Sports.title: World Cup stadium could be demolished to make way for 80,000-seater new arena
Sports.content:
Next

A FORMER World Cup stadium could be demolished to make way for a brand new 80,000-seater arena.

The Deutsche Bank Park was featured multiple times during the tournament in Germany in 2006.



The iconic ground was the setting for England‘s 1-0 victory over Paraguay and four other matches at that edition of the World Cup.

It has also been known as the Waldstadion, the Neues Waldstadion and the Commerzbank-Arena.



The Deutsche Bank Park was also used as a host stadium for other major tournaments such as the 1974 World Cup, the 2011 Women’s World Cup and Euro 2024.

Bundesliga club Eintracht Frankfurt are now planning to undertake a major expansion of the stadium.

This would see its capacity of 60,000 jump to a huge 80,000, which would make it the second largest in Germany.

It would trail Borussia Dortmund‘s Signal Iduna Park by just 1,365 seats.

Frankfurt spokesperson Axel Hellmann has revealed that two options are being considered.

One option would be to keep the current shell of the stadium and build a third tier on top of it.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

The second option would see the existing stadium demolished and a new state-of-the-art arena built on the same site.

A decision is yet to be made on which option will be selected by the 2022 Europa League winners.

Frankfurt are still carrying out research to assess the technical and economic feasibility of each plan.

The club has insisted that a more specific direction will be known in six months.



Hellmann has admitted that the project will not be a swift one to complete and suggested it could take over a decade before finishing.

The expansion would be expected to boost the stadium’s business with the possible addition of major concerts and other big events.

It could also become an important stadium if Germany are to win the hosting rights of future international tournaments.

Sports.title: ‘Livid’ Wayne Rooney’s lawyers demand Andy Carroll retracts claim they drank while on England duty from bombshell book
Sports.content:
Next

WAYNE Rooney is threatening legal action against former team-mate Andy Carroll over his bombshell book.

The ex-England captain, 40, sent a lawyers’ letter to the publishers of Carroll’s upcoming autobiography over claims he drank with him on England duty.



Carroll’s book, Owning It, accuses Manchester United legend Rooney of inviting players to booze in his room during Three Lions training camps around 2010-2011.

Now the former Newcastle and Liverpool striker faces a costly court battle if he does not retract the story. An insider told The Sun: “Wayne is livid. He’s not messing around.



“His legal team have sent a strongly worded letter to the publisher. He wants it retracted as it is completely untrue.

“Wayne knows he’s no angel but this crossed the line. It’s a matter of principle.”

Our source added: “Andy is spiralling over the whole situation. He didn’t think for a second Rooney would kick off like this.

“Andy had a book to sell and now he’s in over his head.



“There may be a public apology coming unless he wants a legal battle on his hands.”

Football pundit Rooney is in advanced talks to join ITV’s I’m A Celebrity . . . Get Me Out Of Here. He is determined to at least equal his wife Coleen’s second place on the show last year.

Since retiring from football in 2018, Rooney tried his hand at management. He has since landed a role on BBC’s Match of the Day and agreed to host a podcast and gameshow.

His and Coleen’s new Disney+ series, The Real Rooneys, is out on Thursday — the same day as Carroll’s book.

Our insider said: “Everything Wayne has been doing recently is marking a fresh chapter in his career.



“He’s lost a lot of weight and cut out drinking — his old habits are firmly in the past. Andy accusing him of bad behaviour is the last thing he wants or needs.”

Sports.title: Arsenal star Max Dowman, 16, in line to link up with England squad after mass withdrawals
Sports.content:
Next

MAX DOWMAN is hoping to land an England training call-up — after Thomas Tuchel was hit by five players withdrawing.

Declan Rice, Cole Palmer, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Tino Livramento pulled out of the four Nations League matches, starting with the opener at home to Spain on Saturday.



Morgan Gibbs-White and James Garner were added to the squad as cover.

And boss Tuchel is considering giving Dowman, 16, his first taste of training with Harry Kane and Co.



Even before yesterday’s withdrawals, Tuchel had already decided to take a look at some of the country’s brightest talents at St George’s Park this week

Unusually, England’s U21s, U20s, U18s and U17s are also training at England’s HQ this week as they prepare for matches.



Midfielder Dowman, 16, is with the Under-19s who will face Ireland in a friendly at St George’s Park on Friday.

In March, Tuchel refused to rule out Dowman making a late run into his World Cup squad.

But while that did not happen, he is likely to receive a senior call-up in the next 12 months ahead of Euro 2028.

Liverpool’s Rio Ngumoha, 18, has been included in this squad.



Chelsea forward Palmer was due to return to Tuchel’s squad after being snubbed for the World Cup.

But a slight injury has seen him withdraw, while Rashford picked up a knock during Manchester United’s 1-1 draw with Fulham on Sunday.

England face world champions Spain in a sold-out Nations League game at Wembley on Saturday night.



The Three Lions will then head to Prague to face the Czech Republic next Tuesday.

The following day, the squad will fly to Rijeka ahead of a Nations League game against Croatia on Saturday October 3.

The match is behind closed doors due to a Uefa punishment for poor behaviour from Croatia’s fans but 100 loyal England supporters will be allowed to watch.

Three days later, England are back at Wembley to face the Czech Republic.

The final two Nations League games against Spain and Croatia will be staged in November and if England finish in the top two, the quarter-finals will be in March.



Another date for Tuchel is the qualifying draw for Euro 2028 in Belfast on December 6.

Sports.title: Granit Xhaka could be facing JAIL for getting fake Covid jab certificate as Sunderland ace issues grovelling apology
Sports.content:
Next

SUNDERLAND’S GRANIT XHAKA could face a whopping fine or even potential PRISON time after admitting to receiving a fake coronavirus vaccination certificate in the pandemic.

The Swiss captain, 33, has pulled out of his country’s upcoming Nations League clashes amid the public prosecutor’s office in the Swiss city of Lucerne criminal investigation.



The controversy came to light amid suspicions that a female doctor in Lucerne issued vaccination certificates without ever administering the jabs.

The doctor has denied allegations. However, a statement on Xhaka’s Instagram admitted his guilt.



The statement read: “In recent days, a lot has been reported about an issue from my past. I would like to address it personally.

“At the time, in connection with the Covid-19 vaccination, I was personally very uncertain and had serious concerns. I had deep distrust of the vaccine and was affected by fear and uncertainty.

“In this emotionally charged situation, I obtained a vaccination certificate instead of having my unanswered questions clarified through the proper channels.

“Today, I clearly see that this was not the right course of action. It was a mistake. I am sorry.

“I take responsibility for the decision, will face the process of clarifying the facts, and will cooperate fully with the relevant authorities.”

Xhaka was still an Arsenal player during the pandemic. He left North London to sign for German club Bayer Leverkusen in 2023 before returning to England with Sunderland in 2025.

A spokesperson for the Lucerne Cantonal Prosecutor’s Office said: “The aim is to clarify whether there has been conduct relevant under criminal law in connection with the possible fraudulent obtaining of a false certification and/or document forgery.”

While there was never a legal requirement to obtain or hold such a certificate, the Swiss office of public health confirmed it was needed for access to various activities, venues and travel. That meant that participation was restricted for anyone who did not possess one.

The measures were in place in Switzerland until the spring of 2022. Covid-19 certificates were still issued after that point, primarily to enable residents to meet entry requirements to foreign countries when travelling.

Swiss cops raided the doctor’s clinic in 2023 and seized evidence as part of investigations involving a number of people believed to have obtained coronavirus certificates.



According to reports in his homeland, the investigations centre on whether Xhaka secured a certificate proving he had received the vaccine despite never actually being vaccinated.

The public prosecutor’s office has confirmed an investigation is underway.

And they added that it aims to establish whether any conduct amounted to a criminal offence, either through obtaining incorrect official proof or forging documents linked to coronavirus certificates.

Xhaka is allegedly expected to appear before the public prosecutor’s office next month to give his statement on the case.

Xhaka missed three matches for Switzerland in September 2021 due to testing positive for coronavirus.



Forging documents in Switzerland is subject to severe penalties, with large fines or imprisonment of up to five years.

Following his confession, Xhaka will not be linking up with his national team-mates this week.

This decision was made jointly in a meeting between the veteran and Swiss Football Association (SFV) management.



SFV president Peter Knabel said: “Granit Xhaka informed us about the situation last night and told us that he will address it publicly and take responsibility.

“We welcome Granit taking this step and facing the consequences.

“At the same time, we jointly concluded that it is in the team’s best interest to complete this training camp without him.

“Our priority now is to calm the situation and focus entirely on the team and the upcoming challenges in the Uefa Nations League.

“After the conclusion of this international match window, we will reassess the situation together with Granit and discuss the next steps.”



Switzerland face away matches against North Macedonia and Scotland before hosting Slovenia and North Macedonia in Lucerne.

Sports.title: ‘Glum-faced’ Marcus Rashford labelled Man Utd’s ‘weak link’ by England legend Michael Owen
Sports.content:
Next

MICHAEL OWEN has labelled Marcus Rashford “glum-faced” and the weak link at Manchester United.

The former Red Devils and England international did not hold back when assessing the forward’s performance against Fulham.



United survived defeat at Craven Cottage thanks to a deflected equaliser from Matheus Cunha.

Rashford, 28, was hooked by boss Michael Carrick in the 76th minute after failing to trouble the scorers.



He is yet to provide a single goal or assist in his five Premier League appearances this season.

Owen believes that Rashford is falling out of love with football and it is visible in his body language.



The retired striker made the claim while speaking on Premier League Productions.

He said: “On the left, Marcus Rashford has probably been the quietest of those attackers.

“He was quiet again today in his body language, just the glum face.

“He just doesn’t seem to be loving his football which has been a permanent frustration with Marcus.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Rashford excelled last season during his loan spell at LaLiga giants Barcelona.

He scored 13 goals and provided ten assists in 45 appearances in all competitions.

Sports.title: Man Utd scout ‘Norwegian JJ Gabriel’, 15, days after ‘Kid Messi’ handed in transfer request
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED are tracking another 15-year-old wonderkid with the name Gabriel.

In the week that teen talent JJ Gabriel stunned Old Trafford by asking to leave, the Red Devils dispatched their top Scandinavian scout to watch a new Norwegian target.



United are now eyeing up 15-year-old Valerenga ace Gabriel Rajkovic, who is creating a stir around Europe’s biggest clubs.

Barcelona have also sent spies to watch the youngster in action this season, but the United scout’s presence in Oslo on Sunday suggests they are firmly in the race for his signature.



Rajkovic turns 16 in February and cannot move abroad until then, although that has not stopped Premier League clubs from snapping them up in the past.

Chelsea sealed a deal to sign Geovany Quenda from Sporting Lisbon last year, loaning him back to the club and waiting a year for him turn 18 and make the move to London.

Rajkovic is a tricky winger with two good feet, although he is predominantly left-footed.

He tends to play on the right and cuts in with devastating effect, often leaving defenders guessing with body feints and quick changes of direction.

The Oslo-born star has played for Norway’s U15 and U16 national teams and is also eligible to represent Serbia, Belgium and Morocco.

He has scored two goals in 13 top-flight appearances this year, becoming the second-youngest player to score in the competition behind Arsenal’s Martin Odegaard when he scored against Bodo/Glimt last month.



Reports in Norway claim he could fetch as much as £16m when sold

This would smash their current domestic transfer record.

But Rajkovic insists he is in no hurry to leave his current club, having already turned down several offers of training stints at major European clubs.

And unlike JJ Gabriel, who is only under contract at United until next summer anyway, Rajkovic’s long-term future it tied up until December 2028 with Valerenga.

Sports.title: Inside rise of Babis Kostoulas who is on way to becoming Brighton’s next £100m star after destroying Arsenal and Man Utd
Sports.content:
Next

BABIS KOSTOULAS has taken the Premier League by storm after devastating Arsenal as well as Manchester United and is making his claim to become Brighton’s next £100million man.

The Seagulls have become famous for discovering hidden gems for bargain prices and polishing them into the Prem’s most in-demand stars that go out for staggering fees after intense bidding wars.



Leandro Trossard, Alexis Mac Allister, Joao Pedro and Carlos Baleba went from relative unknowns to breakout stars with moves to Arsenal, Liverpool, Chelsea and Manchester United respectively.

Then there’s Moises Caicedo who raised the bar with a whopping £115m switch to Stamford Bridge in 2023, which stands as Brighton‘s most expensive sale.



And the Albion could soon find themselves at the forefront of another transfer window with Babis, 19, posing as the club’s newest and brightest prospect.

The striker moved to the Amex from Olympiacos last year following a record sale for a Greek club worth £30m, which includes about £2m in add-ons, and signed a contract worth £1.3m, plus bonuses, until 2030.



The deal was completed by OIS Agency, which is run by Greek super agent Giorgos Panou who represents Greece’s most promising talents along with NBA superstar Giannis Antetokounmpo.

The switch realised a major childhood ambition for the teenage sensation – described as an avid dreamer “without a ceiling” by those close to him – who can now dare to aim for the stars.

The Greece international had been dreaming of following in his father’s footsteps since the tender age of two when he started out with Agia Anna, a club located in his dad Thanasis Kostoulas’ hometown of Volos.

Thanasis, 50, won seven league titles and two domestic Doubles with Olympiacos, where he amassed a total of one goal in 202 appearances during an eight-year run until 2007, when Babis was born.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

The centre-forward and his older brother Konstantinos Kostoulas grew up proudly watching their hero’s 15 Champions League matches that saw him clash with the likes of Man Utd, Real Madrid and Juventus.

Babis and Konstantinos, 21, made it their life’s mission to follow suit as they joined their dad’s beloved club’s academy in 2019 and would often be greeted back home by their mother Irene with shirts drenched in sweat as well as melted boots, ripped socks and crimson-red cheeks.

Their rise was immediate and striking with Babis especially standing out with his raw talent, versatility and personality that saw him smashing 23 goals and nine assists in 51 appearances across the club’s youth ranks.

That quickly earned him the moniker of “Babistuta” as he was compared to Argentina legend Gabriel Batistuta.



The youngest of the two also stuck out thanks to his personality as he always inspired maturity and leadership to his team-mates as well as a gutsy attitude, spontaneous nature and ice-cold demeanour in front of goal.

But those close to him also know there is a sensitive and caring person – who speaks Greek, English and French – behind the tough and ruthless exterior most are accustomed to when they see him perform.

And the brothers made history in 2024 when they led the Under-19s to the UEFA Youth League trophy, which is the first ever European honour won by a Greek club shortly before the seniors lifted the Europa Conference League.



Babis was immediately promoted to the first team where he quickly made history by becoming Olympiacos’ youngest ever league scorer at the age of 17 years, five months and 11 days against rivals PAOK at a fiery Toumba Stadium.

The forward also became a key figure behind the club’s historic centenary campaign that included a domestic Double and a Last-16 run in the Europa League during his debut campaign.

That led to interest from a raft of elite clubs, such as Man Utd, Arsenal, Chelsea, Tottenham, Aston Villa, Newcastle, Bayern Munich, Borussia Dortmund, Juventus and AC Milan before Brighton won the transfer war.

Manager Fabian Hurzeler slowly integrated Babis into the first team during his debut campaign at the Amex but there were still some moments of brilliance, such as his overhead stunner against Bournemouth that saved a last-gasp point in the Premier League.

But the teenage sensation has upped the ante to 11 this season with four goals and three assists in eight appearances across all competitions under his belt already.



Babis was key in Brighton’s dramatic 3-2 comeback win that eliminated Man Utd with a goal and assist at Old Trafford.

The Greek star then handed Premier League champions Arsenal their first defeat of the season with another goal and assist that led to a 3-0 triumph at home.

Babis is now focused to adding to his four caps with Greece as he was called up for the crunch Nations League clashes against Serbia, Germany and the Netherlands.



That will allow him to catch up with his beloved family and exchange stories with his older brother, who is also enjoying a lot of success with Greek minnows OFI.

Konstantinos helped the team from Crete complete a surprise Greek Cup as well as Super Cup double and made history as part of the club’s first ever side to win a Europa League match in the league phase after an upset victory over Hoffenheim.

The brothers are now set for the longest international break recorded in football history but won’t get to play together as the eldest is linking up with the Under-21s.

But Babis might still find some time to unwind with things he doesn’t get to enjoy at Brighton, such as his guilty pleasure which is the famous Greek dish pastitsio.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Premier League ace – who is also a gaming and Greek music enthusiast – will have to wait until next summer to visit his beloved isle of Mykonos, but even then his mind might be far away from the Cyclades.



If the goals keep coming then so could his suitors from two years ago, and this time they will have to reach deep inside their pockets if they want to sign Brighton’s latest young star.

Sports.title: McLaren predict four-way battle for Baku win after confirming more upgrades
Sports.content:
McLaren have confirmed they will bring more upgrades to this weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, where they are expecting a four-way battle for victory with Mercedes, Ferrari and Red Bull.

After failing to claim a victory in the first 10 grands prix of the season, the reigning constructors' champions have come into form, with Lando Norris claiming three pole positions at the last four races and only being denied a third win by the unfortunate timing of a virtual safety car last time out in Madrid.

McLaren have once more exhibited strength in development, with regular upgrades brought to the MCL40 having played a significant part in catapulting them back into contention for victories.

The team's official preview for this weekend's race in Baku, which takes place on Saturday rather than the usual Sunday slot, revealed there will be new parts, and that their rotating 'H-Wing' will return to the car after not being used in Madrid.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Norris lost the lead of the Spanish GP after an unlucky sequence of events which saw a missed a pit-stop opportunity under a VSC, followed by a very slow stop

"As part of the team's continued journey throughout the 2026 season, the team will bring to Baku a set of upgrades aimed to improve the aerodynamic performance of the MCL40," the team said.

"Additionally the H-Wing, that debuted in Monza, will be back in action on a track where the drag reduction can be a factor.

"As has been the approach in previous races this season, all new parts will be evaluated throughout practice before the team makes final decisions regarding the MCL40's Qualifying and Grand Prix setup for the weekend."

McLaren chief technical officer and chief designer Rob Marshall explained the team are keen to continue their development push despite their title hopes being extremely thin, with Kimi Antonelli dominating the Drivers' Championship and his Mercedes team well clear in the constructors' standings.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the moment Norris thought he messed up his lap, which turned out to put him on the pole for the Spanish Grand Prix

"With regulatory continuity into next season and the competition at the front so close, our motivation to keep developing the car remains high," Marshall said.

"We must balance that with work on next year's car, but our immediate focus is on delivering more performance and fighting for more victories in 2026, while carrying forward everything we learn."

The Baku circuit, which features the longest straight on the F1 calendar alongside several slow corners, creates a challenge that Marshall expects to create entertaining competition between the top teams.

"Baku will provide another valuable test of the MCL40 across a very different range of characteristics," Marshall added.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Norris reacts to the news that the Monaco Grand Prix will be a Sprint race in 2027

"Energy management and deployment will be particularly important, as will tyre and brake management with the cars arriving at Turn 1 after the long straight with these areas relatively cold.

"Operationally, there is very little margin for error on a tight street circuit. A small mistake can lead to significant repairs, lost track time and resources being diverted away from performance, so confidence, precision and disciplined execution will be essential throughout the weekend.

"We expect any of the top four teams to be capable of winning in Baku, with the chasing pack also getting closer, and we hope to be firmly in the fight at the front."

Sports.title: F1 race distances set to be reduced for 2027 season
Sports.content:
There is set to be a slight reduction in the length of Formula 1 races for the 2027 season, the FIA has confirmed.

At a meeting of the F1 Commission in London on Monday, the sport's decision makers agreed to reduce Grand Prix distances from 305km to 290km, which corresponds to a reduction of two to three laps depending on the circuit.

The change is being made because fuel flow rates are being increased next season as part of measures the FIA are introducing to optimise the all-new regulations brought in at the start of 2026.

The FIA said: "In line with the refinements to the Power Unit regulations to be introduced in 2027 on fuel flow, a reduction in the total race distance from 305km to 290km was approved, corresponding to a reduction of two or three laps."

The decision must be approved by the World Motor Sport Council, but that is expected to be a formality.

The FIA also announced slight changes to protocols around races disrupted by rain or other factors, with a three-hour limit (including interruptions) from race to start to finish removed, but a "hard stop" time for the end of any racing activity to be introduced.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix.

A limit of two hours of actual racing remains, with those decisions taken "to ensure that the spectators have the best possible chance to enjoy a full race if disruptions occur."

It was also confirmed that there will be "greater flexibility to extend Free Practice sessions should they be interrupted."

The current rules only allow for practice sessions to be extended on Sprint weekends, but such measures may now also be available on a regular schedule.

Sports.title: Wakefield's Guler set to miss rest of play-offs with ban for punching
Sports.content:
Wakefield prop Emre Guler is set to miss the rest of the Super League play-offs after being handed a two-match ban for punching.

The forward was sent off following a clash with Leigh's Owen Trout during Trinity's 26-16 victory over the Leopards in their eliminator last Friday.

The punishment was confirmed following a meeting of the Rugby Football League's match review panel on Monday.

Barring a successful appeal against the grade E offence, Guler will now miss Wakefield's semi-final against Wigan on Saturday and the Grand Final, if Trinity reach it.

Guler only joined Wakefield last month having brought forward his planned arrival from St George Illawarra Dragons from the start of the 2027 season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Super League semi-final match between Wakefield Trinity and Leigh Leopards.

Team-mate Mike McMeeken will be free to play after being fined following a grade B charge of dangerous contact against Leigh's David Armstrong in the same game.

Warrington's James Harrison was also fined following a grade C charge of head contact in the Wolves' win over Hull KR, which set up a semi-final at Leeds. Team-mate Luke Yates will face no further action over a grade A dangerous throw.

Hull KR centre Peta Hiku has also been banned for two matches for punching Warrington's George Williams but, with Rovers now out of the play-offs, his suspension will be served next season.

Sports.title: Cutler beat one McKenna, now he wants world champ brother
Sports.content:
Lee Cutler beat one McKenna brother, now he wants to fight the other for the world middleweight title.

Cutler overcame Stevie McKenna in a thriller in 2024. He lost a technical decision to Sam Eggington in another exciting match-up. Now looking to roar back to form, Cutler stopped Aaron Sutton in a Bournemouth homecoming and will take on Louis Greene next.

Greene, a hard puncher, has a tremendous aggressive style of fighting too. Cutler and Greene will collide at the Copper Box Arena on Saturday, live on Sky Sports.

"It's a dangerous fight," Cutler told Sky Sports. "I don't say no. It's a fight that the fans want to see and it's fight that I believe takes me to another level.

"[Greene is] tough. Punches extremely hard. I've got to be switched on for the full 10 rounds that we're in there. I'm fully prepared for a hard night.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Louis Greene is predicting fireworks in his bout against Lee Cutler on Zuffa Boxing 11.

"It's one of those fights, we're a stepping stone for each other and that's how we've got to see each other," he added.

"I've got to be smart in there and box how I know I can box. If I can do that I'll come away with the victory."

He had been expecting Stevie McKenna to look for a rematch with him.

McKenna levelled Owen O'Neill on the undercard of brother Aaron McKenna's IBF middleweight world title victory.

"It does surprise me. I thought I was going to get a callout after. I thought he might not want to fight me on the Dublin card because it's a big night for the family because of the brother and stuff," Cutler reflected.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lee Cutler and Louis Greene had an intense face-off as their fight was announced on Sky Sports News for Zuffa Boxing 11 in September.

"But I was fully expecting him to get through his opponent and then call me out after that. But the fact he didn't even mention my name, goes to show what he's about."

If he can get through his middleweight 10 rounder with Greene he will look for an eventual fight with new champion Aaron McKenna.

"I think he's very good. I think he's a tough fight for anyone. But he's somebody that I see myself in there with. Bring him on," Cutler declared.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Stephen McKenna and Lee Cutler exchanged a pair of verbal jabs after their respective Zuffa Boxing 07 wins in Bournemouth.

"But as I said I'm focusing fully on Louis Green because he's a very dangerous opponent and if I take my eye off the ball for one second, anything can happen.

"I'm a come forward fighter, he's a come forward fighter, he's a huge puncher, very dangerous.

"All he has to do is touch somebody and then it's lights out."

Sports.title: Spurs bottom of PL but more than £300m spent - where do they go from here?
Sports.content:
This time it was supposed to be different. After multiple false dawns for Tottenham Hotspur, the club had a manager with proven Premier League experience, and had handed him a £300m+ war chest - easily the biggest in its entire history.

Instead, Spurs find themselves bottom of the table after five games for the first time in 18 years, with their only goals a pair of consolation strikes on another dismal afternoon against Aston Villa at the weekend.

Things aren't quite as bad as the table suggests and had Tottenham taken any of a number of presentable first-half chances against Villa, they would have gone into the three-week international break silencing some of the noise around the club.

But instead, two points from five games and such a dismal record in front of goal has kept the spotlight firmly on them.

Though it is only five games, their struggles to find consistency have extended into a third consecutive season. Tottenham have now picked up just 18 points in 2026 and, since the start of 2024/25, still one fewer than a West Ham side who were relegated at the end of last season.

Roberto De Zerbi cannot avoid scrutiny forever, especially after a summer where he was given relative carte blanche in the transfer market and, a top-class left-winger aside, got most of what he asked for.

Speaking before the Villa game, he hinted he would have liked to have done things differently during the summer window, but the club had to respect Financial Fair Play and some players who had been earmarked for sale remained at the club.

That will not afford him much sympathy given the size of Spurs' spend. One of the outgoings who they were happy to let go, Luka Vuskovic, is thriving at Brighton. Meanwhile, the player he replaced, Jan Paul van Hecke, toiled in that Villa defeat and was dribbled past three times.

Regardless, Tottenham were always unlikely to be an overnight fix given money alone will not solve the sizeable task of changing course after finishing 17th in back-to-back seasons.

Spurs' big summer of spending Sandro Tonali - Newcastle, £100m

Savio - Man City, £85m

Mateus Fernandes - West Ham, £85m

Mykhaylo Mudryk - Chelsea, loan

Omar Marmoush - Man City, loan

But fans still expected something more than this, especially from a head coach known for his man-management and getting the best out of limited resources, as he demonstrated across nearly two years on the south coast at Brighton.

Even one win would lift them out of the quagmire - and they will target a similarly under-pressure Man Utd side when the Premier League returns on October 10, live on Sky Sports. However, there are a number of issues of concern even after that mammoth spend.

The naive manner Spurs fell behind to Villa with Micky Van de Ven off the pitch injured and Andy Robertson inadvertently teeing up the opportunity, led De Zerbi to complain that "leaders have to be leaders" in such crunch moments. "We can't lose games in this way," he added.

But does his squad have enough of that kind of player? Van de Ven, Pedro Porro, Ben Davies, James Maddison and Archie Gray were named as De Zerbi's five-man leadership group last month, but none would be considered an out-and-out natural leader, who can hoist his team-mates up by their collars.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch highlights of Spurs' 3-2 defeat at Aston Villa which saw them go into the first international break bottom of the Premier League table

This is nothing new. Despite long-standing allegations of being 'Spursy', in the last two years, that nickname has truly taken on a new form. Tottenham have not won a league game when conceding first in approaching two years and have picked up only nine draws from losing positions since.

It was the right time for Cristian Romero to move on in the summer largely because his aggression could often overstep the mark, but it has left a void which has not been filled.

Instead, it has been compounded by the further loss of perhaps limited but unquestionably combative midfielder Joao Palhinha. In De Zerbi's defence, he made no secret of his desire to keep him.

More worryingly, it does not appear a problem the head coach has a solution to. "It is difficult to explain," he admitted after Saturday's defeat. "In my 14 years as a coach, I've never seen a team like us, so fragile and inconsistent."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Even ahead of Saturday's defeat to Aston Villa, Roberto De Zerbi explained the reasons behind Spurs' dismal start and highlights where they need to improve

He need only look to the home stands if he needs any filling in from a fanbase who are all too used to seeing exactly that over the past two years.

Even without Palhinha he cannot complain too loudly about his midfield given the near £200m sanctioned to sign Sandro Tonali and Matheus Fernandes.

Tonali in particular should be fresh after a summer off from the World Cup, but has yet to hit the heights which made him a fan favourite for much of his time at Newcastle and convinced Spurs to break their transfer record to sign him.

The bizarre sideshow of Richarlison's future has not helped matters either, despite his own limitations. That too is only compounded by Spurs' lack of goals while last season's top scorer watches on from his own, albeit partly self-imposed, spell in exile.

Dominic Solanke has still not returned to full fitness and De Zerbi was almost apologetic for his out-of-form striker after his latest performance against Villa, saying "he's much better than this Dominic Solanke".

But with the average xG of Spurs' shots the lowest across the Premier League and their overall total better only than Coventry's, the real Solanke needs to stand up sooner rather than later - or Omar Marmoush re-find his scoring boots.

It is still very early days in the latest iteration of the Spurs machine, and given the significant turnover in players in the summer - over half of Saturday's starting line-up were not at the club last season - no surprise there have been some teething problems.

But the sight of a Premier League table showing two points, two goals and Spurs holding up the rest of the league will feel like a lot more than that.

There is still a feeling things will come good - there is undoubted quality in the squad and no-one needs reminding of De Zerbi's abilities. But his spells elsewhere have a habit of ending on a sour note. The hope is that it hasn't already set in here.

Sports.title: Brook relishing working with mentor of Pietersen's calibre
Sports.content:
Captain Harry Brook says leaning on a mentor of Kevin Pietersen's calibre will only help the continued upward trajectory of England's white-ball sides.

Pietersen, regarded as one of the greatest batters of the 21st century, has been brought into the England white-ball set-up in a mentoring role by head coach Brendon McCullum in the build-up to next year's 50-over World Cup.

Brook shed light on the impact Pietersen was already having on the squad, both on and off the field, with the team's approach to playing spin already addressed in a masterclass from the former England captain.

"KP has been very good," Brook told a press conference. "He's enjoying the role, he's enjoying himself.

"He's been good to have around, little chats here and there. Away from the game, sat having a coffee and a chat about how he sees the game and how he thinks it should be played.

"He was a hero to many of us growing up, so it's good to have a man of his calibre in our side."

On the masterclass, Brook added: "A lot of it was about picking the length of spin. That is key to facing spin and being able to rotate strike as well as possible.

"In ODI cricket that's an area we probably need to improve as a side. It can make a massive difference to winning games of cricket.

"He [Pietersen] was a hell of a player against spin, alongside [Joe] Root and [Marcus] Trescothick. They were very good players at playing spin, so it's about picking their brains and asking them what worked for them and putting that into your game."

'Higher-octane cricket'

England, fresh from a 3-0 series sweep over Sri Lanka that lifted them to the top of the T20 world rankings, face Sri Lanka again in their first ODI since teaming up with Pietersen.

The three-match series starts in Durham on Tuesday, live on Sky Sports, and Brook has challenged England to maintain their momentum.

"We can take a hell of a lot of confidence from being unbeaten in the T20s," Brook said.

"Going into this ODI series we want more of the same. We're trying to play a higher-octane style of cricket and put them [the opposition] under pressure with bat and ball.

"We want to be one of the fittest sides in the world. To do that, we've got to work hard on and off the field.

"We are trending in the right direction. There are a few touches here and there which we can improve."

Brook - better than Pietersen?

Sports.title: Long-range hits and goals galore: inside the Premier League’s return to chaos | Andrew Beasley
Sports.content:
Goals in the Premier League are up. Chaos is returning. End‑to‑end football is back. The division is more open, in more ways than one.

The figures show a rise from 2.75 goals per game last season to 2.82 this year, a small average increase but one that could easily widen. The goals-per-game rate was at least 0.21 higher in the final 330 games than it was for the first 50 in four of the past five seasons. If 2026-27 has a similar upturn, it will become the second-highest scoring season in the Premier League era.

Goals should be harder to come by at this time of year when teams are fresher, more organised and less ragged. Legs have not yet been drained by the December fixture pile-up or the demands of European football. Evidence of this can be seen in every team averaging more distance per match than they did in 2025-26. Liverpool are bottom for this metric yet are ahead of any club’s final figure from last season.

Teams may be having to run further as more of the football is played in transition. The Premier League averaged the fewest Opta‑defined fast break (counterattack) shots of Europe’s big five leagues in 2025-26, at 1.75 per game. That has risen to 2.08, which would have been second only to the Bundesliga last season (2.26).

While the uplift is not entirely down to Xabi Alonso and Marco Rose joining English football, Chelsea (2.2 fast-break shots per game) and Bournemouth (1.6) are among the top five for this metric. With Matthias Jaissle’s Newcastle joint‑seventh (1.0), perhaps influence from German football is having a mild effect.

Another pointer towards the Premier League becoming a little wilder is the increase in shots and goals from outside the area. Brighton are an extreme example of this as they are already two goals shy of their tally of six last season. They forged a 2-0 lead against Arsenal on Saturday with goals from long-range. Lewis Dunk nominated himself for goal of the season from way outside the area at Coventry, with Yasin Ayari also scoring from beyond the 18-yard line in that match.

Something must fall to allow this rise; close-range goals have declined. The dip in goals from within the six‑yard box may be through the fall in set‑piece strikes. Nine teams have yet to score in this way, including the champions, with another two clubs having only one such goal.

Premier League matches are averaging more shots from set plays than they did last season, 8.2 versus 7.8, yet the expected goal tally from them has dropped from 0.76 to 0.72 xG. Small margins perhaps, but they combine to reduce the average quality of chance teams are producing. Set-piece goals falling (from 0.71 per game to 0.56) is the inevitable by-product. It is unlikely anyone other than Arsenal supporters are disheartened by this development.

The season has only just begun. These changing trends may settle down in time. They could be the result of the season beginning with more new managers than ever before. Transition in the dugout causes uncertainty on the pitch, as it is harder to know what to expect from teams being led by new men.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Very few games are settled early. This is summarised well by 2-2 being the joint-most common scoreline, with six instances. The first three were contested by clubs whose managers were appointed in the summer. Five of the six had either both teams lead or one side go ahead twice before conceding two equalisers.

We have not seen many big leads squandered. Goals are up, but so are the proportion of matches that are drawn, with those won by two or more in decline.

Teams are slugging it out, back and forth. You attack, we counter, and everyone runs further as a result.

The wind could blow these trends back towards last season’s figures soon enough. Fans will hope the increased goal rate remains.

Sports.title: Paper trail of protests: José Mourinho plays the hits in Madrid derby defeat | Sid Lowe
Sports.content:
There were many questions to emerge from the Madrid derby, which Atlético won 2-1 in front of 70,514 very, very noisy people at the Metropolitano on Sunday afternoon, even if not the one José Mourinho was asking. Like: what year is this? Or: what was Dean Huijsen thinking? Why always Arda? And whatever happened to Vinícius Júnior? How come Koke is still the best? And how long before Giuliano Simeone actually bursts, his atlético insides exploding across the pitch? Above all though, you were left wondering: where did Real Madrid’s manager get a printer from? And how did he get the bloody thing to work?

You could still hear the singing outside when Mourinho turned up in the press room, laid down his glasses and sat. In his hand was a piece of paper. Thirteen years after his last derby, on the Santiago Bernabéu night when Madrid lost the Copa del Rey final and a 13-year unbeaten run against their neighbours, Diego Simeone had defeated him again. The stage was new – this stadium didn’t exist then – but his adversary was somehow still the same man, still dressed in black, and the scene was a bit like old times, a classic. Mourinho unfolded the paper and held it up. “We can save ourselves the bother of the press conference,” he said, “because the story is right here.”

Printed on the back side of an Atlético info sheet were two screen grabs from the first half, one on top of the other. Someone had been sent to run off a copy, some footballing Natalie Harp or the manager himself coming back with a couple of gory, freeze-framed, full-colour closeups of tackles. The first showed Cuti Romero’s studs catching Jude Bellingham’s knee; the second showed Kang-in Lee on Fede Valverde’s ankle. Both should have been red, Mourinho insisted, and he was probably right, but neither was. It should have been nine against 11, he said; instead, it was 11 against 10 because early in the second half Huijsen dragged Giuliano Simeone down for the penalty that gave Atlético the lead and got him sent off. And that, Mourinho said, was that. End of story.

View image in fullscreen Real Madrid’s Dean Huijsen was sent off after conceding a penalty to Atlético’s Giuliano Simeone during the derby. Photograph: Juan Carlos Lucas/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

At which point he could have got up and gone, saved everyone the bother of the press conference like he promised, but no one wants that, least of all his president, and that’s the bit he does best so he carried on. Five questions he faced. Four of them were about the referee; so was the answer to the one that was not about the referee. And when he had finished, leaving the paper there for Diego Simeone to have a look at, most agreed: now Mourinho is back, and he’s playing the greatest hits, a hint of the nostalgia that had brought him “home” in the first place, a hint of the conspiratorial mindset too, echoes of him reading out 13 “errors” made by the referee Clos Gómez 16 years earlier.

The “poor ref” – just 41, not an international, and named in advance rather than 24 hours before kick-off – couldn’t handle the pressure, which was “like the 1980s”, Mourinho claimed. The coach, who had already revived his famous “por qué” (why?) line after they lost at Betis, also ran through a list of decisions made by the referee in the VAR room, Daniel Trujillo Suárez – a man supposedly with history – which “make you laugh”. There was talk of “strange things” happening. He insisted he didn’t want to think ill of officials, didn’t want to say the league has been “set up” for others to win, didn’t want to think that these were anything other than honest mistakes – of course not. He congratulated the referees’ committee and vowed to fight for the title despite being six points behind already – if they let us. “I thought I would come back to find a different league to the one I left, but [at Madrid] they told me not and explained why not,” he said.

What Mourinho didn’t say was anything really about the actual football, which might be because there wasn’t much football. The cards might have conditioned the game – of course they might – and he was entitled to insist on the reds, although you could debate Romero’s. But it was hard to avoid the feeling that Mourinho purposely missed a deeper point and revealed a deeper reality, that there could be no escaping the reality he sought to escape: that Madrid are just not very good. That too many questions were avoided and another could be asked: is that it? There was little evidence to back his brief claim that they played well in the first half and were set up to win it in the second – how? – and even if true, it pointed to something limited: wait, counter and it will come.

With the players Madrid have, often it will, but Atlético were aware of that, planned for it; they were aware too of where the damage could be done, overloading Madrid’s left. Simeone’s side took more than twice as many shots and had two-thirds of the possession. They had done so cautiously, it is true, but they, not Madrid, had exercised control. Mourinho’s team had offered little before the potential reds, their first shot on target coming on 39 minutes and from 25 yards, and even less after the actual red, Atlético’s half unoccupied for most of the period except by a pigeon. With Guler withdrawn, their reaction didn’t exist. It’s not easy with 10 men, but there was barely a spark. Even the goal they did get in the 89th minute was an isolated moment and, for all the nerves at the Metropolitano, was followed by more chances for Atlético.

Thank you for your feedback.

None of which would matter so much as a one-off, but these flaws were familiar. Madrid needed last-minute Carlos Espí goals to beat Espanyol and Elche and they’re still six points off the top already. It’s not even close to definitive just seven weeks in and Madrid’s rebuilding process has only just begun, but basic issues they have faced for the last two years remain unaddressed; Fabio Capello’s implausible 2006-07 league title win is the only time Barcelona have ever had a lead that big at the top of the table and lost it. Hansi Flick’s team are flying; and right now you wouldn’t trust Madrid to take advantage even if they did slip up. Claude Makélélé summed them up as: “Nothing, nothing, nothing.” Which leaves only this: a print-out and paranoia, a campaign. Some things don’t change. Some people don’t change much, either.

View image in fullscreen Jonathan David (right) score the winner in a Madrid derby which Atlético dominated. Photograph: Alberto Gardin/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Some, though, do. The last time these two coaches met in a derby, Simeone’s son Giuliano was told he was too little to go to the final so he hung scarves around the living room and watched it from home with his brothers instead. It was late, it was a school night, and he was only 10. He is 23 now and these days he plays for them, a bundle of intensity going at it the way a fan would, and on the day these two “colleagues of war” – as Mourinho called them – met again 13 years later he decided the derby, forcing the penalty for the first and setting up the second. There is some footage somewhere of Giuliano as a ballboy racing up the touchline and leaping into his father’s arms, celebrating wildly when Atlético scored against Madrid. A decade on, another derby day, and it happened again, only this time it was his dad sprinting up the line towards him.

Talking points

“We give him the ball, he scores the goals,” Fermín López said. Over and over and over again. Raphinha, who is filling in at centre forward, has now scored 12 league goals in just seven games, plus two more in the Champions League. He is five ahead of anyone else already. On Saturday night he scored an outrageously good hat-trick, the movement every inch the No 9, the touch and finishing at ridiculous speed all his, as Barcelona beat Sevilla 3-1. Sevilla went a goal up and were as good as anyone against Flick’s side so far this season but in the end just couldn’t live with them, coach Luis García calling them “stratospheric”. That’s seven wins from seven (eight from eight in all competitions), and 31 goals already, the captain leading the way. And not just with the goals, but with everything, taking everyone on a wild intense ride with him. Raphinha says that Lamine Yamal should win the Ballon d’Or but right now there’s no one quite like him anywhere. That said, Lamine Yamal was absurd at the Pizjuan.

At the end of their 0-0 draw with Athletic, Alavés goalkeeper Antonio Sivera walked off saying: “At last, at last!” His record was, he said, “ridiculous” but now at last he had done it. A European champion at U21 level, he is 30 now, and he had just saved the first penalty of his entire career.

“When I played football as a kid in Croatia, everyone wants to play in one of Europe’s top five leagues and on my list Spain was bottom, but in the end it seems like Osasuna and La Liga is my place: God’s path is different to mine,” said Ante Budimir on Saturday, after a lovely chest-and-volley goal took him to 100 in Spain.

Speaking of which, what a way to celebrate the 100th birthday of your home.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Brighton’s organised chaos viciously pecks Arsenal into submission
Sports.content:
CAME IN LIKE A PECKING BALL …

For an elite head coach who isn’t used to seeing his team lose, suffering a rare defeat on the weekend before an international break is particularly hard to take. With the vast majority of your players hightailing it out of Dodge to rack up more air miles than Santa Claus across a decade’s worth of Christmas Eves, the chance to quickly put things right simply isn’t an option. With the first lull of the season set to be longer than any before, the potential for introspection, self-flagellation and over-thinking has never been higher. Luckily, Mikel Arteta has never struck Football Daily as the kind of intense, brooding and meticulous perfectionist likely to spend the next 19 days beating himself up over the monstering his team suffered from Brighton on Saturday. Whether it’s forlornly moving magnets around a tactics board or walking Win the dog around Arsenal’s largely-deserted training ground until her little legs are stumps, we’re confident the Arsenal boss’s every fleeting thought over the next three weeks will not be laser-focused on the manner in which the Seagulls viciously pecked his team of champions into submission and how best to ensure such a humiliation is never repeated.

Of course, while Arteta is sitting on a swing, gazing into the middle distance like a sad Pablo Escobar, Fabian Hürzeler can afford to cut loose and enjoy his early-season hiatus by indulging in his passion for padel, a sport which our older reader may not know is a new-fangled version of tennis for people too lazy to run. Slovenliness when it comes to busting a gut is certainly not an accusation that can be levelled at the German’s players, who tore into Arsenal like a swarm of angry bees and buzzed around them with such scrupulously-organised chaos that after 90 minutes their 3-0 margin of victory seriously flattered the beaten holders. “Extremely disappointed,” parped a shocked and awed Arteta after seeing his players subjected to a rare humiliation. “But first I think we have to congratulate Brighton for the victory. I think they deserve it, I think they were the better team.”

Wearing natty azzurri blue vintage shirts against Arsenal to mark their 125th anniversary, it’s difficult to imagine Brighton have played better since being founded in 1901. In the early Pathé News years, their first team was peopled by club legends like Peter Ward, Johnny Crumplin and a be-headbanded Steve Foster; the current lineup has a decidedly more cosmopolitan feel and, in the likes of Charalampos Kostoulas, Luka Vuskovic and Diego Gómez, boasts future Brighton icons and subsequent, overpriced, Chelsea squad members. “I want to say congratulations to this special club for the history, for everyone who has contributed in the past, for everyone who’s contributing in the present,” cooed Hürzeler, after a special day on the south coast. “I think the history of this club is very impressive and hopefully everyone can enjoy who has been a part of our journey so far.” Hürzeler went on to say that he considered Saturday’s performance more important than the result. Over the coming weeks in London Colney, his Arsenal counterpart will be treating both with equal significance.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“We can skip the press conference because the story of the match is right here. Those were two clear red cards. Given the difficulties we faced playing 11 against 10, we can only imagine what 50 minutes of 11 against nine would have been like. So I’ll just have to limit myself to hugging my players, who gave it their all and played a first half, showed great class and character, setting us up perfectly to win the second half. They’ve put a referee, aged 41, with no international experience – it’s certainly not because he’s a great referee. Then the poor chap has come ‌here and hasn’t been able to cope with the pressure – and it really is intense pressure. I call it ’80s-style pressure’ here in this stadium, which you hardly ever see these days” – judging by José Mourinho and his A4 printout, can you guess if Real Madrid lost the derby against Atlético? Speaking of which, here’s Sid Lowe with his verdict on it all.

View image in fullscreen The Rafa riff! Photograph: Sky

double quotation mark Oxford United’s decision to market an American college-themed ‘United 93’ kit shortly after the 9/11 anniversary, only then to have to recall it (Friday’s Football Daily, full email edition), is a tad unfortunate. But until 1960 they were known as Headington United, from their heady days in the Southern League. So I am eagerly awaiting the ‘1960 Ron Atkinson’ range celebrating both their history and leading appearance maker (still)” – Jon Harris.

double quotation mark Following Andros Townsend’s freak (but miraculously not serious) on-pitch accident, will future fixtures between Prachuap and Pattani be known as the Roller derby?” – Phil Taverner.

double quotation mark OK. I messed up. On 30 August, I made a claim that Emilio Martínez’s transfer to Chelsea for £7.5m might be the bargain of the season. Now five games in and 12 goals conceded, I wish to retract my statement. I will try to do better and stay away from any rash predictions” – Nigel Sanders.

double quotation mark Football knowledge aside, I take great pride in knowing a lot about The Simpsons (earlier years especially … I haven’t watched it in about a decade). It was Wiggum who advised to dig up, not Homer (Friday’s Football Dailly letters)” – Mark Shrewsbury.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s letter o’ the day prize goes to … Phil Taverner, who wins a copy of Behind the Curtain by Big Website’s Jonathan Wilson. It’s out now and available in The Guardian Bookshop alongside loads of other great football titles. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel rocked by five key withdrawals from England squad
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel has been rocked by a host of withdrawals from his England squad, with Cole Palmer, Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento all out because of injury. The head coach has called up James Garner and Morgan Gibbs‑White to boost his options for the upcoming Nations League programme.

Tuchel gave Palmer a high-profile recall on Friday for the beginning of the two-year international cycle that he hopes will end in glory at Euro 2028. England are back in the top division of the Nations League and they kick off against Spain at Wembley on Saturday. They then play Czechia and Croatia away before returning to Wembley to face Czechia.

Palmer has felt a minor muscle issue and, not for the first time under Tuchel, has been forced to make himself unavailable. The Chelsea midfielder, who has started the season in fine form, has made only three appearances under Tuchel. He was left out of the World Cup squad after his form ebbed last season and the head coach spoke at his squad announcement of a fresh opportunity for Palmer. That will have to wait. The 24-year-old has been a virtual ever‑present for Chelsea this season, contributing four goals and two assists in all competitions.

Rice’s withdrawal is not a complete surprise given his workload for a number of seasons. He needed to manage a nerve issue in a hamstring in the second half of last season which also affected his lower back and caused the midfielder discomfort at the World Cup. He has started all of Arsenal’s Premier League matches so far this season – plus their Champions League opener against Napoli. It has been decided that a rest at this point is the wisest course of action.

Mainoo was taken off after 80 minutes of Manchester United’s game at Fulham on Sunday; a move from the manager, Michael Carrick, that led to boos from the travelling support. The midfielder was in the World Cup squad but he was the only outfield player not to get a single minute on the pitch. Tuchel has said Mainoo’s lack of involvement was no slight on him, his ability or application levels. It was, instead, purely down to decisions that Tuchel took for technical reasons. The head coach had promised to give Mainoo minutes over the coming fortnight or so.

Mainoo’s United teammate Rashford was substituted in the 77th minute of the Fulham game and was seen holding the area by the front of his hip and groin as he slowly walked off.

Tuchel has always championed Rashford; he called him up when he named his first squad in March of last year when the player was struggling for form. Tuchel wanted to show Rashford that he believed in him and he has always included the 28‑year‑old when he has been available.

Tuchel seemed to lose a bit of faith after Rashford played poorly against the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the last 32 of the World Cup finals tournament over the summer. Thereafter, Tuchel barely used him until England’s semi-final exit against Argentina, giving him a couple of minutes as a stoppage-time substitute in that game but nothing more. He did play him for the first 45 minutes of the third-place playoff against France.

Livramento was named in the World Cup squad only to sustain a calf injury in training on the eve of the tournament. The Newcastle full‑back had to fly home. He underwent surgery and returned for his club as a substitute against Bournemouth at the start of the month. He had a setback in training before Newcastle’s win against Hull on Saturday and was not in the matchday squad. The 23-year-old is yet to start a game this season.

Garner comes in as a central midfield replacement for Rice and Mainoo while Gibbs-White adds to Tuchel’s options in the No 10 position in the absence of Palmer. Tuchel also has Jude Bellingham, Morgan Rogers and Eberechi Eze as No 10s. The players are due to report on Tuesday to St George’s Park.

Sports.title: Granit Xhaka admits to receiving fake Covid vaccination certificate in 2022
Sports.content:
Granit Xhaka has been withdrawn from Switzerland’s squad after he admitted receiving a fake Covid vaccination certificate in 2022. The Sunderland and Switzerland captain – who was an Arsenal player at the time – has apologised for this “mistake” and will sit out his country’s forthcoming four Nations League matches.

Xhaka is poised to be questioned by the prosecutor’s office in Lucerne next week as it decides whether any criminal proceedings will be initiated regarding the alleged issue of a series of false Covid certificates by a doctor based in the Swiss city during the pandemic. The doctor, who was first investigated in 2023, has denied the allegations.

In a statement issued via Instagram, Xhaka acknowledged he had decided not to be inoculated against the virus. “In recent days there has been much reporting about a matter from my past. I would like to address this personally,” he wrote. “At the time, I was personally very uncertain and had serious concerns regarding the Covid-19 vaccination. I felt deep distrust of the vaccine and was plagued by fear and uncertainty.

“In this turbulent emotional state, I obtained a vaccination certificate instead of clarifying my open questions through the proper channels. Today I clearly see this was not the right course of action. It was a mistake. I am sorry. I take responsibility for this decision, am committed to investigating the matter and am co-operating with the relevant authorities.”

Xhaka tested positive for Covid in September 2022 and the 33-year-old – he turns 34 on Sunday – did not feature in Switzerland’s internationals that month.

A spokesperson for the Lucerne cantonal prosector’s office said: “The aim [of the inquiries] is to clarify whether there has been conduct relevant under criminal law in connection with the possible fraudulent obtaining of a false certification and/or document forgery.”

Should charges be brought, Xhaka could face a heavy fine or, theoretically, a five-year prison sentence. However, the imposition of the latter sanction – or any sort of custodial punishment – is understood to be extremely unlikely.

Given that Xhaka was with Arsenal in 2022, Sunderland have told the Guardian they are not commenting on the matter. The midfielder left north London to join Bayer Leverkusen in 2023 and arrived at the Stadium of Light two years later.

Xhaka, who has been capped 152 times by Switzerland, will now miss the Nations League matches away to North Macedonia and Scotland and at home against Slovenia and North Macedonia.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The president of the Swiss Football Association, Peter Knabel, said: “Granit Xhaka approached us about the situation last [Sunday] night and told us he would admit it publicly and take responsibility. We welcome Granit taking this step and facing the consequences. We jointly concluded that it is in the team’s interests to complete the entire camp without him. Our priority now is to calm the situation.”

Although the Swiss FA possess the power to hit Xhaka with a suspension from football – something they could ask Fifa to apply worldwide – that scenario is regarded as highly unlikely.

Sports.title: The last two seasons were grim for Spurs. This is as bad as it’s ever been | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
In March, Tottenham, fearing possible relegation, spent big to bring in Roberto De Zerbi, who will probably never go into a negotiation with a stronger hand. There was obvious improvement and they stayed up on the final day of the season. Since then, Spurs have spent a net £175m ($234m) on improving the squad. The message seemed clear: the fiscal caution of the Daniel Levy era was over and this was a club willing to spend. Yet Spurs go into the first international break bottom of the Premier League table.

To an extent, the issue is confidence. On the opening weekend at Brentford, with a weird mishmash of a side, a team that was clearly undercooked, they were hammered 3-0 by much better-prepared opponents. That was not hugely surprising given how sensible Brentford’s transfer dealing had been and how early they had done it. More worrying was what happened the following week as Spurs, starting well before fading, lost 2-0 at home to Newcastle.

Goalless draws against Nottingham Forest and Everton seemed to have steadied the ship. Their biggest problem seemed to be a lack of confidence. They were tentative in possession, indecisive when chances did come. The two goals they managed in their 3-2 defeat to Aston Villa on Saturday mean Spurs climbed above Coventry to second-bottom of the goal-scoring charts, but they are ninth for shots. That should be reason for frustration rather than panic; the goals will come eventually.

But there are more concerning things to have come out of Saturday’s game. The lack of confidence in front of goal seems to have curdled into something worse, a more general mental degeneration. Again, they started well. The Villa keeper Zion Suzuki made a string of saves. And then just before half-time Villa scored a shambolic goal. Micky van de Ven was off the pitch receiving treatment. Andy Robertson, in preventing the ball running out for a corner, gifted possession to John McGinn. A cut-back, a scuffed shot and Johan Manzambi was unmarked in the six-yard box to score. It was a horrible goal to concede.

The second goal they conceded was just as bad. A long punt not dealt with, Nicolas Jackson bringing the ball down, Van de Ven not getting tight enough, a shot that bounced in off Antonin Kinsky’s hand. The third Villa goal was whipped brilliantly into the top corner by Emi Buendía, but he had space to line it up before James Maddison, who had been marking João Gomes, got out to him. Perhaps Maddison could have been more aggressive, and the slight turn of his back as Buendía struck his shot is never a good sign, but this was at least as much a failure of structure.

To an extent Spurs were unfortunate. Robertson might have cleared that ball for a throw-in, or at least got distance down the line, and Boubacar Kamara’s mishit cross could have gone anywhere. Jackson will not always be so deft in taking down a chest-high ball. Buendía, enormously technically gifted as he is, will not always pick out the top corner. But equally, each goal followed some sort of error: the Premier League is full of high-class players who will take advantage of any slip.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

De Zerbi spoke of Spurs being “too fragile”, by which he seemed to be talking both of their physicality and mentality. They have players returning from injury. Like so many clubs, they brought in players late. Preseasons have been curtailed, perhaps inadequate.

Where the initial instinct was to be impressed by the numbers and the change of policy, doubts are now emerging about the nature of those summer signings. Is Sandro Tonali really worth £100m? Mateus Fernandes played for a relegated side. Jan Paul van Hecke wouldn’t be the first player to leave Brighton and find his level dip outside that precisely configured environment. Sávio and Omar Marmoush struggled to get into the team at Manchester City. Sávio’s finishing brought just two league goals in two seasons at City and the evidence of Saturday is that it has not improved.

The sense had been that this season couldn’t be as bad as the last two for Spurs. There is no Europe to distract them. The injury crises couldn’t be as bad again. De Zerbi has proved his worth in the Premier League before. They have spent money. And yet this is as bad as it’s ever been. Once a club of Tottenham’s stature could have dismissed this as a blip, the kind of thing that would inevitably sort itself out as the season went on. After the last two seasons, nobody can be quite that confident again.

It’s still implausible Spurs could be relegated, unlikely even that they’ll be in another fight, but those preseason thoughts of European qualification are already beginning to look bafflingly optimistic – and that will inevitably slow the rebuilding of the club.

Sports.title: Ghosts of 2023 quelled after Dortmund return to the Bundesliga summit | Andy Brassell
Sports.content:
Borussia Dortmund would probably rather not think about the last time that they topped the Bundesliga. It was in May 2023, just before all their dreams imploded, with black and yellow Deutscher Meister t-shirts – ‘German champions’ – for sale on the approach to Signal Iduna Park and cold beers at the ready. Now, that is no longer the most recent time Dortmund have led the pack.

It’s four games, four wins to start this season and the Niko Kovac workout plan is hitting the spot. Saturday night’s single-goal win at Stuttgart was a game that had the gravitas of a true Topspiel, if not quite the entertainment value of one. Kovac’s fingerprints were all over it. The conversation of whether his view of the game fits with BVB’s swashbuckling image will no doubt continue, but this was a case in point to show just how good Kovac has been for the club, and for the team.

Dortmund had taken four points from the two games against Sebastian Hoeness and his Stuttgart team last season – and just as Kovac will not be oblivious to criticism of his side’s style, nor is Hoeness to whispers about his impressive team’s waning record against direct rivals – but were hardly overwhelmingly impressive either. It had been a huge improvement on the 2024-25 encounters with Stuttgart, in which BVB had been well beaten, twice, once under the short reign of Nuri Sahin and once in Kovac’s first game in charge, at which point he must have realised the mountainous task ahead of him.

Here, in September 2026, was the clearest of markers of how far Dortmund have come under the former Croatia midfielder and how deeply his ideas have taken root. To see a Dortmund patient, poised and defensively competent enough to grind this game out is still a novelty, and they didn’t have a shot on target until Maximilian Beier prodded in the winner from an inviting ball in by substitute Jobe Bellingham. That Dortmund dealt with everything the home side had in response, with street smarts and limited fuss, was laudable. They made a very accomplished attacking forced look ordinary. “In a top match,” Stuttgart’s Hoeness later reflected, “decent and okay aren’t enough.”

That Bellingham and Beier combined for the goal was noteworthy too; the former frequently rubbished for not being the equal of his generationally-talented elder brother and the latter another player who is simply underrated, both were brought in for big money and accordingly viewed with little patience. Their adaptability was striking, with Bellingham impacting off the bench and Beier thriving in a more advanced role. They are both Kovac’s type: young, willing, athletic and adaptable.

View image in fullscreen Niko Kovac has been in charge of Borussia Dortmund since January 2025. Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Should we call Dortmund contenders? That is, perhaps, a bit strong. But there is talk is about reducing the 16-point gap to Bayern that remained at the end of last season, and there were signs here that they may, at least, be capable of that. “It’s about annoying Bayern a bit”, is how Dortmund managing director Lars Ricken framed it, following the win at Stuttgart.

Dortmund were never going to return to relevance and consistency by trying to relive the Jürgen Klopp years, or by trying to ape Bayern (and yes, both of those approaches have been attempted). To get into the position where they can face the hurt (and potential rewards) of 2023 all over again will take a while, and doesn’t just depend on them – it will take Bayern falling down a rung or two. They are at least climbing the right ladder though, slowly, steadily, and diligently.

Thank you for your feedback.

Talking points

It was only a matter of time and it was probably always going to happen against an ailing Union Berlin, who are enduring a horrible start to the season, but Harry Kane reached 100 Bundesliga goals on Friday night in his 98th game, so much faster than anyone in the league’s history. His double was almost a footnote on a night as Michael Olise scored a dazzling hat-trick, with Jamal Musiala and Ismaël Saibari also netting their first league goals of the season in a 7-0 shellacking. It was a good start to the club’s traditional celebration of Oktoberfest weekend.

Bayern later mourned Peter Hermann, Jupp Heynckes’ popular assistant in the 2013 treble-winning season, who passed away on Saturday at the age of 73. Hermann was also emotionally commemorated at Leverkusen before kick-off on Sunday, having played in their 1979 promotion-winning team and having later served as assistant to Klaus Toppmöller at the helm of the celebrated 2002 Champions League finalists. Die Werkself paid fitting tribute on the field too as they beat RB Leipzig 2-0. The margins were fine, with Christopher Nkunku having an opener ruled out for the visitors before Patrik Schick put the home side ahead from a Miguel Gutiérrez cross. Gutiérrez, Álex Grimaldo’s nominal replacement, scored the second himself. Carles Martínez praised his team for “good balance between keeping the ball and playing forward”, while his opposite number Martín Demichelis has plenty to think about after a fourth straight away defeat.
