View image in fullscreen Bayer Leverkusen players and fans hold a minute of silence for Peter Hermann. Photograph: Martin Meissner/AP

Never before had a team scored three times in successive Bundesliga home games and lost both of them but Borussia Mönchengladbach are managing to find a ledge beneath the edge. Gladbach made a bright start against Mainz (who are under interim coach Jan-Moritz Lichte) – with Florian Neuhaus scoring the opener on his return to the line-up, his first since May 2024 – but ended in defeat again, leaving them bottom, without a point. Alexander Blessin, a former St Pauli coach famed for his defensive work, is expected to arrive in an attempt to plug the leaks.

Hamburg had gone into matchday four pointless and goalless but managed to squeeze past a Köln side who dominated them, with Yussuf Poulsen’s second goal for the club since arriving in summer 2025 proving decisive. It was an endorsement of their faith in head coach Merlin Polzin, who signed a contract extension this week despite that bad start and successive 5-0 defeats.

There are comebacks and there are comebacks, and several coincided on the Weser as Werder Bremen continued their surprisingly good start to the season. They trailed 2-0 to Augsburg but were level after a Niclas Füllkrug netbuster but even better was around the corner, with Mitchell Weiser rattling in a perfect left-foot winner, deep into stoppage time, in his first home appearance after 16 months out with injury. It brought the former Bayern man to tears and his coach Daniel Thoune described it as “a goosebump moment”.

All three promoted teams now have a win after Paderborn’s shock victory over Hoffenheim in Sunday’s late game, with veteran substitute Steffen Tigges sealing it with a header for his first top-flight goal since 2024. It was a third loss in four for Hoffenheim, who also suffered an embarrassing Europa League reverse at OFI Crete on Thursday.

Sports.title: Pierre Sage took Lens to new heights. His replacement left after six games
Sports.content:
It was under cover of darkness that Yannick Cahuzac took his place in the Lens dugout at the Stade Louis II on Friday night. The lights dimmed as the players made their entrance and Cahuzac, who had been named interim manager just three days earlier, sat alone, leaning forward on a seat that Dino Toppmöller would have occupied if not for a dramatic turn of events last week.

Cahuzac’s appointment, much like his entrance in Monaco, had a stealthy quality, as if he had always been there and the switching of the lights was mere confirmation of his presence. Cahuzac left Lorient, where he had been Olivier Pantaloni’s assistant, at the end of last season to return to Lens, where he had finished his playing career before working as Franck Haise’s assistant in the 2022–23 campaign.

He was spoken about as a future No 1, but that was not the role he took in the summer. Cahuzac is still an apprentice who has not yet obtained his coaching qualifications so he returned to the club as an assistant to Toppmöller. The German had the unenviable task of succeeding Pierre Sage, who hastily departed to Crystal Palace after guiding Lens to a maiden Coupe de France triumph and a second-place finish in Ligue 1 last season.

Lens were not expected to soar as high this season. Speaking in the summer, the club’s sporting director, Jean-Louis Leca, said they were “not a Champions League club” and that an eighth-place finish in Ligue 1 would represent success. Toppmöller’s first game in charge brought silverware as Lens beat PSG in the Trophée des Champions; his first Ligue 1 game was a resounding 5-2 win over Auxerre; and his side took all three points away to Slavia Prague in their first Champions League game – not a bad start after a summer of upheaval and the departure of several important players.

Results have dipped in recent weeks but expectations were being met. Hence the shock last week when it was announced that the German had left the club by mutual consent. Having taken charge of just six games, Toppmöller is Lens’s shortest-serving manager since the second world war. His exit says more about the club than it does the man. Explaining the parting of ways, the chief executive, Benjamin Parrot, revealed a divide, not necessarily between Toppmöller and his squad, but rather within the staff itself.

“Even before the Trophée des Champions, we felt, within the staff, that there was a French group and then a more international group,” said Parrot. Toppmöller brought two assistants with him. Lens tried to sack one of them, Nelson Morgado, but Toppmöller stayed loyal to his assistant and refused to accept his dismissal. He left and Cahuzac stepped up in his place.

View image in fullscreen Paris Brunner and Denis Zakaria embrace after Monaco take the lead in their win against Lens. Photograph: Alunno Nicolas/Abaca/Shutterstock

Cahuzac was touted as Toppmöller’s successor before he had even settled at the club. That can’t be a healthy environment for any new manager. Perhaps the writing was always on the wall for Toppmöller, especially given that Leca – Cahuzac’s close friend and former teammate at Bastia – is the club’s sporting director. Leca knows how it looks. “Yes, he is my friend, but inside these walls he isn’t my friend. Inside these walls, I am his line manager,” said Leca.

To suggest that Cahuzac’s appointment is pure nepotism is unfair. Lorient were one of the most tactically interesting teams in Ligue 1 last season and while Pantaloni – who was nominated for the manager-of-the-season award – earned most of the plaudits, Cahuzac played a key role too. He also knows the club, having played for them for three seasons and worked under Haise as an assistant.

His first game in charge, against Monaco, did not begin well. The hosts were 1-0 up at half-time but they had the ball in the Lens net on three occasions, denied by the assistant referee’s flag. Cahuzac changed tactics at the interval, which helped, and Matthieu Udol headed in a deserved equaliser. Franjo Ivanovic and Thorgan Hazard had chances as Lens pushed for a winner. In the end, it was a Lens player who scored but, unfortunately for Jonathan Gradit, it was into his own net.

So, Cahuzac’s tenure begins with a valiant 2-1 defeat. The 41-year-old was a pitbull of a player but he was almost inert in his dugout. He stood like a statue, with his hand on his chin in a pensive pose that exuded a studious serenity. After the turbulent week Lens have had, the club need a sense of calm.

Quick Guide Ligue 1 results Show Auxerre 2-1 Brest Nice 2-1 Lille Marseille 1-2 PSG Paris FC 2-1 Strasbourg Angers 2-0 Troyes Le Mans 2-1 Lorient Lyon 4-0 Rennes Toulouse 3-2 Le Havre Monaco 2-1 Lens Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Talking points

On the topic of messy break-ups, there was an unhappy reunion between Liam Rosenior and Strasbourg on Saturday. The pair had not met since Rosenior was hurried out the door to join sister club Chelsea in January. There is no love lost. The Englishman led Paris FC to a 2-1 win, continuing his unbeaten run since returning to Ligue 1 this summer. He celebrated the win in front of the travelling Strasbourg fans, a response, Rosenior said, to insulting chants about his family from the away end. An unsavoury confrontation between both sets of players and staff ensued. Rosenior said the chants had gone “too far” and that “celebrating like that was clearly a message”. His players also sent a message, confirming that they are in the mix for Champions League qualification.

View image in fullscreen Liam Rosenior celebrated Paris FC’s win in front of the travelling Strasbourg fans. Photograph: Matthieu Mirville/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

PSG beat Marseille 2-1 in a Classique that encapsulated the clubs’ seasons so far; both are struggling. For PSG, the points are at least now flowing. Ferran Torres continues to prove a fine signing. He came off the bench to score the opening goal. Marquinhos redeemed himself for his own goal in this fixture last season, which gave Marseille their first win over PSG at the Vélodrome in Ligue 1 in 14 years. That feels like a long time ago now. The concerns for Marseille only deepen. There were bright moments, notably Angel Gomes’s equaliser, but Bruno Génésio’s side have now lost four of their first five league matches. “A Ligue 2 project?” read a banner from the home fans. They go into the international break in the relegation zone.

Despite the game being briefly suspended after the home fans unfurled an insulting banner that targeted their fierce rivals Saint-Étienne, Lyon made a statement with a 4-0 win over Rennes. They rotated in their midweek Europa League win over Anderlecht, a clear but disappointing sign of where their priorities lie. It paid off, however. Rennes fielded a stronger side against Sturm Graz but did not take the three points, and their striker Esteban Lepaul was consequently not involved from the start against Lyon. A full-strength Lyon made short work of Franck Haise’s side, who may struggle to balance their European and league commitments. Rennes did not lay a glove on Lyon, whose own fans posed the greatest threat.

Sports.title: Paul Scholes accuses Man United of 'a lack of ambition' and 'buying players for the sake of it' - rather than trying to win the Premier League - and claims Michael Carrick will feel 'let down' by his bosses
Sports.content:
Paul Scholes has claimed that Michael Carrick has been let down by the Manchester United hierarchy with their 'lack of ambition' over the summer.

United have managed to win just one of their opening five games of the season, a 5-2 victory over promoted side Ipswich Town. Otherwise, they have lost to Hull City and Manchester City, and have drawn against Everton and Fulham. They have also been knocked out of the Carabao Cup at the first time of asking.

United had a modest summer in the transfer market. With Casemiro leaving for Inter Miami and Manuel Ugarte - now injured - deemed not good enough, Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes emerged as Carrick's top midfield targets. But Anderson joined Man City from Nottingham Forest in a £116million deal, while Fernandes chose Tottenham over United for £85m.

The club also considered Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes, but baulked at the fees required to sign the pair, who eventually joined Spurs (£92.5m) and Arsenal (£75m) respectively.

Instead, United signed Carlos Baleba for £70million, though the Cameroon international is yet to feature after arriving with an ankle injury. Andrey Santos joined for £48m but has started only once, while Youri Tielemans arrived for £35m and Karl Darlow on a free transfer.

Carrick also wanted a new left back, but the club failed to provide cover or a long-term successor for the 31-year-old Luke Shaw.

Scholes has claimed that Carrick has been let down by the Manchester United hierarchy with their 'lack of ambition' over the summer

United have managed to win just one of their opening five games of the season, a 5-2 victory over promoted side Ipswich Town and have lost to Hull City and Manchester City

United legend Scholes has voiced his concern over the situation, with the club sitting in 12th after five games.

'It feels quite sad to say this but Man United are a club now that are not trying to win the league with recruitment,' he said on The Good, The Bat & The Football podcast.

'Santos, Baleba, they've brought players in that physically they may be better. Santos played 11 games for Chelsea, they paid £50million for him.

'But he's not getting into the team, now Baleba might make a bit of difference. But again, if you're recruiting at the start of the season for Manchester United, it should be for players that you think you can go and win the league with. I think they're a million miles away.

'I think they're just trying to consolidate from what Michael did last year, which is hard to get your head around. Were United trying to buy an Elliot Anderson? Probably. Now that's a signing where you think that might help you get a lot better. The players they've bought aren't making them any better.'

Centre-forward appears to be a particular sticking point for Scholes and his podcast partner Nicky Butt. United appeared willing to let forward Joshua Zirkzee leave the club in the summer, although a move failed to materialise.

Carrick has remained reluctant to play the Dutchman in Benjamin Sesko's absence and he has made just two substitute appearances in the Premier League so far, with Matheus Cunha getting the nod up top instead.

Butt said: 'Playing Cunha as a nine - it kills him, he's not a nine. He's nowhere near the player he is when he's playing off the side. We haven't got a number nine other than (Benjamin) Sesko. Zirkzee doesn't look anywhere near a Man United number nine. How can Man United have one centre forward that they can rely on?'

Carrick has been reluctant to play Zirkzee in Benjamin Sesko's absence and he has made just two substitute appearances in the Premier League

Carrick guided United to third in the Premier League last season, and both Scholes and Butt have claimed that Carrick has been let down by the club's hierarchy.

Scholes said: 'Michael must be really disappointed with what has happened in the summer. I reckon behind the scenes he thinks he's been let down. What Michael did last year was very, very good.

'The most important time for Michael was the start of this season. These games now are where you put a marker down, it gives you a foundation for the rest of the season.'

United have already seen two managers depart since Sir Jim Ratcliffe's INEOS took over footballing operations in February 2024. Erik ten Hag was sacked three months after being handed a new deal in October 2024. His replacement, Ruben Amorim, was then sacked in January this year after 14 months in charge.

Butt said: 'As a fan, the bit that gets me, I no longer think "it's a no-brainer we're going to win this game". Who can you point the finger at, and for me, it has to be the people upstairs that are pointing the people into place to pick the managers, the players, the coaches.

'I don't understand it. (Omar) Berrada the CEO said they're going to win the league by 2028. That's never going to happen the way it's going, never in a million years.

'I don't understand it. (Omar) Berrada the CEO said they're going to win the league by 2028. That's never going to happen the way it's going, never in a million years,' Butt said

'Without literally ripping them to shreds, it has to be said they've come in, they gave Ten Hag an extra few years on his contract, that didn't work. They went and got two other managers after that and it's still not working.

'There's got to be a real question being asked - is it being run right off the pitch, in recruitment and then that translates onto the pitch. So it's a massive big problem I think.'

Scholes added: 'I don't think we can keep blaming managers all the time. You can't just keep going through managers like we are doing. Recruitment will have an awful lot to answer for, especially after this summer.

'Are they looking at these top targets, Morgan Rogers, Elliot Anderson? It feels like we're buying players just for the sake of it. It feels like they're settling for third, fourth, fifth-best signings - and that isn't good enough. I'd rather just keep the money, and say "sure we can find someone in the academy who can do what these lads are doing".'

Sports.title: Brighton's demolition of Arsenal dissected: The Seagulls' power press, Bart Verbruggen's clever tactic, exploiting Mikel Arteta's new idea and preying on David Raya's weakness
Sports.content:
So much, then, for Arsenal’s uncontested stroll to a second Premier League title under Mikel Arteta. So much for the idea that this impenetrable fortress would remain unconquered all season, for who could possibly possess the weapons with which to breach it. Brighton have quickly put paid to that. ‘There was only one team who tried to play football today,’ was Fabian Hurzeler’s pointed remark after the Gunners clung on to a 1-0 lead at the Amex Stadium back in March. Six months later, it was the Brighton boss who provided Arteta with his own brutal lesson of how to do so and one, perhaps, that Arsenal’s rivals could look to follow on their quest to dethrone them. PRESS, PRESS, PRESS The biggest of Brighton’s weapons was their relentless press. From the first minute until the last, the Seagulls swarmed around Arsenal, man-to-man, as high and as wide up the pitch as possible. It was in complete contrast to the trick used by Manchester City last season under Pep Guardiola where their front four would sit off the Arsenal backline, refuse to press them, and instead cut off the passing lanes into midfield. Brighton wanted to harass Arsenal so much that they either won possession high up the pitch – the Seagulls won the ball back 10 times in the final third, the most of any team this season, and the last side to do so more often against Arsenal was Liverpool in April 2023 – or panic them into dangerous passes into midfield where they would be waiting. Brighton allowed Arsenal no time to settle on the ball at the Amex Stadium on Saturday as they ran out 3-0 winners Brighton won possession from Arsenal 10 times in the final third of the pitch These two examples (below) came from inside the first five minutes. On one occasion in between, Arsenal keeper David Raya was so flummoxed he passed the ball straight out for a throw in. Brighton crowd the Arsenal players high up the pitch and win the ball back Again, Brighton's press has Arsenal in all sorts of trouble in their box with nowhere to go The key was Brighton just didn’t stop. It’s all well and good harrying and hustling and chasing down all over the pitch from the first minute but, eventually, you tire and you fade and don’t jump up as quickly or aggressively as you did at the start. Only Brighton didn’t. They kept going. Even at 3-0 up, with nearly an hour gone, they swarm around Arsenal’s players to create another chance. The Seagulls push up and force Ezri Konsa to play a pass into midfield towards Bukayo Saka only for Brighton to nick it back, burst into the area and Charalampos Kostoulas goes down in the box looking for a penalty. Ezri Konsa plays the ball into midfield to try to find Bukayo Saka... ...but Saka is immediately under pressure and Brighton win the ball back Just a minute later, Arsenal get the ball back on the other side of the pitch. By the time Bruno Guimaraes receives the pass, he is surrounded by four blue shirts with nowhere to go. Brighton keep the Gunners where they want them. Bruno Guimaraes is swamped by Brighton players and can find no way out That came, as it happens, from Brighton lumping the ball upfield from just outside their own box and out for a throw-in. This, too, was a key aspect of their play. GO LONG, CAUSE CHAOS We’ve seen it with other high-pressing teams like Bournemouth when they lump the ball, rugby-style, into touch from the kick-off because they would rather try to win the ball back as close to the opposition goal as possible. Brighton did it frequently, in open play, and often via goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen. For Brighton’s first goal, the Seagulls had a throw-in deep in the final third, almost level with the edge of Arsenal’s box, but still they eventually worked the ball all the way back to Verbruggen, who stood with his studs on the ball while the centre backs split and, eventually, went long to the right. After some neat passing, the ball found Pascal Gross, who fired in from range. The Brighton keeper frequently targeted that side, as you can see from his pass map (below). The feeling was that even if the usually physically dominant Arsenal side won the first ball, the Seagulls would be there to flock around the second. The map shows Bart Verbruggen using the long ball a lot and frequently favouring Arsenal's left-back position Right back Ferdi Kadioglu pushed up high down that side to frequently box Arsenal in. A look at their average position maps, too, shows just how Brighton locked down that side of the pitch. The average position of Brighton players in their victory over Arsenal and how they doubled up on their right wing EXPLOITING ARTETA’S EVOLUTION It was not all about the press for Brighton, though. Whenever Arsenal did get on the ball inside the Seagulls’ half, the hosts dropped into a deep, deep block. They either wanted to win the ball close to Arsenal’s box, or near their own - and spring a counter. Look here (below), how Brighton have all 11 players behind the ball as Arsenal look to find a way through just before the hour. Brighton are back in shape with all their players behind the ball as Arsenal try in vain to find a way through Brighton eventually win possession back just outside their box and break. Not even a minute later, after pressing to win the ball back high up the pitch, they win the corner from which they score their third goal. Brighton’s four ‘fast breaks’, Opta’s phrase for a counter attack, and their three shots that came from them, were their most in a Premier League game since 2019. The last time Arsenal faced more in a match was 2018. Hurzeler was exploiting Arteta’s changing style. For so long, the complaint about Arsenal is how they were so obsessed with control that they never took enough risks to create enough in open play. That appears, maybe, to be changing. After just four matches this season, Arsenal have attempted the third most fast breaks themselves with 10. This is a change. Last season they were ranked ninth. The season before that 12th and, two seasons before that, 16th with just 18 all campaign. It adds an extra dimension to their play but they are yet to find the balance and, as Brighton showed, you can hurt them in transition. Their second goal comes straight from an Arsenal counter attack, where Saka fluffs a shot straight into Verbruggen’s hands, and Brighton spring one of their own. TEST RAYA FROM RANGE Brighton’s first two goals came from shots from outside the box. So was the one Arsenal conceded against Chelsea, the only other league match in which they have been breached. Seven of the last 18 Premier League goals Arsenal have conceded have come from distance. Is this becoming a weakness? A stat from Opta did the rounds after the match stating that among goalkeepers that have conceded at least 100 Premier League goals only Hans Segers (22 per cent) has conceded a higher percentage from outside the penalty area than David Raya (20.6 per cent).

Your browser does not support iframes.

Arsenal's David Raya was beaten from distance again during the defeat at Brighton It is slightly unfair to pick him out as Arsenal’s defence is so good that teams are often reduced to having to shoot from miles away but of the 22 goalkeepers to start at least 40 league matches since the start of the 2023-24 season, when Raya joined the Gunners, only two have a worse save percentage from outside the box (Raya's is 78 per cent). You can bet that teams, even if they aren’t already, will start to pepper Raya’s goal from range now. HAVE THEY BEEN FOUND OUT? Is this the key, then, to beating this unbeatable Arsenal? Well, for a start, Brighton’s approach was exceptionally high risk with so many bodies committed to press so high. Arsenal had plenty of chances, including Kai Havertz missing a one-on-one. Few teams, too, have the energy, physicality and tactical discipline to pull it off for 90 minutes like Brighton did. Not every long-range shot, too, will nestle in the bottom corner, let alone two. However, the manner of the defeat, the lack of balance and control, has certainly given Arteta three weeks to think about what went wrong. The Gunners still boast one of the best defences in world football but Brighton have proved they are not quite so untouchable after all.

Sports.title: How Gary Neville is missing the point over Man United's running stats, why Michael Carrick isn't worried about 'lack of effort', the way he's copying Sir Alex Ferguson and the numbers that tell the other side of the story
Sports.content:
The truth is, Michael Carrick made his feelings clear on running statistics long before fronting up at Fulham on Sunday night. Where others such as Gary Neville are apoplectic with rage at the lethargy ('lack of effort' as Neville put it) with which Manchester United are playing – he described a spell in the first half as the worst 15 minutes he had seen from United in 45 years – Carrick is not. He didn’t focus on running stats as a player, and certainly doesn’t now. ‘David [Moyes] was right that in terms of “distance covered” we weren’t one of the top sides in the Premier League,’ Carrick wrote in his 2018 book Between the Lines, recalling one of Moyes’ first meetings with the squad upon succeeding Sir Alex Ferguson, in which he vowed to have them running more. ‘But if you look back over the years, all the good years, teams might come to Old Trafford and run a lot more than us, but quite often we ended up winning 2-0, 3-0 or 4-0. Under Sir Alex, we were very efficient with the ball.’ At Middlesbrough, though, ask their supporters what the biggest weakness of Carrick’s Boro side was and they will unanimously cite the lack of intensity in the press and the defensive issues that arose because of it.

Gary Neville was fuming at United's lack of effort in their 1-1 draw with Fulham at the weekend Then he had Jonny Howson and Hayden Hackney as a midfield pair, now it’s Kobbie Mainoo and Youri Tielemans. On the ball both pairs are brilliant. Without it, the shortcomings are strikingly similar. The thing is, win games and nobody talks about running stats. Win the game and the number of minutes spent at high intensity is likely airbrushed from the conversation. Win the game and the pros and cons of your system and your beliefs are saved for another day. But United aren’t winning. They lost at Hull City in abject fashion. They lost to the 10 men of Manchester City. They drew at Everton and they drew at Fulham. Even with a 5-2 win against Ipswich Town, this is United’s worst start to a Premier League season since 2013-14. Fail to beat Tottenham Hotspur and Carrick will officially have masterminded United’s worst ever start to a Premier League campaign. Fundamentally there is a chasm between a fanbase that want to see intensity, a buzzword that has stalked United for years, and effort, versus a manager that believes distance covered, sprints made and sheer physical output is not the only way to win a football match. So, you end up here, United heading into the international break dead last in sprints made, dead last in distance covered at high intensity, dead last in the amount of time spent at high intensity, dead last in the amount of time sprinting, and with only three teams spending more time walking without the ball than United do. And with a manager who rejects all criticism about those metrics. ‘I didn't think we did [look passive]. Did you think we were passive? Football is a difficult game,’ Carrick said as the inquest into the drab Fulham draw began with haste. ‘We controlled a lot of the first half and we played a lot of good football today. There are going to be spells when you don't have it go your own way.

Your browser does not support iframes.

Youri Tielemans is brilliant on the ball for United but without it his shortcomings are there for all to see Michael Carrick refuses to get hung up on Manchester United's running statistics 'To expect total dominance for the whole game, I don't think anyone gets that in this league.’ Passivity has been a trigger word for Carrick all season long. He rejected that assessment at Hull, and did so again at Everton and now at Fulham. Where he sees control and patience, others see laziness and a lack of ideas. To indulge Carrick, let’s look beyond the surface numbers that went viral soon after the final whistle. What we know to be true is that United ran 6.5 kilometres less than Fulham on the day, the second biggest disparity between teams when 11 v 11 so far this season. What we also know to be true is that Fulham started their passing sequences – when moves in attack begin – 36.9 metres from Senne Lammens’ goal, on average. In this latest round of matches, no side started closer to their opponents' goal than Fulham did. We also know that Bryan Mbeumo was the only United player to sprint more than 305 yards against Fulham, with 408.4. Bruno Fernandes, for example, was recorded to have sprinted just 35.2 yards in total. Kobbie Mainoo clocked in at 71.5 yards. It can also be pointed out that of the top 70 players in the league this season for number of sprints made, only two play for United in Mbeumo and Marcus Rashford. Brentford and Bournemouth combine for 11 players in this category. But then you need to look at the numbers Carrick cares about. The numbers he is focusing on. Numbers that show United had 29 shots against Fulham, taking their overall total to 113, ranking first of all 20 Premier League sides. Or the fact that Carrick’s side rank third in the league for expected goals (xG), with 9.9. Or the fact they rank first in the league for touches in the opposition’s box (182) and have allowed the fewest touches in their own penalty area (92). They are fourth in the league for possession and second in the league for most accurate passes per match.

Your browser does not support iframes.

All of the above statistics point to the conclusion that this so-called 'lethargic' United has to be, in part, by design. No, Carrick will not be explicitly telling players not to run and not to work hard, no manager would. Yet he fundamentally disagrees that those metrics represent the keys to success. Liverpool, for example, are the side which cover the least ground in the league under Andoni Iraola, yet they also top the sprint charts. It doesn’t have to be one or the other, that’s the gripe among United fans. Carrick wants to evolve into a possession-focused, pass-dominant side that can manage matches at their own pace, strangling the life out of teams through control. His own style as a player, going back to his dismissal of Moyes in his book, has unquestionably influenced his ideology. ‘Naturally, we all see the game for certain things,' Carrick explained to reporters at a sit-down during pre-season. 'We enjoy seeing different things and your eye naturally takes you to different parts of the game. We can all watch the game and see something a little bit different. ‘Just being a midfielder, that's how I've seen the game. In some ways, it helps because you kind of connected to all parts of the team over time. ‘I'm not saying you have to be a midfielder to be a good coach, but I think it's just how my reference points are in some ways and what I feel's worked over the years, what kind of football I think the supporters want to see as well, and hopefully that fits together.’ Supporters want to see wins but they crucially want to see effort and application upon the eye test, regardless of the more detailed data. Bruno Fernandes sprinted for just 35.2 yards at Craven Cottage on Sunday Calvin Bassey celebrates United's own goal that put Fulham ahead ‘It's about intensity, body language, physicality,' Ralf Rangnick explained in December 2021. 'This was always the case. If you want to keep control of a game like this you need to be physically present, and this wasn't the case in all positions.' ‘I think the main problem, that we did before in games much better, is intensity,' Erik ten Hag mused in October 2022. 'We have to bring the intensity in every game on the pitch. That was the big difference between City and us.' ‘Most important is the intensity,' Ruben Amorim bluntly pointed out in December last year. 'You can feel it right away, when we start the game. We can feel when we are at the top level in intensity and when we are not, and you cannot win games in this way.’ All that sounds and feels painfully familiar. Fans believe intensity holds the key, as does Matheus Cunha, who spoke passionately about it after the Fulham game. Three of Carrick’s predecessors believe success is built on the foundation of intensity, while director of football Jason Wilcox previously talked up the ‘intensity’ in training sessions day in, day out. But if you have a head coach whose philosophy goes against everything the Premier League has become in terms of blood and thunder football played in fast forward, is a three-week break really going to deliver the change required? Doubtful. Carrick is determined to do it his way and that’s why United are never going to be the Duracell bunnies of the Premier League under his watch. This feels like a hill that Carrick is very much willing to die on.

Sports.title: Benjamin Sesko becomes latest Man United star to withdraw from international duty - after Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford pulled out of Thomas Tuchel's squad
Sports.content:
Benjamin Sesko has become the latest Manchester United player to withdraw from international duty, the club have confirmed.

Sesko has pulled out of the Slovenia squad after Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford were ruled out of action for England, and goalkeeper Karl Darlow for Wales.

The 23-year-old striker missed United’s draw at Fulham on Sunday due to a recurrence of a niggling shin injury that kept him out of the final three games of last season and the club’s entire pre-season programme.

Sesko, who has made six appearances for United this season, has undergone scans and will have further tests this week to determine the best treatment plan. The initial results have been sent to Slovenia’s medical team, and Sesko will remain in Manchester to be assessed rather than travel to Ljubljana.

A club statement read: ‘Manchester United can confirm that Benjamin Sesko has withdrawn from the Slovenia squad ahead of the upcoming three-week international break.

‘The striker had been called up by head coach Bostjan Cesar for two games against Scotland, plus meetings with North Macedonia and Switzerland, but he will now no longer join the squad.

Sesko has pulled out of the Slovenia squad after Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford were ruled out of action for England, and goalkeeper Karl Darlow for Wales

‘Sesko last appeared in our Carabao Cup tie with Brighton & Hove Albion, but was absent from the matchday squad for our most recent encounter with Fulham. Benjamin will undergo tests this week before defining his individual recovery plan.’

Slovenia FA sources have said that it is up to United to give updates on Sesko’s fitness and plans for his recovery, adding that Cesar will not be commenting on the situation either.

United’s £74million signing from RB Leipzig has been at the centre of club-versus-country tensions in the past after Slovenia insisted on assessing the player when he withdrew from international duty in March and Cesar warned United that his country would not be pushed around.

The coach struck a more conciliatory tone when he named Sesko in his squad last week, but the latest pullout has raised more questions in Slovenia over his absence from the national team for a year.

Both United and Slovenia are keen to get to the bottom of Sesko’s shin problem after the striker claimed earlier this month that it was ‘perfect’ following an extended summer break.

‘It was basically just to make sure that it doesn't get worse because this was kind of a problem,’ he said. ‘We just need a little bit longer than usual, because if you start too early it might appear again. I think waiting a little bit longer was a great decision and now it's healed, so it's perfect.’

Sports.title: Now that's a Super Sunday! Arsenal vs Man City and Everton vs Liverpool among SIX games on blockbuster Premier League day as TV picks for November are revealed... with Man United landing first 3pm Saturday kick-off of the season
Sports.content:
Now that's a Super Sunday! Arsenal vs Man City and Everton vs Liverpool among SIX games on blockbuster Premier League day as TV picks for November are revealed... with Man United landing first 3pm Saturday kick-off of the season

Arsenal will host Manchester City to cap a six-game Premier League Sunday in November – starting with the Merseyside derby.

The revised schedule for the month was released on Monday afternoon, with Everton kicking off a busy day of action on November 29 at 12pm when they host Liverpool for the second time at Hill Dickinson Stadium, having lost the first one 2-1 last season to a late header by Virgil van Dijk.

Four games follow at 2.05pm, with Brighton v Newcastle, Crystal Palace v Hull, Fulham v Bournemouth and Sunderland v Tottenham – a repeat of Roberto De Zerbi's first match in charge of Spurs, a 1-0 defeat in April.

Champions Arsenal will then welcome Manchester City at 4.30pm, in what could prove a key early game in the title race. After five games this season, City lead the Gunners by three points at the top of the table having enjoyed a perfect start to the season under Enzo Maresca.

The glut of Sunday fixtures is partly explained by Palace, Bournemouth and Sunderland all playing in the Europa League three days earlier, with Brighton in Conference League against Romanian side Craiova the same night.

Nottingham Forest v Chelsea start the weekend on Friday at 8pm, and as a result of those changes just three matches will take place on the Saturday.

Erling Haaland and Gabriel will rekindle their rivalry at the Emirates on November 29

Leeds welcome Coventry in the traditional 3pm slot and Manchester United host Brentford at the same time – the first Saturday 3pm kick-off for the Reds in their 12th league game of the season.

Ipswich host Aston Villa at Portman Road in the 5.30pm match that day.

There are just three rounds of Premier League fixtures in November, with a two-week international break to factor in.

In other changes, Liverpool v Manchester United at Anfield is the headline game at 4.30pm on Sunday, November 22.

Sports.title: Here is the transfer Man United should pull forward to January - or risk being gazumped by Liverpool... and the new best pundit on TV is NOT on Sky Sports: IAN LADYMAN on My Football Weekend
Sports.content:
Gary Neville said the period after half-time was the worst he had ever seen from a Manchester United team. I would dispute that. The bar since the Sir Alex Ferguson years has been set desperately low. As we have talked about in this column before, one of the greatest challenges facing any United manager is the giddiness that follows a victory and the hysteria that follows a defeat. Michael Carrick knew that before this season started and he is being reminded of it with every passing disappointment. The truth is that the United we are watching now is the one that some of us saw coming. They will not remain in the bottom half of the Premier League. They are better than that. Michael Carrick is being reminded of the giddiness following a win and the hysteria following a defeat as United manager Equally, they are not equipped for a title challenge. Carrick lifted them into the top four during a perfect storm last season. His team – not in Europe and out of both domestic cups early – played one game a week in the absence of key injuries at a time when other big clubs were under-performing hugely. Now it’s different and United don’t have the depth – and quite possibly the manager – to cope. Look at Carrick’s bench yesterday. Where are the game changers? Until that changes – until United build a roster of players fit for the rigours of a 50+ game season – nothing else does. Hall will have other offers There has been understandable criticism of United’s transfer policy, particularly an apparent decision to focus on the midfield and attacking positions this year and the defence the next. With that in mind, United are keen to sign Lewis Hall from Newcastle next summer. But if the gifted 22-year-old continues to play like he did for his current club in the defeat of Hull on Saturday, then United would be fools to wait that long. Will Liverpool need a left back next summer? Possibly. What about Hall’s old club Chelsea? Maybe. United cannot presume the field will be clear at the end of the season. There is a transfer window in January and they may wish to use it. United would be fools to wait until the summer to sign Lewis Hall - other clubs will be interested Questions will have to be asked if Arsenal fail to defend their Premier League title this season Gunners beware Arsenal have the deepest squad, the best back four, the top goalkeeper and a manager who has won the Premier League before. If the Gunners don’t defend their title successfully this season they will have to ask themselves why. They say going back-to-back on a Premier League title is harder than actually winning it in the first place. I would dispute that this season, particularly now that it already looks like a two-horse race between Arsenal and Manchester City yet again. Liverpool, Chelsea and Manchester United already look short – by a distance in some cases – of what it takes. Tottenham? There must be a joke there somewhere. Arsenal’s start to the season had been imperious until they arrived at Brighton on Saturday. What took place at the Amex Stadium looked and felt like a huge wake-up call, not just for Arsenal but for the Premier League as a whole. A day to remind us that we may yet have a title race and a day when Arsenal learned that you can’t just turn up and win a football match, whoever you are. If it serves to remind the champions of some basic fundamentals of the game, it may serve them in the long run. But Arteta’s own words after the game were telling. ‘They were another gear from us in the basics of the game,’ said the Arsenal manager. It's too early to make sweeping statements on the champions, but this is their opportunity to put the league in a choke hold ‘We were not respecting the game. This cannot happen again.’ Footage of the game backed Arteta up. Given that Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler accused them of playing anti-football last season, Arsenal should not have lacked motivation. But they were outrun and outfought by their opponents. Declan Rice should be embarrassed by his kick out at Malick Yalcouye – he should have been sent off – while Gabriel’s dive under zero contact from Yasin Ayari was not befitting of a Sunday parks player, never mind the best defender in the land. Given the way Arsenal have started the season – with a 100 per cent record prior to the weekend – it’s too early to make sweeping statements about the champions. They showed last season that after two or three near misses, they have matured into the real deal. Arteta’s squad is frighteningly good. He has the type of quality on the bench that is reminiscent of peak City under Pep Guardiola. In these days of five substitutes, it is arguably the biggest advantage they have. None of it means much if you don’t run, though. Season 2026-27 represents Arsenal’s opportunity to put the Premier League in a choke hold and make it their own. If they don’t do it, they will have the rest of their careers to regret it. It will be a long international break for some Arsenal players. Arbeloa has failed his team Fulham are yet to win but look to have plenty about them and in Josh King, have a young midfielder who is just joyful to watch. Manager Alvaro Arbeloa would be advised to do better than throwing wild accusations about referee bias around, however. All it does – apart from getting him a well-deserved FA sanction – is draw attention away from some of the excellent things his team did. Fulham manager Alvaro Arbeloa should not be throwing round wild referee accusations Hart now holds the title Joe Hart's analysis of United goalkeeper Senne Lammens' difficulties in conceding the Fulham goal was excellent on Match of the Day and bettered only by his superb dissection of Rayan Cherki's for City against Sunderland. The likes of Neville and Jamie Carragher on Sky continue to set the standards for soundbites and candour but when it comes to breaking down the minutiae of what actually happens on the field, Hart has established himself as the best pundit in the country. The question is: Will the BBC be able to afford to keep him? Wirtz problem was clear at the World Cup Carragher went big on his criticism of Florian Wirtz, saying the German wouldn’t be in his Liverpool team to face Manchester City the other side of the international break. I have seen marginal improvement in Wirtz this season but it still feels as though the £115million signing of summer 2025 has some big steps to take if he is ever to become a Premier League star. Wirtz can do some wonderful things and was not without influence as Liverpool edged a close one 1-0 at Bournemouth. But one worry is that the way he can sometimes look half a yard off the pace exactly mirrors the way he appeared to me for Germany during the World Cup. The 23-year-old was taken off in the two World Cup games that really mattered to his country – against Ecuador and Paraguay. When Germany needed impetus and influence, they looked somewhere else. I hope it doesn’t get to that stage at Liverpool too. Florian Wirtz has a way to go to to become a Premier League star and his problems were clear at the World Cup Coaching worth its weight in gold We have only played five Premier League games but already some of our big clubs are being shamed by the likes of Brentford and Brighton. It won’t last but it’s good to know that, for a short time at least, top-class coaching and indeed recruitment can get you ahead of those who spent large parts of the summer setting fire to money. Scrap the Friday games I was at the Gtech to watch one of our big spenders – Chelsea – being taught a lesson at the start of the weekend and we could talk about their deficiencies all day. More broadly, the whole experience merely convinced me that Friday night is not a time for football. It just doesn’t feel the same and I don’t think it ever will. Over the years I have come to understand and appreciate the rhythms of a football weekend TV schedule that goes Saturday 12.30pm & 5.30pm and then Sunday 2pm & 4.30pm. But Friday will always feel wrong. Friday night is a time for anticipation of the sporting weekend, a time to dream and get excited by what is to come. I mean imagine being a Chelsea fan. You haven’t even had time to change out of your work clothes and the weekend is ruined already. Friday night is not a time for football - it should be a time to feel anticipation for the weekend Is Cole truly committed? Cole Palmer looked fleetingly impressive against Brentford and it’s disappointing to see him withdraw from the England squad after playing 90 minutes. Full details will doubtless emerge but at the moment it seems the decision has been made to enable him to manage a muscle concern. It’s a three-week international period and it’s hard not to wonder whether Palmer could not have reported to camp and played limited minutes or at the very least spent some time reintegrating himself with a squad that travelled to the World Cup without him. It would be a surprise at this stage if he makes the England cut for the next squad in November. And where would that leave him? Fab for Fabio It was uplifting to watch Fabio Carvalho come off the bench to score Brentford’s third goal. The Portuguese midfielder is still only 24 but much has happened – not much of it good – since his early move from Fulham to Liverpool back in 2022 didn’t work out. Carvalho has suffered injuries at Brentford and his goal on Friday was his first in the Premier League for a year and only his second since one for Liverpool back in August 2022. I was lucky enough to spend some time with him last season and he’s a good player who cares deeply about the game. Fingers crossed for better luck as he is a talent. Fabrio Carvalho is a talented player and came off the bench for Brentford to score against Chelsea on Friday Nicolas Jackson appears to be loving life under Unai Emery and could recapture his form Was I wrong on Jackson? Emi Martinez continues to look a little bemused by life at Chelsea – if Premier League crowds could stop booing all the Argentina players it would be nice – while Aston Villa may just have found an upgrade. Zion Suzuki – Japan’s American-born international goalkeeper – was outstanding as Villa withstood Tottenham pressure to win on Saturday lunchtime. He is only 24 so we can expect him to improve, too. Meanwhile Nicolas Jackson gave me cause to reconsider my view after leading the line magnificently for his team and scoring a super goal. Erratic at Chelsea, I expressed in an earlier column my amazement that Villa paid £45.5m plus add-ons for the centre forward. But Jackson feels that being reunited with his former Villarreal coach, Unai Emery, will be the key to a good season. ‘I am with the coach I wanna be with,’ said Jackson. We will see…

Sports.title: Michael Owen claims 'glum-faced' Marcus Rashford could be Man United's 'weak link' following 1-1 draw at Fulham
Sports.content:
Former Manchester United and England striker Michael Owen has called Marcus Rashford the 'weak link' in the Red Devils' forward line, following a difficult return to life at Old Trafford.

Rashford has started four of United's five Premier League matches since returning to the club, following loan spells at Aston Villa and Barcelona, including their 1-1 draw with Fulham at Craven Cottage on Sunday.

The winger has shown flashes of brilliance at times early this season, but is yet to register a single goal or assist in over 400 minutes of football in all competitions.

The 28-year-old was substituted during the second half in west London due to a hip issue, which has seen him pull out of the upcoming England squad, and Owen has voiced his concern about the output and mentality of the England international.

‘On the left, Marcus Rashford has been probably the quietest of those attackers,’ Owen said on Premier League Productions. ‘He was quiet again today in his body language, just the glum face. He just doesn’t seem to be loving his football which has been a permanent frustration with Marcus.

‘It does look like the weight of the world is on his shoulders and you just think how? Why? He’s living everybody’s dream. Surely there’s something behind the scenes that is making him look as if he’s not enjoying his football at the moment.’

Marcus Rashford is yet to register a goal or assist since his return to Manchester United

Rashford notched up 25 goal contributions during his impressive but short stint at Barcelona, with 14 of those goals. But the confidence he gained during his campaign in Catalonia seems to be wilting away already.

Owen added: ‘Last chance saloon was Barcelona. I couldn’t believe his luck in getting a team like Barcelona.

‘He does reasonably well out there, but not well enough for them to keep him and then they end up spending fortunes to replace him by buying Anthony Gordon. So, it wasn’t all perfect. It wasn’t all rosy despite any spin that people put on it.

‘And then he comes back to Manchester United. He’s done okay, but only okay. And he needs to probably do a little bit better in that front three because his is the position in the attack that would be vulnerable.

‘There’s a bit of a demand for Benjamin Sesko to come back in and start, injury permitting of course. But if that happens, Cunha is going to go on the left and Rashford would be the weak link in that attack as things stand.’

Despite Owen being disappointed with Rashford’s start to the season, he still has faith in the forward coming good again at United, if he can get in the right mental space.

Rashford picked up a hip issue against Fulham which has seen him pull out of the upcoming England squad

‘There is nothing that that lad hasn’t got,’ Owen continued. ‘He is so tall, such a great athlete. His touch and his skill levels are unbelievable. He’s quick.

‘He’s got everything that you would want in a player, and it just shows you if you haven’t got that [mentality], that is the most important thing in football. Not even a question. If you’re mentally strong, then you can go far in the game and he has got absolutely everything.

‘When he’s confident, when he’s happy and everything then he can be a world beater. But it’s not often he’s got that between his ears ticking. It’s not often that he’s in the right frame of mind.

‘He’s 28 now, he should be in his prime. He should be absolutely tearing defences apart, scoring loads of goals. We’re talking about what records he can break. He has got that ability to do it, and he’s shown it in patches, but just not seeing it on a consistent basis.’

Rashford’s return date from the hip injury he sustained at Craven Cottage is unknown; however, he will miss England’s upcoming Nations League fixtures against Spain, Czechia and Croatia, which will take place over the next three weeks.

Sports.title: Declan Rice leads FIVE stars in pulling out of England duty - with just two new players called up - as Thomas Tuchel faces exodus after his stern warning
Sports.content:
Declan Rice leads FIVE stars in pulling out of England duty - with just two new players called up - as Thomas Tuchel faces exodus after his stern warning

Declan Rice is the new big name among a five-man England exodus - days after Thomas Tuchel warned his players of a need to 'step up' to prove their worth after the World Cup.

Rice, Cole Palmer, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento have all now pulled out of Tuchel's squad - with Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White and James Garner of Everton the only replacements.

Arsenal midfielder Rice played the full 90 minutes of their defeat by Brighton on Saturday but has been declared unavailable for England. The Gunners are yet to offer any other details on his injury.

Chelsea sources say Palmer has a muscular injury, while Manchester United boss Michael Carrick said Rashford had an 'issue' after their weekend draw with Fulham. Mainoo was also assessed over an injury today.

Livramento was forced to pull out of the World Cup squad with a calf injury, did not play for Newcastle United at the weekend and is yet to start a game this season.

England are due to face 2026 World Cup winners Spain first, before two games against Czechia and another versus Croatia. Tuchel is scheduled to speak this Friday, when he will be able to offer his opinion on losing five players.

Declan Rice has been removed from the England squad for their upcoming internationals

Cole Palmer has pulled out of the England squad with a small injury and to manage his work load after an injury-hit season last campaign

Tuchel previously warned Palmer, who was left at home for the World Cup, that he had a 'point to prove' and needed 'to step up' to 'keep his shirt and justify the nomination'.

He added: 'So now it is a new competition. Some players, some positions, have more injuries. Some have less injuries. Cole has his starts that he always had but he has his numbers back - he has his assists back, he has decisive goals back - so that is why he is in the squad.'

Gibbs-White, 26, had been on holiday with his family in Dubai after playing in the defeat by Coventry on Saturday but is immediately returning to answer England's call.

Everton midfielder Garner is selected ahead of Crystal Palace's Adam Wharton.

Tuchel cited having too many attacking midfielders to include them all as the reason for Gibbs-White's initial omission.

'It makes no sense to nominate three, four, five No 10s,' Tuchel said. 'It just does not help anyone.

Manchester United duo Kobbie Mainoo (left) and Marcus Rashford (right) have also withdrawn

Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White has been called up in place of the midfielder - leaving his family holiday in Dubai to answer his country's call

'We can see the form he is in. He ended the season very strongly and is a key player for Forest. We can see him stepping up now.'

Rashford has been battling a hip issue since the World Cup. He started Manchester United's 1-1 draw with Fulham on Sunday but the injury needs management.

Mainoo is also struggling with an issue. The 21-year-old was in the squad at the World Cup, but did not play a single minute.

Sports.title: Meets the Jets 'Swiss Army knife' whose NFL career is down to military background
Sports.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Meets the Jets 'Swiss Army knife' whose NFL career is down to military background

EXCLUSIVE: Ahead of Week 1, Jets fullback Andrew Beck spoke to The Mirror about how his father's military background influenced his career and the wise words of Patriots Julian Edelman

View 3 Images Andrew Beck and the Jets begin the 2026 season against the Titans on Sunday (Image: Getty Images)

The NFL is a unique league, one armed with strict positions that match any given player’s specific skill set. Then there is Andrew Beck.

‌



Across stints with the Houston Texans, Denver Broncos, and New York Jets, where he currently plies his trade, Beck has been deployed at tight end, fullback, and on special teams having started his college football career as a linebacker. He has gradually carved out a uniquely valuable role, establishing himself as the kind of player coaches could trust to do whatever was required.

‌



His versatility stems directly from his upbringing. His father, Chris Beck, was a U.S. Army officer who eventually became a colonel and later a brigadier general - and this career meant home was wherever he was deployed. Born in Tampa in 1996, Beck bounced around the United States and Europe, moving 11 times before getting to college, including time in Texas and two separate stints in Germany.

‌



New York Jets star explains how chess helps him excel in the NFL READ MORE :

Lewis Hamilton weighs in as message sent to Macklemore after Ed Sheeran row READ MORE :

This background has had a significant impact on Beck. His father’s commitment to the military, which meant he missed the first time Beck wore football pads due to an assignment in Iraq, has played a key role in the Jets’ do-it-all star’s mentality.

“It influenced a lot, the commitment to his career,” Beck exclusively told The Mirror. “There's a lot of similarities between football and the military. I think it's the commitment to a band of brothers is huge. It's a group of guys that are not from the same background, not from the same area, working towards a common goal, and at the end of the day, it's just us out on the field, so it's figuring out a way to be successful because there's no other option.

“That's the same way it is with those military guys. None of them are from the same hometowns, but they get thrown into a sticky situation, and they've got to figure it out. That's the only choice, and I think that mentality and upbringing definitely benefited me in the long run on the football field, and it's something that I try to bring along with me with other guys around me.”

‌



View 3 Images Andrew Beck scored two receiving touchdowns for the Jets alongside his ever-present role on special teams (Image: Getty Images)

Even with roots all over the place, Beck never forgets; his family was stationed at Fort Carson, Colorado, for some time, and years later, when with the Broncos, he returned to the post to work with military families. Beck became heavily involved with military charities and veterans' organizations, and even won the NFL's 2021 Salute to Service Award.

“My wife, she grew up, born and raised in the same house her entire life - and it's something that I can't even fathom. But I think it was great for me,” Beck said. “I’ve got a lot of good friends all over, and I've gotten to meet a lot of great people and see a lot of cool things that I wouldn't have been able to otherwise. I lived in two places in Germany growing up, which, again, never would have even crossed my mind.

‌



“It forces you into learning how to develop quick relationships and to build rapport with people quickly, which is important in a locker room. NFL locker rooms are constantly changing. It's never the same 53 guys, and I think that skill and growing up in situations like that have molded me and helped me be successful in the league now.”

In his own words

Was the military ever an option for you rather than football in the NFL?

“I always thought about it, man. It got really serious towards the end of high school, beginning of college, and my parents were like – I started getting offers and then talking to schools. My parents made me promise that I would at least see college out, and then afterwards I started thinking about the NFL, and they told me to play this out as long as you can. It’s still going eight years in.”

‌



You arrived at Texas as a linebacker, and became a tight end. How did that change alter the trajectory of your career?

“I had early enrolled at Texas, so I did spring training and a little bit of training camp as a linebacker, and there was a pretty established senior linebacker corps at Texas when I got there. I had played a little bit of tight end in high school - just enough to put it on my highlight tape to tell colleges that I played the position. Florida was the only school that offered me to play tight end, and I laughed and told the coach, ‘There’s no way I’m playing tight end in college,’ which worked out great.

“We got halfway through training camp, and all but one of the tight ends got hurt. Charlie Strong, the Texas head coach at the time, held me up after a team meeting and said, ‘I’m not going to make you, but I need someone who can go to tight end right now and play.’ Sure enough, I spent the next couple of weeks grinding and trying to learn the playbook, and ended up playing my freshman year as a tight end. I haven’t looked back.”

‌



View 3 Images Andrew Beck is preparing for his second season with the Jets after being Darren Mougey's first signing as Jets GM (Image: Getty Images)

Coach Glenn has talked about the value of having a fullback, because it's a position that's being phased out a little bit across the league. What do you think you can give the Jets that doesn't necessarily show up on a box score?

“It’s versatility. The fullback spot is huge, I think. Not a lot of teams use it, and when you talk to AG, it makes it harder for defenses. It's one more thing they've got to prepare for. It changes run fits, and usually draws them into base defense, so it opens up things on the outside, and then being able to contribute on special teams is the key, but I think if I had to pick one thing, I would say it's my value in the run game and being able to get downhill and get vertical. We've got a pretty special group of running backs, so I just help them do what they do best, man. It's a lot of fun.”

‌



When did you embrace the mentality of being the versatile player who can and will do whatever to help the team?

“When I started my NFL career, I signed with New England back when it was [Bill] Belichick, [Josh] McDaniels was the OC, Tom Brady was the quarterback, and Julian Edelman was there. One day, he grabbed me, him and James Devlin, and they were like, ‘Seriously, man, the more you can do, that is the key to this league, that's the secret.’ And so I took it to heart. I started long snapping, so I'm a backup long snapper. I’ve talked to [Jets special teams coach Chris] Banjo about being a backup kicker and punter. I argue that I should be a backup quarterback for emergencies. I'm absolutely the worst about it. I tell any coach that, yes, I can do it, and I'll just figure it out later.

“I mean, my path is not the standard one that everybody takes. I'm in a room with a first-round pick, a second-round pick, and two third-round picks or something like that, and I was an eighth-round pick - and they only got seven, man. It’s left a permanent chip on my shoulder. I don’t take any days that I walk in this building for granted, and that mentality is what keeps guys around. I think we've got a gritty room and a gritty team, and it's because everybody thinks that way.

‌



“I think that's been the secret: the more you can do in this league. It's hard to find guys that want to do that, but if you can, then it's just another way to stick around.”

Behdad Eghbali's net worth compared to Premier League rivals ahead of full Chelsea takeover READ MORE :

Week 1 versus the Titans

Armed with a new deal, confirming the Jets deemed him more than a one-year experiment, Beck and the AFC East franchise kick off the 2026 season against a familiar face, going on the road to Nashville to take on former head coach Robert Saleh’s Tennessee Titans in Week 1. Beck is confident the new-look Jets offense is ready to go.

“As a team, as an offense, as a special teams unit - everything that I'm qualified to speak on - I would say that we're extremely prepared,” Beck said. “We've been waiting for this opportunity to go out and compete against another team.

Article continues below

“Obviously, training camp's about evaluating guys and finding the best 53, but in the back of our mind, we all knew that this was where we wanted to get to, and now it's time to go prove to the rest of the world what Jets football is going to be about for this season, and I think everybody's excited about it.”

The Jets open up their 2026 NFL season on the road against the Titans on Sunday, September 13.

Sports.title: JJ Spaun makes comments about English culture as Rory McIlroy shocked by winner's omission
Sports.content:
JJ Spaun makes comments about English culture as Rory McIlroy shocked by winner's omission

There has been plenty to discuss after JJ Spaun left Rory McIlroy forced to settle for joint-second at the BMW PGA Championship

View 2 Images Rory McIlroy finished tied for second at the BMW PGA (Image: Warren Little, Getty Images)

It was close but no cigar for Rory McIlroy at the BMW PGA Championship. The Northern Irishman put up a good fight but ended up in a tie for second as JJ Spaun finished two clear of the field.

‌



American star Spaun has been enjoying his time in England and fought off a fierce challenge to triumph at Wentworth. However, he won't be involved in the upcoming Presidents Cup.

‌



That's one of a number of big events left to play between now and the end of the year. Spaun isn't the only one with plenty of play ahead of him, with McIlroy aiming to chase down Patrick Reed and claim top spot in the Race to Dubai.

‌



Spaun and McIlroy both spoke after their weekend's exertions, with the former making comments which will have left an impression with local fans. Here's our round-up of the latest lines.

Spaun's unexpected Jeremy Clarkson influence

JJ Spaun revealed his affection for England even before securing victory at Wentworth, reflecting on his and his family's love for 'Clarkson's Farm' as well as an enjoyment of the local crowd. The American posted a final round 67 to claim the title ahead of McIlroy, Aaron Rai, Adam Scott and Manuel Elvira.

‌



“We love coming here, as far as being in the atmosphere, the English culture, we love it," the American said at the midway point in the tournament. He expanded on this after his victory, revealing that he and his family are particularly fond of the TV programme 'Clarkson's Farm'.

"I think we really enjoyed it because we went to the Cotswolds before watching his show, and it gravitated to how we understood the culture there, the community, and then obviously looking like an idiot trying to farm. It's a good laugh. We enjoy the show and we love the Cotswolds," the 36-year-old added.

View 2 Images JJ Spaun enjoyed his trip to the UK (Image: Warren Little, Getty Images)

‌



"We've grown fond of him along with English culture. We take holidays in December in the Cotswolds and really enjoy his show. I went to his pub, The Farmer's Dog, with hopes to catch a glimpse but he wasn't around."

McIlroy's Spaun surprise

Rory McIlroy spoke about how impressed he was by Spaun over the weekend. This made it all the more surprising when he learned his rival wasn't part of the United States team for the upcoming Presidents Cup.

"He's been playing great for the last couple of years. I think it's great of him to come over here [to the UK} and play," the world No.2 said. "He made the Presidents Cup, didn't he? He didn't? Oh, geez,".

Article continues below

"I was going to say, that's a good way to go into the Presidents Cup. Sorry. But it's great that he's over here, and he's obviously had a great week."

Sports.title: Michael Vaughan makes big claim about Kevin Pietersen's new England coaching role
Sports.content:
Michael Vaughan makes big claim about Kevin Pietersen's new England coaching role

Pietersen has made a surprise return to the England fold as a specialist mentor to Brendon McCullum’s white-ball teams, beginning with the T20 and ODI series against Sri Lanka.

View 3 Images Former England captain Michael Vaughan at Lord's

Michael Vaughan believes Kevin Pietersen could one day help England’s Test team and reckons the red-ball side may need him more than the white-ball set-up he has just joined.

‌



Pietersen has made a surprise return to the England fold as a specialist mentor to Brendon McCullum’s white-ball teams, beginning with the T20 and ODI series against Sri Lanka. The 46-year-old is also due to be involved in England’s winter white-ball tours of Australia and South Africa before returning for next summer’s home series against Pakistan and New Zealand and the 2027 World Cup. But former England captain Vaughan believes Pietersen’s influence could eventually stretch much further.

‌



“I just look at the white-ball team and say, do they need Kevin in white-ball cricket, or do they need him helping the Test match batters? I kind of look at that and think it’s the Test match team that’s had more of an issue,” said Vaughan, speaking at Lord’s during the first-ever finals day of the Barclays Knight-Stokes Cup.

‌



“We’ll wait and see what else is in line for change with the Test team, but I would think once he starts working with players, those that cross from white-ball cricket into Test match cricket, Kev’s the kind of character who will want an involvement in both formats.

“Not that he’ll be there [with the Test team], but he’ll certainly be on the phone to the players, making sure that they’re doing what he’s been working on. At the minute, it’s just white-ball cricket, but it wouldn’t surprise me in time if Kev helped the Test team as well.”

View 3 Images Kevin Pietersen, Coach of England looks on during an England nets session (Image: 2026 George Wood - ECB)

‌



Pietersen’s appointment represents quite a turnaround after his successful and sometimes turbulent international career, which saw him win four Ashes series and be named Player of the Tournament during England’s T20 World Cup win in 2010, ended in 2014 after Andy Flower’s side lost the Ashes 5-0 in Australia. He played 104 Tests, scoring 8,181 runs, while also making 136 ODI and 37 T20 appearances for England.

Since retiring, Pietersen has forged successful careers as both a commentator and content creator while he has mentored in the Indian Premier League for Delhi Capitals in 2025.

But Pietersen is now officially back as part of McCullum’s white-ball coaching set-up, with the England boss, who was sacked as Test boss in July, describing his experience, knowledge and stature as hugely valuable and particularly highlighting the opportunity for the team’s batters to work with him.

‌



Vaughan, who knows Pietersen well from his England days, believes that his directness could be one of his greatest assets and that his personality could make him a particularly valuable sounding board for England’s next generation of batters.

“He’s very driven, he’s very enthusiastic, he’s very hard-working, and I don’t think he’ll play the party line,” Vaughan said. “I think he’ll tell them the home truths, which is pretty much what Kevin Pietersen’s all about.”

Pietersen is also another high-profile name that has joined England’s set-up in some capacity in recent times and Vaughan believes England, who have invested heavily in expertise throughout their cricket structure, must now start winning some silverware.

‌



“Winning’s the key,” he added. “English cricket has got pretty much everything. You look at the infrastructure of our teams and everything that the players get with the preparation.

“We’ve had Freddie Flintoff, Baz McCullum, Stephen Fleming now, Kevin Pietersen, Marcus Trescothick. You’d want to start winning trophies, and that’s going to be key.

“They’ve got to start being on the podium with trophies in their hands, because they’re spending a huge amount of money on expertise and some of the best brains in the game. Now you want to see a trophy or two.”

‌



View 3 Images Altrincham Grammar School boys celebrate winning the inaugural Barclays Knight-Stokes Cup (Image: Jed Leicester/MCC)

Vaughan was speaking at the final of the Barclays Knight-Stokes Cup, which was held at Lord's in front of 2,000 people. The nationwide state school competition was the brainchild of the former England captain and saw Altrincham Grammar School and Chelmsford County High School for Girls lift the boys and girls trophies respectively.

“The Barclays Knight-Stokes Cup has been a huge success,” said Vaughan. “The standard has been great, the enthusiasm for the tournament has been amazing. It just proves to you that there is a real want for cricket in the state sector. They just need an opportunity. They need tournaments like this."

Sports.title: Man Utd striker Benjamin Sesko set to undergo MRI for possible injury issue
Sports.content:
Man Utd striker Benjamin Sesko set to undergo MRI for possible injury issue

Benjamin Sesko missed Manchester United’s Premier League draw with Fulham on Sunday and there appears to be fear that his injury could see him miss a chunk of the season

View 2 Images Sesko was ruled out against Fulham with a shin injury (Image: Getty Images)

Manchester United star Benjamin Sesko is set to undergo tests to determine whether he has aggravated his troublesome shin injury. The Slovenian forward missed the Red Devils’ draw with Fulham on Sunday.

‌



Asked for an update, United boss Michael Carrick said: “No, I think that just because you get setbacks in certain positions, you can’t sign a player for cover in every one. We’re not sure with Ben yet, he felt some pain after the [Brighton] game and we are assessing him at the moment.

‌



“He definitely wasn’t ready for today. I haven’t got any more news to give you, just that he felt pain on his shin."

‌



It appears that there is now serious concern for United and Sesko’s national side that he could be sidelined for some time. Sesko will of course undergo further testing, with reports suggesting that he will have a MRI scan in London to get a closer look at the issue.

The striker only joined United from German side RB Leipzig last summer but missed seven games through injury.

He still managed to score 12 goals across just 19 starts in all competitions. Sesko had already made six appearances for the Red Devils this season, scoring against Everton and Sabah in the Champions League.

He is not the only injury concern that United have heading into the first international break of the season. Marcus Rashford was also taken off against Fulham at the weekend and Carrick seemed somewhat downbeat in the aftermath.

"We had to bring him off as he had a bit of an issue," Carrick told beIN Sports. Asked if Rashford was alright, he replied: "I'm not sure." The issue has been severe enough to see Rashford pull out of England duty for the forthcoming international break.

United will certainly be hoping that both Rashford and Sesko are back to full fitness ahead of their next game in a little under three weeks' time. Their next Premier League clash pits them against struggling Spurs.
