Chile political reform is one step from becoming law. Congress votes this week on a bill that makes new parties harder to create and small ones harder to keep.

The Senate is expected to vote on Tuesday 22 September 2026, according to Pauta and La Tercera. The Chamber of Deputies follows on Wednesday 23 September.

The bill, Bulletin 17640-06, is titled in Spanish as a law “to promote the governability and representativeness of the political system”.

A Boric bill that Kast adopted

The Senate record shows the bill was sent by the executive on 30 June 2025, under former President Gabriel Boric. La Tercera credits it to Álvaro Elizalde, then interior minister and a Socialist.

It survived a change of government. José Antonio Kast, founder of the Republican Party, took office on 11 March 2026 and at first moved cautiously, La Tercera reported.

His government formally sponsored the bill and gave it “suma urgencia”, a priority status that shortens deadlines, on 11 August 2026. It renewed that urgency on 8 September.

José García Ruminot, of National Renewal, is minister of the Segpres, the ministry that steers the president’s bills through Congress. He told El Mercurio that “strengthening our democracy is also a priority for this government”, Emol reported.

Where the bill stands

Most of the text has already passed. The Senate approved it on 6 January 2026, and the Chamber approved it with changes on 4 March 2026.

On 9 June the Senate accepted every Chamber change but one. That article went to a joint committee of senators and deputies, which agreed a wording unanimously on 31 August.

That article concerns party manifestos. Every party would have to condemn totalitarian rule and the use or incitement of violence as a political method.

It also asks parties to affirm their commitment to probity and transparency.

The clause amends an organic constitutional law, a class of law that needs an absolute majority of members in office. That means 26 of 50 senators and 78 of 155 deputies.

If it fails, only that clause drops out, according to Pauta and La Tercera. The rest would go to the Constitutional Court for review and then to Kast to sign.

A joint session of Chile’s Congress in Valparaíso. File photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

What the Chile political reform changes

Today a party can register in eight regions or in three neighbouring ones. The bill scraps the three-region route, so every new party must organise in at least eight.

The membership floor also rises. It moves from 0.25% of those who voted in the last Chamber election to 0.3% of all registered voters, region by region.

Existing parties get 18 months to meet the minimum membership needed to survive. Founders of a party cannot run for a different party for four years.

Only parties with seats in Congress would receive the state’s regular funding for party running costs. Independents could fill at most half of a party’s congressional candidacies, or the whole slate is rejected.

Signatures for independent candidates would also be counted against the full electoral roll, which raises the number needed. That applies to congressional, municipal and regional races, Pauta reported.

What it does not do

The bill does not set a 5% national vote threshold for winning seats. Pauta notes that idea sits in a separate constitutional reform.

It keeps the rule that a party dissolves if it wins less than 5% of the vote in at least eight regions. But it drops the easier option of meeting that bar in three neighbouring regions.

Nor does it change the number of deputies, the districts or proportional voting.

Party-switchers keep their seats. Instead, a party keeps the full state payment linked to a lawmaker who quits, and the new party gains nothing.

Congressional party groups would be recognised in law and could set proportional sanctions for breaking group agreements. Those sanctions cannot strip lawmakers of their power to vote or legislate.

The case for: fewer, stronger parties

Chile’s party system is crowded. In February 2026 the electoral service, Servel, rejected the accounts of 14 of 24 parties, La Tercera reported.

The same outlet said 14 parties with seats in Congress now share state funding. Kast’s Republicans won 32 of the Chamber’s 155 seats in November 2025, the largest group, according to ADN Radio.

Senator Iván Flores, a Christian Democrat, told CNN Chile the reform may hurt smaller parties. “What has done most damage to Chilean democracy is the atomisation and polarisation of the parties,” he said.

Iván Moreira of the conservative Independent Democratic Union (UDI) said the aim is “to reduce the fragmentation that affects governability”. Fragmentation gives “disproportionate power to small parties”, he added.

The case against: a closed club

Jaime Mulet, a deputy who leads the small Regionalist Green Social Federation (FRVS), called the bill a big-party pact. “This law cartelises politics,” he said, as quoted by La Tercera.

He also told CNN Chile it lacks “a method to sanction parliamentarians who switch party”. The Communist Party’s political commission decided to oppose the bill, although two Communist senators had backed its changes.

Lorena Pizarro, who led the Communist deputies in March, called it “a step back very similar to the binominal”. That was the old two-seat district system, which favoured the two big blocs.

Johannes Kaiser, now president of the National Libertarian Party, voted against it as a deputy in March. He argued that rule changes will not cure public distrust of politicians.

Who has to go out and recruit

El Mercurio calculated which parties already meet the new survival floor, Emol reported. The Socialists, National Renewal, the Broad Front, the Party of the People and the Libertarians already qualify.

The Liberal Party would need 10,106 more members, the centre-right Evópoli 9,755 and the FRVS 9,087, on the same calculation. Kast’s Republicans would need 2,392.

For the big parties, the Chile political reform means paperwork. For the smallest, it sets an 18-month deadline to grow or disappear.

More: Chile coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Chile political reform being voted on this week?

It is Bulletin 17640-06, a bill to promote the governability and representativeness of the political system. It raises the membership needed to found and keep a party, requires presence in at least eight regions, limits public funding to parties with seats in Congress and caps independent candidates on party slates. Only one article, on party manifestos, is still pending.

Does the bill punish lawmakers who switch parties?

Not with loss of their seat. A lawmaker who quits keeps the seat, but the original party and its congressional group keep the state funding and allowances linked to that member. Congressional groups may also adopt proportional internal sanctions for breaking group agreements, without removing any lawmaker’s right to vote or legislate.

Does it create a 5% vote threshold for Congress?

No. According to Pauta, a 5% national threshold for winning seats belongs to a separate constitutional reform. This bill does not change the number of deputies, the electoral districts or the proportional voting system.

What happens after the final votes?

If the Senate and Chamber approve the joint committee’s wording, the bill goes to the Constitutional Court and then to President José Antonio Kast to sign. If that article fails, only the manifesto clause drops out and the rest still proceeds, according to Pauta and La Tercera.

Sources: Chilean Senate legislative record for Bulletin 17640-06, Report of the joint committee of senators and deputies, Pauta on this week’s votes, Pauta on what the bill does and does not change, La Tercera on supporters and opponents, Emol on the government’s urgency, Emol on which parties need more members, CNN Chile on the debate, La Tercera on state funding for parties, ADN Radio on the new Chamber

World.title: Colombia Gripen Contract Faces Court Bid to Freeze Payments to Saab
World.content:
Colombia · Defense

Key Facts — What happened Lawyer Guillermo Rodríguez Martínez asked the Administrative Tribunal of Cundinamarca to suspend the purchase of 17 Saab Gripen fighters.

— What he wants Suspension of the whole contract until its financing is disclosed, plus an urgent order halting payments or at least future disbursements.

— What the deal is worth About €3,135.5 million (about US$3.6 billion), signed on 14 November 2025, with deliveries planned from 2028 to 2032.

— The catch No admission, ruling or freeze has been reported, and nobody has been found to have done wrong.

— Where the government stands Sources close to President Abelardo de la Espriella told El Espectador the jets will be received.

A lawyer wants a court to halt payments on one of Colombia’s largest defense purchases until the state discloses how it will be paid for. No admission, ruling or freeze has been reported.

A Swedish Air Force Saab JAS 39 Gripen at the Kaivopuisto Air Show in Helsinki, June 2017. File photograph.

A Colombian lawyer has gone to court to freeze payments on the Colombia Gripen contract, one of the country’s largest defense purchases. He wants the state to reveal how it will pay for 17 Swedish fighter jets first.

The case was filed by lawyer Guillermo Rodríguez Martínez before the Administrative Tribunal of Cundinamarca, the regional court for Bogotá. Infobae reported it on 21 September 2026, citing El Tiempo.

No admission, ruling or freeze has been reported, and no court has found any wrongdoing in the deal. The filing is a request, not a decision.

What the lawsuit asks for

Rodríguez seeks the “suspensión inmediata y total de la ejecución del contrato,” a total halt to the contract. That would cover disbursements, transfers and approvals of future-year budget commitments.

He also seeks an urgent provisional order, known as a medida cautelar, against the Aerospace Force and the defense and finance ministries. It would halt payments, or at least future disbursements, while the court studies the case.

The suit names seven respondents. They include the Aerospace Force, as the air force is now called, the Presidency and the Navy.

El Tiempo called it the first known court action seeking to intervene directly in the deal with Saab. Saab is the Swedish defense group that builds the Gripen.

The complaint is about secrecy, not the jets

The lawsuit does not attack the aircraft itself. Its target is the financing, the budget and the payment terms.

Rodríguez says he sent formal information requests to several agencies on 20 August 2026. He asked for the disbursement schedule, the preliminary and cost-benefit studies, and the contract text.

The Aerospace Force withheld part of the material, citing national defense and security. The lawyer argues that the secrecy was applied in blanket fashion, without specifying which documents it covered.

The filing also cites the earthquake of 10 August, a magnitude-7.4 quake centred in Chocó that killed more than 300 people. Paying without disclosing interest and cost could strain public finances, it says.

Reports of the filing describe no allegation of corruption. It centres on disclosure and a pause.

Colombian Air Force Kfirs, the fleet the Gripen is meant to replace, during Exercise Relampago VI on 26 July 2021. File photograph. (U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Duncan C. Bevan)

What an acción popular is

The case is an acción popular, or popular action, an action enshrined in Article 88 of the 1991 Constitution. Anyone, person or organisation, can file one to protect collective rights rather than personal ones.

Law 472 of 1998 lists those rights. They include “la defensa del patrimonio público,” the defense of public assets, and “la moralidad administrativa,” integrity in public administration.

Under that law, a judge should decide within three working days whether to admit a suit. Judges may also order precautionary measures, such as halting an activity, before a final ruling.

Admission is not a finding against anyone. It only means the court will hear the case.

What Colombia signed

Colombia signed the deal with Saab on 14 November 2025 in Cali, on the anniversary of the air force. It covers 15 single-seat Gripen E jets and two two-seat Gripen F trainers.

The lawsuit puts the value at €3,135.5 million (about US$3.6 billion). The jets are meant to replace Colombia’s ageing Israeli-made Kfir fleet.

Separately, the economic-policy document Conpes 4155 programs 16.86 trillion pesos (about US$5.3 billion) for the whole project from 2026 to 2032. That is a budget line, not the contract price.

Conversions here use the European Central Bank reference rate of 1.1490 dollars per euro on 21 September 2026. For pesos, they use Colombia’s official rate of 3,192.92 to the US dollar, valid that day.

Pedro Sánchez, then defense minister, said the peso allocation includes a margin in case the euro strengthens.

According to a January 2026 report on the Comptroller General’s review, jets arrive between 2028 and 2032. Forty percent is paid in advance and 60% on delivery.

The Comptroller General, Colombia’s public-spending watchdog, found no inconsistencies in the deal’s structure in its January review. On 10 June, the House of Representatives’ Accusations Commission opened a preliminary inquiry into the purchase.

That commission, which investigates presidents, is looking at then-President Gustavo Petro and his wife, Verónica Alcocer. Nobody has been charged.

The new government and the offsets

Abelardo de la Espriella became president on 7 August 2026. His government is analysing whether to renegotiate price and after-sale terms, El Espectador reported on 10 August.

Sources close to the president told El Espectador the jets will be received. Before handing over, Sánchez had warned that the deal “no se puede reversar,” cannot be reversed.

The sharper debate is over offsets, the benefits Saab promised Colombia alongside the sale. Under Petro, 85% were earmarked for social programs and 15% for the national aerospace industry.

Those social projects included solar panels for towns off the national grid, water in La Guajira and a hospital project. Officials are reviewing the offsets, Infobae reported on 13 September, citing El Tiempo and an unnamed source.

The idea is that part of the offsets could become technology transfer and military capabilities for the Aerospace Force. No official has announced a formal renegotiation, and Saab has not been reported to respond.

What happens next

Under Article 20 of Law 472, the tribunal must decide whether to admit the suit. No court order currently stops payments under the Colombia Gripen contract.

Under Article 25, it may also decide on precautionary measures, such as the freeze requested. Either step would be the first judicial decision on the case.

More: Colombia coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has a court frozen the Colombia Gripen contract?

No. A lawyer has asked the Administrative Tribunal of Cundinamarca to suspend the contract and all related disbursements, and to grant an urgent provisional measure. No admission of the case or provisional order has been reported, and no court or authority has found wrongdoing in the purchase.

What is an acción popular?

It is an action enshrined in Article 88 of Colombia’s 1991 Constitution and regulated by Law 472 of 1998. Anyone, person or organisation, can file one to protect collective rights, such as public assets or integrity in public administration. Judges can order precautionary measures while the case proceeds.

How much are the Gripen jets costing Colombia?

The contract value cited in the lawsuit is €3,135.5 million (about US$3.6 billion) for 15 Gripen E and two Gripen F aircraft. Separately, the Conpes 4155 programming for the whole project sets aside 16.86 trillion pesos (about US$5.3 billion) through 2032, including a margin in case the euro strengthens.

Will the new government cancel the deal?

It has not said so on the record. Sources close to President Abelardo de la Espriella told El Espectador the jets will be received, while price and after-sale terms are analysed. Officials are also reviewing the offsets, Infobae reported on 13 September, citing El Tiempo and an unnamed source.

Sources: Infobae on the acción popular, Infobae on the offsets review, Infobae on the Comptroller’s review, Infobae on the outgoing minister’s position, El Espectador on the new government’s review, El Espectador on the congressional inquiry, El Espectador on the 2025 information ruling, Law 472 of 1998 on popular actions, European Central Bank reference rates, Colombia’s official peso-dollar rate

World.title: 8 January Convict Pictured With Police Baton Ordered to Start 14-Year Term
World.content:
Brazil · Justice

Key Facts — What happened Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered Jackson Uriel de Souza Vieira, 30, to start a 14-year prison term.

— The order Moraes issued the warrant on 8 September 2026, after the conviction became final; Metrópoles reported it on 21 September 2026.

— Where the baton fits Images from 8 January 2023 show him holding a police baton outside Congress, and they led to heavier charges.

— The catch His defence told Metrópoles the warrant had not yet been served; he had been free under an ankle tag.

— The wider tally A Supreme Court report of 29 April 2026 counted 850 convictions and 552 plea-style deals over the riots and wider coup plot.

The baton dates from the 2023 riots in Brasília, not from this month. Images of it helped turn a minor case into a coup conviction, and the sentence is now final.

Security forces in riot gear confront supporters of Jair Bolsonaro on the ramp of the Planalto presidential palace in Brasília on 8 January 2023. File photograph. (Photo: EFE/Andre Borges)

An 8 January convict who was photographed with a police baton at Brazil’s Congress has been ordered to prison. Justice Alexandre de Moraes of the Supreme Federal Court, Brazil’s top court, issued the warrant on Tuesday 8 September 2026.

The man is Jackson Uriel de Souza Vieira, 30, from Ji-Paraná in the Amazon state of Rondônia. He was sentenced to 14 years over the riots in Brasília on 8 January 2023.

The order came to light on Monday 21 September 2026, when the news site Metrópoles reported it. The warrant is under seal and addressed to the Federal Police.

The baton dates from 2023

The baton is not a new incident. It appears in images from the day of the riots, and those images later raised the stakes of his case.

According to Metrópoles, a Federal Police forensic analysis turned up images of him outside Congress on 8 January 2023. In one of them, he is holding a police baton.

A police report cited by the site found signs that he at least walked across the roof canopy of Congress carrying it. The Curitiba newspaper Gazeta do Povo said the photo, which he had sent, surfaced on another suspect’s phone.

From a plea deal to a coup conviction

He was arrested on Monday 9 January 2023 at the protest camp outside Army headquarters in Brasília. Prosecutors first charged him only with incitement to crime and criminal association.

The case was paused while the two sides negotiated a non-prosecution agreement, a deal used for lesser offences. The images changed that.

The Office of the Prosecutor General withdrew the offer after the forensic findings, Metrópoles and IstoÉ reported. It charged him instead with attempting a coup and the violent abolition of democratic rule of law.

The other charges were armed criminal association, aggravated damage to property and damage to listed heritage.

The analysis also identified him as an administrator of two WhatsApp groups. In them, according to the Federal Police, messages organised seats on free buses to Brasília.

Investigators found no messages sent by him in those groups, Metrópoles reported. He was convicted on all five counts, according to Gazeta do Povo.

A majority of the full court backed Moraes’s proposed 14 years, starting in the closed regime, meaning an ordinary prison. Justices Kassio Nunes Marques, Luiz Fux and André Mendonça voted against, Gazeta do Povo reported.

Like other convicted rioters, he shares a joint R$30 million (about US$5.8 million) bill for collective moral damages. The conversion uses the Central Bank’s reference rate of 5.1575 to the US dollar on 18 September 2026.

The colonnade of the Supreme Federal Court in Brasília, with the twin towers of the National Congress in the background. File photograph. (Photo: “Congresso Nacional (30890615792)” by Marcos Oliveira/Agência Senado, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

Why he was still free

He remains at liberty, according to Metrópoles and IstoÉ; his defence says the warrant has not been served. He has been monitored by an electronic ankle tag, and the warrant followed the conviction becoming final.

The sentence begins “in view of the final judgment of this criminal case”, Moraes wrote in the order quoted by Metrópoles. He ordered the warrant sent to the Federal Police.

Gazeta do Povo said it could not reach his lawyer, Geneci Apolinário. Neither outlet reported a date for the arrest.

What happened on 8 January 2023

On Sunday 8 January 2023, thousands of Jair Bolsonaro’s supporters stormed Congress, the presidential palace and the Supreme Court. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had taken office as president a week earlier.

Many had spent weeks camped outside army bases, refusing to accept Lula’s narrow election win over Bolsonaro, the Guardian reported. Police in Brasília said 300 people had been arrested that day, the BBC reported.

How many have been convicted

A Supreme Court report published on 29 April 2026 counted 1,402 people held to account. The total covers the riots and the wider coup plot, according to Estadão.

Of those, 431 received prison terms and 419 lighter penalties such as community service. Another 552 cases ended in non-prosecution agreements.

The 431 include 29 members of the plot’s core groups, among them Bolsonaro himself. He was sentenced in September 2025 to 27 years and three months.

Congress later passed a law that would shorten sentences for the 8 January convicts. Moraes suspended its application on 9 May 2026 until the full court rules on it, BBC News Brasil reported.

For the 8 January convict from Rondônia, the next step is the arrest itself, carried out by the Federal Police.

More: Brazil coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Jackson Uriel de Souza Vieira?

He is a 30-year-old resident of Ji-Paraná, in the Brazilian state of Rondônia, according to Metrópoles and IstoÉ. He was arrested on 9 January 2023 at the protest camp outside Army headquarters in Brasília. The Supreme Federal Court later sentenced him to 14 years over the riots of the previous day.

Was he caught with a police baton recently?

No. The baton appears in images from 8 January 2023, which show him holding it outside Congress, according to Metrópoles. A Federal Police forensic analysis found those images. They led prosecutors to drop a plea-deal offer and charge him with attempting a coup.

Why does Moraes decide on these cases?

Justice Alexandre de Moraes is the rapporteur of the 8 January cases at the Supreme Federal Court, Brazil’s highest court. He wrote the vote that set this 8 January convict’s sentence at 14 years, which the majority of the court followed. Once the conviction became final, he ordered the sentence to begin.

How many people have been punished over 8 January?

A Supreme Court report published on 29 April 2026 counted 1,402 people held to account over the riots and the wider coup plot. Of those, 850 were convicted in court, 431 of them to prison terms. Another 552 cases were settled through non-prosecution agreements, which involve alternative penalties such as community service and fines.

World.title: Cuban Doctors in Uruguay: Government Weighs Paying Them Directly After US Listing
World.content:
Uruguay · Politics

Key Facts — What happened Búsqueda reported on 17 September 2026 that ministries are studying direct payments to the Cuban eye-care brigade.

— Why A State Department report to Congress in late August listed Uruguay among 15 countries paying Cuba directly for medical workers.

— The catch US law bars aid only to countries named two years running; Uruguay has been named once.

— What ministers said Between 8 and 14 September, senior officials told local media the programme would continue.

— Who the doctors are The State Department counted 21 Cuban workers in Uruguay in 2026, based at a Montevideo eye hospital.

— What Uruguay pays The social security institute pays US$250,000 a year; its president says this covers expenses, not salaries.

A US report to Congress named Uruguay among 15 countries paying Havana for medical staff. Ministers defended the programme in public; officials are now studying a change in how the doctors are paid.

Avenida 18 de Julio, the main avenue of central Montevideo, in 2021. File photograph. (Photo: Intendencia de Montevideo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The government is studying a way to pay the Cuban doctors in Uruguay directly, the weekly Búsqueda reported on 17 September 2026. The aim is to answer a US complaint without ending a programme ministers have defended.

At stake is a Cuban eye-care brigade at a public hospital in Montevideo. Washington calls Havana’s medical missions forced labour and has put Uruguay on a list that could eventually cost it US aid.

The plan for direct payment

The foreign ministry is working with the health ministry, the state health provider ASSE and the Banco de Previsión Social, Búsqueda said. That is Uruguay’s social security institute, which funds the programme.

Government sources told the weekly that direct payment would not alter the agreement with Cuba but would resolve the US criticism. No decision has been announced.

What Washington put on paper

The trigger was a State Department report on forced labour and trafficking of Cuban medical professionals, sent to Congress in late August. Búsqueda obtained a copy.

The report says Cuba’s government keeps “a policy or pattern of forced labour” in its labour-export programme. It lists 15 countries, Uruguay among them, whose governments pay Havana directly for the workers.

The report adds that some of those 15 “may also be paying a stipend to the workers themselves”. It counted 21 Cuban workers in Uruguay so far in 2026.

A budget law passed by Congress in February 2026 requires the report each year, the US embassy in Montevideo told Búsqueda. The same law bars US assistance to any country named in two consecutive years.

Uruguay was listed because “the payments go directly to the Cuban embassy”, the embassy said. It added that there is “no evidence” the doctors themselves are paid for treating Uruguayans.

According to Búsqueda, Washington notified Uruguay’s foreign and defence ministries on Friday 4 September 2026. A foreign ministry source called the note a “non-paper”, an informal diplomatic communication.

How ministers responded last week

The story broke on Tuesday 8 September, when journalist Gabriel Pereyra of Radio Sarandí reported the warning. He said US military aid was at stake.

Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin told reporters that day that there had been “no official communication from the United States” on the subject. He added that it was “one of the many subjects on which we are in dialogue”.

On the programme itself, Lubetkin called the Cubans’ work “extraordinary”. “Very good things we have to preserve, and we are going to preserve them,” he said.

Alejandro Sánchez, secretary of the presidency and a close aide to President Yamandú Orsi, was blunter. “We obey the Uruguayan people,” he said on Sunday 13 September, as reported by the state media portal.

Sánchez had spoken to the newspaper El Eco on 12 September, in an interview it published on 21 September. “We are going to keep working with the Cuban doctors,” he told it.

Deputy Foreign Minister Valeria Csukasi struck a softer note on Monday 14 September. “Pressure is not the best term,” she said, describing embassies voicing concern as routine diplomacy.

“At the end of the day Uruguay acts as it sees best,” Csukasi added, according to the news agency FocoUy.

Cuban doctors are greeted by supporters and reporters on arrival in Brasília for a Brazilian programme in August 2013. File photograph. (Photo: Rogério Tomaz Jr./Flickr, CC)

The eye hospital at the centre of the row

The Cubans work at the José Martí Eye Hospital, which sits on the grounds of the Saint Bois public hospital in Montevideo. The programme rests on a 2007 agreement between the two governments.

It treats mainly low-income patients and pensioners, many for cataracts. Up to July 2025 it had carried out 118,029 eye operations, according to government figures cited by Búsqueda.

Álvaro Danza, president of ASSE, said on 8 September that “about 15” Cuban professionals were working there. He said they included technicians as well as doctors.

The Banco de Previsión Social pays US$250,000 a year, its president, Jimena Pardo, told a morning television programme on 15 September. The sum covers stipends, fares and travel costs under a 2011 agreement, Búsqueda reported.

“What Uruguay reimburses is called a stipend; it is a reimbursement of expenses,” Pardo said. She said Uruguay pays no salaries, which the Cuban government handles.

Why Washington targets the missions

Cuba has sent doctors abroad since the 1960s, and many host countries pay Havana for them. Washington calls the scheme forced labour, arguing that Cuba keeps much of the fee and controls the workers.

In February 2025 Secretary of State Marco Rubio expanded US visa restrictions to officials, including foreign ones, involved in the programme. On 23 July 2026 Washington sanctioned Cuba’s health minister and the state agency that sells medical services abroad.

A White House spokeswoman told ABC News the missions are “a forced labor scheme that exploit Cuban workers”. The US embassy also cites an April 2026 report by the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, an independent regional body.

What Havana says

Cuba rejects the forced-labour label and presents the missions as solidarity. Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez said in July that Washington was punishing Cuba “for providing a humane and solidarity-based service.”

The missions also bring in hard currency. Professional services supplied over 40% of Cuba’s export value from 2018 to 2020, official statistics cited by EFE show.

Other governments have adjusted

Guatemala, Honduras, Jamaica and others have suspended or modified their Cuban medical agreements under US pressure, OnCuba News reported in July. Guyana announced in February that it would pay its Cuban doctors directly, Al Jazeera reported.

Uruguay says it will keep the programme while it looks at changing how the doctors are paid. Nobody in Uruguay has been accused of wrongdoing.

No US penalty applies yet, because the aid ban takes effect only after a second consecutive listing. For now, the Cuban doctors in Uruguay keep operating.

More: Uruguay coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is the US criticising Uruguay?

A State Department report sent to Congress in late August 2026 named Uruguay among 15 countries that pay the Cuban government directly for medical workers. Washington considers Cuba’s medical missions forced labour. The US embassy in Montevideo said payments go to the Cuban embassy and there is no evidence the doctors are paid for their work in Uruguay.

Will Uruguay lose US aid?

Not yet. Under a US budget law passed in February 2026, assistance is barred only for countries named in the report two years in a row, the US embassy told Búsqueda. Uruguay appeared for the first time in 2026.

How many Cuban doctors are in Uruguay?

The State Department counted 21 Cuban workers in Uruguay during 2026. On 8 September the head of the state health provider ASSE said about 15 professionals, including technicians, were working at the José Martí Eye Hospital in Montevideo.

What has the government said about the Cuban doctors in Uruguay?

On 8 September Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin said Uruguay was in dialogue with the United States on the issue. Separately, he said the programme had done very good things that Uruguay would preserve. Presidential secretary Alejandro Sánchez said the government would keep working with the Cuban doctors, and ministries are now studying paying them directly.

World.title: Pope Leo in Argentina: Visit Schedule Set as Government Weighs Days Off
World.content:
Argentina · Religion

Key Facts — What happened The Holy See published the full programme on Monday 21 September 2026 for Leo XIV’s 6 to 17 November trip.

— The route Uruguay from 6 to 8 November, Argentina from 8 to 11 November, then Peru until 16 November.

— The big events in Argentina Masses in Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Luján, plus a youth vigil in the capital’s Palermo district.

— The crowd planning Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva cited a combined capacity of about 7 million across all events, a cumulative figure, not distinct people.

— The catch No holiday has been decreed; the scope is still undefined, to be analysed by locality, the foreign minister said.

— Why it matters It is the first papal visit to Argentina since John Paul II in 1987.

The Vatican has published the day-by-day programme for Leo XIV’s first trip to South America as pope. Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor, gets four days, three open-air masses and a youth vigil.

Pope Leo XIV waves in white and red papal vestments. File photograph. (Photo: Edgar Beltrán / The Pillar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Vatican has set the schedule for Pope Leo XIV in Argentina, a visit from Sunday 8 to Wednesday 11 November 2026. It includes three open-air masses, a youth vigil and a meeting with President Javier Milei.

The Holy See Press Office, the Vatican’s official press office, released the programme on Monday 21 September 2026. Argentina’s government then said it is preparing the largest security operation in the country’s history.

Three countries in twelve days

The journey was first announced on Wednesday 5 August 2026 by Matteo Bruni, director of the press office. It runs from 6 to 17 November, counting the flights to and from Rome.

Uruguay comes first, from 6 to 8 November, with stops in Montevideo, Paysandú and the town of Florida, north of Montevideo. Argentina follows, and Peru closes the tour from 11 November.

The pope leaves Lima for Rome on Monday 16 November and lands on 17 November. The Peruvian leg takes in Lima, Chiclayo, Cusco and the Amazon city of Pucallpa.

The Argentina programme, day by day

Leo XIV flies in from Montevideo to Buenos Aires’ city airport, Aeroparque Jorge Newbery. He lands at 4:30 p.m. Buenos Aires time on 8 November.

He first honours independence hero José de San Martín at his monument. He is then received at the Casa Rosada, the presidential palace, and visits Milei.

His first speech, to authorities and diplomats, follows at the Palacio Libertad cultural centre.

On Monday 9 November he visits the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole, south of the capital. La Nación reports the home cares for people with disabilities.

At 11:30 a.m. Buenos Aires time he celebrates mass at the Monumento de los Españoles in Palermo. That afternoon he addresses the world of work at the Catholic University of Argentina.

He also meets leaders of other Christian churches and faiths at the Palacio San Martín. The day ends with vespers alongside Argentina’s bishops in the Metropolitan Cathedral.

On Tuesday 10 November he flies to Córdoba, Argentina’s second city, for a 10 a.m. mass at the Military Aviation School. That evening he returns to Palermo for a youth vigil.

On Wednesday 11 November he starts at 8 a.m. with a visit to the Federal Penitentiary Complex of Buenos Aires. Two hours later he says mass outside the Basilica of Our Lady of Luján, a major pilgrimage shrine.

He leaves from Ezeiza international airport at 2 p.m. for Lima. The Vatican notice says Aerolíneas Argentinas flies him into Argentina, around it and on to Peru.

The floodlit facade of the cathedral of Santa María in Chiclayo, northern Peru, the diocese Leo XIV led before moving to Rome. File photograph from 15 September 2018. (Photo: Danny Miguel Hoyos Wepio, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Seven million, counted across every event

The government set out its plans at a press conference at the Casa Rosada on Monday. Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno spoke alongside Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva.

Monteoliva called the security operation “the largest in our history”, according to Clarín. She listed three jurisdictions, three airports, three cities, four mass events and 11 closed events.

She also cited a unified command running for 120 uninterrupted hours and “a global capacity of approximately 7 million people”. La Opinión Austral reports that figure covers all the events combined over the four days.

It is therefore a cumulative planning number, not a forecast of 7 million different people. Monteoliva said the city of Buenos Aires, Buenos Aires province and Córdoba each have a unified command.

A holiday is an idea, not a decision

Quirno said the government would study whether to declare a public holiday, an asueto or non-working days. An asueto is a day off for public employees.

“Only today did we have official confirmation of the calendar,” Quirno said, as quoted by La Nación. He added that the scope, the days and the places covered “are not yet defined”.

The five-day figure comes from the calendar, not from the government. If Monday to Wednesday were declared days off, they would join the weekend of 7 and 8 November.

La Opinión Austral framed that scenario as a possible five-day break, while stating that no such decision exists. El Cronista reports a separate bill in the Chamber of Deputies.

That bill, by Peronist deputy Jorge Taiana, a former foreign and defence minister, would make 9, 10 and 11 November non-working days. More than 20 legislators back it, and the executive has not adopted it.

Why this trip matters

Leo XIV, born Robert Prevost in Chicago in 1955, is the first pope from the United States, says his Vatican biography. He is also a naturalised Peruvian citizen since 24 August 2015.

He spent much of his career as an Augustinian missionary in Peru. He led the diocese of Chiclayo, in the north, from November 2014 until Pope Francis called him to Rome in January 2023.

His predecessor Francis was Argentine, yet never returned to his homeland after becoming pope, the BBC noted when he died. No pope has visited Argentina since John Paul II in 1987.

The papal nuncio, the Vatican’s ambassador in Buenos Aires, is Michael Wallace Banach. He said the pope comes “as head of state, but principally as a pastor”.

For Argentines, Pope Leo in Argentina is the visit Francis never made in twelve years as pope. For Peru, it is a return to the diocese he led for more than eight years.

More: Argentina coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will Pope Leo XIV be in Argentina?

The Vatican programme has him arriving in Buenos Aires from Uruguay at 4:30 p.m. Buenos Aires time on Sunday 8 November 2026. He leaves for Lima, Peru, at 2 p.m. on Wednesday 11 November 2026. In between he visits Claypole, Córdoba and Luján.

Where are the big public masses?

There are three open-air masses in Argentina. The first is at the Monumento de los Españoles in Palermo, Buenos Aires, on 9 November. The second is at the Military Aviation School in Córdoba on 10 November, and the third outside the Basilica of Luján on 11 November. A youth vigil is held in Palermo on the evening of 10 November.

Is there a holiday while Pope Leo is in Argentina on his visit?

Not yet. Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said on 21 September 2026 that the government is studying holidays, an asueto or non-working days. He said their scope is not yet defined and will be analysed according to the places the pope visits. A bill by deputy Jorge Taiana proposing 9 to 11 November as non-working days has not been adopted.

Is it true that 7 million people will attend?

That is the security plan’s figure, cited by Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva. It is a combined capacity across all events during the four days, so the same people may be counted more than once. It is not an estimate of distinct visitors.

Sources: Holy See Press Office programme of the journey, Holy See Press Office flight notice, Holy See Press Office announcement of 5 August 2026, Vatican biography of Leo XIV, Clarín on the Casa Rosada briefing, La Nación on the holiday analysis, La Opinión Austral on the five-day scenario, El Cronista on the Taiana bill, BBC on Francis never returning to Argentina

World.title: Chile Online Gambling Crackdown Widens as Subtel Orders 37 More Domains Blocked
World.content:
Chile · Technology

Key Facts — What happened Telecoms regulator Subtel announced on 21 September 2026 that six internet providers must block 37 more betting domains within 48 hours.

— Who is targeted New domains, subdomains and mirror sites linked to 15 brands, including Betano, Betsson, Bet365, Betfair and 1xbet.

— The legal basis A Supreme Court ruling of 30 September 2025, won by Lotería de Concepción, a lottery owned by the Universidad de Concepción.

— The catch Chile online gambling brands have repeatedly answered blocks by opening new addresses, so the lists keep growing.

— How big the lists are Subtel’s orders this month cover 79 web addresses, after 12 sites named in the original ruling.

— What is still missing A licensing law. The bill has passed the Chamber of Deputies and is before the Senate’s economy committee.

A court ruling, not a new law, is driving the campaign. The betting brands keep opening mirror sites, and the bill to license them is still in the Senate.

A sports betting app on a smartphone, with a match on a laptop behind. File photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Chile online gambling brands lost another batch of web addresses this week. The Undersecretariat of Telecommunications (Subtel), Chile’s telecoms regulator, announced it on Monday 21 September 2026.

Entel, Movistar, Claro, GTD, WOM and VTR must block 37 more betting domains within 48 hours of notification. It is the latest round in a court-ordered campaign that betting brands keep sidestepping with new addresses.

A court ruling, not a new law

The blocks do not come from new legislation. Subtel said it acted “in strict compliance” with rulings of the Supreme Court and the Santiago Court of Appeals.

The case was brought by Lotería de Concepción, a lottery owned by the Universidad de Concepción. It sued the country’s main internet providers for letting unlicensed betting sites reach Chilean users.

On 30 September 2025 the Supreme Court ruled in its favour, by majority. The state lottery Polla Chilena de Beneficencia backed it as a supporting third party.

The court held that games of chance are illegal in Chile unless a law expressly authorises them. For online games, only the two lotteries and the racing firm Teletrak hold such permission.

What the 37 domains are

According to Subtel, the new list covers domains, subdomains and mirror sites tied to 15 brands. They include Betano, Betsson, Bet365, Betfair, Betway, 1xbet and Marathonbet.

The Superintendency of Casino Gaming, the state casino watchdog, validated the list. Subtel then sent it to the providers for blocking at the level of the Domain Name System, the internet’s address book.

The providers must prove compliance directly to the Santiago Court of Appeals, under the penalties that court has set. They must also tell Subtel the exact date and time of each block.

A game of whack-a-mole

The original ruling named 12 sites, which the providers said they had blocked by November 2025. The operators simply changed their addresses, La Tercera reported.

The lotteries asked for the mirror sites to be blocked as well. In April 2026 the Supreme Court overturned a finding that its order had been met.

The Santiago Court of Appeals then set a five-step procedure, reported on 8 August 2026.

Under it, the lotteries report suspect addresses, the casino watchdog validates them and Subtel instructs the providers. The first list under it, of 42 addresses, went out on 1 September 2026.

Within days, more than ten online casinos had told customers of new addresses, BioBioChile reported. Monday’s 37 domains are the answer, and Subtel says the procedure will keep repeating.

That brings Subtel’s two lists this month to 79 addresses. La Cuarta, a Santiago tabloid, described Monday’s order as the third blocking request of the campaign.

Casino chips on a roulette table. File photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

A grey zone that pays tax

For foreigners, the Chilean position looks contradictory. International betting brands advertise openly, and many have sponsored the country’s professional football.

When the Supreme Court ruled in 2025, nine of the 16 first-division clubs carried online betting sponsors, the broadcaster Cooperativa counted. The national team had none.

The state is also preparing to tax these platforms. Chile’s tax service, the SII, has registered 39 platforms to pay value-added tax.

The first quarterly payment is due in October, and the SII expects it to reach about US$100 million. Its director, Jorge Trujillo, says charging the tax does not validate the activity.

The Association of Gaming Casinos, which represents Chile’s licensed physical casinos, calls that a “gigantic contradiction”. Its members are barred from offering games online.

The law that would license them

A bill to regulate Chile online gambling platforms is bulletin 14838-03. It has passed the Chamber of Deputies and is before the Senate’s economy committee.

Successive governments have repeatedly marked it urgent, most recently in May 2026, but that urgency has lapsed. It has not been enacted.

A working group of Senate and Finance Ministry advisers was agreed in June. Three senators, including the economy committee chair, want licences, age checks and a specific betting tax.

The betting firms are fighting back in court. W&C N.V., which operates Latamwin, filed a constitutional protection action against the casino watchdog and Subtel over the 42-domain order.

The Santiago Court of Appeals admitted it on 11 September, the trade outlet Gaming Intelligence reported.

What it means for users

The block works at the level of the providers’ DNS servers. A user may find the page unavailable, law academic Juan Ignacio Contardo of the Universidad del Desarrollo told Canal 9.

Apuesta Legal Chile, a gambling affiliate site, has said such blocks affect only access to a domain, not deposits or balances. It has also warned of fake mirror sites posing as known brands.

None of these firms holds a Chilean licence for online betting. The casino watchdog had sent 123 complaints to prosecutors since 2018, its then head told senators in June.

Most came from customers of online platforms, including over trouble collecting winnings.

More: Chile coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is online gambling legal in Chile?

Not for private operators. The Supreme Court ruled on 30 September 2025 that games of chance, online or not, are illegal unless a law expressly authorises them. That is the basis for Chile online gambling blocks. Only the lotteries Polla Chilena and Lotería de Concepción and the racing company Teletrak are authorised for certain online games. A bill to license private platforms is still in the Senate.

Who is behind the blocking campaign?

Lotería de Concepción, a lottery owned by the Universidad de Concepción, filed the original case against the internet providers. The state lottery Polla Chilena de Beneficencia backed it. Both report suspect domains. The Superintendency of Casino Gaming validates them, and the Undersecretariat of Telecommunications (Subtel), Chile’s telecoms regulator, orders the blocks. Licensed physical casinos, through their trade association, also oppose the online platforms.

Which providers must block the sites?

Entel, Movistar, Claro, GTD, WOM and VTR. They have 48 hours from notification to block each listed domain through the Domain Name System. They must then prove compliance to the Santiago Court of Appeals and tell Subtel the exact date and time of each block.

What happens to my betting account if a site is blocked?

The block works at the level of the six providers’ DNS servers, so the site may simply stop loading. Apuesta Legal Chile, a gambling affiliate site, says such blocks affect access to a domain, not deposits or balances. The operators hold no Chilean licence for online betting. The casino watchdog’s then head told senators in June 2026 that most of its 123 complaints to prosecutors since 2018 came from online platform customers.

World.title: Bachelet UN Bid: Former Foreign Ministers Blame Kast, Cite US Snub
World.content:
Chile · Politics

Key Facts — What happened Eleven former Chilean foreign ministers and deputy ministers said on 21 September 2026 that Kast’s government damaged the Bachelet UN bid.

— Who signed Seven former foreign ministers, including José Miguel Insulza and Heraldo Muñoz, plus four former deputy foreign ministers.

— What they say about Washington The US ambassador to the UN refused to meet Bachelet, they say, and a Brazilian-Mexican request went unanswered.

— The catch On 8 September, US ambassador to Chile Brandon Judd told CNN Chile that Washington had not said it would veto her.

— The government’s line The Foreign Ministry said on 19 September that it dropped Chile’s sponsorship in March over the spread of regional candidates.

— Why Washington counts Any of the five permanent Security Council members, including the United States, can veto a Secretary-General nominee.

Eleven former senior officials of Chile’s Foreign Ministry say the government’s March decision to drop the former president hurt her campaign. They also say Washington refused to meet her.

Michelle Bachelet, then UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, at a UN session. File photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Seven former Chilean foreign ministers and four former deputy ministers blame President José Antonio Kast’s government for damaging the Bachelet UN bid. Their joint statement, released on Monday 21 September 2026, also says Washington refused to meet the former president.

Michelle Bachelet, twice Chile’s president and a former UN human rights chief, quit the race for UN Secretary-General on Saturday 19 September. The signatories hold Kast, in office since 11 March 2026, responsible for weakening it.

They also describe the American refusal to receive her as “very significant”. The dispute follows Kast to New York, where he is making his debut at the UN General Assembly this week.

Who signed, and what they said

The former foreign ministers served centre-left and left-wing governments across three decades. José Miguel Insulza and Juan Gabriel Valdés held the post under Eduardo Frei Ruiz-Tagle in the 1990s.

Ignacio Walker served under Ricardo Lagos, while Mariano Fernández and Heraldo Muñoz served in Bachelet’s own two governments. Antonia Urrejola and Alberto van Klaveren were foreign ministers under Gabriel Boric, Kast’s left-wing predecessor.

The four former deputy foreign ministers are Cristián Barros, Gloria de la Fuente, Ximena Fuentes and Edgardo Riveros. All eleven supported the candidacy, and Valdés worked on her UN campaign, according to the Santiago radio station Cooperativa.

Their harshest words were for Kast’s decision in March to withdraw Chile’s sponsorship. They called it “an inexplicable and unprecedented act” that “will go down in the annals of Chile’s diplomatic history”.

“The withdrawal of the Chilean government’s support represented a hostile gesture that caused evident damage to the candidacy,” the statement says. It adds that the move created doubts in countries that had shown interest in backing her.

“For the first time in the UN’s 80-year history, a Chilean woman had a real chance of leading the organisation,” they wrote. “If that did not happen, responsibilities must be established.”

The claims about Washington

The signatories say senior officials of every permanent Security Council member received Bachelet, except those of the United States. The other four permanent members are China, Russia, the United Kingdom and France.

The foreign ministers of Brazil and Mexico asked in writing for a senior Trump administration official to receive her, the statement says. That request “was not even answered,” the former ministers wrote.

They also say the US ambassador to the UN interviewed most candidates but refused Bachelet a meeting. “We consider these facts very significant,” they added.

The statement does not say that the United States vetoed or voted against her. No US response to Monday’s statement has been reported.

On 8 September the US ambassador to Chile, Brandon Judd, told CNN Chile that Washington had not said it would veto her. He said it was still weighing her candidacy.

“No. We have not said that we are going to veto her,” Judd told the interviewer Mónica Rincón. Kast’s view would be taken into account but would not decide the matter, he added.

The entrance of Chile’s Foreign Ministry on calle Teatinos in Santiago. File photograph. (Photo: Rodrigo Fernández, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Insulza, a former secretary general of the Organization of American States, went further in an interview with the news site El Mostrador. He asked whether Kast had discussed the candidacy with President Donald Trump before dropping it.

“Or did they decide to do the United States a favour by withdrawing the candidacy to avoid vetoes?” Insulza asked. He put it as a question, and no such contact has been reported.

The government’s answer

No government reply to Monday’s statement had been reported at the time of writing. Its position is on the record, however.

On Saturday 19 September the Foreign Ministry said it “takes note” of Bachelet’s decision. The same written statement defended the March withdrawal.

As its reasons, it cited “the dispersion of candidates in the region and its impact on the chances of success”. It added that Chile had not committed its support to any rival candidate since.

The foreign minister is Francisco Pérez Mackenna, in office since 11 March 2026. He is accompanying Kast to New York for the General Assembly.

Kast answered his critics over the Bachelet UN bid on Cooperativa radio on 31 August 2026. He said “certain former ambassadors” blamed him, adding: “I think the main people responsible are themselves.”

How the campaign unravelled

Chile, Brazil and Mexico jointly nominated Bachelet on 2 February 2026, under Boric. Kast’s government announced on Tuesday 24 March that it was withdrawing Chile’s nomination.

A UN letter dated 25 March confirmed that she remained a candidate of Brazil and Mexico alone. Kast said at the time that he had foreseen “the result was not going to be the one sought”.

The 15-member Security Council then held three secret straw polls, in which members encourage, discourage or give no opinion. Unofficial, unconfirmed tallies published by 1 for 8 Billion, a campaign group monitoring the race, show her support falling each time.

She drew six encouragements, five discouragements and four no-opinions on 30 July, according to the group. On 21 August the figures were two, six and seven.

On Friday 18 September she received one encouragement, 11 discouragements and three no-opinions. Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan led that round with nine encouragements.

Bachelet withdrew the next day, thanking Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum. “I do not regret having taken on this great challenge,” she wrote on social media.

Why Washington’s view matters

Under the UN Charter, the General Assembly appoints the Secretary-General on the Security Council’s recommendation. That recommendation needs nine votes and the concurrence of all five permanent members.

In practice this gives the United States, like China, Russia, Britain and France, a veto over any candidate. It is why the signatories treat a refused meeting in New York as more than a matter of protocol.

More: Chile coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who blamed the Kast government for the failed Bachelet UN bid?

Eleven former senior officials of Chile’s Foreign Ministry, in a joint statement released on 21 September 2026. Seven are former foreign ministers: José Miguel Insulza, Juan Gabriel Valdés, Ignacio Walker, Mariano Fernández, Heraldo Muñoz, Antonia Urrejola and Alberto van Klaveren. The other four are former deputy foreign ministers. All had backed Michelle Bachelet’s candidacy.

Did the United States veto Michelle Bachelet?

No formal veto was cast, because Bachelet withdrew before any Security Council vote on a recommendation. The straw polls are secret and informal. The former ministers say the US ambassador to the UN refused to meet her, but their statement does not say Washington voted against her. On 8 September the US ambassador to Chile, Brandon Judd, told CNN Chile that Washington had not said it would veto her and was still weighing her candidacy.

Why did Chile withdraw its support for Bachelet?

Kast’s government announced the withdrawal on 24 March 2026, less than two weeks after taking office. The Foreign Ministry says it acted after weighing the number of Latin American candidates and their effect on her chances. Kast has said he warned Bachelet before taking office that he saw the bid as very difficult.
