World.title: Moody’s cuts Poland’s credit rating to lowest level since 2002
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, has lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The decision is likely to push up borrowing costs for Poland and reduce investor confidence. The last time the agency had Poland at such a low level of creditworthiness was in 2002. It is also the first time any of the big three agencies has downgraded Poland’s rating since 2016, when Standard & Poor’s shifted it from A- to BBB+ on its scale. However, it restored Poland to A- two years later. Moody’s obniżył dziś rating Polski z A2 do A3. To pierwsza obniżka ratingu Polski przez Moody’s od 2002 r. Przez lata agencja utrzymywała A2, nawet gdy zmieniała perspektywę na negatywną. Trwałe wysokie deficyty i rosnące koszty obsługi oznaczają pogorszenie perspektyw dla Polski pic.twitter.com/iGeuBb5hih — Piotr Arak (@piotrarak) September 18, 2026 “The downgrade of Poland’s ratings to A3 reflects our expectations of a sustained deterioration in Poland’s fiscal strength,” said Moody’s in an announcement late on Friday. “Large fiscal deficits persist, leading to a material increase in public debt and, together with rising interest costs, weaken debt affordability metrics,” added the agency. It also warned that “fiscal policy effectiveness has weakened”, including a “limited willingness or ability on the part of the Polish authorities to rebuild fiscal buffers during favourable economic conditions”. “Political constraints, including the continued standoff between the government and the president and the proximity of the November 2027 parliamentary elections, also limit the scope for meaningful fiscal consolidation,” concluded Moody’s, pointing to Poland’s high social and defence spending. In response to the announcement, Poland’s finance minister, Andrzej Domański, noted that Moody’s had previously “had the highest rating for Poland among the three major agencies”. After the downgrade, it is now aligned with Standard & Poor’s and Fitch, the other two agencies, he added. “We take this decision seriously, but calmly,” continued Domański. “The Polish economy is growing rapidly, and its fundamentals remain strong. We will consistently strengthen public finances, but this requires cooperation from all state institutions, including the president.” The latter comment was directed at President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has blocked many of the government’s initiatives, including some of its fiscal policies. However, the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker, blamed the situation on the government. “They steal, they lie and they burden our homeland with debt,” he wrote on social media. “Unfortunately, we Poles will have to pay for it all.” Dziś agencja ratingowa Moody’s obniżyła rating Polski do poziomu A3, jednocześnie podnosząc perspektywę ratingu z negatywnej do stabilnej. Dotąd Moody’s miała najwyższą ocenę Polski spośród trzech głównych agencji – po obniżce dostosowała ją do poziomu agencji Fitch i S&P.… — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) September 18, 2026 Poland’s worsening fiscal situation has been drawing the attention of the rating agencies for some time. The government’s budget deficit has ballooned, reaching 7.3% of GDP in 2025, the second-highest figure in the European Union. That was despite Poland being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024, at which time it set out a plan to reduce the deficit. Instead, the deficit has risen. The draft budget for 2027 puts the deficit at 7.1%, almost double the 3.7% the government had previously committed to reach by that year. As a result, Poland’s level of debt has risen rapidly. In the first quarter of this year, it went above 60% of GDP for the first time on record, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. Poland's government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence and healthcare as spending priorities, while continuing heavy borrowing The deficit, at 7.1% of GDP, remains well above the EU limit of 3% that the government has pledged to reach https://t.co/gxLdsHjYPz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2026 Meanwhile, the ability to introduce measures to better balance the budget has been hindered by hostility between the government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right – and Nawrocki. Since coming to power just over a year ago, Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills, including a proposed tax increase on alcoholic and sweet drinks. He also recently blocked a windfall tax on fuel companies. The situation led both Fitch and Moody’s to shift their outlook for Poland from stable to negative last year, indicating that they may lower the country’s score. Moody’s has now done so, although in Friday’s downgrade announcement it also shifted Poland’s outlook back to stable, saying that it forecasts strong economic growth in the coming years and government debt stabilising around 70-75% of GDP by the late 2020s. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Fitch has so far maintained its credit rating for Poland at A-, where it has been since 2007. However, in March this year, the agency warned that the “political gridlock” between the government and president is hindering efforts to tackle Poland’s “large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt”. Standard & Poor’s, meanwhile, has so far maintained both Poland’s credit rating at A-, where it has been since 2018, and its outlook at neutral. In a comment on the Moody’s decision on Friday, Ignacy Morawski, editor-in-chief of Polish business daily Puls Biznesu, wrote that the downgrade had “happened faster than most market participants had predicted”. He cited “uncontrolled political inertia” in tackling public finances as the primary reason behind the downgrade, which he said should provide “even more reason for the government and president to start seeking agreement”. World.title: Poland joins European Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has announced during a visit to Ukraine that Poland has joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries that are jointly developing an integrated air defence system for the continent. “Yes, Poland is now part of this great project,” said Tusk, “a group of countries and companies that will work together to protect against ballistic missiles…mean[ing] much safer European, and therefore also Polish, skies.” He added that he had “established the form and framework for this cooperation” during talks today with President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was hosting a summit of eight countries from around the Carpathian Mountains: Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary. Speaking at a press conference alongside Tusk, Zelensky also confirmed that “we will be partners” in the missile coalition and Poland “is welcome there”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Jesteśmy w Koalicji Antybalistycznej. pic.twitter.com/prtqKznHnB — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 18, 2026 The Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition was established in mid-July this year during a meeting in Paris of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries that are supporting Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. Alongside Ukraine, the coalition also included Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. In late July, Kyiv announced that it wants a prototype anti-ballistic system, which has been codenamed Freyja, ready in the first half of next year. Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point is the lead industrial partner in the project. At the time, there was some confusion and criticism in Poland regarding the fact that the country had not been included in the coalition. Speaking today, Tusk admitted that there had been “a certain misunderstanding” at the time, but it is “now clear that Poland is also part of this initiative”. The alliance is hoping to develop a cheaper complement to the US-made Patriot air-defence systems, which Ukraine and many other European countries use but which rely on American supplies. Zelensky has recently called on Ukraine’s allies to provide it with Patriot missiles. However, that issue caused political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition criticised the government for handing over some of its missiles to Kyiv, arguing that it would weaken Poland’s own defences. Speaking today alongside Tusk, Zelensky said that the new missile coalition would bring Poland and Ukraine “even closer to each other” and provide benefits to both countries, reports PAP. “Ukraine possesses unique technologies developed during the war, and we are ready to share them with Donald [Tusk] and our Polish partners,” said Zelensky. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 Both leaders made reference to recent tensions between their countries, in particular over the Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians. “We may sometimes speak very directly, but if we are friends, we must openly discuss topics that are sensitive to both sides,” said Zelensky, quoted by PAP. “We are friends, and Russia is the enemy. If we begin a dialogue based on common understanding, we will manage everything.” Tusk, meanwhile, thanked Zelensky “for your willingness to at least try to understand our Polish sensitivities” regarding “difficult, painful issues from the past”. He pledged to “always support Ukraine in your fight against aggression”, regardless of “adversities and negative trends”. Meanwhile, Tusk expressed hope that the newly formed Carpathian Eight group of countries, which met today in that format for the first time, would help provide further impetus for Ukraine on its path towards European Union membership. Today, for the first time, here in Ukraine, in our part of the Carpathians, we hold a Summit that brings together all the Carpathian states, the regions and communities of our countries. We are launching a new format – “C8,” the Carpathian Eight – bringing together us and our… pic.twitter.com/tcIupMsBBK — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: American Nobel laureate receives Polish citizenship
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros, whose father emigrated from Poland after World War Two, has received Polish citizenship. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him to give him the good news personally. Ambros, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on microRNA, revealed earlier this year during a visit to Warsaw that he was seeking Polish citizenship and hoped to help strengthen Poland’s scientific standing worldwide. Jesteś obywatelem najlepszego państwa na świecie!🇵🇱❤️ pic.twitter.com/cBDfMDS3Ax — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 16, 2026 “I have great news for you: you are a Pole, you have a Polish passport,” Tusk told Ambros during the call. “You are a citizen of the country that is the best place on Earth – at least I believe that.” Ambros told Tusk that he was “honoured” to receive the news. Speaking later to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), the scientist said that he was “very grateful to Prime Minister Tusk and to Poles for awarding me Polish citizenship”. “I hope that my having dual citizenship – American and Polish – will honour both my father’s Polish roots and the opportunities that America created for him and me.” Ambros, who is already chair of the scientific council of the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences, also expressed hope that there would be “additional opportunities to help improve the international position of Polish science, especially in the field of biomedical research”. Ambros’s father, Longin, was born in 1923 in what was then the village of Dordziszki in Poland but which, after postwar border changes, is now Dordishki in Belarus. He later attended high school in the city then known as Wilno, and which was part of Poland, but is now Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania. During World War Two, Longin Ambros was deported to Nazi Germany and used as forced labour, before being liberated at the end of the war by American forces, who then employed him as an interpreter. In 1946, Longin emigrated to the United States, where he settled on a farm and raised a family. Victor was one of eight children and the first scientist in the family. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros has announced that he is seeking Polish citizenship in order to honour his family “and all those who fought and survived so that I could exist today” He also wants to contribute to the development of science in Poland https://t.co/70uXhh1fj6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026 There has been a growing trend in recent years for foreigners to seek Polish citizenship. There are three paths for those wishing to obtain it. The first is through Polish ancestry. People with a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who lived in Poland after 1920 and never lost their citizenship can apply to have their status as a Polish citizen officially confirmed. Last year, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Poland, received Polish citizenship, describing it as the “honour of a lifetime”. His Oscar-nominated 2024 film A Real Pain was set entirely in Poland. Eisenberg is currently starring in a new state campaign promoting Poland abroad, along with football star Robert Lewandowski and supermodel Anja Rubik. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The second route is for foreign residents in Poland who meet requirements relating to their length of residency, language skills and personal situation to apply to the governor of the province where they live. The third is by applying directly to the president, who has discretion to grant citizenship without any specific legal requirements being met. Applicants are expected to show personal ties to Poland and explain their reasons for seeking citizenship. One recent example was Russian-born speed skater Vladimir Semirunniy, who fled to Poland and was granted citizenship last year by President Karol Nawrocki. This allowed him to win a medal for Poland at the recent Winter Olympics. Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago. Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 Last year, Poland granted citizenship – either through provincial governors or directly from the president – to a record 19,135 people. Over half of the recipients were Ukrainians, who constuitute by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. In 2024, the figure stood at 16,342. However, the Polish government is currently working on measures to make it tougher for foreigners to obtain citizenship, including increasing the minimum residency period and requiring applicants to take a test proving they are integrated. They would also have to sign a declaration of loyalty. Applications to confirm citizenship through descent have also risen sharply, in particular among Israelis, many of whom have roots in Poland. Last month, rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski announced that he was also applying for Polish citizenship with a view to representing and winning medals for the land of his ancestors on the international stage. Rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski has announced he wants to represent Poland, the country of his ancestors. His best 100m time of 9.89 seconds is the 9th fastest in the world this year and over a tenth of a second faster than Poland's national record https://t.co/S2tZsiSAhh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish ruling party MP stripped of immunity and detained at request of EU prosecutors
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. An MP from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s party, the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has been detained by anti-corruption officers after parliament approved a request from the European Public Prosecutor’s Office to lift his legal immunity. It is the first time in history that the EPPO, which Tusk’s government signed Poland up to in one of its first actions after taking power in 2023, has taken action against a sitting Polish member of parliament. Poseł Wojciech Król został doprowadzony do biura Prokuratury Europejskiej w Katowicach. Śledczy zamierzają przedstawić mu zarzuty dotyczące przestępstw korupcyjnych i przesłuchać.https://t.co/AknEyHwIHL — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) September 18, 2026 The MP in question, Wojciech Król, is accused of trading in influence in relation to the EU-funded modernisation of tram infrastructure in the Upper Silesian-Zagłębie Metropolis, an agglomeration of municipalities in southern Poland that includes Katowice, a major city. The EPPO says it has found evidence of “a system of corruption” that involved inflated costs and fictitious work on the project, for which 1.9 billion zloty (€435 million) of EU funds was designated. Its investigation found that, as part of this system, a member of parliament – not named directly by the EPPO but who is known to be Król – had “accepted financial benefits in exchange for arranging favourable outcomes for several companies”. Polish news website Interia reports that the EPPO suspects Król of accepting over 1.4 million zloty in bribes. The MP has publicly denied the accusation. Eleven other people have already been charged in relation to the alleged corruption scheme, reports broadcaster TVN. They include senior executives from a municipal tram operator. In May, the EPPO submitted a first request to Poland’s parliament to lift the immunity that Król enjoys as an MP and bring him into detention. At the time, Król was deputy head of KO’s caucus in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, but he has since lost that position and been suspended from the caucus entirely. In late July, a majority of MPs in the Sejm approved the lifting of Król’s immunity to face prosecution. However, at the same time, they rejected the EPPO’s request for Król to be taken into detention, after MPs from the ruling coalition voted against it. The same week those votes took place, the EPPO issued a second request, outlining additional evidence and suspicions regarding Król’s alleged involvement in corruption. On Thursday this week, the Sejm voted almost unanimously in favour of that second request, again lifting Król’s immunity to face further charges but this time also approving his detention. A few hours later, officers from Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) arrested Król in Warsaw. Po południu decyzja Sejmu, wieczorem działanie służb. Tak działa państwo prawa, w którym legitymacja poselska i barwy partyjne nie dają żadnego immunitetu od odpowiedzialności karnej. Nie ma świętych krów! https://t.co/7DpmV7q4RF — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 17, 2026 “This is how a state of law operates, in which parliamentary credentials and party colours offer no immunity from criminal liability,” wrote justice minister Waldemar Żurek on social media. “There are no sacred cows.” A Polish prosecutor delegated to the EPPO, Agnieszka Marcińczyk, told the Sejm this week that bringing Król into detention was necessary to prevent potential obstruction of the proceedings against him. She also said that Król had not complied with some of the preventative measures imposed on him after his immunity was previously stripped, including failing to post the required bail and to appear at a police station as part of his supervision order, reports news website Wirtualna Polska. Oświadczenie ws. drugiego wniosku o uchylenie immunitetu Uprzejmie informuję, że zapał do mojego aresztowania skończy się w grudniu. Do tego czasu będą składane kolejne wnioski o uchylenie immunitetu oraz zgodę na zatrzymanie i aresztowanie. Przypomnę, że pierwszy wniosek o… — Wojciech Król (@wojciech_krol) September 11, 2026 The EPPO was established in 2021 in order to investigate and prosecute crimes against the financial interests of the EU. However, under Poland’s former national-conservative, eurosceptic Law and Justice (PiS) government, the country initially did not join the body. After Tusk’s more liberal, pro-EU coalition replaced PiS in December 2023, one of its very first actions was to begin the process of joining the EPPO, which was completed in March 2024. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. Addressing parliament on Thursday, the prime minister said that “citizens absolutely have the right to know what scenario can be expected based on the information available today”. Intelligence from allies, including the United States and Ukraine, indicates that various scenarios are possible, but one is most likely, said Tusk. Over the next few months, Russia’s recent tactic of using jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine near the Polish border will likely continue, said Tusk, as well as attacks on Ukrainian economic and logistics infrastructure, such as railways. “Russia’s plan, according to intelligence, also includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,” continued Tusk. “These possibilities have been discussed for some time. This information is now very consistent and, unfortunately, convincing.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Istnieje realne ryzyko, że na teren któregoś z państw NATO mogą wlatywać drony, dokonywać zniszczeń. I te „przypadkowe” według Rosji uderzenia mogą się powtarzać. pic.twitter.com/bScJBjQQF1 — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 17, 2026 The aim, said Tusk, would be to “weaken NATO member states’ motivation to apply appropriate NATO regulations in the event of aggression against any member state”. Russia’s “official narrative will be that this is an accident and there’s no reason for anyone to consider any kind of NATO response”. The prime minister said that the incidents could be similar in nature to the night one year ago when around 20 Russian drones entered Polish airspace across its eastern border. “These ‘random’ attacks could repeat themselves, becoming an increasingly glaring illustration of NATO’s helplessness, as conceived by the Russians,” said Tusk. In response to last year’s drone incursions, Polish and allied NATO jets shot down some of the drones. Poland then invoked article 4 of the NATO treaty and received increased air-defence support from a number of NATO allies. Russia has recently stepped up its attacks on western Ukraine, including a number of strikes close to the Polish border. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has begun reinforcing security at border crossings, including installing 28 new bomb shelters and expanding air-defence systems. The prime minister also confirmed that he would be travelling to Kyiv later on Thursday. He planned, among other things, to discuss with President Volodymyr Zelensky how they would cooperate on air defence and utilise Ukraine’s experience and capabilities in this area. On the night of Thursday to Friday, the latest round of Russia attacks on Ukraine prompted Poland to scramble aircraft, activate air-defence systems, and close parts of its eastern airspace – actions that have recently become increasingly common. A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around 2 km from the Polish border, amid the latest mass Russian attacks on Ukraine. Warsaw has launched special joint patrols by its municipal police and roads authority to check whether electric scooters are being parked legally and in keeping with rules introduced under a recent agreement with rental firms. According to the city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, more than 140 improperly parked scooters have been towed away within just a few days. Under the agreement, their operators now face potential fines. Nie ma miejsca dla hulajnóg tam, gdzie nie ich miejsce. Zdecydowałem o uruchomieniu specjalnych patroli Straży Miejskiej i ZDM. W ciągu ostatnich kliku dni dzięki ich pracy odholowanych zostało ponad 140 nieprawidłowo zaparkowanych hulajnóg elektrycznych. Taką możliwość daje… pic.twitter.com/U5fd7YDN8U — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) September 16, 2026 “There’s no place for scooters where they don’t belong,” Trzaskowski said in a social media post announcing the patrols. “There are specific provisions, agreements and legal regulations – and action is being taken. No leniency.” An agreement reached between the city and three scooter operators – Bolt, Dott and Lime – in May expanded the number of streets where the vehicles are subject to a maximum speed of 12 km/h (7.5 mph) and increased the areas where their use is entirely prohibited. It also introduced measures to prevent scooters from being left in places where parking is illegal. Riding and parking electric scooters was banned in several areas of Warsaw, including popular tourist attractions such as the Old Town, Krasiński Garden and Łazienki Park. Trzaskowski added that the city has now expanded the list of areas covered by the ban, as permitted under the agreement. He did not, however, provide the new list. The agreement requires operators to programme their scooters so they cannot enter areas where riding is prohibited or be parked in places where parking is illegal, including on bridges, in tunnels, in residential areas and on streets where the pavement is too narrow to allow legal parking. Operators can be fined when scooters are left in violation of the rules. The city says that, despite electric scooters accounting for just under 8% of all traffic on cycle lanes, their riders were found to be responsible for 39 of the 66 accidents recorded on cycle lanes last year. Those accidents resulted in 73 injuries. Concerns over the safety of electric scooters have also prompted the national government to introduce stricter rules, including a nationwide requirement for children under 16 to wear a bicycle helmet when riding bicycles and electric scooters, which took effect in early June. Poland first introduced regulations governing electric scooters in 2021, formally setting out rules for their use. Under those rules, scooters are generally required to use cycle lanes where available, with their maximum speed capped at 20 km/h. The Polish government has moved to introduce new rules on the use of electric scooters. A year after the legislation was introduced, after the first report on e-scooter-related accidents showed that they had caused hundreds of injuries and three deaths in 2021, Poland’s police launched a campaign publicising the new rules. At national level, infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak has announced further restrictions the government is working on, including a new law requiring scooters to be collected and left only in specially designated zones. World.title: Heating Season Starts Across Czechia as Temperatures Fall
World.content:
District heating plants across the Czech Republic are beginning to supply heat as temperatures drop, with conditions for the start of the heating season now being met in much of the country.

Some plants have already begun providing additional heat during the colder morning and evening hours. The first systems to respond were mainly in mountainous parts of northern and western Czechia and in the Vysočina region.



Other heating plants are expected to gradually start operating in the coming days, depending on local temperatures and weather forecasts.

Since 2010, district heating systems have generally started supplying heat after September 20, although the exact timing varies considerably from year to year.

If temperatures rise again in late September or early October, heating can be suspended. Under the standard rules, heating is normally interrupted when the average outdoor temperature exceeds 13°C for two consecutive days and the forecast indicates that temperatures will continue to rise.

Last winter was colder than average

The previous heating season placed greater demands on heating systems than the years immediately before it.

According to figures from the Czech District Heating Association, the season was 4.9 percent colder than the previous year. It was also 3.2 percent colder than the average of the preceding 15 years.

The colder conditions translated into higher demand for heat, particularly during periods of sustained low temperatures.

Heating costs could increase next year

Households are not currently expected to face a direct increase resulting from a recent change in the interpretation of a fuel tax exemption, but some other users of district heating could see higher costs.

The issue concerns combined heat and power (CHP) generation. This year, the state changed how an existing fuel tax exemption is interpreted, limiting its application to the amount of heat supplied to households.

Heating companies say the change could increase annual heating bills for institutions such as hospitals and schools by tens or even hundreds of thousands of Czech crowns.

World.title: Crowdfunding Campaign Launches for Book Tracing the History of Prague’s Roxy Club
World.content:
A new book documenting the history of Prague’s Roxy club and the alternative cultural scene that grew around it is seeking public support ahead of its planned publication this autumn.

Titled Kopneš do plechovky a dva dny se tančí (“Kick a Can and Dance for Two Days”), the book looks at Roxy’s development from its beginnings in the early 1990s to its current role in Prague’s music scene.



A crowdfunding campaign to finance the publication has been launched on Donio.cz.

Rather than focusing solely on the history of one nightclub, the project examines the people, artists and cultural movements connected with the venue.

More than 40 musicians, promoters, artists and other figures associated with Roxy contribute their memories and perspectives.

Roxy opened in 1992 and quickly became an important venue for alternative music in Prague. Over the years, its programme has covered genres including hardcore, house, trip-hop, hip-hop and drum’n’bass.

The book is the result of almost five years of research by cultural journalist Ondřej Horák. He examined thousands of archival documents, located previously unpublished photographs and interviewed nearly 50 people connected with Roxy and its history.

The campaign will also feature newly created artwork. Graphic designer and typographer Jozef Ondrík has produced a series of three screen-printed posters based on visual elements from Roxy’s history.

The design draws on three pages from the original handover document for the non-residential premises at Dlouhá 33, which were transferred to the Linhart Foundation.

Large-format photographs and works by artists connected with Roxy and the NoD Gallery are also expected to be among the campaign rewards.

World.title: Prague and the 15-Minute City? Only for One in Seven Residents
World.content:
In the first year of the Friendly City Index, Prague ranked second among Central and Eastern European metropolises.

Yet only 13.82% of residents can reach most daily destinations – work, schools, shops, or healthcare – within 15 minutes. The best metropolises in the region remain closer to “30-minute cities.”



Young Czechs are closest to the ideal: 34% of those aged 18–24 said they can reach everyday destinations within 15 minutes. Middle-aged people, especially 45–54, scored the worst at 14.7%.

Smaller Czech cities outperform Prague. Olomouc (36%), Ostrava (29.7%), and Brno (21.8%) all ranked better in their categories. Compact urban structures and shorter distances explain much of this advantage. Polish cities also dominated the rankings, including Krakow, Szczecin, and Lublin.

Among metropolises, Warsaw leads with 15.9%. In other categories: Krakow (30.3%), Split (44%), Rijeka (53.3%), and Zadar (53.6%). Riga ranked worst at 9.8%, while Zagreb scored only 20%.

The smaller the city, the better the accessibility

Around 10–15% in metropolises, 30% in large cities, 40%+ in medium-sized cities, and over 50% in small cities. Even cities with metro systems like Prague or Bucharest show little improvement, confirming that compactness and urban structure matter more than infrastructure alone.

Transport habits

In Central and Eastern Europe, 46% rely on cars and 27% on public transport. In Czechia, the split is nearly even: 42.6% drive, 42.4% use public transport. Among 18–24-year-olds, more than half (51.1%) rely on public transport. Alternative mobility options such as bikes, scooters, and carsharing remain marginal.

Urban planner Peter Bednár explains: “The point is not that all journeys must be short, but that most daily activities can be done without a car. Achieving this requires higher density and a mix of functions. Without enough services and destinations nearby, the most practical walk still leads to the parked car.”

About the index

The Friendly City Index is an international survey on quality of life and urban development. In 2025, it covered 54 cities in nine countries with 4,500 respondents, including 500 in Czechia. The study was carried out by Syno International in partnership with Bolt.

World.title: Where to See Prague’s Best Autumn Colors Without Leaving the City
World.content:
Autumn in Prague does not have to mean a crowded walk across Petřín or a stroll through Stromovka.

Beyond the city’s best-known parks, forests, valleys and protected natural areas offer quieter routes where the changing season can be enjoyed without leaving Prague.

Many of these places are also surprisingly easy to reach. A tram, bus or train can take you close to the starting point, making it possible to plan a two- or three-hour walk without a car or a full-day trip.



Vinoř Park and the Satalice Pheasantry

In northeastern Prague, a marked trail links Vinoř Park with the Satalice Pheasantry through a narrow wooded valley.

The landscape is shaped by the Vinořský Stream, sandstone formations and small springs. Along the route, walkers can also come across traces of the area’s history, including rock carvings, the remains of an old hillfort and the entrance to a water cave.

The area is especially attractive in autumn, when old oaks and other trees turn yellow and brown. A long avenue between Vinoř and Satalice adds another distinctive feature to the route.

The official educational trail is about 3.5 kilometers long and takes roughly two hours. It starts near the Malá Obůrka pond and finishes close to the Chapel of St. Anne in Satalice. From there, buses and trains provide connections back into Prague.

Hvězda offers more than its main avenue

Hvězda Game Reserve is one of Prague’s better-known green spaces, but many visitors stay on the central avenue leading from Vypich to the white Renaissance summer palace.

The quieter parts begin once you leave the main route and head into the surrounding woodland.

Oaks, beeches and hornbeams dominate the reserve. According to Prague’s records, more than half of its forest stands are over 150 years old. Several notable beech trees date from plantings carried out after 1763, including a tree recognized as the oldest and largest beech in Prague.

A loop through the reserve can lead from the summer palace toward the pond and Světlička wetland meadow before returning along one of the smaller paths.

Dalejské Valley offers a different side of Prague

Prokopské Valley is familiar to many Prague residents, but the landscape continues west toward Řeporyje in the quieter Dalejské Valley.

Here, limestone cliffs, former quarries, open slopes and the Dalejský Stream create a landscape that changes frequently along the trail.

One option is to follow the green-marked hiking route from Řeporyje toward Hlubočepy. Rather than forming one continuous wall of autumn foliage, the valley combines yellow trees with exposed rock and brownish grass-covered slopes.

The area forms part of the northeastern section of the Bohemian Karst and is recognized for its geological features. Prague’s Nature Portal recommends following the valley along the stream.

Hostivař Forest Park changes after summer

Hostivař is closely associated with its reservoir and summer swimming, but the area takes on a different character once the bathing season ends.

The woods surrounding the water offer numerous walking routes, with more than 35 kilometers of paths and trails running through the forest park.

A shorter walk can follow the reservoir, while longer routes continue through woodland and meadows and pass the animal enclosure near the gamekeeper’s lodge. The Botič Stream Basin educational trail also crosses the area.

Autumn brings changing colors to the oak and larch trees, while the reservoir provides views that are particularly noticeable on cooler mornings.

World.title: New Dog Playground Opens in Central Prague with Agility Course
World.content:
Prague 1 now has its first public dog playground, giving dog owners in the city center a dedicated space for exercise and training.

The new facility is located on Ludvík Svobody Embankment, next to the Ministry of Transport’s traffic playground and close to Lannov Park. It has been open to the public since September 16.



At the center of the site is an approximately 92-meter-long agility course. It includes a tunnel, slalom poles, an A-frame and several jumping obstacles. The playground is freely accessible and does not require prior booking.

“Space in the center of Prague is very limited, so we want to use every suitable location to serve local residents,” said Kateřina Klasnová, Prague 1’s deputy mayor responsible for the environment.

The playground is currently unfenced, meaning dogs can enter and leave the area freely.

Some dog owners raised concerns about the lack of a fence during the opening, and Prague 1 said it would consider adding one.

An information board at the site explains the operating rules and provides instructions for using the agility equipment. The playground also has a waste bin and two dispensers containing bags for dog owners to clean up after their pets.

Responsibility for the site lies with the Prague 1 Department of the Environment. Visitors can report damaged equipment or other defects directly to the municipal district.

World.title: Emeli Sandé to Bring Her Biggest Hits to Prague at O2 universum
World.content:
One of Britain’s most acclaimed contemporary singers, Emeli Sandé, returns to Prague on November 3 for a special live concert at O2 universum.

The singer-songwriter will perform her best-known hits alongside music from her latest album, How Were We to Know.

Tickets are available through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal.

Select 2 tickets and enter promo code EXPATPRAGUE at checkout. You’ll only pay for 1 ticket. The offer is valid from 14 to 21 September 2026 for tickets in sectors 102-109, subject to availability.

Emeli Sandé’s biggest hits

Sandé became an international star with songs including Next to Me, Heaven, Read All About It, Clown and My Kind of Love, combining soul, pop and powerful vocals with deeply personal songwriting.

Her debut album, Our Version of Events, became one of the most successful British albums of its era and was the UK’s best-selling album of 2012. It also produced several of her biggest hits and established Sandé as one of the country’s leading vocalists.

She further cemented her place in British music history with performances at both the opening and closing ceremonies of the London 2012 Olympic Games.

In Prague, fans can expect a set spanning her career, including songs from her latest album, How Were We to Know. Released as part of a new chapter in her career, the album combines her distinctive soul influences with a contemporary pop sound.

ADONXS joins as special guest

Sandé will be joined by ADONXS, singer, songwriter and one of the newer names on the Czech and Slovak pop scene.

ADONXS represented the Czech Republic at the Eurovision Song Contest 2025, where he performed his song Kiss Kiss Goodbye. He has also released tracks including Wasted and Perfume, while his latest single, Cherry on Your Cake, continues his development as a songwriter and performer.

His appearance at O2 universum will open the evening before Sandé takes the stage.

Emeli Sandé live at O2 universum

The Prague concert will bring together Sandé’s most recognisable songs with material from her more recent work, giving audiences the chance to hear her signature voice in a live setting.

With hits that have become familiar to audiences around the world, the concert offers a chance to revisit songs such as Next to Me, Heaven and Read All About It, while discovering the latest direction of her music.

World.title: EU Citizens Can Vote in Czechia’s October Elections: Here’s How
World.content:
EU citizens living in Czechia can vote in the country’s municipal elections this October, but those who are not already registered will need to take action before election day.

The elections will take place on October 9 and 10, with voters in Prague choosing representatives for both the Prague City Assembly and their local municipal district.

EU citizens aged 18 or over who have permanent or registered temporary residence in Czechia can vote in municipal elections. However, they must be registered in the relevant electoral register.

Registering to vote

The deadline for registration is October 7, but the civic initiative Volby pro všechny recommends registering as soon as possible.

Its EU Voter Registration Tool generates the necessary application form and explains how to submit it to the relevant municipal or district office.

Registering early also means voters should receive their ballot papers at home before election day, giving them time to understand the unfamiliar Czech voting system. Those who register closer to the deadline will receive their ballots at the polling station.

There is also an important option for those who miss the registration deadline. According to Volby pro všechny, EU citizens will have a special possibility this year to register directly at their polling station on election day, provided they bring the required identification and proof of residence.

Find your polling station

Voters cannot simply choose any polling station. Their home address determines where they can vote.

The Polling Station Finder allows residents to enter their address and find the correct polling place. It can also create a calendar reminder for election day.

Voters should bring a valid ID or passport and the relevant Czech residence document.

What will Prague residents vote for?

Prague voters will cast two votes: one for the Prague City Assembly, covering the capital as a whole, and one for the council of their municipal district.

For those unfamiliar with the division of responsibilities, Volby pro všechny has created a “Who Does What?” quiz explaining which level of local government deals with different issues.

The organization has also published an overview of political parties and groups and is preparing a quiz that will allow users to compare their answers on policy questions with the positions of Czech political parties.

A guide in 23 EU languages

Volby pro všechny has also prepared a seven-step checklist for EU citizens, available as a downloadable PDF in 23 EU languages.

For EU citizens who have never voted in Czechia before, the resources provide a straightforward way to check their registration, find their polling station and understand what to expect on election day.

World.title: Prague Unveils Future Metro Stations in Nusle and Náměstí Míru
World.content:
Prague’s future Metro Line D has taken another step toward becoming a reality, with new preliminary designs released for two stations planned along the route.

The Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has presented renderings of the future Náměstí Míru interchange and Nusle station, offering an early look at how the new metro line could change the city’s underground transport network.

The images do not represent the final appearance of either station. DPP plans to select the architectural solutions through a two-stage competition, which will focus on the design of the interiors and the public spaces around the stations.

DPP intends to organise the competition in two stages, using a workshop format. The winning designs are expected to be selected within 18 months of signing the contract with the competition organiser. Preparations for that contract are currently underway.

Náměstí Míru station will connect Metro Lines A and D

The future Náměstí Míru station is planned beneath Sázavská Street, approximately 40 metres underground. It will be built using underground mining methods and will feature a single-vault design with an island platform.

The new station will be located above the existing Line A station, creating a new interchange between the two metro lines.

The design includes two vestibules equipped with escalators and a third access point with an elevator. The renderings show the planned exits towards Vinohradská, Francouzská, and Sázavská streets, as well as an elevator entrance on Korunní Street.

Metroprojekt has also presented a possible design for the outlet of a ventilation shaft in Riegrovy Sady. The structure will form part of the station’s technical infrastructure, although its final appearance may change following the architectural competition.

New Nusle station will serve Náměstí Bratří Synků

The second station featured in the new designs is the future Nusle station, which was previously known as Náměstí Bratří Synků.

The station will be built using cut-and-cover construction methods, with its island platform located approximately 13 metres below ground level. It is planned between Náměstí Bratří Synků and Otakarova Street.

Plans also include an underground parking garage for local residents above the station.

The new renderings show the proposed station entrances on Náměstí Bratří Synků, the northern vestibule beneath Otakarova Street, and the planned completion of the existing urban block.

When will Prague’s Metro Line D open?

Construction of Metro Line D began in 2022 with the section between Pankrác and Ryšánka. Work on the following section, extending towards Nové Dvory, began in June 2026.

The Pankrác–Nové Dvory section is planned to be the first part of the new metro line to open to passengers. DPP currently expects the section to enter service in the second half of 2032.

World.title: Hungary’s biggest restaurant awards 2026 announced – here are the Dining Guide winners
World.content:
On the evening of Monday 21 September, the Dining Guide announced this year’s outstanding achievements in Hungarian gastronomy at the Dining Guide Restaurant of the Year Gala. The evening’s biggest success was for Stand Restaurant, which, in addition to the Restaurant of the Year award, also won the Hungarian Restaurant Best of the Best title, thus rounding off the evening with two major accolades. Stand’s new management structure also played a part in the awarding of the Master Good Restaurant of the Year prize. In the absence of Szabina Szulló, the restaurant has been operating under a revised culinary leadership structure since October 2025, led by head chefs Tamás Széll and Benjamin Morris. The accolade recognises both the work of the current team and the achievements made under the new management structure.

A number of special professional awards were also presented at the gala: the Dining Guide – TORTER Promising Restaurant of the Year award went to Cova Budapest, whilst the Dining Guide – Innovative Kitchen of the Year award was presented to Alkimista Culinary Workshop. The Dining Guide – VLM Chef of the Year title was awarded to Márton Tatai, chef at Hoppá! Bistro, whilst Ádám Berecz, chef at Sulyom Tájétterem, was chosen as the Dining Guide – DEBIC Young Chef of the Year. The Dining Guide – Gosset Sommelier of the Year award went to Krisztián Juhász, sommelier at Borkonyha and Textúra, whilst the Dining Guide – KAVIÁRI Service Staff Member of the Year award was presented to Zsolt Király for his work at the Rumour by Jenő Rácz restaurant. The Dining Guide – Dallagiovanna Pizza of the Year award was won by Anyukám Mondta.

“The history of the Dining Guide began twenty-six years ago, and we presented the first Restaurant of the Year award to Fausto’s in 2005. It gives us particular pleasure that, more than two decades later, this iconic restaurant remains a defining force in Hungarian gastronomy. This also clearly demonstrates that, for us, truly great restaurant performance is not about a single successful year, but about the long-term, consistent delivery of quality. Over more than two decades, not only has Hungarian gastronomy changed enormously, but an audience has also emerged that chooses restaurants consciously, pays attention to quality and seeks well-founded recommendations. The Dining Guide’s rating system is based on the professional principles also applied by Michelin, but we combine this with our in-depth knowledge of the Hungarian hospitality sector, gained over several decades. This is important because we are not simply looking for the performance on a single evening, but also assessing a restaurant’s character, its development and its performance over the longer term. “This year, we visited nearly five hundred dining establishments to ensure that the 2026 guide provides a truly accurate picture of the current state of Hungarian gastronomy” – said Zoltán Herczeg, editor-in-chief of the Dining Guide and head of the professional jury.

The Dining Guide carries out the evaluation and ranking independently. Fausto Arrighi, the legendary former director of the Michelin Guide, also assists with the guide’s professional work in an advisory capacity, having been involved in the production of the publication for nine years now. The 2026 edition of the Dining Guide TOP100 Restaurant Guide features 180 restaurants alongside nearly 70 alternative dining venues.

If you missed it: Gordon Ramsay chooses Budapest for first Central European restaurant – opening date revealed

The finest of Hungarian gastronomy in one place

The Dining Guide TOP100 Restaurant Guide has been tracking and evaluating developments in the Hungarian hospitality sector for over two decades now. The ever-changing gastronomic scene takes shape year on year with new restaurants, changes of chefs and evolving concepts, and the guide reflects these changes to showcase the current cutting edge of Hungarian hospitality.

Stand Restaurant was named Restaurant of the Year 2026

Hungary’s finest dining establishment is Stand Restaurant, whose stable backbone is provided by co-owners including Ibolya Csahók, Zoltán Hamvas, Tamás Széll and Szabina Szulló, amongst others. In October 2025, Szabina Szulló took a break from intensive kitchen work for a while, but Benjamin Morris – who has been part of the team since 2020 – stepped up to the role of head chef and, together with Tamás Széll, the two of them now handle all the tasks that were previously carried out by the three of them. This is how they ensure the consistency that is the hallmark of the restaurant. Every single element of this top-class restaurant is characterised by a refined, strong ‘fine’ concept, which blends Hungarian cuisine with international trends in a unique way. Since its opening, Stand has represented a refined, elegant, contemporary Hungarian gastronomic movement based on local ingredients.

Jenő Rácz embarked on his international career at a young age: he worked in world-class kitchens in London, Copenhagen, Singapore and Shanghai. Upon his return, he opened Rumour by Jenő Rácz in May 2021, becoming the first to introduce the chef’s table concept to Hungary. Guests sit at a 21-seat counter surrounding the open kitchen, allowing them to watch the precise preparation and presentation of the dishes up close. The evening, with its gastronomic theatre atmosphere built around the chef’s personal presence, is complemented by playful elements and humorous touches, whilst the secret entrance door establishes a sense of exclusivity from the moment guests arrive. On the menu, Jenő Rácz’s Hungarian roots meet the global influences he has absorbed during his travels, carefully crafted and presented in an unconventional style.

Located in the heart of the Őrség region, Pajta opened its doors in 2012: the young couple, Ferenc Kvasznicza and Flóra Marjai, who left Budapest behind, realised their dream in an old barn, where gastronomy, nature and culture come together. The kitchen is led by the chef duo István Akács and Yazmin Salazar: Yazmin brings Latin American flavours to the plate, drawing on her Mexican roots, whilst István draws on his experience gained in leading European and Scandinavian restaurants – the fusion of the two forms the basis of Pajta’s distinctive, progressive international cuisine, built around strongly local ingredients. The farm-to-table philosophy is part of their daily routine: they often venture into the woods in search of wild mushrooms and fresh inspiration. The head chef at Pajta is Krisztián Paksa, who comes from the world of international haute cuisine, whilst Márton Király, a sommelier who previously spent many years as part of the Dining Guide’s team of writers, is in charge of the wines.

The 42 Restaurant & Bar in Esztergom has undergone a major transformation over the past year or two. In the summer of 2025, Kuzin Bistro took over the former ground-floor premises in the iconic building on Széchenyi Square, whilst the fine dining restaurant moved one floor up to a space featuring frescoes, which once served as the living room of a middle-class family. The owner, Sándor Varga, is the visionary behind and creator of the Alexander the Guest YouTube channel, which showcases the world’s leading fine-dining restaurants and boasts over half a million subscribers. Kevin Szabó has been at the helm of the kitchen since December 2025; his approach has been shaped by his background in competitive gastronomy – including his experience with the Hungarian Bocuse d’Or team – into technical precision and discipline. Kevin Szabó’s cuisine is rooted in Hungarian ingredients, whilst drawing freely on international gastronomy; the menu changes seasonally and includes a full vegetarian option. Every few weeks, the ‘Gastronomic Adventure’ evening, which draws a full house, brings the two establishments together, sometimes featuring a guest chef

SALT Budapest’s chef, Szilárd Tóth, continues to forge ahead as a pioneer of the farm-to-table restaurant style, which is still rarely seen in Hungary. The cuisine is shaped by the techniques of new Scandinavian gastronomy, but the dishes are rooted in the culinary heritage of Szilárd Tóth’s homeland, Szatmár and north-eastern Hungary. A book dedicated to this connection was published in 2026, in which memories of Szatmár appear on the plates in a dense, concentrated form. The restaurant’s interior is characterised by raw wooden surfaces, minimalist, pastel-coloured furnishings and shelves lined with jars from his own collection, filled with fermented or dried vegetables and fruit – all tangible evidence of the kitchen’s philosophy. The centrepiece of the dining area is the chef’s table, where Szilárd Tóth finishes preparing the dishes right before our eyes. SALT offers a fourteen-course tasting menu with wine and juice pairings; the restaurant, which seats around thirty people, welcomes guests from Wednesday to Saturday. The team is using home-grown produce in an increasing number of dishes; the vegetable garden is hosted by the SZIA Garden in Gödöllő.

Kornél Kaszás joined the Babel Budapest restaurant as executive chef in 2021. In 2022, they reopened with a completely new team and with the expert guidance of Swedish consultant chef Daniel Berlin. To this day, the spirit of the place is shaped by the joint efforts of Kornél Kaszás and his team, who continue to refine the restaurant’s mature Hungarian and regional identity through an ingredient-led approach. The restaurant is housed within the walls of a building originally constructed between 1913 and 1917 as a Piarist monastery; the historic setting and the minimalist, warm décor create a unique contrast. This fine-dining restaurant in the city centre offers friendly service and skilfully composed, intelligent and subtly elegant dishes that draw on the traditions of the Carpathian Basin whilst casting them in a modern, innovative mould. Good examples of this are their now-iconic casino eggs or their venison dish.

Tiago Sabarigo first made a name for himself in Hungary as the chef at Costes Downtown; then, in 2020, he and his wife, Éva Jenei, opened their own restaurant, Essência Restaurant Tiago & Éva, in the 5th district. Their Portuguese-Hungarian fusion cuisine has now established its own distinct identity and remains firmly at the forefront of the Hungarian culinary scene. Octopus and cod feature prominently on the restaurant’s menu as iconic ingredients that represent the meeting of Portuguese roots and Hungarian gastronomy. The tasting menu, which debuted in May 2026, begins with duck liver, apricots and fennel, followed by a dish featuring tomato essence, stracciatella and caviar; the ‘Palóc-style’ lamb loin with green beans and dill has become one of the most popular dishes. At Tiago Sabarigo and Éva Jenei’s restaurant, the contemporary, rustically elegant interior is dominated by Portuguese stylistic elements, whilst the open-plan kitchen at the back adds to the atmosphere.

The team at Sauska Padi, a new entry in the top 10, brings Hungarian home-cooking traditions, local ingredients and flavours designed to complement Tokaj wines to the plate; for them, the hallmarks of the wine region are just as important in the kitchen as they are in the glass. The kitchen at the Rátka estate’s restaurant is led by resident chef Máté Gerák, based on the concept of executive chef Attila Bicsár, who draws inspiration from, amongst other things, the forests and gardens of Zemplén and the region’s gastronomic heritage. The kitchen produces dishes that are worthy companions to Tokaj wines and sparkling wines, as they never lose sight of the fact that the restaurant is housed within the winery. The dishes are both familiar and innovative. They are based on different ingredients depending on the season: for example, game, mushrooms, various vegetables and fruits, poppy seeds, walnuts and aszú berries all feature on the menu.

Borkonyha, which has been operating on Sas Street in central Budapest since 2010, was the first top-tier Hungarian restaurant to win over the country’s culinary elite not through formal service, but through quality and a friendly atmosphere; it has maintained this reputation ever since. The concept is the brainchild of Ákos Sárközi, the executive chef, whilst the kitchen has been led for many years by Csaba Puskás, the head chef, with a stable team that has worked together for a long time. Pastry chef Anett Béres is responsible for the extraordinary desserts – at both Borkonyha and the neighbouring Textúra restaurant. Borkonyha combines modern international influences with a Transylvanian character: the menu regularly features pasta stuffed with Transylvanian ordá, tortellini filled with tripe and grilled hot peppers, or bulz, polenta balls with sheep’s milk cheese. The plates clearly bear the mark of artist Ákos Sárközi’s visually inspired use of form and colour, which lends a unique visual quality to the fine bistro-style dishes.

The highest standard of gastronomy in the South Transdanubia region is undoubtedly represented by Sauska 48 Villány in Villány, which has embodied the concept of ‘a restaurant at the heart of the winery’ since 2017. The head chef, the highly experienced Attila Bicsár, coined the term ‘uninhibited village gourmet’ here, for which the internationally renowned entrepreneur Krisztián Sauska, owner of the iconic Sauska wine estates, provides a fitting setting. Over the years, the restaurant has moved towards more complex tasting menus, whilst retaining its original Swabian-Hungarian identity. A favourite among guests is the duck liver terrine, served with apple compote, walnut cream and brioche. The elegant service allows time for wine presentations and conversation. The menu follows the availability of seasonal produce and the offerings of local producers, and the dishes are, of course, accompanied by Sauska wines from Tokaj and Villány. The wine list also features a section unique in Hungary,

‘A Glimpse into the Wider World: A Selection from the Sauska Family’s Cellar’, where guests can choose from the finest vintages – dating back as far as the 1960s, ‘70s and ‘80s – from the world’s most highly regarded wineries.

One of the flagships of Budapest’s fine dining scene, Arany Kaviár, celebrated its 35th anniversary in 2025. According to owners Attila Molnár and Szása Nyíri, the secret lies in their ability to always sense what guests might be craving at any given time. The memorable dining experience they provide stems from their attention to detail and their friendly, high-quality hospitality. The kitchen is led by executive chef Bence Molnár, who presents traditional Russian flavours with a contemporary twist, building on classic foundations whilst bringing a fresh perspective to the dishes. The caviar that gives the restaurant its name is a clear indication that guests at the Ostrom Street restaurant can sample the world’s finest caviar. The exceptional wine list is curated by sommelier Dávid Kincses, featuring rare wines from around the world as well as an outstanding selection of sparkling wines and champagnes.

Located on the ground floor of the Matild Palace Luxury Collection Hotel Budapest is the restaurant bearing the name of the legendary Austrian-American chef Wolfgang Puck, Spago Budapest by Wolfgang Puck, which opened its doors in 2021 as the brand’s first European outlet. The chef, who has been creating the menus for the Oscars for nearly three decades, is regarded as the pioneer of Californian cuisine, whilst his restaurants present classic dishes from various national cuisines through Wolfgang Puck’s unique interpretation. Since the restaurant opened, the kitchen has been led by István Szántó, executive chef, who has gradually expanded the international Spago concept with local flavours and a distinctive identity; indeed, a strong selection of sushi has also been added to the menu. Among the dishes that have become iconic are the goulash soup, created in István Szántó’s adaptation, tender game beef cheek and Somlói galuska ‘in a walnut shell’, as well as Wolfgang Puck’s signature dishes, including smoked salmon pizza, Wiener schnitzel, Scottish steamed salmon ‘Hong Kong’ style and Kaiserschmarrn.

World.title: Working in Hungary could become easier for non-EU professionals under new EU rules
World.content:
Working in Hungary could become considerably easier for some non-EU professionals under a new European Commission proposal designed to speed up the recognition of qualifications obtained outside the European Union. The planned rules could cut procedures that currently take more than a year to around four months.

The European Commission unveiled the measures on 15 September 2026 as part of its new Fair Labour Mobility package, a broader set of proposals aimed at making it easier for workers to move across the EU while reducing administrative burdens for employers.

According to the European Commission, recognition procedures for qualifications obtained outside the EU currently take an average of around 14 months. Under the proposed common standards, that could fall to approximately four months. The Commission says the changes could also cut employers’ administrative costs related to recruiting qualified workers from abroad by as much as half.

What could change for non-EU professionals working in Hungary?

At present, third-country nationals who want to work in a regulated profession in an EU member state generally have to have their professional qualifications recognised under the national rules of the country where they intend to work.

That means someone planning on working in Hungary may face a different procedure from a professional with the same qualification applying in Austria, Germany or another EU country.

The Commission now wants to introduce common EU standards for recognising qualifications obtained outside the bloc. The planned system would cover both EU citizens who obtained their qualifications in a non-EU country and third-country nationals who are already in the Single Market or are applying from abroad.

The objective is not to remove professional requirements, but to make the assessment process quicker and more predictable across member states.

For foreigners considering working in Hungary, this could therefore mean less uncertainty about how long recognition will take and what documents and procedures they will face.

If you missed it: Hungary has a record number of foreign workers – now businesses want the government to ease the rules

Seven professions could receive special treatment

The proposal goes particularly far for seven regulated professions for which EU-wide minimum training requirements already exist.

These are doctors, general care nurses, dentists, midwives, pharmacists, veterinary surgeons and architects.

Working in Hungary could become easier for non-EU professionals under new EU rules. Source: Depositphotos.com

Under the Commission’s plan, qualifications awarded by accredited institutions outside the EU could be recognised automatically if the institutions and programmes concerned have undergone the required European quality-assurance assessment.

The seven professions already benefit from an automatic recognition system for qualifying EU credentials under existing European rules. The new proposal could extend a comparable route to certain qualifications obtained outside the bloc.

This could be especially significant in professions where European countries are struggling to recruit sufficiently qualified staff.

Recognition would not automatically give the right to work in Hungary

There is, however, an important distinction for non-EU citizens.

Having a professional qualification recognised would not in itself grant someone the right to enter Hungary, live in the country or take up employment.

The European Commission explicitly states that EU member states would retain control over who is admitted to their territory and over the standards professionals must meet before they can practise a regulated profession.

In practice, a third-country national interested in working in Hungary could therefore still need the appropriate residence and employment authorisation even if recognition of their professional qualification becomes faster.

The proposal is consequently aimed at removing one major administrative obstacle rather than replacing national immigration rules.

When could the new rules take effect?

Nothing will change immediately. The measures presented by the Commission are legislative proposals and still need to be considered and adopted by the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union.

If approved, the changes would be introduced gradually. The Commission says simpler recognition of non-EU qualifications should become available within two years of the legislation being adopted. Other elements of the wider package, including digital qualifications and changes affecting regulated professions, are expected to follow within three years.

The wider package would also introduce digital tools for qualifications and social security documents, while strengthening EU-level cooperation against abuses involving mobile and third-country workers.

For non-EU professionals considering working in Hungary, the proposal is therefore worth following closely. It would not remove immigration requirements or guarantee that every foreign qualification is accepted, but it could make one of the most complicated parts of entering a regulated European profession substantially faster and more transparent.

World.title: Korean Film Festival returns to Budapest with 24 films and three visiting directors
World.content:
What happens when three generations set off from Gwangju to Budapest in an electric car? Can you save a family member who has turned into a zombie? And what secrets can surface from a family’s past after forty years? From 25 September to 2 October, the Korean Film Festival returns to Corvin Cinema with 24 feature films. From historical drama and road movies to occult action, this year’s programme brings a remarkably varied selection of stories to the big screen, while three Korean directors will also meet audiences in person at post-screening talks.

These days, Korean cinema is about much more than Parasite or Squid Game. What is perhaps less visible behind these international successes is just how diverse the country’s film scene really is. Organised by the Korean Cultural Center, the 19th Korean Film Festival sets out to showcase exactly that diversity, with this year’s programme built around four sections: Fresh, Faces, Focus and Extra.

It All Begins with a Child King

The festival opens on 25 September with Chang Hang-jun’s historical drama The King’s Warden. Set in 15th-century Joseon, the story follows the head of a poor mountain village who hopes his community might prosper by taking in an exiled nobleman. There is just one catch: the man entrusted to his care is no ordinary noble, but Yi Hong-wi, the young king who has been forced from the throne.

The historical drama was a major success in South Korea, attracting more than 16 million cinemagoers by April following its February release. It also won the Audience Award at the Udine Far East Film Festival and received several Baeksang Arts Awards.

Romance, Family Secrets and Demon Hunters

The Fresh section is perhaps the best place to see just how difficult it is to define contemporary Korean cinema by any single genre.

In Heartman: Rock and Love, a former musician’s first love unexpectedly reappears in his life. In The Ugly, human remains discovered after forty years set off an investigation into a family’s past, while Project Y follows two women who risk everything on a dangerous plan. At the other end of the spectrum is Holy Night: Demon Hunters, in which a trio with supernatural powers must save Seoul from a criminal organisation that worships the devil.

What Is It Like to Be a Child in Yoon Ga-eun’s World?

This year’s Faces section turns the spotlight on the films of Yoon Ga-eun. The director is particularly interested in childhood and adolescence, but not in an idealised version of them. In her films, friendships fall apart, families face crises, and young characters discover far too early what it means to feel like an outsider.

Four of her works will be screened at the festival, including The World of Love, which had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, as well as The World of Us and The House of Us.

If you missed it: K-pop in Hungary is no longer just a teenage trend: it is becoming a cultural movement – interview

From Gwangju to Budapest – by Electric Car

In this year’s Focus: On the Road selection, everyone is heading somewhere – although where they end up may not be where they originally intended to go.

The film with the most direct connection to Hungary is 3 Gen. Journey. A grandfather, a father and two children travel from Gwangju to Budapest by electric car over the course of 80 days. Elsewhere in the selection, a family heads to Gyeongju in search of revenge, two strangers set off into the unknown together, and another family embarks on one final trip, only to uncover a long-held secret along the way.

Festivalgoers will also have the chance to meet three Korean directors in person. Song Jinuk and Jang Kunjae will take part in CineTalk events on 26 September, followed by Lee Seonyeon on 27 September. The post-screening conversations will be held in Hungarian and Korean.

Five Films from Jeonju

The Extra section presents five films selected by the festival’s official partner, the Jeonju International Film Festival. The selection offers a glimpse into a less familiar side of Korean independent cinema, exploring relationships, financial insecurity, family ties and historical trauma.

Living Through the Same Season traces the memories of a relationship across four seasons, while Insomnia confronts a young married couple with a brutal moral dilemma after they lose all their savings in a housing rental scam. Two award-winning filmmakers will also be in Budapest in person: Jang Kunjae will meet audiences after the screening of Spring Snow, while Lee Seonyeon will discuss her debut feature, The Summer That Slipped Away.

One of the most distinctive films in the selection is the documentary Horoomon. The history of a now-popular Japanese dish is closely intertwined with the past of the Korean minority living in Japan. Beginning with something as everyday as food, the film opens up a much larger story about identity, exclusion and a century of historical memory.

Saving the Zombie for Last

The festival closes on 2 October with the comedy My Daughter is a Zombie. The premise sounds familiar enough: an outbreak begins and someone turns into a zombie. This time, however, that someone is a young girl – and her father refuses to give up on her.

He takes her to the countryside to stay with her grandmother, hides her from the outside world and attempts to teach her how to be human again. Adapted from a popular webtoon, the film playfully turns the conventions of the zombie genre on their head while telling, at its heart, a story about the relationship between a father and his daughter.

Audiences will once again be able to vote for their favourite film throughout the festival, with the Audience Award presented before the screening of the closing film.

Event: 19th Korean Film Festival

Dates: 25 September – 2 October 2026

Venue: Corvin Cinema (1082 Budapest, Corvin köz 1.)
