The assessment includes specialists in international aviation law, aviation personnel licensing, airworthiness and flight operations.

Assessment builds on work started in 2024

The 2026 assessment follows a preliminary technical review the FAA conducted in Kazakhstan from Aug. 26 to 30, 2024. Since then, Kazakhstan’s aviation authorities and the FAA have continued working to prepare for the current assessment and address areas relevant to the country’s aviation safety oversight system.

On Sept. 24, the FAA team is scheduled to make a technical visit to Air Astana in Astana. The airline has applied to the U.S. Department of Transportation for authorization to conduct commercial operations in the U.S.

According to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport, the visit is intended to verify information provided to the Aviation Administration of Kazakhstan as part of the transparency process. It is not an inspection of Air Astana as an air operator certificate holder.

After completing the assessment, the FAA is expected to hold a final briefing with the Aviation Administration of Kazakhstan and then provide a written report covering the areas reviewed.

Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport said the IASA represents an important step in strengthening the country’s state aviation safety oversight system and advancing work toward launching direct air services between Kazakhstan and the U.S.

World.title: Kazakhstan Wins Four Golds on First Full Competition Day at Asian Games 2026
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan won six medals, including four golds, on Sept. 20, the first full day of competition following the official opening of the 20th Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, reported the Kazakh National Olympic Committee’s press service.

Triathlete Arlan Zhanabay secured Kazakhstan’s first medal of the games in the men’s individual triathlon, finishing third in 53:11. Japan’s Takumi Hojo won gold, finishing 15 seconds ahead of Zhanabay, while another Kazakh athlete, Ayan Beisenbayev, placed ninth.

Kazakhstan’s first gold followed soon after, with cyclist Rinata Sultanova winning the women’s individual time trial in road cycling. Sultanova completed the course in 36:23.72, finishing 4.86 seconds ahead of China’s Zhang Hao. South Korea’s Shin Chieun took bronze.

Alexey Lutsenko then added another cycling gold in the men’s individual time trial with a time of 41:24.05. Japan’s Shunsuke Imamura took silver and Mongolia’s Jambaljamts Sainbayar won bronze. The victory was Lutsenko’s fifth Asian Games gold medal. It also marked his fourth consecutive title in the individual time trial, following victories in 2014, 2018 and 2022.

Kazakhstan claims two karate golds

Kazakhstan added two more gold medals in karate. Zholaman Bigabyl won the men’s under-55-kilogram category after defeating Tajikistan’s Makhsatullo Muminov and Indonesia’s Muhammad Zanuar before beating Uzbekistan’s Khumoyunmirzo Khalimov 9-1 in the final. The title marked Bigabyl’s first Asian Games medal.

Sofya Berultseva claimed gold in the women’s over-68-kilogram category. She defeated Saudi Arabia’s Dina Mostafa and Nepal’s Arika Gurung on her way to the final, where she overcame Thailand’s Manivan Butsuwan. Berultseva, who won gold at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, secured her second Asian Games title.

Men’s pentathlon team takes bronze

Kazakhstan also earned bronze in the men’s modern pentathlon team competition. Temirlan Abdraimov recorded the best individual result among the Kazakh athletes, finishing seventh. Tikhon Varekhin placed ninth, Lev Chuvashov 13th and Kirill Stadnik 18th.

The combined results of the three best Kazakh athletes were enough to secure bronze in the team standings. China won gold, while South Korea took silver. The women’s modern pentathlon team finished fourth. Yuliana Petrova placed 14th, Ayana Kazbekova 17th and Diana Shchedrova 18th.

Kazakhstan advances in team sports

Kazakhstan’s men’s table tennis team opened its group campaign with two victories, defeating Bangladesh 3-0 and Singapore 3-1. The team will face Laos in its final Group G match on Sept. 21. The women’s team lost its opening match to South Korea 0-3. Kazakhstan will next play the Maldives.

In beach volleyball, Sergei Bogatu and Kirill Gurin defeated Indonesia’s Imam Ahmad Faisal and Fairuz Baihaqi 2-1 (22:24, 21:19, 15:12). Another Kazakh pair, Abdulmajid Mohammad and Dmitry Yakovlev, lost to Japan’s Juntaro Tachie and Yusuke Ishijima 1-2. Kazakhstan’s women’s volleyball team lost to South Korea in the quarterfinals, 24:26, 25:27, 21:25, and will continue in the matches for fifth through eighth places.

Kazakh athletes also advanced in wushu-sanda. Ayan Tursyn defeated Turkmenistan’s Bibirmeriem Akmukhammedova in the under-52-kilogram category to reach the quarterfinals, while Abdurasid Abdullaev advanced in the under-75-kilogram category after defeating Laos’ Anong Theunchaleun.

In traditional MMA, Erkingali Burkitalin defeated Lin Ming-dian of Chinese Taipei in the opening bout of the men’s under-77-kilogram category and advanced to the quarterfinals. Aigerim Torekhanova was eliminated in her opening bout in the women’s modern MMA under-54-kilogram category.

Kazakhstan finishes seventh in mixed triathlon relay

Kazakhstan’s triathlon team finished seventh in the mixed relay, with Ayan Beisenbayev, Aida Kim, Diana Yerzhanova and Yegor Krupyakov recording a time of 1:31:45. China won the relay in 1:25:54, followed by Japan in 1:26:45 and Hong Kong in 1:27:25.

The result came a day after Zhanabay won bronze in the men’s individual triathlon, giving Kazakhstan its first medal of the 2026 Asian Games.

World.title: Kazakhstan Raises Irrigation Support to Accelerate Water-Saving Technologies
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has expanded the use of water-saving irrigation technologies to 702,300 hectares of irrigated farmland as of Sept. 1, 2026, nearly three times the area recorded in 2023, as the government seeks to reduce agricultural water losses and improve irrigation efficiency.

Modern irrigation systems were used on 237,100 hectares in 2023. The area increased to 389,900 hectares in 2024 and 543,500 hectares in 2025, before reaching 702,300 hectares this year. Water-saving technologies now cover 36% of the country’s 1.9 million hectares of irrigated farmland, the Prime Minister’s press service reported.

The expansion comes as Kazakhstan faces growing pressure on water resources and seeks to improve the efficiency of agricultural water use, particularly in regions dependent on transboundary water sources.

Drip irrigation expands nearly sixfold

Drip irrigation has recorded the fastest growth among modern irrigation technologies, with its coverage increasing from 42,500 hectares in 2023 to 254,300 hectares in 2026. Sprinkler irrigation expanded from 188,300 hectares to 379,000 hectares over the same period.

Since the beginning of 2026, drip irrigation systems have been introduced across 86,500 hectares, while sprinkler systems have been installed on another 65,900 hectares. The government plans to expand water-saving technologies to 912,200 hectares in 2027, 1.1 million hectares in 2028, 1.2 million hectares in 2029 and 1.3 million hectares by 2030. At the planned 2030 level, the technologies are expected to save up to 2.2 billion cubic meters of water annually.

According to the government, modern irrigation systems can reduce irrigation water consumption by an average of 20–30%. The actual savings depend on the crop, climate, soil, terrain and condition of on-farm irrigation infrastructure.

In 2025, water-saving systems covering 543,500 hectares were estimated to have saved around 874 million cubic meters of irrigation water.

Southern regions remain a priority

The expansion is concentrated in regions with extensive irrigated agriculture and high demand for water. Of the additional 158,800 hectares brought under water-saving irrigation in 2026, around 50,000 hectares were in the Turkistan Region, 25,500 hectares in the Almaty Region, 19,200 hectares in the Kyzylorda Region, 11,800 hectares in the Zhetisu Region and 10,200 hectares in the Zhambyl Region.

The Zhambyl, Kyzylorda and Turkistan regions have been given priority in government support measures. Together, they account for about 905,000 hectares of irrigated land and have significant dependence on transboundary water resources. The government is also supporting measures including laser field leveling, subsidies for electricity used to pump groundwater, moisture-charging irrigation and washing of saline soils.

Domestic irrigation equipment production expands

The expansion of modern irrigation is also creating demand for locally manufactured equipment. The number of domestic producers in the sector has increased from four to seven over the past two years. Three plants operate in the Turkistan Region, two in Astana, and one each in Almaty and the Atyrau Region.

Their combined production capacity reaches 3,390 sprinkler machines annually, enough to irrigate about 205,000 hectares. With domestic demand estimated at 1,000–1,200 machines a year, current production capacity is described as broadly sufficient to meet farmers’ needs.

Since the beginning of 2026, agricultural producers have purchased around 1,010 sprinkler machines for irrigation of 65,600 hectares. The government’s longer-term target is to bring 1.3 million hectares under water-saving technologies by 2030, linking investment in irrigation infrastructure and domestic equipment production with efforts to reduce agricultural water consumption.

World.title: From Astana Events to Xi’an Rail Links, Kazakhstan Expands Tourism Reach
World.content:
ASTANA – Nearly 830,000 tourists visited Astana in the first half of 2026, a 12% increase from the same period last year, as Kazakhstan’s capital expands its tourism offering and strengthens international connectivity, including through a new tourist train linking China and Kazakhstan.

Of the total visitors to Astana, about 187,000 were foreign tourists, Deputy Mayor of Astana Yevgeniy Glotov said at the opening of the Kazakhstan Travel Forum 2026 in the capital on Sept. 18.

According to him, Astana is developing several segments of tourism, including business, cultural, medical and event tourism. The capital receives more than 1.6 million tourists annually, with visitor numbers growing by an average of 10–12% each year.

“Astana has long ceased to be a city that people visit only for work. More than 1.6 million tourists visit the capital every year, and this flow is growing by an average of 10–12% annually. Today, our task is to make sure that a guest who comes to Astana for a concert or business meeting stays here longer and returns again. Cities around the world are competing for this kind of tourist today, and Astana is actively participating in this competition,” he said.

Event tourism remains one of the city’s key priorities. International concerts, sporting competitions and major business and cultural events are being used to attract additional visitors and encourage them to extend their stays.

The city is also expanding its tourism infrastructure, with new attractions and international hotel brands adding to its offer.

Xi’an–Almaty tourist train strengthens China links

Meanwhile, Kazakhstan is expanding its railway tourism connections with China. An international tourist train operating on the Xi’an–Almaty route arrived in Almaty after departing from the Chinese city of Xi’an on Sept. 14. The route passes through northwestern China and Xinjiang along the historic Silk Road before crossing the Kazakhstan–China border at Khorgos.

Passenger transportation within Kazakhstan is provided by Passenger Transportation, which has established a special timetable for the international service to account for border procedures and the connection between the railway systems of the two countries.

“Developing tourist trains is of strategic importance to us. Railways make it possible to create comprehensive tourist routes, connecting cities, regions, historical and natural sites. Our task is to jointly develop this format with foreign partners, expand the geography of travel across Kazakhstan and create a quality tourism product for passengers,” said Anuar Akhmetzhanov, chairman of Passenger Transportation.

A cultural and sightseeing programme has been prepared for the Chinese tourists arriving in Almaty. The itinerary includes the Independence Monument, the 28 Panfilov Guardsmen Park, the Ascension Cathedral, the Central Mosque, Kok-Tobe, Shymbulak, the Central State Museum and other attractions.

The Xi’an–Almaty international tourist train was first launched by the Chinese side in 2025. In June 2026, the first service using Kazakhstan’s national carrier’s trains was operated. The current service is the second such trip this year.

World.title: B5+Italy Turns Italy’s Central Asia Strategy Into Working Platform
World.content:
The launch of B5+Italy in Astana matters because it gives Italy and the five Central Asian states a standing mechanism to turn last year’s summit diplomacy into investment, industrial partnerships, and regional economic cooperation.

The Central Asia-Italy Business Forum may look like another event in the region’s crowded calendar of international meetings. Its significance, however, lies in what it creates between high-level summits: a platform linking governments, businesses, and economic institutions around practical projects in energy, critical minerals, manufacturing, agriculture, transport, and the Middle Corridor.

B5+Italy is a direct follow-up to the first Central Asia–Italy summit, held in Astana in May 2025, which brought together Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and the leaders of the five Central Asian countries. Italy’s Foreign Ministry has presented the forum as a way to convert that political momentum into investment, industrial cooperation, and new opportunities for companies.

That shift from political declarations to an institutional mechanism capable of producing commercial results is why B5+Italy matters.

From summit diplomacy to economic infrastructure

The 2025 summit was an important political signal. It demonstrated that Italy sees Central Asia not as five separate markets, but increasingly as a region with common strategic and economic potential.

But political summits, however important, do not automatically generate commercial integration.

The more difficult question is what happens between summits.

This is precisely where B5+Italy could become consequential. The new platform is intended to facilitate regular dialogue between governments and businesses, support the preparation of joint investment projects, and expand direct contacts between companies from Italy and Central Asia. Priority areas include industrial production, critical minerals, energy, agribusiness, transport infrastructure, connectivity, and the Middle Corridor.

Italy already has a substantial economic presence in the region. Italian-Central Asian trade grew by 46.5 percent between 2019 and 2025, according to Italy’s Foreign Ministry. Rome increasingly sees Central Asia as a market of roughly 80 million people located at the crossroads of Europe and Asia.

The challenge now is to turn this growing interest into a deeper and more diversified economic relationship.

The real obstacle is not political will

There is no shortage of political support for stronger Italy–Central Asia relations. The more fundamental question is whether companies can operate across borders with sufficient predictability and manageable transaction costs.

For businesses, connectivity is not limited to railways, ports, and logistics corridors. It also means customs procedures, regulatory requirements, certification, investment protection, financing mechanisms, access to information, and the ability to identify reliable local partners.

This makes the simplification of procedures for business cooperation one of the most important issues on the agenda.

The launch of B5+Italy creates an opportunity to address precisely these practical barriers. If the platform can help companies navigate administrative procedures, identify partners, and move from initial discussions toward concrete projects, it could develop into something more significant than a traditional business forum.

The question should therefore not simply be how much Italy and Central Asia trade today.

The more important question is: what prevents that trade and investment relationship from becoming significantly larger?

A role for think tanks

There is also an important space between government and business that should not be overlooked: independent policy research, education, and skills development.

Italian officials have expressed interest in continuing the dialogue through a think-tank format that could bring together policymakers, businesses, academics, and experts from Italy and Central Asia. Such a forum could help identify common priorities not only in trade and investment, but also in research, education, and human-capital development.

This matters because the next stage of Central Asia’s economic development will depend not only on capital and infrastructure, but also on qualified people, technological expertise, and stronger links between universities, research institutions, and industry.

A structured expert dialogue could therefore provide an additional bridge between political ambitions and practical cooperation.

The next test: ministerial diplomacy

The next important step will be the planned ministerial engagement between Italy and the five Central Asian countries.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has already expressed his intention to organize a new ministerial meeting with the five countries in order to further strengthen dialogue and cooperation.

Such a meeting could help move the agenda from broad political support toward implementation: investment facilitation, trade procedures, connectivity, critical minerals, industrial partnerships, agriculture, technology, and energy.

It would also provide another opportunity to prepare the political ground for the next Central Asia–Italy summit, which is planned to take place in the Kyrgyz Republic in 2027. The decision to hold the next leaders’ meeting in the Kyrgyz Republic was included in the joint declaration adopted at the 2025 summit.

If this sequence develops as intended — business platform, ministerial dialogue, and then a second leaders’ summit — Italy and Central Asia will have created something increasingly valuable in international diplomacy: continuity between high-level political meetings.

Italy is part of a larger transformation

The significance of B5+Italy becomes even clearer when viewed against the wider transformation of Central Asia’s external relations.

The region has witnessed a rapid expansion of the C5+1 model, through which external powers engage the five Central Asian states collectively.

The latest example came only days before the Italy–Central Asia business forum.

On Sept. 16, South Korea hosted the first Central Asia–Republic of Korea summit, bringing together the leaders of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan with the South Korean president. The summit focused heavily on critical minerals, energy, supply chains, industrial cooperation, technology, and investment. More than 70 agreements and memoranda were reportedly concluded during the broader summit process.

The significance of the Korean example is not simply the number of agreements.

It demonstrates that the C5 format is becoming increasingly useful as an instrument through which external powers can engage Central Asia as a regional economic space.

This does not mean that Central Asia is becoming a formal bloc. The five countries retain different economic structures, national priorities, and foreign-policy interests. Bilateral relations will remain essential.

But the regional format is becoming complementary to bilateral diplomacy.

For external partners, it offers access to a larger regional market and a coordinated political dialogue. For the Central Asian states, it provides an additional mechanism for presenting regional priorities and attracting investment, technology, and expertise.

Competition is creating opportunity

The growing number of C5+1 initiatives also reflects a broader change in how the world perceives Central Asia.

The region is increasingly relevant to discussions about supply-chain diversification, critical minerals, energy security, transport connectivity, food security, and new trade routes between Europe and Asia.

Italy has a potentially distinctive role in this process.

It is not simply another external power seeking access to Central Asian resources. Italy has considerable industrial and manufacturing expertise, strong agricultural and engineering capabilities, logistics companies, and a large network of small and medium-sized enterprises.

At the same time, Central Asian economies are looking for partners capable of providing not only capital, but also technology, industrial expertise, and access to international value chains.

The potential complementarity is therefore considerable.

But potential alone is not enough.

The real test of B5+Italy will be whether it can help businesses overcome the practical barriers that currently stand between political agreements and commercial projects.

A quiet but important milestone

The Astana forum therefore deserves to be viewed as more than another business gathering.

Its importance lies in the institutional architecture being built around it.

The 2025 leaders’ summit created political momentum. B5+Italy creates an economic mechanism. The forthcoming ministerial dialogue can provide political direction. A possible think-tank track can help generate ideas and identify areas of convergence. And the planned 2027 summit in the Kyrgyz Republic can consolidate the progress made.

Taken together, these developments suggest that Italy–Central Asia relations are moving from episodic diplomacy toward a more continuous partnership.

The development is also significant for Central Asia itself.

As more global and middle powers return to the region with concrete economic proposals, the C5 format is gaining practical value. The question is no longer simply whether Central Asia can attract international attention. It is increasingly about whether the five countries can use that attention to build mutually beneficial projects, diversify external partnerships, and strengthen their collective economic position.

The launch of B5+Italy may have passed relatively quietly in the international media. But beneath the headlines, a more important process is underway: the gradual construction of a denser network of institutions linking Central Asia with the major economic centers of Europe and Asia.

For Italy, the task is to turn political interest into business reality.

For Central Asia, the task is to ensure that growing international competition translates into investment, technology, industrial capacity, skills, and greater connectivity.

And for the C5 format, the expanding number of external partnerships suggests that its most important phase may only now be beginning.

The authors are Sapargali Shalgimbayev, the president of the CFive Intellectual Platform, and Domenico Palmieri, the secretary general of the Italian Institute for Asia (ISIA).

The article is published as part of the partnership between The Astana Times and CFive think tank.

World.title: Making of World No. 1: Elena Rybakina’s Journey
World.content:
ASTANA – On Sept. 12, Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina defeated Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 in the US Open final to claim the third Grand Slam title of her career.

The victory ended Sabalenka’s 19-match winning streak at the tournament and completed a remarkable rise for Rybakina. A few days before that, she became the world No. 1, the 30th woman in WTA history to reach the top of the rankings and the first player representing Kazakhstan to do so.

Rybakina had technically secured the No. 1 ranking before the final, after defeating Zheng Qinwen in the quarterfinals. But winning the title made the achievement even more significant.

It was also an unexpected conclusion to a tournament that had begun with uncertainty. Rybakina arrived in New York after spending a week away from the court because of a left-foot injury. She had retired during the first set of her Cincinnati match against Iga Swiatek, and that tournament could have given her an earlier opportunity to reach the top of the rankings.

Instead, she reached No. 1 in New York.

“I don’t want to put too much pressure on myself,” Rybakina said before the final, explaining that regardless of the result, she would still have other opportunities ahead.

The Grand Slam

Before 2026, the US Open was Rybakina’s least successful Grand Slam tournament.

Across eight previous appearances, she had never advanced beyond the fourth round. This time, however, she defeated Thea Frodin, Jessica Bouzas Maneiro and Yuliia Starodubtseva before overcoming former champion Naomi Osaka.

Her quarterfinal against Zheng Qinwen became another test of her ability to recover. Rybakina lost the opening set but fought back to win the match.

The semifinal against Coco Gauff followed a similar pattern. After losing the first set 3-6, Rybakina won the next two 6-4, 6-4 to reach her first US Open final.

Three consecutive comeback victories were significant for a player whose game has often been associated with a straightforward formula: a powerful serve, flat groundstrokes and an aggressive style of play.

In New York, she demonstrated another side of her game: the ability to adapt, recover and win when a match does not follow her preferred script.

A tennis player almost by accident

Rybakina was born in Moscow on June 17, 1999. She initially tried several sports with her elder sister Anna, including gymnastics and figure skating. Tennis came later.

Because of her height, gymnastics and figure skating eventually became less suitable, and her father, who was interested in tennis, suggested that she try the sport. She was six years old.

Rybakina trained first at Dynamo and later at Spartak, where she worked with former Top-10 player Andrei Chesnokov and former world No. 100 Evgenia Kulikovskaya.

For years, she did not have an individual coach. Until the age of 15, she trained in a group of around eight players and later in a smaller group of four.

Her daily schedule also looked different from that of many young elite athletes. She spent roughly two hours on tennis and another three hours on physical preparation while attending a regular school rather than a specialized sports school.

This became an important part of her development. Rybakina was not raised through one of the highly structured tennis academies that produce professional players from an early age. Much of the work that would eventually turn her into an elite athlete came later.

From junior success to an uncertain future

Rybakina entered the ITF junior circuit in November 2013, at the age of 14.

Her strongest junior season came in 2017. By the end of that season, she was ranked No. 3 in the world among juniors. But her path was not always smooth.

At the 2016 US Open junior tournament, Rybakina fainted because of low hemoglobin and withdrew in the first round. According to her account, her family did not receive sufficient assistance from representatives of the Russian Tennis Federation at the tournament.

After the incident, her parents decided that she would no longer travel to tournaments without them.

That created another problem: the cost.

Professional tennis requires constant travel, accommodation, coaching and tournament expenses. Her family could not indefinitely finance that lifestyle on its own.

As a result, Rybakina and her family seriously considered another route of moving to the United States or Canada, studying at a university and playing college tennis.

For a teenager who would eventually become world No. 1, a professional tennis career was still far from guaranteed.

The decision that changed her career

In 2018, shortly before turning 19, Rybakina received Kazakh citizenship and switched her sporting representation from Russia to Kazakhstan.

The initiative came from her father, Andrey Rybakin, who was born in Almaty. He contacted the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation, which offered financial support in exchange for her representing Kazakhstan.

Rybakina chose that opportunity instead of pursuing university tennis in the U.S.

The change affected her career in practical ways. The support allowed her to travel to tournaments, build a professional team and most importantly, work with a full-time coach who could accompany her on the tour.

In February 2019, Croatian coach Stefano Vukov became her coach. He was the first coach in her career to regularly travel with her to tournaments.

Rybakina later described Kazakhstan’s support as crucial.

“They believed in me,” she said in an interview with the WTA. “I was not so good when they offered. So they believed in me and they’re helping me a lot.”

The decision therefore meant more than simply changing the flag next to her name in the rankings. It came at a moment when Rybakina had to decide whether tennis would remain an after-school activity or become her profession. With Kazakhstan’s support, she chose the latter.

The first signs of a breakthrough

Rybakina’s first major breakthrough on the WTA Tour came in St. Petersburg in 2018.

After winning her first WTA-level match, she moved up from around No. 450 to No. 268. The following year brought an even bigger step. In July 2019, Rybakina won her first WTA title in Bucharest, which pushed her into the Top 100 for the first time, at No. 65. She ended the season ranked No. 37.

Then came 2020. Rybakina reached five finals during the season, more than any other women’s player that year, and won the title in Hobart. By the time the COVID-19 pandemic interrupted the tennis season, Rybakina had risen to No. 17 and become the first Kazakh player to enter the WTA Top 20.

In 2021, she reached her first Grand Slam quarterfinal at Roland Garros, defeating Serena Williams on the way, and finished fourth at the Tokyo Olympics.

Rybakina was no longer simply a promising young player. She was becoming one of the strongest players on tour.

Wimbledon 2022: the title that changed everything

The biggest moment of her career came at Wimbledon in 2022. At 23, Rybakina became the first player representing Kazakhstan to win a Grand Slam singles title.

The victory also created a complicated situation because Wimbledon had banned Russian and Belarusian players following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Rybakina had been born in Moscow and had represented Russia as a junior, leading to considerable discussion around her nationality and sporting identity.

There was another unusual consequence: Wimbledon did not award ranking points that year. As a result, winning the tournament did not improve Rybakina’s ranking in the way a Grand Slam victory normally would.

She ended 2022 ranked No. 22 and did not qualify for the WTA Finals.

From Grand Slam champion to a Top-3 player

The next major step came in 2023. Rybakina reached the Australian Open final and then won two WTA 1000 titles, in Indian Wells and Rome. In June, she reached a career-high No. 3 in the WTA rankings.

But the following two years were less straightforward. Injuries and health problems affected her schedule, while changes to her coaching team added another layer of uncertainty.

She split with Vukov after the 2024 US Open and briefly worked with former Wimbledon champion Goran Ivanisevic. She later reunited with Vukov, who was subsequently suspended by the WTA for 12 months. Rybakina also worked with Davide Sanguinetti during this period.

While she had fallen to No. 11 in April 2025, the year of 2025 became another turning point.

At the 2025 WTA Finals in Riyadh, Rybakina entered the tournament as the final qualifier among the eight players. She then won the entire tournament without losing a match. The victory brought her back into the world’s Top 5 and gave her the biggest title of her career since Wimbledon.

2026: the season that took her to the top

Rybakina began 2026 by winning the Australian Open. Rybakina won 6-4, 4-6, 6-4 in a match against Sabalenka to claim her second Grand Slam title.

She later won in Stuttgart and reached the finals in Indian Wells and Toronto.

When she arrived in New York, she was ranked No. 2. The gap between Rybakina and Sabalenka at the top of the rankings had become one of the central storylines of the season.

Rybakina secured the No. 1 ranking after defeating Zheng Qinwen in the quarterfinals. But she still had two matches to play.

“You never know how long you’re going to stay. I want to win the titles still in tournaments, so all my thoughts are just for the next match,” she said.

That mentality carried her through the semifinal against Gauff and into the final against Sabalenka.

Rybakina’s victory over Sabalenka in the US Open final completed perhaps the most successful season of her career.

She became a three-time Grand Slam champion, won her first US Open and became the first world No. 1 in the history of Kazakh tennis.

Rybakina said she would like to win the French Open one day and complete a career Grand Slam. The achievement matters, she said, but she does not want to spend too much time thinking about it. There will always be another tournament, another opponent and another problem to solve.

That perspective is consistent with the story of her career.

Rybakina was not a child prodigy who was destined for the top from the beginning. She started tennis because other sports were not a good fit. She trained without an individual coach for years. At 17, she was still considering university instead of professional tennis.

Her career changed when Kazakhstan offered her the support needed to make professional tennis financially and logistically possible. From there, the progress came step by step and the ranking is only one part of the story. The girl who once played tennis simply because it was something to do after school had become the best-ranked women’s player in the world.

And, for Rybakina, there was still another match ahead.

World.title: Armenia marks 35 years of independence: the country’s gains and losses, according to AI
World.content:
Armenia’s 35 years of independence: an AI assessment

Armenia is marking Independence Day. Thirty-five years ago, on 21 September 1991, an overwhelming majority of the population (99.51%) voted in a referendum to leave the USSR and establish an independent democratic state.

JAMnews asked artificial intelligence to analyse Armenia’s journey over the past 35 years.

According to the AI assessment, the past 35 years present a highly mixed picture. Armenia has made significant progress in democratisation, international integration and the development of state institutions.

At the same time, Armenia has suffered major losses. Wars have cost thousands of lives, driven emigration and resulted in the loss of territory. Above all, the country has yet to fully resolve its security concerns.

“The greatest achievement is the survival of an independent state. The greatest loss is the human cost and demographic price Armenia has paid over 35 years,” the AI concluded.

From survival to state-building

“35 years can be divided into three major stages.

1991–1998: survival and state-building — the declaration of independence, war, blockade, an energy crisis and economic collapse, but also the creation of the foundations of state institutions.

1999–2017: stabilisation and economic growth — macroeconomic stability, rapid growth and infrastructure development, but also emigration, corruption, a closed political system and the unresolved Karabakh conflict.

2018–2026: democratic transformation, war and a new foreign policy strategy — the 2018 “Velvet” Revolution, the 2020 war, the loss of Nagorno-Karabakh, the exodus of Karabakh Armenians from their homeland in 2023, the arrival of more than 100,000 forcibly displaced people in Armenia, and efforts to build a new security system and new foreign policy relationships.”

Key achievements

“Building an independent state”

The greatest achievement is that Armenia has existed for 35 years as an internationally recognised independent state, with its own Constitution, state institutions, army, currency, diplomatic system and international commitments.

Developing an international presence

Armenia joined the UN in 1992 and later joined numerous international organisations. This means that the Armenian state acts as an independent subject in international relations and makes its own decisions.

Building an army and defence system

During the war of the 1990s, Armenia established its armed forces. This became one of the key institutions underpinning its independent statehood.

Economic recovery and long-term growth

After the severe crisis of the early 1990s, the economy began to recover in 1994, followed by rapid growth in the 2000s. According to the World Bank, Armenia’s economy grew by an average of around 6.3% a year between 2000 and 2023. During this period, the economy shifted significantly from agriculture towards industry and services.

Development of the technology and services sectors

IT, services, finance and tourism now play a much larger role in the economy than they did during the early years of independence. This is particularly important for a small landlocked country.

Some improvement in living conditions

The World Bank notes an increase in life expectancy and improvements in several social indicators. Extreme poverty has been virtually eliminated. However, “ordinary poverty” remains a serious problem, particularly in rural areas.

Political change and the ability to transfer power

The peaceful transfer of power in 2018 demonstrated the potential for mass civic mobilisation and political change. Subsequent elections, including the 2021 early parliamentary election, were competitive and well organised, according to international observers, although political polarisation persisted.

Strengthening civil society and national identity

Independence created an environment in which the Armenian language, state symbols, national culture and the idea of statehood became the foundations of an independent country rather than a Soviet republic.”

Losses and setbacks

“Human losses

The First Karabakh War, the four-day war of 2016 and especially the 2020 war claimed thousands of lives and left deep trauma across Armenian society.

Consequences of the 2020 war

Armenia lost control over a significant part of the territories of Nagorno-Karabakh and its previous security system. After 2020, Armenia’s security environment changed radically. In 2024, the prime minister himself described 2020 as a moment when Armenia found itself on the verge of losing its independence.

The loss of homeland for Karabakh Armenians and population displacement

After the military escalation in September 2023, more than 100,000 people moved to Armenia. The International Committee of the Red Cross noted that Armenian social services and the accommodation system struggled to cope with such a large influx of displaced people. For Armenian society, this became not only a territorial loss but also a major demographic, social and psychological one.

Emigration and demographic problems

Mass emigration, which began in the early years of independence, became one of Armenia’s most persistent long-term problems. The World Bank identifies low birth rates, an ageing population and significant emigration as serious constraints on the country’s economic future.

Social inequality and poverty

Despite years of strong economic performance, economic growth has not always translated evenly into higher living standards. According to the World Bank, as of 2022, around half of the population still lived below the international poverty line of $6.85 a day. This threshold applies to upper-middle-income countries.

Weak institutions and political polarisation

Over 35 years, Armenia has not achieved full judicial independence, eliminated corruption or overcome political polarisation. A 2026 analysis by Human Rights Watch says that, despite reforms, serious problems remain concerning the independence of the judiciary, the media and the police, as well as the protection of human rights.

Excessive reliance on external security partners

For 35 years, Armenia has had to build its security system amid difficult regional and geopolitical conditions. Its long-standing reliance on Russia for security and, in recent years, the need to diversify its partnerships show that full strategic autonomy remains a work in progress.”

Independence as a fact

“Armenia has managed to create and preserve an independent state, but it has not yet transformed that independence into a state system that is sufficiently secure, demographically sustainable and socially prosperous.

It is important to distinguish between independence as a legal and statehood fact and independence as a real characteristic of a state. Armenia achieved the former in 1991. The latter — economic, military, demographic, institutional and diplomatic independence — remains an ongoing process.

At the same time, the picture of recent years is not limited to losses. In 2025, Armenia and Azerbaijan made progress towards a peace settlement. The prospect of restoring regional ties has also created an opportunity for a new stage to begin, although it is still too early to assess its long-term results.”

Armenia’s 35 years of independence: an AI assessment

World.title: ‘Intergenerational solidarity’ and avoiding payments: how pensions work in Abkhazia
World.content:
A 71-year-old resident of Abkhazia Marina Kachubeevna recently submitted documents to apply for Russian citizenship. Without a Russian passport, she cannot receive a Russian pension, which is relatively generous by local standards.

Her Abkhaz pension, which totals 6,000 roubles [$65] a month including all basic payments and supplements, is not enough to live on. So the woman has to continue working to have money of her own.

“I have wonderful children. My son and daughter-in-law never refuse me anything. When I started having health problems last year, they took full responsibility for paying for my medicines and doctors.

But every time I have to ask them for money for the pharmacy or basic personal needs, I feel uncomfortable. I don’t want to be a burden. At 71, I want to remain independent and be able to buy even small gifts for my grandchildren myself, without having to ask my children for the money,” Marina Kachubeevna says.

This desire to ease the financial burden on her family is the only reason she decided to apply for Russian citizenship.

Intergenerational solidarity and the reality of pension payments

The story of Marina Kachubeevna reflects broader systemic trends in Abkhazia’s social welfare system.

At present, around 33,000 people receive the basic old-age pension of 6,000 roubles. As the chairman of the republic’s Pension Fund, Denis Gularia, acknowledges, this amount falls far short of what is needed to live on.

However, Gularia points to a traditional model of social support in Abkhaz society, based on assistance from relatives.

“There is such a concept as intergenerational solidarity: children should help their parents. Of course, some pensioners do not have children, but this is the kind of society we have. Neighbours help each other as much as they can.

We constantly hear criticism directed at us. We hear it and understand it. But people have to help each other,” the Pension Fund chairman says.

He also stresses that the number of people receiving additional domestic payments continues to grow:

“The number of people receiving supplementary payments is approaching 17,000 and will continue to grow. Many of our citizens no longer have enough Soviet-era work experience to qualify for a pension from Russia’s Social Fund, so they will receive only our payments. We will try to find the funds to increase these payments in the future.”

41,000 workers supporting 50,000 pensioners

The main obstacle to a significant increase in pensions is the imbalance between the number of officially employed residents and the number of people receiving pensions and benefits.

According to statistics, Abkhazia has a working-age population of 144,000. Of these, around 40,000–41,000 people officially work and pay social insurance contributions. Meanwhile, around 51,000 people receive supplementary payments or pensions.

“With this ratio, high pensions are simply impossible. The remaining part of the population, around 100,000 people, work but do not contribute to the Pension Fund,” Gularia explains.

Commercial businesses also create an additional problem by avoiding full payment of social insurance contributions:

“Unfortunately, not everyone declares their full salary. The minimum salary in commercial organisations here is 20,000 roubles [$215]**. But if someone earns more, employers and employees often agree to declare only the minimum.

People themselves should have an interest in ensuring that social insurance contributions are paid. Remember, the contributions made by the 40,000 people who work today support the entire older generation.”

Reforms, collection orders and individual records

To change the situation, the Pension Fund plans to introduce individual records for insurance contributions and tighten fiscal discipline.

“A flat-rate system is unfair to those who pay honestly. One person pays contributions based on their actual salary, while another declares the minimum, yet they both receive the same pension. That is unfair.

Once we introduce individual records for insurance contributions, it will benefit people who plan to remain economically active: in addition to the basic 6,000 roubles, they will receive substantial payments based on the contributions recorded in their personal account,” Gularia says.

At the same time, the fund is actively working with employers who fail to meet their obligations. According to the chairman, the agency can issue collection orders when contributions are overdue. A collection order allows a bank to debit money from a payer’s account without prior consent. In 2025, the fund recovered 49.9 million roubles [around $537,000] in this way.

Some businesses also voluntarily repay old debts.

“We need to adopt legislation that strengthens the responsibility of managers and accountants who fail to submit reports on time,” Gularia says.

Re-registration for oversight and transparency

The re-registration of pensioners, which runs from 1 September to 1 December 2026, is another necessary step towards putting the system in order.

“There are cases when relatives do not always register a pensioner’s death promptly or submit the death certificate to social welfare offices. The money saved as a result of these checks will go into a fund for future increases in supplementary payments to the most vulnerable groups,” the official explains.

Apparently, bringing businesses out of the shadow economy, introducing individual records and ensuring that people pay their contributions properly offer the only way to ensure that, in a few years, pensioners such as Marina Kachubeevna can retire without financial worries, feel secure and afford to buy gifts for their grandchildren without having to work at the age of 71.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Features of the pension system in Abkhazia

World.title: Georgian authorities ‘suspect’ Tbilisi School of Political Studies of receiving grant without their consent
World.content:
The Georgian State Audit Office has launched an investigation into the financial activities of the Tbilisi School of Political Studies. The Audit Office’s Financial Transparency Department said the investigation concerns the possible receipt of a grant without the Georgian government’s consent.

“To examine the matter comprehensively, the State Audit Office will act within the powers granted to it by Georgian law, including the Law of Georgia on Grants,” the Audit Office told Interpressnews.

The Tbilisi School of Political Studies was founded in 1999 as a non-governmental organisation. The school operates under the auspices of the Council of Europe and is headed by politician Armaz Akhvlediani.

What happened

Government officials have repeatedly spoken about the Tbilisi School of Political Studies in recent weeks. Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said the school had held a seminar in the village of Bakhmaro with funding from the Council of Europe. He suggested that the funding for the event may have bypassed Georgian law.

According to Papuashvili, the school did not seek the government’s consent to receive the grant, while the Council of Europe’s media office said the event in Bakhmaro did not constitute a grant.

“So what was it, then?” Papuashvili asked.

He said the original version of the Law on Grants required government approval for all forms of foreign funding, including direct spending by organisations. The final version retained an exception for diplomatic activities. However, Papuashvili argued that organisations should not use this exception to circumvent the law.

ПPapuashvili suggests that, in the case of the seminar in Bakhmaro, the Council of Europe’s local office directly paid for hotel accommodation, transport and food, as well as fees for experts and speakers.

“If that is the case, we are dealing with an attempt to circumvent the law,” the speaker said.

According to Papuashvili, the law also covers cases where an agreement is described as a service contract but in substance amounts to a grant.

What the Law on Grants provides

The legislative package approved on 4 March 2026 significantly broadens the definition of a “grant”. It covers both financial and non-financial support if it can be used to influence the country’s domestic or foreign policy, including activities linked to the interests of a foreign state or political force.

The law also strengthens the State Audit Office’s oversight of the awarding and receipt of grants. If a foreign legal entity funds a branch operating in Georgia without government approval, it can face sanctions, including a fine equal to twice the value of the grant.

Violating the grants law can also result in criminal liability. Penalties include a fine, community service or up to six years in prison.

The changes also affect the political process. People who work for organisations that receive predominantly foreign funding will be barred from joining political parties for eight years. At the same time, restrictions imposed on political parties also apply to entities that are not formally parties but effectively engage in political activity.

The legislative package also tightens administrative liability for private companies if they become involved in public political activity.

Georgia’s Law on Grants

World.title: New interpretation of Georgia’s relations with Russia? How history is presented in new school textbooks
World.content:
Protest against new Georgian history textbooks

From September 2026, state and private schools in Georgia have been teaching the country’s history using new textbooks. They immediately sparked widespread criticism.

Many teachers are angry that they had no opportunity to review the new Georgian history textbook for the 10th grade in advance. This is the penultimate grade in state schools.

The Education Ministry published the first part of the new textbook on 11 September — just four days before the school year began.

The textbook immediately became the subject of widespread criticism. Historians say it contains factual errors, inaccuracies, questionable wording and, in their view, distorted interpretations.

One of the main areas of criticism concerns the interpretation of historical events. This is particularly evident in the sections covering Georgia’s relations with Russia.

Key new elements in the Georgian history textbook

So far, only the first part of the new textbook has been published. It contains 185 pages. Its cover features King David the Builder and Queen Tamar, monarchs associated with the “golden age” of Georgian history.

The textbook follows the “individual in history” approach.

This means that historical processes are presented through specific historical figures rather than in chronological order.

The authors explain their approach in the very first chapter:

“Perhaps everyone has asked themselves this question: do individuals make history, or does history shape individuals? Why does history remember some people for centuries while others fall into oblivion?

The centuries-old history of our homeland is closely linked to outstanding individuals who played a major role in the development of the Georgian state and national unity.”

The textbook begins with King Pharnavaz, who lived at the turn of the fourth and third centuries BC, and ends with the national liberation movement of the 20th century in the 1980s and 1990s.

Each lesson ends with sources, questions and exercises. Some sections also contain an “Expert opinion” box, which provides an assessment of a particular historical event.

The first page features a QR code. Scanning it with a mobile phone plays the Georgian national anthem.

Historians’ assessments: “Errors, outdated sources, no room for analytical thinking”

After finally getting an opportunity to examine the new textbook, many Georgian historians published sharply critical comments and reviews.

Scholars say the textbook contains factual errors and inaccuracies, while some of the historical sources it cites also raise questions.

“The authors make insufficient use of the latest research and new sources and often rely on historiographical views that took shape decades ago,” historian Shota Matitashvili writes in a detailed and highly critical review.

Historian and researcher of contemporary history Giorgi Arkania says the new textbook resembles a set of lecture notes, with no logical links between individual lessons.

According to him, the exercises in the book do not aim to develop students’ analytical thinking, encourage discussion or help them form alternative views.

Arkania also notes that the book’s content does not match its stated principle of studying history through individuals. The biographies are presented schematically and do not give students enough material for analysis.

Shota Matitashvili also notes that despite the “individual in history” approach, the textbook omits some important historical figures. In his view, these chronological gaps make it harder to understand the historical process.

“Students learn a lot about whom they should consider the makers of Georgian history. They learn much less about why history developed the way it did. And they learn even less about how we know, analyse and debate what this history means,” Professor Oliver Reisner wrote in his brief review.

According to him, teaching history with the aim of developing a democratic understanding of citizenship should not be limited to learning authoritative interpretations of the national past.

Students need to learn how historical knowledge is constructed, how to compare conflicting sources and interpretations, and how to develop their own evidence-based views of history, Reisner argues.

Giorgi Saakadze — unequivocal hero or controversial figure?

Giorgi Arkania pointed out numerous problematic passages in the textbook. One concerns Giorgi Saakadze, one of the most prominent figures of the early 17th century.

According to Arkania, the textbook presents Saakadze unequivocally as a positive hero, much as Soviet-era textbooks did.

The historian says, however, that Saakadze was a highly controversial figure. For example, during the devastation of Kakheti and the forced relocation of Georgians from the region, he served as one of Shah Abbas’s advisers and planned military operations for him.

“The section on Giorgi Saakadze should have presented both sides, allowing students to consider for themselves what role he should play in the history of the modern state,” the historian says.

Because of such details, some historians compare parts of the textbook to a toast — a story celebrating a legendary historical figure.

“The textbook fails to teach students the fundamental principle of history as a science — a critical approach to sources,” Shota Matitashvili writes.

He also criticises the authors for failing to use the latest research and new sources, and for often relying on historiographical views that took shape decades ago.

For example, one of the sources about King Vakhtang Gorgasali says:

“At the time, Vakhtang was 22 years old. And he was the greatest of all kings. He had a handsome appearance and great strength, so that he could hold up a building and a heavy iron hammer, lift a Georgian horse onto his shoulders and climb from Mtskheta to the fortress of Armazi.”

“A table toast” — this is how historian Giorgi Astamadze described the passage.

Many other excerpts from the book also reminded him of toasts.

A new, more positive interpretation of Georgia’s relations with Russia

Giorgi Arkania examined in detail one of the lessons — “Leaders of the national liberation movement” [of the late 20th century]. The lesson covers seven pages. The historian says he found at least ten errors in those seven pages alone.

In his assessment, the book misrepresents the main content of a proclamation issued by the Gorgasliani organisation.

Gorgasliani was an illegal underground anti-Soviet youth organisation. Among its members were Zviad Gamsakhurdia and Merab Kostava [well-known leaders of the national liberation movement — JAMnews], as well as other young people. They founded the organisation while they were still school students.

The textbook says that members of the organisation put up proclamations on the streets of Tbilisi condemning Soviet violence in Hungary.

However, the main purpose of the proclamations was not Hungary, but to call on people to fight for Georgia’s independence and freedom. They referred to the 9 March tragedy (1956) in Tbilisi and the events of 1924 and 1937, and called for resistance to Moscow’s rule. The proclamations described the Soviet regime as an occupier.

Context. According to various estimates, between 100 and several hundred people were killed in Tbilisi on 9 March 1956, when Soviet forces violently dispersed mass demonstrations. Security forces also opened machine-gun fire from the windows of the Ministry of Communications building at tens of thousands of people gathered on Rustaveli Avenue. The protests were sparked by Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev’s speech denouncing Stalin’s cult of personality, in which he emphasised Stalin’s Georgian origins. In August–September 1924, a large-scale armed uprising against Soviet rule, established in Georgia in 1921, swept across the country. 1937 — the peak of Stalinist repression and the beginning of the mass Great Terror.

“That was the main message of the proclamation. At the same time, its authors addressed the Hungarian people, who were gradually breaking free from Soviet control. This served as an example for Georgians: just as the Hungarians had raised their voices, the people of Georgia had to raise their voices against Soviet rule,” Arkania says.

From the text of the proclamation: “Georgians! Have you forgotten the bloody night of 9 March? Have you forgotten the bloody years of 1924 and 1937, the years of the expulsion and extermination of the Georgian people? How much longer must we bow our heads beneath the swords of the Communists? … Today, when all conscious humanity is outraged by Moscow’s terrible atrocities, when the very existence of our nation is at stake, the time has come to unite under a common flag and fight against the occupiers of our homeland … Down with the occupiers and their military hordes, whose hands are stained with the blood of our people!”

Historian Giorgi Arkania points to other factually inaccurate interpretations in the textbook.

“For example, the seventh paragraph of the lesson mentions only the arrest of Merab Kostava: ‘Merab Kostava was first arrested in 1956 … and for the second time in 1977.’ This gives students the impression that the Soviet regime did not persecute Zviad Gamsakhurdia,” the historian says.

He also disagrees with the textbook’s description of the events in Tbilisi from 22 December 1991 to 6 January 1992 as the “Tbilisi War”.

“In other words, a direct armed coup, the overthrow of Georgia’s constitutional order and the ousting of its democratically elected president are described as the ‘Tbilisi War’. The word ‘coup’ is not mentioned at all. Yet the state classified the event as a coup as early as the 2000s.

This was not simply the ousting of Zviad Gamsakhurdia. It was the overthrow of Georgian statehood. Ignoring this enormous crime and presenting it to schoolchildren in a distorted way is tantamount to a crime,” Arkania says.

Interestingly, the textbook Contemporary History of Georgia, published in 2008, assesses the events of 1991–1992 as follows: “In December 1991–January 1992, the legitimate government in Tbilisi was overthrown by military force. The military coup led to civil unrest in the country.”

A 2012 history textbook for 12th-graders published by Diogene begins its account with the escalation of the confrontation between the government and the opposition, while the relevant section is devoted entirely to the topic “The coup in Georgia (1991–92)”.

A new interpretation of the Treaty of Georgievsk, which brought Georgia into the Russian Empire

Historian Giorgi Astamadze took a particularly close look at the sections covering the later period of Georgian history and the country’s relations with Russia, especially the reign of King Erekle II and the Treaty of Georgievsk.

The Treaty of Georgievsk was signed on 24 July (4 August New Style) 1783 between the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and the Russian Empire. King Erekle II renounced an independent foreign policy and accepted the protection of the Russian emperor. In return, Russia pledged to defend Kartli-Kakheti’s territorial integrity, preserve the rule of the Bagrationi dynasty and provide military assistance. However, Russia did not fully honour its commitments. In 1795, when Agha Mohammad Khan invaded Kartli-Kakheti and devastated Tbilisi, Russian military assistance did not arrive in time. A few years later, Russia itself violated the treaty’s principles. In 1801, it abolished the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and incorporated it into the Russian Empire.

The new textbook devotes a rather dry, informational section to the Treaty of Georgievsk.

The authors write that Erekle II unsuccessfully sought help from European monarchs. The Caucasus was a distant region for them. Therefore, the textbook says, Erekle II had to seek an alliance with the Russian Empire.

“On 24 July 1783, the Treaty of Georgievsk was signed. Under the treaty, Kartli-Kakheti accepted Russian protection while retaining internal independence and the autocephaly of its church. Under the agreement, Russian troops were also supposed to be stationed in Georgia to defend the country.” The lesson ends its discussion of the treaty there.

The textbook also includes a separate “Scholar’s opinion” box featuring the views of literary scholar Geronti Kikodze.

“In the quotation, Geronti Kikodze says that Erekle II had good judgement. He is referring to the treaty with Russia, which Erekle II himself was actually very dissatisfied with during his lifetime. It is interesting to ask who Geronti Kikodze was and why his opinion on this issue should appear in a school history textbook. Geronti Kikodze was not a historian at all. He was a literary scholar and therefore could not claim professional expertise in history,” Giorgi Astamadze says.

The historian recalled Kikodze’s ties to the Bolshevik authorities and the senior positions he held in the Soviet occupation administration. Giorgi Astamadze argues that “the openly collaborationist views of such a person on the national question have no basis, either in terms of his competence or from a moral standpoint.”

“The current Georgian regime’s publicly stated position that ties with Russia supposedly saved us has now been officially incorporated into a school textbook. And they have done so through the words of the writer Geronti Kikodze, presenting his opinion as a scholar’s view,” the historian says.

Interestingly, the previous Georgian history textbook included an assessment of the Treaty of Georgievsk by Ivane Javakhishvili, a classic of Georgian historical scholarship. He sharply criticised the treaty.

“The 1783 treaty brought nothing to Georgia. But the harm was enormous. Instead of improving Georgia’s political position, it made it dramatically worse. Much has been said about this treaty and the protection offered by the Russian state. In reality, however, the assistance Russia provided to Georgia was very limited,” Ivane Javakhishvili wrote.

Are the years 1918–1921 — the period when Georgia gained independence — missing from the textbook?

After the first part of the textbook was published, social media users actively discussed the absence of events from 1918–1921 — Georgia’s declaration of independence, the establishment of the First Democratic Republic, its political leaders and the subsequent Soviet occupation of Georgia in 1921.

Previous history textbooks treated this period as a separate and important topic.

Does this mean that 1918–1921 has been removed from the curriculum?

“It is not known yet. Historians consider this unlikely. Most likely, this material will appear in the next parts of the textbook. The introduction to the first part says that the textbook will consist of four parts.

In principle, the other parts should cover the First Republic, the Soviet occupation, the Soviet totalitarian system, the Russian-Georgian wars, including the August 2008 war. We are waiting. I hope the authors will write these sections in a way that dispels doubts and preserves the textbook’s factual character,” Giorgi Arkania says.

Does the textbook create the impression of a party narrative?

The authors of the new textbook are Jaba Samushia, Giorgi Kalandia and Aleksandre Boshishvili. Samushia also serves as a reviewer.

Jaba Samushia and Aleksandre Boshishvili are affiliated with the academic community of Tbilisi State University. Samushia has served as the university’s rector since 2022.

Giorgi Kalandia heads a state cultural institution. Since 2019, he has served as general director of the Art Palace of Georgia.

Because of these connections, some historians consider the authors affiliated with the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Additional questions concern the selection process: the state chose the authors, but it is unclear exactly how it did so.

“I hope that political considerations did not lead to certain issues being deliberately left unaddressed. However, after reading the textbook, one definitely gets the impression that some issues have been overlooked. For example, the coup I mentioned earlier.

The word ‘coup’ still creates a certain degree of political discomfort, and perhaps that is why the textbook does not give this period enough attention. The same applies to the proclamation.

Perhaps the authors considered it inconvenient to emphasise the word ‘occupation’ and remind students about the repressions,” historian Giorgi Arkania says.

Historian Giorgi Astamadze puts it more directly. He says the interpretations do not surprise him because historians close to Georgian Dream wrote the textbook. “I was completely certain that this was how it would turn out,” he says.

“We cannot allow new generations to remain unaware of what Russia has done to Georgia for more than two centuries: occupation, deception, humiliation, the abolition of the monarchy and the Church’s autocephaly, and the constant struggle against the Georgian Orthodox Church. These are facts that every young person in the country should know,” politician Pikria Chikhradze says.

On 14 September, she held a special briefing dedicated to the history textbooks. She said directly that “the authors linked to Georgian Dream used the opportunity to bring party narratives into school textbooks”.

Can schools refuse to use the new textbook?

For around two decades, Georgia had an entire textbook evaluation system. Different groups of authors and publishers produced textbooks, which the ministry then evaluated. Schools could have several approved textbooks for the same subject and grade and choose between them.

In 2026, the government began gradually replacing this system with a single state textbook model. Under the new system, the Education Ministry takes responsibility for producing textbooks.

Education Minister Givi Mikanadze said that the main principle would now be: “one grade — one subject — one standard textbook”.

Once the reform is complete, this principle should apply to both state and private schools. The ministry plans to complete the process by 2028.

But schools have no choice when it comes to the Georgian history textbook for the 10th grade discussed in this article. They must teach from this new book.

The replacement of school textbooks is part of a large-scale reform announced by the education minister. He spoke about the reform as early as October 2025.

The minister said the changes were necessary to ensure that school textbooks focused on “national values” and aimed to “raise citizens with a state-oriented mindset and national values”.

He also warned that the design of textbook covers would change, with “patriotic themes” appearing on them.

Protest against new Georgian history textbooks

World.title: Why can Russia conscript students from Abkhazia?
World.content:
Russia conscripts Abkhaz students

A schoolteacher, lawyer and blogger from Abkhazia, Said Beya, has looked into the issue of Abkhaz students studying in Russia being conscripted into the Russian army.

Said Beya: “Recently, there has been active public discussion of reports that the Abkhaz Foreign Ministry is trying to reach an agreement with Russia so that our students with dual citizenship are not required to register for military service in Russia.

Many people are asking: ‘How is this even possible? We are already registered for military service at home!’

Let’s look at the legal side of the issue and see where exactly the mistake was made.



What is the legal basis?

The status of people holding both passports is governed by the Agreement between Russia and the Republic of Abkhazia on resolving issues of dual citizenship. The document was signed by the Abkhaz and Russian sides in Sukhumi on 19 September 2022. Following a lengthy ratification process, the agreement fully entered into force on 25 April 2025.

The main source of the problem lies in Article 5 of the agreement. It states:

‘Persons holding citizenship of both parties shall perform compulsory military service in the party in whose territory they permanently reside at the time of conscription.’

The agreement protects those who have already completed military service in Abkhazia, meaning they cannot be conscripted in Russia. But if a young man has not yet served in the Abkhaz armed forces and travels to Russia to study, he becomes vulnerable to conscription.”

Why does Russia have the right to do this?

For the Russian authorities, anyone holding a Russian passport while in the country is regarded exclusively as a Russian citizen. An Abkhaz passport carries no weight with Russian military recruitment offices.

Under Russia’s law on military service, any Russian citizen who moves to a new place for more than three months is required to register with the local military authorities.

Students who come to Russia to study obtain temporary registration in halls of residence or rented accommodation, usually for several years. The Russian side interprets this unequivocally: if a young man lives and studies in Russia, then under Article 5 of the agreement, Russia is his current place of residence. This means the military recruitment office is entitled to require him to report for registration and conscript him for military service, unless he is eligible for a student deferment.

Why did the Abkhaz side fail to address this issue when signing the agreement in 2022?

This is now the main question facing the Abkhaz diplomats and officials who drafted and signed the document in 2022.

There appears to be a significant legal omission:

A crucial exemption is missing. Article 5 of the agreement does not contain wording along the lines of: “…with the exception of citizens temporarily staying in the territory of the other Party for the purpose of receiving an education.”

Had such a provision been included, Russian military recruitment offices would have had no grounds to make such demands of Abkhaz students.

In 2022, our authorities signed a framework agreement without taking some of the legal nuances into account.

Years later, after large numbers of students were told to register for military service in Russia, the Abkhaz Foreign Ministry has been forced to hold urgent meetings with the president and seek to renegotiate the issue with Moscow.

While these negotiations continue, the requirements imposed by Russian military recruitment offices on students temporarily registered in Russia unfortunately remain lawful.

For now, the only way for these students to avoid conscription is to make sure they obtain an official student defermentin Russia in time.”
