World.title: Azerbaijan’s 2027 budget: how will fall in oil revenues be offset?
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s 2027 budget

The Azerbaijani government forecasts lower state budget revenues from the oil and gas sector in 2027, while tax revenues are expected to rise. Preliminary figures point to moderate growth in government spending and a greater role for non-oil revenues in financing the budget.

These changes will also affect working people. From next year, the income tax rate on salaries in the private non-oil sector will increase. As a result, higher tax payments on wages will partly drive the growth in budget revenues.

According to a statement published by the Finance Ministry on 16 September, these figures are only preliminary. The figures may change before the government submits the draft budget to parliament.

How will budget revenues and spending change in 2027?

In 2027, state budget revenues are forecast at 39.234 billion manats, while spending will reach 42.4 billion manats (around $25 billion). Compared with the approved figures for 2026, revenues will rise by 1.6% and spending by 1.7%. The difference between revenues and spending — the budget deficit — is expected to reach 3.166 billion manats (around $1.86 billion).

This comparison uses the planned figures for 2026 and 2027. If actual budget execution in 2026 differs from the approved figures, the growth rate in 2027 compared with the actual results will also differ.

Higher spending in monetary terms does not automatically mean that the state will provide more services. Price rises must also be taken into account. If maintaining schools, buying medicines or repairing roads becomes more expensive, some of the additional funding will go towards maintaining the existing level of services.

A 1.7% increase in the overall budget also does not mean that funding for all sectors will rise at the same rate. The government may increase spending in one area while cutting it in another. For citizens, therefore, the overall size of the budget matters less than which services receive the funding.

Why are oil revenues falling?

Budget revenues from the oil and gas sector are forecast at 15.48 billion manats (around $9.1 billion). This is 955 million manats (around $562 million) less than the amount planned for the current year. Of this reduction, 935 million manats (around $550 million) comes from a cut in transfers from the State Oil Fund. Next year, the government plans to transfer 11.9 billion manats (around $7 billion).

The main change, therefore, is a reduction in the amount the State Oil Fund transfers to the state budget. This should not be interpreted as an equivalent fall in the country’s oil sales revenues. The fund’s revenues and the amount it transfers to the state budget are separate indicators.

The budget will nevertheless continue to receive significant support from the State Oil Fund. The planned transfer will account for 30.3% of budget revenues, meaning roughly one in every three manats will come from the fund.

Where will the additional funds come from?

Revenues collected by the State Tax Service are forecast at 18.43 billion manats (around $10.85 billion). This is 1.52 billion manats (around $894 million), or 9%, more than the amount planned for the current year. Customs revenues will increase by just 3 million manats and are expected to reach 6.865 billion manats (around $4.04 billion).

Personal income tax revenues are expected to rise by 690 million manats (around $406 million) to 3.07 billion manats (around $1.8 billion). This is around 29% more than the amount planned for the current year.

Corporate income tax revenues are planned at 6.983 billion manats (around $4.01 billion). The government therefore expects higher tax revenues from both personal incomes and corporate profits.

The increase in tax revenues cannot be explained solely by stronger economic activity. Revenues can rise not only because of higher wages, employment and corporate profits, but also because of changes in tax rates and more effective tax collection. More detailed calculations are needed to determine how much each factor contributes.

However, the additional revenues will not be enough to cover all spending. According to preliminary calculations, the government plans to finance 2.751 billion manats (around $1.62 billion) of the 3.166 billion-manat budget deficit through borrowing. It plans to cover the remaining amount with funds left in the Treasury account and proceeds from privatisation.

Overall, the government plans to cover around 87% of the deficit through borrowing. Borrowing allows the government to finance current spending, but it also creates obligations for future budgets to pay interest and repay the debt. Assessing budget sustainability therefore requires looking at borrowing terms and how the government plans to use the funds it raises.

What will change for salaried workers?

According to an official explanation from the State Tax Service, in 2026 the tax rate on the first 2,500 manats (around $1,470) of monthly taxable income for employees in the private non-oil and gas sector is 3%. In 2027, it will rise to 5%, and to 7% from 2028.

For example, if monthly taxable income after allowances is 1,000 manats (around $588), income tax will rise from 30 to 50 manats (around $17.65 to $29.40). With the tax base unchanged, this means an additional 20 manats (around $11.80) a month, or 240 manats (around $142) a year.

This calculation covers income tax only. The final amount a worker receives after tax also depends on other mandatory deductions and the tax allowances that apply to them. The changes do not affect workers in all sectors.

If an employer does not increase the gross salary and other deductions remain unchanged, the higher tax will reduce the worker’s take-home pay. To keep take-home pay at the same level, an employer may need to increase its labour costs.

Will higher social payments offset the higher tax burden?

Vugar Bayramov, a member of the Milli Majlis Economic Policy Committee, views the expected increase in the share of non-oil revenues to more than 60% positively. He considers this important for budget sustainability. According to him, structural reforms and greater transparency in public procurement could allow the government to allocate additional funds to social needs.

Economist Natig Jafarli said on 8 September, before the publication of the preliminary budget figures, that he expected pensions and salaries for public-sector employees to rise by 8–10%. He stressed that higher social payments sometimes only offset rising prices. This is the economist’s expectation.

Even if such increases take place, it cannot be said that they will offset the additional tax burden on private-sector employees. Higher salaries, pensions and benefits affect different groups of the population.

The preliminary figures point to the following trend: as transfers from the State Oil Fund decline, the government plans to increase tax revenues. What this will mean for citizens will depend on which services receive the additional funding, as well as on how their incomes and everyday expenses change.

World.title: Azerbaijan security service terrorism case spans five countries – what  is known so far?
World.content:
Azerbaijan security service operation in five countries

Azerbaijan says money collected for religious ceremonies was transferred to terrorist organisations using cryptocurrency. In a statement issued on 18 September, the State Security Service (SSS) said the alleged financing scheme and preparations to assassinate public and religious figures were being investigated as part of the same criminal case.

However, the statement published by the media does not specify the amount of money involved, the organisations alleged to have received it, or the five countries where the operations were carried out.

Information available from open sources does not allow the scale of the case to be independently verified. Available reports largely repeat the account provided by the agency conducting the investigation.

Charges brought

The SSS named the defendants as Vugar Abdullayev, Jalal Hajiyev, Javid Aliyev, Nijat Ahmadov, Nazim Aliyev, Ilkin Hasanzade, Aykhan Huseynov, Elshan Asgarov, Fakhraddin Imanov, Nail Rasulov and Elgun Ismayilov. Although the statement says 10 people were detained, it lists 11 defendants. The reason for the discrepancy is not explained.

They have been charged under Criminal Code articles relating to financing terrorism, forming a criminal organisation, preparing an assassination attempt against a state or public figure, and other offences. According to the SSS, a court ordered the defendants to be remanded in custody.

Link between two strands of case

In the SSS account, Jalal Hajiyev’s name appears both in connection with the alleged assassination plot and the financing scheme. The agency says Vugar Abdullayev and other defendants gathered information about the movements and security arrangements of the alleged targets. Hajiyev, meanwhile, is alleged to have used his contacts abroad to arrange money transfers to people involved in armed conflicts, as well as to terrorist organisations.

Although the two strands are being investigated as part of the same case, the SSS does not specify how they are linked financially. Were the funds allegedly transferred abroad used to finance preparations for the assassination attempts in Azerbaijan? Although some of the same individuals feature in both strands of the case, no evidence has been presented to establish a link between the movement of funds and the planning of the alleged attacks.

How was money traced?

According to the SSS, the funds were collected through fake s posted on social media, purportedly seeking donations for religious ceremonies. The agency says investigators obtained evidence showing where the money came from and how it was transferred.

To independently assess these claims, key evidence would include an archive of the s, payment details, transaction dates and information about the recipients. It is also unclear whether those who transferred the money knew its alleged true purpose or were themselves deceived – a distinction that could imply different degrees of responsibility.

The reference to cryptocurrency alone does not explain how the alleged financing scheme worked. The SSS does not say which digital assets were used, who controlled the addresses involved in the transactions, or how investigators established links between the recipients and terrorist organisations.

A 2023 report by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) describes the risks of social media fundraising and the use of virtual assets for terrorist financing. It also highlights the difficulty of proving that funds were intended for terrorist purposes and stresses the importance of protecting legitimate charitable activity.

International experience suggests that the mechanism described by the SSS is possible in principle. However, the allegations against specific individuals would need to be supported by evidence in the criminal case. So far, that evidence has not been made public.

World.title: Abkhaz punk rock: TOM SQUARE leader Salima Sagaria tells her story – VIDEO
World.content:
Punk rock in Abkhazia

This story is about a rare phenomenon: Abkhaz punk. Salima Sagaria and her band TOM SQUARE could be described as unique.

Salima began her career in pop music and turned to punk several years ago.

“People say different things to me. Many are supportive and say they are glad that this kind of music has finally appeared in Abkhazia. But there is also a lot of hate. At the beginning of the year, I posted a clip from my new song online. I wasn’t wearing any make-up, I was in ordinary clothes at home, just sitting there and shaking my hair around. For some reason, that really shocked a lot of people. I received threats and was even cursed.

“Our latest track is about exactly that: why so many people are afraid of change, and why our society does not want to move forward and change. This attachment to tradition also manifests itself in preventing creative people from expressing themselves,” Salima says.

“But I’m going to keep going, releasing new tracks and mixing different styles. I want to bring traditional instruments and choir into punk rock. I like introducing something new.”

World.title: Azerbaijani Speaker highlights AI’s role in education at IPU briefing (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 21. The Speaker of the Azerbaijani Parliament, Sahiba Gafarova, stated that artificial intelligence (AI) can make education more inclusive and accessible during an online briefing organized by the Inter-Parliamentary Union’s Committee on the Rights of Children.

This was reported by the Press and Public Relations Department of the Milli Majlis (Azerbaijani Parliament).

According to the information, the meeting was dedicated to the topic "Artificial Intelligence – the Opportunities and Risks in Providing Children’s Right to Inclusive and Quality Education" on September 21.

The speaker noted that the issue of artificial intelligence and education is not merely about technology; it also concerns children's futures and the quality of education provided to them.

According to her, while technology can enhance education, it cannot replace teachers or human interaction.

She also noted that AI can tailor the learning process to each child's needs, expand educational opportunities for children with disabilities, and help deliver quality educational resources to remote communities. AI can also assist teachers in identifying gaps in students' learning.

The speaker emphasized that the opportunities created by AI aren't automatically accessible to everyone. The fact that access depends on family income and place of residence could further deepen inequalities. Therefore, she stressed the importance of considering risks associated with privacy, algorithmic bias, harmful content, and the ambiguity of human accountability in this field.

Gafarova said that children's rights must be the guiding principle for the use of artificial intelligence in education. She noted that AI should assist teachers rather than replace their professional judgment, and it shouldn’t reduce children to mere collections of data.

She highlighted the important role parliaments play in this area.

The speaker remarked that the AI ​​initiative could assist parliaments in exchanging legislative experiences, developing practical recommendations, strengthening oversight, and fostering dialogue among educators, technology companies, international organizations, civil society, and children.

In conclusion, Gafarova said that AI is already entering classrooms; the key issue is not whether to use this technology, but rather how to implement it fairly and in the best interests of children.

The primary goal is to utilize artificial intelligence to make education more inclusive, accessible, and of higher quality, while simultaneously preserving the human-centric nature of education. She pointed out that no child should be left behind due to their geographical location, family income, disability, or limited digital access.

World.title: Azerbaijani Parliament commemorates State Sovereignty Day (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 21. Azerbaijan’s State Sovereignty Day was commemorated in the country’s parliament.

This was reported by the Press and Public Relations Department of the Milli Majlis (Azerbaijani Parliament) following the first meeting of the Human Rights Committee during the parliament’s 2026 autumn session, held on September 21.

According to the information, Committee Chairperson Zahid Oruj opened the meeting by congratulating the members on the start of the new session and wishing them success in their work. Referring to the festive atmosphere in the country marking September 20—State Sovereignty Day—the chairperson highlighted significant events that have taken place in Azerbaijan’s modern history on this date. He emphasized that September 20 symbolizes the full restoration of state sovereignty and holds special significance as the beginning of a new stage in modern Azerbaijani statehood.

The chairperson then presented a report on the activities of the Human Rights Committee during the 2026 spring and extraordinary sessions. He said that 19 meetings were held, 31 issues were addressed, and nine draft laws were discussed by the committee during the previous session.

During the meeting, it was noted that the committee received 453 applications, letters, and other inquiries during the spring and extraordinary sessions, and that appropriate measures were taken regarding them in accordance with the law. The committee chairperson said that, throughout the previous session, the chairperson and members held regular meetings with constituents, listened to their appeals, and carried out relevant work concerning the issues raised. Furthermore, the committee chair and members actively participated in the country’s socio-political life.

Then, information was presented regarding the draft work plan of the Human Rights Committee for the autumn session of 2026. The information noted that the upcoming session is expected to include the discussion of draft laws submitted to the committee, the strengthening of legal and institutional mechanisms to counter disinformation and manipulation technologies, and the holding of public hearings on other matters. The document also addresses issues concerning the execution of administrative decisions, the physical and digital accessibility of services for persons with disabilities, and social and legal protections for the families of martyrs and veterans.

Regarding the draft law on the agenda, the committee chair stated that the draft law on amending certain laws of Azerbaijan—drafted in connection with the implementation of the law of Azerbaijan "On state services" No. 279-VIIQ dated October 31, 2025- is of an alignment nature and was prepared to improve existing regulations for the efficient organization of state service delivery.

During the discussion of the documents, the Committee Deputy Chairperson Arzukhan Alizade and members Razi Nurullayev, Hikmat Mammadov, Nagif Hamzayev, Sevil Mikayilova, Azer Allahveranov, Sayyad Aran, Vugar Rahimzade, Elman Nasirov, and Mirjalil Gasimli spoke, offering their views and proposals on issues such as increasing accessibility to state services, expanding the use of private medical facilities within the compulsory health insurance system, the social protection of martyrs' families and other citizens, enhancing the socio-economic and investment appeal of the regions, and improving transport infrastructure in the capital.

At the conclusion of the meeting, the work carried out by the committee during the past two sessions was deemed satisfactory, the draft work plan for the autumn session of 2026 was approved, and the draft law on the agenda was recommended for discussion at the plenary session of the parliament.

MP Bahruz Maharramov and other officials attended the event.

World.title: Salesman's 'superhero' branding triggers DC Comics trademark dispute
World.content:
A western NSW man who dresses as a caped superhero to promote ceiling fans has found himself in a legal dispute with comic book giant DC Comics.

Dubbo Lighting Centre owner Matthew McKay created "Fanman" after becoming tired of customers walking into his store and asking whether it also sold fans.

What started with a personalised number plate grew into social media videos and a brightly wrapped car featuring the red-and-blue superhero.

Mr McKay said the character was originally intended to promote the business, but these days he mostly dresses up for fun.

"I just enjoy having kids laugh at it; I drive past schools and they yell at you on the fence," he said.

But the joke took a serious turn when Mr McKay received an email from representatives for DC Comics alleging elements of his Fanman branding infringed its trademarks.

Matthew McKay developed the character after customers repeatedly asked whether his store also sold fans. (ABC Western Plains: Zaarkacha Marlan)

The letter argued Fanman "adopts key features" that are "deceptively similar" to Superman, including the red, blue and yellow colour scheme, cape and boots, and a chest emblem resembling Superman's shield.

It suggested the branding could "likely mislead consumers" into believing Mr McKay's business or products were authorised, licensed or endorsed by DC Comics, and requested he remove all Fanman-related content.

"I was very shocked. I thought it was a scam," he said.

"I understand what their standpoint is in similarities, but [they're] trying to state that I am using their brands to deceive people into thinking that I am endorsed by them.

"I don't think anybody thinks I'm affiliated with the real DC comic universe."

DC Comics has been contacted for comment.

The Dubbo business owner says he was in disbelief when he was contacted by DC Comics. (ABC Western Plains: Zaarkacha Marlan)

Small businesses on the radar

Mr McKay is not the only Australian small business to attract the attention of a major international brand.

Western Australian swimwear company Swim Shady successfully defended its trademark against a challenge from US rapper Eminem, while Australian fashion designer Katie Taylor this year won a long-running trademark battle with pop star Katy Perry.

University of Technology Sydney intellectual property law expert Sarah Hook said such disputes were not new, but social media had made potentially infringing material much easier to find.

Sarah Hook thinks brands are using AI tools to track down infringements. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"You go to any rural town and look at the names of businesses and they're quite funny and most of them would be trademark infringements," Dr Hook said.

"But now, because of social media, people are able to kind of clamp down on instances."

In western NSW, organisers of Coonamble's "Cowchella" festival recently changed its name to "Cowchilla" after being contacted by representatives of US music festival Coachella.

Dr Hook said Coachella had also pursued uses of its name online, including through hashtags about similar events or fashion, and believed artificial intelligence (AI) tools could be used to automatically search for references to major brands.

"My thought is they're probably using AI tools now to really roam the internet and find any kind of instances," she said.

"That's probably why there's going to be an uptick in a lot of these letters going out and a lot more enforcement."

Protecting an icon

Dr Hook said major companies had an incentive to pursue unauthorised uses of their trademarks to prevent their brand identity from weakening over time.

In 2013, DC Comics also took legal action against an Australian gym over the use of Superman-related branding for a workout program.

"DC Comics are quite litigious, and there's a reason why and that's because Superman is such an unbelievably important part of popular culture," she said.

"Everyone knows who Superman is … they really are at risk if they don't clamp down on unauthorised uses that they would start to see a generic type of Superman come through.

"And they might even lose some of that power they have of their brand identity, if they allow other people to start using things that look and feel like Superman."

Dr Hook said small businesses should consider potential trademark issues before investing heavily in a brand.

"The problem is that businesses will go and get advice about things like trademarks after they've already created their brand, their logos, or painted their vans," she said.

She recommended businesses search IP Australia's free trademark register for similar names and imagery early in the process.

Matthew McKay has spent significant time and money building his character. (ABC Western Plains: Zaarkacha Marlan)

How close is too close?

Mr McKay has engaged a lawyer to contest the allegations, with no plans yet to retire Fanman or delete the content at the centre of the dispute.

He said he understood why major companies protected their intellectual property, but questioned the decision to pursue a small regional business.

"You've got to pick your battles," he said.

"We're not in the same industry. No-one thinks I'm affiliated with them. There's no way their sales are being affected by me."

Dr Hook said operating in a completely different industry did not necessarily protect a business from a trademark dispute.

DC Comics argues the Fanman branding adopts key features associated with its Superman trademark. (ABC Western Plains: Zaarkacha Marlan)

While Australian trademark law did not provide a specific parody exception, she said a court would consider how closely the branding resembled registered trademarks and whether consumers could be confused about an association between the businesses.

"It may or may not be a trademark infringement. It would depend on how close it looks to Superman's trademarks," she said.

"If he had used different colours, he probably would have been able to get away with this a bit more. The red and blue superhero imagery might be too far."

World.title: More than one in four Brisbane council parking spots now pay by app only
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

More than one in four paid parking spaces in Brisbane City Council can now only be paid for through a third-party mobile app, making it the only major city in Australia where motorists are forced on to a digital-only option.

The latest council data shows of the roughly 9,000 metered parking spaces within Brisbane City Council, 2,483 are in pay by app only zones.

But advocates have warned the move to meter-less parking risks widening a digital divide.

Paid parking spaces in inner-city Brisbane are increasingly 'pay by app' only. (ABC News: Stephen Clarke)

Elissa Ferguson lives near the Wesley Hospital in the inner-north suburb of Auchenflower, where about 60 per cent of paid parking spots are app-only.

Ms Ferguson said she "often" comes across visitors to the hospital confused by how to pay for parking.

"The last person I came across was an elderly woman who was just looking very confused and sort of grabbed me as I walked by and asked if I could help her," Ms Ferguson said.

Ms Ferguson said together they worked out that the woman had previously downloaded the app but could not access it because she had forgotten her password.

"To access her password, she needed her email account, which wasn't linked to her phone," she said.

Ms Ferguson said eventually she had to point the woman in the direction of a parking meter she knew was located at the top of a nearby steep street.

"Visitors to the Wesley often come from Toowoomba, Boonah," she said.

" For them to have to download an app for a one-off visit is also a bit ridiculous. "

Apps 'creating barriers' for vulnerable people

In Newstead, retiree Margaret McCormack was running late for an appointment when she found a parking spot.

Instead of a parking meter she came across a QR code which she was able to scan and download an app after a bit of "fooling around".

"By that stage I'm browned off and I'm thinking I don't care if I get a parking ticket, I'm going," Ms McCormack said.

Ms McCormack said she was also concerned about the cyber security risks of scanning a public QR code.

Brisbane City Council has rolled out new parking enforcement technology at more than 40 locations. (ABC News: Stephen Clarke)

Seal Chong Wah is the Greens Councillor for Paddington Ward, which includes suburbs with high numbers of pay by app parking.

In a statement she said parking apps can "create barriers" for vulnerable people, including the elderly and low-income earners.

"There's no reason to remove parking meters, other than cutting costs at the expense of accessibility."

CEO of the Council on the Ageing Australia, Patricia Sparrow, said she has seen a move towards digital only practises "right across the board".

"Many older people don't like being online or doing things online at all, not unreasonably," Ms Sparrow said.

Ms Sparrow said the issue of digital exclusion would not disappear with changing generations. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

"We understand that things are changing and things are going digital, but it can't be digital only."

"Councils need to serve their resident base, and that includes making sure people can access those services," Ms Sparrow said.

Ms McCormack said she used to have paying for parking "down to a fine art" when regularly visiting the Mater Hospital in Brisbane.

"You weren't going into the clouds and hoping that someone was going to take your money," she said.

A spokesperson for Brisbane City Council said there are "no plan to remove all parking meters in Brisbane."

"We will continue to operate the physical meters, along with our two parking payment providers, CellOPark and PayStay," the spokesperson said.

"Parking payments can also be paid over the phone or online via our payment provider's websites."

World.title: Wet winter increases risk of active hayfever season in Victoria
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Much of Victoria could experience a more active hayfever season after this year's warm, wet winter.

Seasonal hayfever affects people who are allergic to tree and grass pollen, which are released into the air during spring.

Tree pollen season is already underway in Melbourne, with cypress trees responsible for a number of extreme ratings being issued by air-monitoring service Melbourne Pollen already this spring.

Grass pollen season starts on October 1.

Last year, there were five extreme grass pollen days and 15 high grass pollen days in Melbourne.

With Victoria recording its wettest winter in a decade and above-average temperatures, Melbourne Pollen said the state was likely to see more extreme grass pollen days this year.

"We are seeing conditions that look more favourable to a larger year than we did last year," said Edwin Lampugnani, the CEO of AirWatch, which runs Melbourne Pollen.

"That's really driven by the satellite data that we're seeing, with lots of greenness in those north-western pasture lands."

Melbourne Pollen has already issued a number of extreme ratings this season due to tree pollens. (Supplied: Melbourne Pollen)

Dr Lampugnani said western and central Victoria could be affected by the more active season, but there was better news for the east of the state.

"In the Gippsland region, we are seeing dry conditions and the prediction is that we are going to have lower amounts of rainfall in that area, and so for the Gippsland area we're expecting a subdued pollen season," he said.

Western and central Victoria are likely to record higher levels of pollen this hayfever season. (iStockphoto)

And there is hope that the current El Niño weather pattern affecting Australia could give rise to a shorter hayfever season.

"We're not going to be having those wet summers," Cenk Suphioglu, a professor of biomedical science at Deakin University, said.

"Those grass, with the recurring heat, will essentially dry them up and desiccate them so … the season is short."

Melbourne the hayfever capital of the world

Melbourne's geography and climate, including the state's wind patterns, had led to the city being dubbed the world's hayfever capital by Professor Suphioglu's pollen science centre, AirWatch.

Professor Suphioglu said rye grass was grown extensively for livestock feed on farmlands to the north-west of Melbourne.

He said the grass produced large amounts of pollen, which was carried on northerly winds to the city.

Rye grass is grown in abundance on Victoria farmlands and produces large amounts of pollen. (ABC News: James Jooste)

He said residents of Melbourne's west were the most affected, while those living to the east of Port Phillip reaped the rewards of a naturally occurring pollen filter.

"We have this large body of water in our bay," Professor Suphioglu said.

"As the pollen is travelling over the water, if they then suddenly settle on top of the water, it's going to be a water filtration effect.

"If you can relocate to the [Mornington] Peninsula, or the further you go on the other side of the water, … the better for you."

Experts weigh in on common hayfever treatments Which hayfever remedies are most effective, and can you use more than one at the same time?

Hayfever symptoms include sneezing, coughing and an itchy nose, eyes and throat.

Medical experts have previously told the ABC antihistamine tablets can help those suffering mild symptoms of hayfever, but people with more moderate cases may need a nasal spray, including a corticosteroid or anti-inflammatory spray.

Eye drops from a pharmacy can help soothe watery, itchy eyes.

Those with severe symptoms can speak to their doctor about whether they should be referred to an allergy specialist for desensitisation immunotherapy.

10 years since world's worst thunderstorm asthma event

Under certain conditions, hayfever sufferers can experience respiratory distress.

"Thunderstorm asthma is a particular condition that occurs when certain types of storms, combined with very high or extreme levels of grass pollen, occur simultaneously," Dr Lampugnani said.

"Under those conditions, grass pollen can rupture, turn into very small particles, and those small particles can go down into your lungs and cause asthma-like symptoms."

Thunderstorms help break grass pollen grains up into particles small enough to inhale into lungs. (Supplied: Asthma Australia)

November 21 will be the 10th anniversary of Melbourne's thunderstorm asthma event that killed nine people and forced thousands to seek urgent medical help.

At the end of a hot day, a severe thunderstorm swept across Melbourne and Geelong.

"The storm was followed by an epidemic thunderstorm asthma event, the likes of which, in terms of size, severity and acuity, had never before been seen, nor even imagined, let alone planned for," then-Victorian chief health officer Charles Guest said in a 2017 report.

"It resulted in thousands of people developing breathing difficulties in a very short period of time, creating extraordinary and unparalleled demand across the health service system.

"For many of those affected, this was their first asthma attack."

The health department has since declared it the world's largest epidemic thunderstorm asthma event.

What is thunderstorm asthma? Why can people with no history of asthma suffer from thunderstorm-induced asthma?

Professor Guest's report said there was a 672 per cent increase in respiratory-related presentations to Victorian emergency departments over the following 30 hours, and a 992 per cent increase in asthma-related hospital admissions in Melbourne and Geelong.

He said there was a 3,000 per cent increase in asthma-related intensive care admissions.

Thunderstorm asthma forecasts are issued by the Department of Health and are available through the Vic Emergency app.

The daily forecasts will begin next week, coinciding with the grass pollen season.

"It's really important that you start preparing now," Dr Lampugnani said.

"Make sure you have an asthma action plan in place and that you've spoken to your GP about treating your condition.

"You can treat it, of course, once you start experiencing symptoms, but by that time, some of the treatments are not as effective."

World.title: Bushfire strategy must change, expert says, after Tasmanian scare
World.content:
Conducting more burn offs in winter and implementing an earlier official start to the fire season are just two things bushfire expert David Bowman is suggesting for Tasmania after the state experienced a shock start to the fire season on the weekend.

Sixty fires were reported around the state on Sunday, with the Tasmania Fire Service (TFS) confirming a large number were connected to burn-offs by people who "weren't prepared for the weather".

The Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) said while its normal to have a couple of "spike days" in spring where there are strong winds, warmer temperatures and dry air over the state, Sunday's heat did arrive early.

"The conditions that we saw particularly across south eastern parts of the state were abnormally warm with temperatures around 10 degrees or even more above average" BOM meteorologist Urshla Connor.

The burnt fireground at Seven Mile Beach on Sunday. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

TFS wary of 'crying wolf', fire expert says

There has been criticism of the TFS for not calling a total fire ban for Sunday given the predicted conditions.

Instead, it held a press conference on Friday, "strongly discouraging" residents preparing registered burns "from continuing with those activities.

Residents angry at lack of fire ban despite dire forecast Residents east of Hobart are questioning why a total fire ban was not imposed over the weekend, after they spent the evening fearing a potential ember attack from a nearby blaze.

Professor of Pyrogeography and Fire Science at the University of Tasmania, David Bowman, said implementing more fire bans isn't necessarily the answer to worsening fire seasons.

"The problem is if you overcall total fire bans, and it turns out it's a fizzer, then you're getting into the 'oh they're crying wolf, so we won't worry about this total fire ban," Professor Bowman told 936 ABC Hobart.

"There are going to be some summer days coming where we are talking about an extraordinarily terrifying risk … now what happened on the weekend was bad and frightening, but I'm talking about way, way, way dialling up the stress levels

"A management agency has to be very careful to use an instrument like a total fire ban because the community could just get complacent," he added.

Ned Bramich's photo of a bushfire in north-east Tasmania, December 9, 2025. (Supplied: Ned Bramich)

'Extremely challenging summer' ahead

Professor Bowman said he sympathised with fire authorities given they're now dealing with fire conditions that are becoming increasingly unpredictable and potentially catastrophic.

The state can expect "an extremely challenging summer," he said.

" The thing that I really emphasise is expect the unexpected, so err much more on the side of caution because these landscapes are able to dry out very fast, given the right conditions. "

That meant "a whole lot of consequences for administrative processes, for practices; what used to work clearly isn't going to keep working into the future," he said.

David Bowman says authorities are faced with bushfires that are becoming increasingly unpredictable and potentially catastrophic. (Supplied: David Bowman)

Professor Bowman suggested implementing an earlier official start to the fire season and more burning off in winter.

"It's totally consistent with what's happening around the world, more extreme fire weather, longer fire seasons, and so an early start is very consistent with what we would be expecting"

People watch the Dolphin Sands bushfire, December 4, 2025. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The Queenstown hotel and town were bathed in eerie light during the bushfire emergency on Tasmania's west coast in February 2025. (Supplied: Joy Chappell)

Professor Bowman said he was recently in the Northern Territory and some planned burns there were being started at night.

"That's because fuels are so dry now, it's actually safer to start burning at night, so that's a very good example of adaptation and adjustment.

" Those sorts of things in a Tasmanian context would be thinking about burning much earlier in the winter and trying to readjust our thinking about the ramping up of danger. "

Fires on Tasmania's east coast in December last year could be seen from space. (Supplied: NASA/MODIS)

Asked about the progress of this year's fuel reduction program, a spokesperson for the Tasmania Fire Service said its partner agencies "are continuing to make the most of favourable weather conditions … to progress planned burning activities ahead of the bushfire season".

"Fuel reduction burning is just one part of Tasmania's broader bushfire preparedness effort, alongside mechanical fuel management, mitigation works and community preparedness activities."

Crews in Tasmania battle bushfires with air and ground support. (Instagram: Fire Rescue Tasmania)

The role of climate change and El Niño

As well as the intensity and nature of bushfires changing, experts said the ability to predict conditions has become tougher.

"Events are getting harder to predict as we move into a warming climate and with climate change and especially warmer sea surface temperatures around not only Tasmania's coast but the whole of Australia", Urshla Connor said.

"We are in an El Niño year, as well as a positive Indian Ocean dipole phase, which both do lead to to generally drier and warmer conditions in Tasmania.

"While the whole state will be susceptible to seeing bushfire conditions, parts of the east and north-east coast have been flagged as being of particular worry for the upcoming fire season," she said.

Experts are predicting this El Niño could be the strongest on record.

World.title: Two new stick insect species emerge from Queensland forests
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Some look to the stars in the hope of finding alien life forms, but others hunt for outlandish creatures living much closer to home.

For entomologist Braxton Jones, searching for insect life was far more exciting than waiting for extra-terrestrials to show up.

"In movies, they try to design all these crazy aliens, but all you have to do is just look at the insect world because they already exist," he said.

The University of Sydney researcher has discovered two new stick insect species, Anchiale robusta and Anchiale mabiensis, in Far North Queensland.

Anchiale robusta, which has large, mottled wings and grows to a length of about 160 millimetres, was found to live in coastal rainforest from Tully to north of Cooktown.

An example of a male Anchiale robusta, one of two new species found in Far North Queensland. (Supplied: Paul D. Brock)

Anchiale mabiensis has only been observed in the Mabi Forest on the Atherton Tablelands and is slightly smaller and more slender, growing to about 115mm.

Dr Jones's findings have been published in the scientific journal Austral Entomology.

Spotting a new species

Dr Jones said the first indication of a potential new species was how it looked.

"So the colour of the wings, or the shape of the wings, or the length of their wings, and that's very consistent within that species, but it's very different between species," he said.

Braxton Jones collected samples from a number of regions. (Supplied: Braxton Jones)

Dr Jones said he was always keen to collect living females so that the eggs could be examined.

"I don't know any other organism where this applies, but you can take the egg alone, and from the egg you can identify the species," he said.

Dr Jones said Anchiale mabiensis had particularly unusual eggs, featuring a series of rings and a lid.

He said the eggs of other species were sometimes glued, buried, or featured a silk-like substance, but nothing like the new discovery.

"It's the only stick insect or the only egg that we've been able to find that has these rings on it," he said.

An under-discovered field

Dr Jones said the identification of new species was important for conservation efforts, particularly for creatures only found in small areas.

Terry Carmichael from the Wet Tropics Management Authority said the biodiversity of the region was well known and growing.

But he said the understanding of different invertebrate species was lagging behind other groups of animal life.

"It's the number one thing we hear from researchers — we don't know enough to make some decisions sometimes" Mr Carmichael said.

He said large parts of the original Mabi Forest, a home to Anchiale mabiensis, had been cleared for agriculture.

Anchiale mabiensis have so far only been found in one area of rainforest on the Atherton Tablelands. (Supplied: Angus J. Emmott)

"Mabi rainforest itself is a threatened ecological community under the Commonwealth legislation for protecting the environment," Mr Carmichael said.

"Now we have a very rare stick insect living in that Mabi Forest, it just makes it more and more special."

Dr Jones said his love for finding stick insects had never wavered and encouraged other would-be entomologists to follow his lead.

"If you have a passion for insects, pursue it, because you never grow up. You're just a kid forever," he said.

"You're just having so much fun going through the one life that you have, just looking at how amazing the outside world is."

World.title: Brownlow simply latest chapter as Daicos continues rewriting AFL history
World.content:
When Nathan Buckley's decade-long tenure as Collingwood coach came to an end midway through 2021, there was a silver lining for the club amid the painful exit of the club legend.

Buckley's tenure had seen the Pies flirt with winning a premiership in 2018 and 2019 before ultimately failing, but by the time he wrapped up, Collingwood seemed well out of the premiership window.

The silver lining came in the form of a player who was yet to set foot on an AFL field: Nick Daicos, then a teenager touted as a generational prospect years before he was eligible to be drafted.

Daicos wins first Brownlow Medal and sets new modern-day voting record Nick Daicos breaks Patrick Cripps's record in the 3-2-1 voting era by winning the first Brownlow Medal of his career.

The AFL world was no stranger to the Daicos surname due to the exploits of Nick's famous father Peter, who had become immortalised at Collingwood as a member of the club's 1990 premiership side.

You did not need to be a Collingwood fanatic to know about Nick Daicos. Everyone around the game knew the kid was on his way because of his prolific exploits at the junior levels.

The weight of expectation that comes with the level of hype Daicos had as a draft prospect can prove crippling. Unfortunately, years of evidence support this.

Sometimes even the most hyped prospects can take time to fit into the AFL system, and it makes sense. These are boys coming to a man's game.

The more rigorous training regimes, expanded playbooks, media commitments, dietary requirements, and everything else that comes with being an AFL player can be too much. That is even before we get to the pace of the game being completely different.

Nick Daicos with his parents. (Getty Images / AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

That hasn't been the case with Daicos, who, as an audacious Nike advert claimed on the morning of the Brownlow count, has proven it inevitable from day one.

From his first game, Daicos showed an ability to bend the game to his will in ways not seen in teenagers, and we have all been blessed to witness it.

Daicos's arrival helped catapult Collingwood from second-last in 2021 to fourth in his first season in the AFL.

Collingwood fell one point short of a grand final appearance in Daicos's debut season, but went all the way in his second.

After collecting boatloads of the football across halfback while occasionally dipping his toes in the midfield as a rookie, Daicos supercharged the Pies engine room in 2023, helping them claim the flag, and he has not looked back since.

Daicos helped propel Collingwood to a premiership in just his second season in the AFL. (AFL Photos via Getty Images: Dylan Burns)

From very early on in Daicos's career, the Brownlow win appeared to be a question of when rather than if, but it was the one accolade he was frustratingly made to wait on.

Daicos followed up his premiership by polling a ridiculous 38 votes in 2024, the most by any player in the league's history up until that point, only for that year's winner, Patrick Cripps, to poll 45.

Last year, he was again a seemingly unbackable favourite before being stunned by Gold Coast's Matt Rowell.

Missing out on a Brownlow after being among the favourites for a few years can be something that follows you.

Marcus Bontempelli, despite being widely considered the best player of his generation, has yet to win the prestigious medal.

Bulldogs star Marcus Bontempelli's career is an example of just how hard Brownlow Medals are to come by. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Buckley was famously made to wait year after year before eventually breaking through in 2003, his 11th season, while Gary Ablett Jr was even denied by his own teammate before his maiden Brownlow triumph. It is almost a rite of passage if you're an all-timer.

Despite Bontempelli, Zak Butters and Bailey Smith all challenging him at various points during the count, Daicos would not be denied this year.

Almost in revenge for the previous two seasons, this year, Daicos turned in an individual season that would ultimately prove impossible to ignore for the umpires.

Daicos broke Cripps's record with 47 votes and set a few more records along the way.

He is now the only player in league history to poll over 30 votes in three consecutive seasons, the only player to put together six straight three-vote games, and the only player to put together 13 three-vote games in a single season.

Daicos celebrates his Brownlow triumph with his parents after the count. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Given the ease with which Daicos has played from his first contest in the AFL four seasons ago, it was surprising to talk about the weight of expectation actually weighing on him after winning his elusive first Brownlow.

You get the sense that the weight of expectation might be the only thing that is capable of slowing him down, because efforts from his AFL counterparts to do so have so far proven futile.

For a player so metronomic and seemingly superhuman on the field, it was refreshing to hear Daicos admit he too deals with nerves and struggles with criticism, just like the rest of us.

Daicos admitted to the Brownlow win being a relief after being denied for so many years as a favourite, even saying he had given up trusting in betting markets.

Daicos is likely to put together more dominant seasons now that the weight of winning a Brownlow is no more. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Now that the Brownlow box has been ticked off, it is frightening to think of what an unburdened Daicos could potentially achieve.

Still just 23 years of age, Daicos has gone from being the precocious youngster to one of Collingwood's veterans, and he will act as the bridge from one era of Collingwood premiership contention to the next, just as Scott Pendlebury did.

He seems good enough to single-handedly wrench Collingwood's premiership window open for as long as he wants.

Daicos has the chance to eclipse Scott Pendlebury (right) as Collingwood's greatest-ever player. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Adding premierships to his 2023 triumph will be at the top of Daicos's to-do list, and the hope will be that in the process of achieving that goal, his resume ultimately becomes undeniable.

The chance to be Collingwood's greatest player is in play. The chance to be the greatest player in league history is as well, as premature as that shout may seem.

The records Daicos set with his maiden Brownlow win will eventually be just another footnote for a player who is poised to rewrite the game's history books.

Like the commercial said: inevitable.

World.title: Victoria unveils data centre strategy with renewables requirements
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

All new data centres built in Victoria will have to source their own renewable energy and will be banned from using drinking water under the state government's new rules for the booming sector.

In the face of community backlash to data centres being built near residential areas across the state, the Victorian government will also introduce a 150-metre buffer between any new data centres and homes.

The policy comes amid rising opposition to data centres, including from some Labor MPs and candidates.

On Wednesday a Senate inquiry into AI and data centres will hold hearings in Melbourne to air community concerns.

Ben Carroll says communities need to benefit from data centre development. (ABC News)

The government is backing the sector, arguing data centres are creating jobs and investment, resulting in $5.8 billion in capital expenditure last year, but says the growth cannot come at the expense of Victorians.

"If we get that right, we can all share in their economic benefits, especially the local community,'' Premier Ben Carroll said.

Water use has also sparked concerns that the sector will drink up supplies for cooling.

The government says less than 1 per cent of the state's drinking water is being used for data centre cooling, but concedes it should be zero.

The rules will require data centres to use recycled or non-drinking water. Developers will be forced to find offsets if they cannot meet those requirements.

Some rule changes can be made quickly through regulation but other requirements will take longer to come into effect. It is also not clear how the state will enforce the requirements.

The state government has fast-tracked multiple planning applications for data centres under its controversial Development Facilitation Program, which allows companies to bypass local councils and apply directly to the planning minister.

ASX-listed tech company NextDC had a $1 billion data centre in Port Melbourne approved by the minister in 75 days earlier this year.

Under the state's proposed new rules data centres will soon have to provide their own renewable energy and storage to cover the increased demand data centres put on energy supplies.

Several data centres have been established in Melbourne's inner west over the past decade. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

This could be through their own renewable programs, or investing in new generation projects.

The developers will also have to pay for energy infrastructure upgrades.

According to advocacy group Data Centre Australia, the country had 162 data centres with a combined IT capacity of 1.5 gigawatts as of March of this year.

Melbourne is the fastest-growing market and there are 50 already operating in Victoria, concentrated around the city's west.

By 2030, data centre energy consumption in Victoria is set to quadruple — a major issue as the state transitions away from coal-fired plants to renewable energy.

Mr Carroll has put data centre regulation on his agenda, appointing Anthony Carbines to be the state's first minister for artificial intelligence and the digital economy.

"Data centres power our lives and support banking, healthcare, transport and emergency services '' Mr Carbines said.

"Companies like Amazon and Microsoft choose to invest in Victoria. That will continue within sensible guardrails."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has tried to establish a national approach to data centres but could not reach consensus with all the states on renewable energy requirements.

The state says its plans fit within the Commonwealth framework.

Under Mr Carroll's plan developers will also have to pay towards a local investment fund to help build TAFEs and parks.

The state will also introduce procurement rules requiring data centres to properly train Victorian workers.

The Victorian strategy will require data centre developers to bankroll local Investment funds. (ABC News: John Gunn)

The state government says it is already working on other planning rules for data centres including "fair community consultation".

Earlier this month, electricity distributor Jemena was forced to pause the installation of high-voltage power poles in Melbourne's inner-west following fierce backlash from residents.

The 15-metre-high poles were designed to facilitate increased power loads, particularly from NextDC's West Footscray data centre, and were also opposed by Maribyrnong council, which accused Jemena of failing to consult the community.

The data centre, located metres from homes, has also come under fire for the air pollution emitted by its back-up diesel generators, constant hum, and plans to expand further.

The Greens have pinpointed data centres as a key election issue, campaigning heavily in Melbourne's inner west, and have called for a moratorium on all new data centres.

World.title: Thirteen-year-old surfer breaking records as first Indigenous world champ
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Leihani Zoric almost didn't compete in El Salvador, but now the 13-year-old is the youngest International Surfing Association (ISA) Under 18 World Junior Champion in history.

"When I went over there, I was extremely sick," Zoric told ABC Weekend Breakfast.

"I wasn't even going to go, my mum and dad were like, 'Leihani don't go, you're that sick'."

But the teenager was committed.

"I was like, 'no, I'm going to go. I believe that I can go all the way'," she told her parents.

And all the way she went, using visualisation to help her through.

"I wrote it down about 1,000 times [and] I said to myself, 'I'm going to become this year's Under 18 ISA gold medallist'," Zoric said.

"So, when it happened, I was like, oh my God, this is crazy."

Zoric, from Byron Bay in northern NSW, is the youngest ever surfer to win the ISA Under 18 World Championship. (Supplied: Surfing Australia)

Across more than a week of competition, Zoric was part of a 12-strong Australian team that went head-to-head with the world's best junior surfers.

She competed three age divisions above her own, to take out the title.

"It feels amazing," Zoric said.

"I'm really proud of myself for all my hard work and effort I've put in, and all the people that have helped me along the way."

It comes after a stand-out year so far, which includes winning the Junior Girls and Open Women's divisions at the 2026 Indigenous Surfing Titles.

She's now back home not only as a World Champion, but a history maker.

And she's taking it all in her stride, with a maturity that's beyond her years.

"I'm just so grateful to have been able to go to El Salvador and represent my culture and my country as best as I can," she said.

Loading Instagram content

Creating a proud history

Zoric, from Byron Bay in northern New South Wales, is also the first Indigenous world champion surfer at any level.

"I'm really proud to have represented my Yued mob over in Western Australia," she said.

"We have such important history in our culture and I feel like [that] has really shaped me as a person."

Zoric first got a feel for surfing at two days old, when her dad put her on a surfboard in the shallows at Broken Head.

From then on, she just loved the water.

Thirteen-year-old Zoric has had a stellar year, also winning the Open Women's division at the 2026 Indigenous Surfing Titles. (Supplied: Surfing Australia)

She takes inspiration from Soli Bailey, the first pro surfer to compete under the Aboriginal flag in the World Surfing League, and Cathy Freeman.

"Having those people inspire me has definitely made me want to be like them one day," she said.

Along with looking up to others, Zoric wants to be a positive role model herself.

When she's not in the water, she's busy creating connection, with things like Lei's Lu'au, a community day celebrating girls and women in surfing.

Loading Instagram content

"I hope that I inspire, not just as an athlete, but being a good person and always caring about others, being encouraging and just having a positive attitude all the time," she said.

"Bringing people up and lifting their spirits and attitudes and just [making] them feel like they belong here in this world.

"Because everybody is important and special in their own unique ways."

Locana Cullen (Under 16 men's) and Lucy Darragh (Under 16 women's) also claimed individual golds at the World Junior Championships, with Australia winning three out of the four divisions.

The Australians also won their third consecutive team gold at the event.

World.title: ‘I’d love to see more of it’: Telstra backs data centre boom amid backlash
World.content:
Exclusive TechnologyTelecommunications ‘I’d love to see more of it’: Telstra backs data centre boom amid backlash David Swan September 22, 2026 — 5:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Telstra says Australia has a natural advantage in the global race to build artificial intelligence data centres, and wants to see more of them built here despite growing community backlash. Nathan Gumley, the telco’s executive for software engineering and IT, said the country’s combination of renewable energy and water set it apart from much of the United States, where developers are often forced to choose between the two. Data centres like NextDC’s building in Footscray, Victoria, are popping up around Australia. Eddie Jim “If you look here in the US, you can go where power is cheap because renewables exist, but there’s no water,” Gumley said in an interview at Salesforce’s Dreamforce conference in San Francisco. “Or you can go where water exists and there’s no renewables and power’s really expensive.” “We’re kind of blessed that we have both.”





Treasury has estimated $150 billion could be spent on Australian data centres by 2030. There are 162 already operating and about 130 more at the planning stage. Community resistance is building alongside the investment. Residents are campaigning against a $1.47 billion facility proposed for Spotswood in Melbourne’s inner west, which would draw 240 megawatts, roughly the consumption of 250,000 Victorian households. Telstra’s AI boss Dayle Stevens said the national resilience question for Australia lay in that infrastructure rather than in developing local AI models. Peter Rae In the United States, 18 states have passed moratoriums on new data centres. The company stands to benefit directly from any expansion of the build. It is constructing the Aura Network, a terrestrial fibre network connecting Australian capital cities, and has deployed more than 8500 kilometres of fibre with six routes ready for service. It owns or operates about 400,000 kilometres of subsea cable.



“We’re just incredibly well-placed to be able to connect to those things, particularly with intercity network,” Gumley said. “I’d love to see more of it.” Related Article Newsletter

Telecommunications Telstra had no shortage of warnings before its outage. How did it miss them? Telstra has signed long-term contracts across its fibre and subsea assets with Google, Amazon Web Services and Australian AI infrastructure company Firmus. Microsoft is the foundational partner on Aura. The company lifted its expected investment in Aura and a related satellite project to about $1.8 billion through to FY28 in results released last month, up from a previous estimate of $1.6 billion, citing inflation and site conditions. It expects a mid-teens internal rate of return and a payback period of around nine years. Chief executive Vicki Brady told investors the sales pipeline for Aura had increased significantly over the past six months.



Dayle Stevens, who leads Telstra’s data and AI function, said the national resilience question for Australia lay in that infrastructure rather than in developing local AI models. “Telstra’s role is connectivity,” she said. “It is not our job to be building sovereign models.” Stevens said the critical infrastructure underpinning AI, including subsea cables, would matter more as the broader economy adopted the technology. Inside the company, Telstra has deployed AI agents built on Salesforce’s Agentforce platform to process customer refunds and check security permissions, targeting internal processes staff had complained about for years. Gumley said the refunds agent removed 15 to 20 steps from what a call centre worker must complete while holding a conversation with a customer. Telstra keeps a person accountable end to end for each automated process, he said, with thresholds determining when a human must intervene.



Not every deployment has gone smoothly. Gumley said staff given an internal assistant to navigate about 5500 knowledge articles reported that it was producing poor results. Telstra has signed long-term contracts across its fibre and subsea assets with Google, Amazon Web Services and Australian AI infrastructure company Firmus, with Microsoft the foundational partner on Aura. Craig Sillitoe “Unsurprisingly, it wasn’t the agent that was broken, it was actually the knowledge articles,” he said. Late last year Telstra deployed what it calls an AI control plane, monitoring cost, performance, risk and compliance across its AI systems in real time. Stevens said it had not stopped any deployment yet, describing it as early days. Telstra executives have said reductions in software engineering came largely through attrition and slower hiring rather than redundancy, and that the company expects to be smaller again by 2030. Telstra’s direct workforce fell by 1219 roles over the past year, to 29,334.



Related Article Updated

Telecommunications ‘Accountability rests with me’: Telstra boss rakes in $6.8m but Triple Zero outage costs her “Most people at most companies have some amount of uncertainty about what the future of their roles are,” Salesforce’s chief product officer for Agentforce John Kucera told this masthead. “All of our roles are impacted by AI, and they evolve every day, which is uncomfortable.” Kucera argued that automating repetitive tasks is meant to free up staff rather than eliminate them: “You want to have the human when you need them most, while having the agent handle all the routine things.” Stevens declined to discuss July’s network outage, which cut off Triple Zero. She said Telstra was examining what AI could do for network resilience and for the staff who work on it. David Swan travelled to San Francisco as a guest of Salesforce. World.title: ASX set to rise as Wall Street surges; Oil prices fall; Road clears for $154b Paramount-Warner Bros merger
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise as Wall Street surges; Oil prices fall; Road clears for $154b Paramount-Warner Bros merger Stan Choe September 22, 2026 — 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks are climbing with markets worldwide after oil prices and yields in the bond market gave back some of their jumps from last week. The S&P 500 rose 1.5 per cent and pulled within 0.4 per cent of its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 348 points, or 0.7 per cent, in mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 2.2 per cent higher. Easing oil prices and bonds yields brought relief to markets. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 4.52am AEST pointing to a gain of 36 points or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX closed flat on Monday. The Australian dollar was steady at US71.22¢. They got help from the price for a barrel of Brent oil falling 3.4 per cent to $US100.29. While that’s still much higher than its roughly $US72 price from earlier this summer, it’s down from the nearly $US110 it touched last week.



Oil prices are swinging up and down as some crude from the Middle East is able to sail through the Strait of Hormuz, though nowhere nearly as much as the industry and customers would like because of the war with Iran. Morgan Stanley’s Michael Wilson said another leg higher in prices for oil, gasoline and other refined products is the main risk he sees in the near term that could keep the US stock market from rising to his forecasted target for the year’s end. The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline across the United States has already climbed to nearly $US4.48, according to AAA. That’s up from less than $US4.32 just a week earlier and from $US3.18 a year ago. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Trump’s war is strangling the world Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Monday’s pullback in oil prices helped lower the pressure coming from the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury eased to 4.97 per cent from 5.01 per cent late Friday after it crossed above the 5 per cent threshold last week for the first time in three years. Yields have been on the rise because of worries about inflation, big debt loads for governments worldwide and other factors. That hurts the economy because high yields make it more expensive not only for the US government to borrow money to pay its bills but also for households and businesses.



Worries remain about how much oil is available for customers worldwide, ING commodities strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson wrote in a commentary on Monday. However, they said profit-taking by investors after the recent jump in oil prices, together with hopes for constructive discussions at this week’s UN General Assembly and at a meeting between China’s and the United States’ leaders, helped improve optimism. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters following talks Sunday with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York that the US had “a very successful engagement” with the Chinese side. Bessent said talks with China touched on trade and AI. China and the United States have been discussing reciprocal tariff reductions on $US30 billion ($42.1 billion) worth of goods from each side. In Beijing, China’s Foreign Ministry on Monday confirmed that Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to the United States between September 23 and 25. Experts and policymakers believe trade, tariffs, and AI safety are likely among the topics to be on the agenda. The war in Iran and developments in the Middle East and ties between China and Iran could also be discussed. On Wall Street, stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry continued to stabilise following their worldwide slide at the start of last week. Leaders of the AI industry have recently warned a slowdown is needed in the industry’s development for the safety of humanity. Advanced Micro Devices rallied 8.8 per cent and could finish the day with a total market value above $US1 trillion, while Nvidia added 2.2 per cent.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Why higher interest rates are the new normal Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor Stocks enmeshed in the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, rallied after bitcoin’s price rose back above $US85,000 and returned to where it was in January. Coinbase Global jumped 4.8 per cent, and Robinhood Markets rose 4.2 per cent. Skydance-owned Paramount fell 1.6 per cent as it reached a settlement in lawsuits brought by 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild trade union challenging its $US110 billion ($154 billion) acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, which jumped 10.8 per cent. The parties worked through the weekend to reach the deal, which includes protections designed to limit the market power and ensure the editorial independence of the media giant, which will control two of Hollywood’s biggest studios, two major subscription streaming services and dozens of TV channels ranging from CBS to HBO. Paramount has promised to release 30 movies a year at the combined studios, a move designed to placate cinema owners and Hollywood talent who believed the merger would reduce film output. Under the terms of the deal , half of those films must be produced by the new company.



Stock indexes around the world also climbed thanks to the easing of oil prices and bond yields. Indexes gained 0.9 per cent in France, 1.2 per cent in Hong Kong and 1.6 per cent in South Korea. AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
