World.title: Super wars escalate as Coalition leans in to mortgage plan
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalSuperannuation Super wars escalate as Coalition leans in to mortgage plan Paul Sakkal September 22, 2026 — 5:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Coalition has locked in a three-way election battle with One Nation and Labor over superannuation, floating a plan to use retirement savings to make securing a home loan easier. The opposition was split this month when Pauline Hanson announced a policy to allow people to pocket a quarter of their super contributions as a wage top-up, which Labor said had set up an effective referendum on the multitrillion-dollar scheme. Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg. Alex Ellinghausen Some shadow ministers wanted to avoid a fight on superannuation after the Coalition lost two elections in a row advocating to use retirement savings for housing. Since then, however, senior MPs have largely united around the idea of making a splash with a fresh policy to give people more choice over how their funds can be used. Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg will use a speech on Tuesday to float a proposal, which is under consideration but not yet adopted, to use superannuation as collateral for a mortgage or to increase the size of a loan.



The Coalition’s policy at the last election allowed first home buyers to take up to $50,000 out of superannuation for a home purchase. The idea to use superannuation funds as collateral is seen as less radical because people would not draw the funds from of the super account. Related Article Exclusive

Superannuation Superannuation shouldn’t be untouchable, says expert: ‘People get hysterical’ The Coalition will also explore an expansion of the $50,000 proposal, though this is seen as less likely. “Policy must factor in the big changes since 1992, when superannuation started, such as the fact that it was assumed that most people would own a home in retirement. That is not assured today. It is even less assured in the future,” he will say, according to a copy of his speech. “The idea that we are stuck with the exact design features of the current system and there is no possible way to improve it is incredibly lazy thinking and exemplifies the frustration Australians have about their leaders.”



Labor will probably use Bragg’s speech to portray the opposition as willing to risk a world-leading pension scheme whose power to invest trillions has attracted the interest of the Trump administration. But there are growing calls to consider whether the $4.8 trillion retirement savings pool can help address contemporary economic problems. Emily Millane, author of an upcoming history of the private pension system, said a fortnight ago that the political debate on super had become “hysterical” and proposals to use the money for housing should be debated. Nicholas Gruen, a prominent economist who worked for Labor treasurer John Dawkins when Paul Keating established compulsory super, conjured World War I battlelines as he said Labor was defending “the Maginot Line they’ve spent the last generation building”. “It’s a neat trick for finance to pull off requiring people to pay them for mortgages which are necessary because they’re … forced to invest their savings in securities when they need to fund a home,” Gruen said on LinkedIn last week.



A Morrison-era review and the Grattan Institute have argued that the superannuation guarantee rate of 12 per cent is too high and probably depresses wages. Like Gruen, Bragg raised the issue of superannuation’s cost to the federal budget. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has argued that the Intergenerational Report, released on Monday, demonstrates that Australia is one of very few nations where spending on the pension is on track to decline. However, Bragg argued the concessional tax treatment of superannuation was projected to overtake age pension spending in the 2040s. Treasurer Jim Chalmers at the Australian National University on Monday prior to the release of the Intergenerational Report. AAPIMAGE Before entering politics, the Liberal senator worked for the Financial Services Council, which competes with industry super funds. He has been a frequent critic of the pension scheme. The MP was chastised by some colleagues for freewheeling on a range of policies in a press club speech in August. He is not in charge of superannuation policy for the Coalition, but leads ideas on housing. Bragg argues Labor was ideologically tied to super because many MPs, unionists and staffers moved onto the boards of industry super funds.



“Housing was always part of this discussion. Back in 1993, Paul Keating himself proposed a policy where $10,000 could be taken from superannuation for a first home deposit. His policy said ‘for most people, a debt-free home is as important a part of retirement security as superannuation income’,” Bragg will say. “The architect of compulsory superannuation was right that home ownership should be part of the system. In later years, Mr Keating has lost his imagination. He now subscribes to the groupthink position that super preservation until 60 years of age is a sacred cow which can never be discussed, reviewed or reformed.” Keating’s policy was eventually dumped because of fears about stoking house prices. Bragg said his looming policy on super-for-housing must be coupled with a radical unleashing of home building, which he argued was the main game in housing. But he said the super policy was also key because there was a growing group of renter retirees and nearly a third of lump sum payouts of super were used to pay mortgages. “If it is good enough for Singapore, New Zealand and Canada with these similar super schemes to allow for housing, surely it’s a debate we can have without scare campaigns,” Bragg will say. “The psychological benefits of a home that belongs to an individual are equally immense. We must be clear that housing sits at the heart of retirement policy alongside private savings, superannuation and the pension. Each element should work together.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Albanese signs declaration with world leaders calling for international AI safeguards
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAI Albanese signs declaration with world leaders calling for international AI safeguards Rob Harris Updated September 22, 2026 — 5:01am ,first published 2:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia has joined a call for international safeguards on artificial intelligence amid warnings from scientists and industry executives that the rapid development of powerful systems could outpace governments’ ability to control emerging risks. At the United Nations in New York, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese signed a declaration with leaders including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz calling for mandatory safety testing, independent evaluations and greater international oversight of so-called frontier AI models. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, pictured on the weekend as he visits the US. Dominic Lorrimer The declaration warns that capable AI systems have already been seen circumventing testing safeguards, exploiting vulnerabilities and gaining unauthorised access to real-world systems. “Leading scientists and executives are warning that the pace of development could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks,” the leaders said.



The release comes ahead of Thursday’s meeting between Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, with AI expected to be a major topic of discussion. Albanese has cited Australia’s role in shaping international rules for AI as a key plank of its bid for a seat on the UN Security Council. He said he hoped for a positive meeting between Trump and Xi. Related Article AI ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates The US and China are locked in a race to develop increasingly powerful AI systems, while Washington and Beijing have resisted calls from industry figures including Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, backed by OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceX founder Elon Musk, to slow the development of frontier models amid warnings that humans could lose control. The leaders on Monday (US time) stopped short of calling for a halt to development, instead arguing that AI’s potential to improve lives, advance science and strengthen economies should be preserved while stronger controls are imposed.



“AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control,” they said, insisting that it must be developed and used in accordance with international law. Albanese said AI had the potential to improve lives, strengthen the economy and productivity, and advance science and medical breakthroughs, but “humans need to be in control of it”. The prime minister said Australians wanted to know that “artificial intelligence won’t be in control of us” and that governments needed to shape how the technology rolled out. “Artificial intelligence will have a massive impact on the way that our lives and our work is conducted,” he said, arguing that humans needed to remain “at the centre of it” and in control. The declaration calls on AI companies to develop transparent safety protocols, including mandatory testing before systems are deployed and independent assessments by qualified evaluators given sufficient access to identify risks.



Governments and regional organisations are also urged to develop common standards, strengthen transparency and share reports of serious AI safety incidents. Related Article Data centres This is the data centre capital of the world. They’re starting to regret it The leaders want countries across all regions to have access to the scientific expertise, technical capacity and trusted evaluation needed to assess advanced AI systems. The declaration also calls on UN member states to explore creating an international institution that could set standards, enable verification and convene governments when AI systems cross agreed capability thresholds. The group warned that efforts to control frontier AI should not widen the gap between countries with access to the technology and those unable to benefit from its advances. World.title: John’s cancer patients were prescribed opioids. This key warning was missing
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCancer John’s cancer patients were prescribed opioids. This key warning was missing Courtney Kruk September 22, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cancer survivor Suellen Kirkegaard had been given six months to live when she was prescribed opioids, a group of strong, highly addictive painkillers. Doctors had discovered a metastatic melanoma three years after her breast cancer surgery and treatment. Immunotherapy – then limited and expensive – offered the only hope of improving her prognosis. “The oncologist I’d had for my breast cancer … [was able to get immunotherapy] for me on compassionate grounds,” she said. “Otherwise, six months wasn’t a lot to look forward to.” Cancer survivor Suellen Kirkgaard was not informed about the dangers of driving when she was prescribed opioids. Courtney Kruk Kirkegaard responded well to the treatment, but needed opioids to curb painful side effects; arthritis, joint pain, fatigue and regular bouts of pancreatitis.



“Without the pain medication, I just would not have been able to function at all,” she explained. While Kirkegaard understood opioids could be addictive, it wasn’t until she met Dr John Gillett, a Toowoomba-based palliative care doctor and Queensland University of Technology PhD researcher, that she learned about the risks associated with driving. “The medications say ‘do not operate heavy vehicles’ and I’m thinking, yeah, I’m not going to be driving a truck,” Kirkegaard said. “It was only when he [Gillett] mentioned opioids and the capacity to drive [that it] crossed my mind.” Nearly 3 million Australians are prescribed opioids each year. While strong painkillers such as morphine, oxycodone and fentanyl are not classed as sedatives, they can cause heavy drowsiness and fatigue.



Related Article Drug reform ‘Pick between driving or treating yourself’: Calls for change to zero-tolerance laws Patients rely on health professionals to explain possible cognitive impairment, but through his research, Gillett found both doctors and pharmacists were failing to perform this duty of care. “I [spoke] to a couple of younger women who said, ‘can we drive? Can we drop the kids off to school? I’m taking these drugs, but nobody can tell me what to do’,” Gillett said. “They wanted to ask the question, but nobody wanted to answer.” Reasons for the oversight were varied, Gillett explained.



In one study focused on pharmacists, many discussed the risk of impairment, but did not explicitly tell patients this related to driving, assuming they would make the connection themselves. “No, I probably never ask if they are driving or not,” one pharmacist told Gillett, continuing that they encourage patients to “decide how impaired you are and then you decide if you think you’re right to drive”. Another pharmacist implied that GPs bore greater responsibility to manage driving and opioid use: “I’ve even seen them drive their car and they haven’t even been able to walk in the door, so to me they shouldn’t be driving,” they said. “But the doctors will still sign off that they’re capable of driving, and I don’t know how they can do that.” Separate research exploring doctors’ role in assessing drivers found GPs gave mixed advice depending on their experience and relationship with patients.



Many doctors had not received consistent education on driving-impairing medications. “The book is very clear on epilepsy and it’s pretty clear on diabetes, but on medication, it’s quite vague,” one senior doctor said. “I think that pushes a lot of … responsibility and guesswork back onto the GP.” Overall, Gillett found health professionals leave it up to patients to self regulate driving and initiate concerns. “[Doctors are] not going to say ‘oh, I’m worried about these drugs you’re taking, but I know nothing about them’, and then pass that over to the patient,” Gillett said.



“That’s probably going to be worse than saying nothing.” Gillett was recently asked to be involved in GP training on the topic of auditing driving privileges, and has written submissions on assessing fitness to drive guidelines. He said recent cases highlight the importance of improving education across the health sector and ensuring GPs and pharmacists give patients consistent advice. In 2024, bus driver Brett Button was sentenced to more than two decades in prison for the fatal crash that killed 10 people and injured 25 following a wedding in the NSW Hunter Valley the previous year.



Related Article Science Jess gave birth on an opioid treatment program. It inspired her to start a PhD Throughout the case, the court heard that Button had an opioid dependency and had taken a large amount of the painkiller Tramadol through the day of the accident. He admitted he was impaired as a result of the drugs, but did not believe when he got behind the wheel on the day of the crash. “No one’s mentioned about the responsibility of doctors and pharmacists to inform [the driver],” Gillett said. Kirkegaard no longer takes opioids but agreed with Gillett’s calls for consistency and education. “You lose so much with a cancer diagnosis, from your hair to your dignity, your self-image … you want your independence [and] some form of normality,” she said.



“But you don’t want to put other people at risk either. A car on the road with someone behind it that’s not fully switched on, so to speak, isn’t good either.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Four satisfying new Sarah Pound salads you’ll actually want to eat
World.content:
RecipesCookbook extracts Four satisfying new Sarah Pound salads you’ll actually want to eat Packed with texture, zippy dressings and generous layers, these midweek-friendly dishes put crunch back on the table. Sarah Pound September 22, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A great salad shouldn’t be an afterthought or a bowl of leaves you force yourself to finish. It needs weight, contrast and purpose. For me, assembling a salad is about building layers: pairing hearty bases such as grains, roasted root vegetables or noodles with sharp herbs, big-hitting proteins, and a dressing strong enough to hold all the elements together. Once you stop treating salads like a diet requirement and start treating them like an actual meal, the options open up fast. The recipes below from Wholesome Made Easy reflect that exact approach – generous, textured and punchy enough to take centre stage at the table. Sarah’s salad tips Remember the crunch. Nuts, seeds, croutons, crispy noodles, fried shallots or even crushed tortilla chips can completely change a salad.

Nuts, seeds, croutons, crispy noodles, fried shallots or even crushed tortilla chips can completely change a salad. A great dressing matters. It’s what brings everything together, but add it gradually. You want to coat the ingredients, not drown them.

It’s what brings everything together, but add it gradually. You want to coat the ingredients, not drown them. Think beyond leaves. Grains, noodles, potatoes, roasted vegetables and legumes can turn a simple salad into a really satisfying meal.

Grains, noodles, potatoes, roasted vegetables and legumes can turn a simple salad into a really satisfying meal. Use what you have. You don’t need to follow a salad recipe religiously. Swap the herbs, vegetables, grains or protein depending on what’s in the fridge.

You don’t need to follow a salad recipe religiously. Swap the herbs, vegetables, grains or protein depending on what’s in the fridge. Balance is everything. I love having something fresh, something creamy, something crunchy and a little acidity or sweetness. That combination makes you want to keep going back for another bite.



Raw asparagus, hazelnut, celery and parmesan salad is simple but impressive. Mark Roper The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Raw asparagus, hazelnut, celery and parmesan salad Raw asparagus is unbelievably good. If you’ve never tried it, you simply must give this salad a go to understand how fresh, zesty and crunchy it really is. I’m completely obsessed with how simple this is, too. It uses just a handful of ingredients, comes together quickly and tastes so much better than you would ever expect. INGREDIENTS 4 bunches of asparagus (about 600g), trimmed and finely sliced on the diagonal

4 celery stalks, finely sliced

140g (1 cup) hazelnuts, toasted and roughly chopped

50g (½ cup) finely grated parmesan

25g (¼ cup) shaved parmesan, to serve

freshly ground black pepper



Shallot, lemon and chilli dressing 1 French shallot (eschalot), finely diced

3 tbsp extra virgin olive oil

juice of 1 large lemon

1 tsp salt flakes

pinch of chilli flakes

1-2 tsp honey or maple syrup METHOD Place the asparagus and celery in a large bowl. Whisk the dressing ingredients together well in a small bowl. Taste and adjust the seasoning if needed. Pour half the dressing over the vegetables and toss gently to coat evenly. Add the hazelnuts and grated parmesan and toss again. Transfer the salad to a large bowl and finish with the shaved parmesan and a good grind of pepper. Serve straight away. Serves 4



Storage tip: Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Chargrilled zucchini and broccoli salad with corn and rocket is a riot of interesting textures and flavours. Mark Roper Chargrilled zucchini and broccoli salad with corn and rocket The crunchy parmesan, seed and pine nut topping on this salad will change your life. Seriously, it’s so moreish you’ll find yourself sneaking some straight from the pan, and it works beautifully on other salads too. This vibrant and utterly delicious salad is the perfect combo of textures and flavours, and I love that it’s easy enough for a weeknight but impressive enough for weekend entertaining. INGREDIENTS



750g zucchini, cut diagonally into 1cm slices

300g broccoli florets

1-2 tbsp extra virgin olive oil

salt flakes and freshly ground black pepper

2 tbsp apple cider vinegar

2 corn cobs, husks removed

2 handfuls of rocket leaves

1 large handful basil and mint leaves Creamy basil dressing 2 tbsp salted capers, rinsed and drained

1 handful of basil leaves

1 garlic clove, roughly chopped

juice of 1 lemon

125g (½ cup) Greek yoghurt

pinch of salt flakes Crunchy topping 2 tbsp pine nuts

2 tbsp pumpkin seeds

2 tbsp finely grated parmesan



METHOD Heat a large chargrill pan or barbecue over medium-high heat. Toss the zucchini and broccoli with the olive oil in a large bowl, then season with salt and pepper. Cook for 3-4 minutes each side, until golden and slightly charred. Transfer to a large serving bowl, drizzle on the vinegar while still warm and toss to coat. Next, chargrill the corn cobs for 8-10 minutes, turning occasionally, until lightly charred and cooked through. Set aside to cool slightly, then cut the kernels from the cobs and add to the zucchini and broccoli. Next, add the rocket, basil and mint leaves. Combine all the creamy basil dressing ingredients in a food processor and blend until smooth. Add 1 teaspoon of water at a time, processing after each addition, until a nice thin consistency is reached. Taste and adjust the seasoning if needed. Combine the crunchy topping ingredients in a dry frying pan over medium heat and lightly toast for 3-4 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Drizzle the dressing over the salad and toss gently to coat everything evenly. Finish with the delicious crunchy, chewy and savoury topping. This salad is best served while the chargrilled vegetables are still slightly warm. Serves 4 Storage tip: Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Mediterranean pasta salad, with a choice of dressings, is ideal for summer entertaining. Mark Roper



Classic Mediterranean pasta salad Everyone loves a good pasta salad. I think the best ones are where all the ingredients come together – the juicy tomatoes, salty olives, crunchy capsicum, fresh herbs and creamy cheeses – to create the perfect mix of flavours and textures. It is full of the Mediterranean flavours I adore and is always a crowd-pleaser, wonderful for family meals, picnics or summer entertaining. INGREDIENTS 300g dried short pasta (such as spirals, fusilli or small shells)

200g cherry tomatoes, halved

60g (½ cup) pitted black or green olives, sliced (optional)

1 small Lebanese cucumber, diced

1 small red capsicum, diced

1 small green capsicum, diced

1 small red onion, finely sliced

1 handful of flat-leaf parsley leaves, chopped

100g salami, cut into small pieces (optional)

125g mozzarella, cubed, or cherry bocconcini

50g (½ cup) freshly grated parmesan, plus extra to serve (optional)

salt flakes and freshly ground black pepper

1 tsp dried Italian herbs DRESSING OPTIONS



1: Classic vinaigrette 80ml (⅓ cup) vegetable oil or half extra virgin olive oil, half vegetable oil

3 tbsp red wine vinegar

1 tsp Dijon mustard

1 tsp caster sugar

salt flakes and freshly ground black pepper 2: Creamy Italian dressing 125g (½ cup) Greek yoghurt

2 tbsp mayonnaise

1 tbsp red wine vinegar or freshly squeezed lemon juice

1 tsp Dijon mustard

½ tsp dried Italian herbs

1-2 tsp extra virgin olive oil (optional, for extra silkiness)

salt flakes and freshly ground black pepper METHOD



Cook the pasta according to the packet instructions until al dente. Drain and rinse under cold water to cool. Prepare your chosen dressing by whisking all the ingredients together in a small bowl until smooth. Taste and adjust the seasoning if needed. Combine the cooled pasta with the cherry tomatoes, olives, if using, cucumber, capsicums, onion, parsley, salami, if using, and cheeses in a large bowl. Pour the dressing over the top, season with salt and pepper and toss gently until everything is evenly coated. Chill the pasta salad in the fridge for at least 30 minutes before serving. Serve cold with a sprinkle of dried Italian herbs and some extra parmesan or black pepper, if desired. Serves 6-8 Storage tip: Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Expect to have roasted carrot salad with almond harissa crunch on high rotation. Mark Roper Roasted carrot salad with almond harissa crunch



Carrots are such an underrated and very affordable vegetable. I’ve made this salad so many times recently because it is easy, uses very few ingredients and comes together quickly to create a beautiful side dish. Plus, it is ideal for entertaining or taking somewhere – simply prep all the parts separately and pop them together just before serving. INGREDIENTS 1kg small carrots, washed and halved lengthways

2 tbsp extra virgin olive oil, plus extra for drizzling

1 tbsp honey

1 tbsp fennel seeds

1 tbsp dukkah or zaatar

salt flakes and freshly ground black pepper Almond harissa crunch 155g (1 cup) whole almonds (honey-roasted almonds are even better), roughly chopped

1 tbsp unsalted butter

1 tbsp harissa paste



Creamy dill base 250g (1 cup) Greek yoghurt

zest of 1 lemon

juice of ½ lemon

2 tbsp finely chopped dill, plus extra to serve

pinch of salt flakes To serve 2 spring onions, finely sliced

handful of mint leaves

100g soft goat’s cheese or feta, crumbled METHOD



Preheat the oven to 200C fan-forced (220C conventional). Place the carrots on a large baking tray and drizzle on 2 tablespoons olive oil and the honey, then scatter on the fennel seeds, dukkah or zaatar and salt and pepper, to taste. Toss to coat. Roast for 30-40 minutes, until the carrots are tender and caramelised. Meanwhile, make the almond harissa crunch. Heat a frying pan over medium heat, add the almonds and butter and toast for 5-8 minutes, until the nuts are golden. Stir in the harissa and cook for 1-2 minutes, until fragrant. Set aside to cool slightly. - Combine the creamy dill base ingredients in a bowl until smooth. Taste and adjust the seasoning if needed. Spread the creamy dill base over a serving plate. Arrange the roasted carrots on top. Sprinkle on the almond harissa crunch, spring onion, mint and extra dill, then finish with the goat’s cheese or feta and a drizzle of olive oil. Serves 4-6 Storage tip: Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. World.title: Climate change could push many Melbourne women out of work. This app aims to keep them in it
World.content:
Petite Gardens owner Lisa Nicholson isn’t afraid of a tough day’s work. But, as Melbourne gets hotter, her workdays are getting earlier.

As temperatures rise, Melbourne will shift towards a nighttime economy. We trial a new app which makes walking more comfortable and safer.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

The morning has just turned light when Lisa Nicholson’s alarm sounds. She taps her phone screen to turn it off, before sitting up and stretching muscles still tired from the day before. After saying good morning to her teenage son, she walks out to her carport, where she hauls a lawn mower, whipper snipper, leaf blower and hand tools into the back of her little green Mazda 2. Peering above the pile of metal in her rearview mirror, she backs out of her driveway, and sets off to create lush sanctuaries in Melbourne’s neighbourhoods of concrete and brick. Monash University gender and urban design expert Nicole Kalms and CrowdLab founder and director Anthony Aisenberg, who co-created the YourWalk app. Eddie JIm Tomorrow, she’ll do it all again – but as the city heats up, her days are getting earlier. “I’ll try to get out and get all my work done in summer by midday,” says Nicholson, owner of gardening business Petite Gardens. “It’s a killer in the afternoon.



“Once the weather starts to really crank up – sometimes it’s earlier in the year, sometimes it’s later – it does affect the business.” Gender and urban design expert Nicole Kalms says that, as temperatures rise with climate change, cities including Melbourne will shift their work, commerce and recreation to the nighttime economy. Prioritising green space is a focus for Kalms, but she knows the shift to an after-dark economy also comes with an unintended cost for women. If women don’t feel safe out at night and in unlit areas, will they be excluded? The topic of healthy places and people is one of the key pillars of Melbourne Assembly, a civic forum The Age is hosting in October, bringing together the world’s brightest minds, industry leaders, key decision-makers and the community to shape the city’s future. Nicholson says that, if she didn’t have the agency to work around the heat, “I certainly wouldn’t do the work I’m doing”. “I’m not averse to being out there and working hard, and being sweaty and all the rest of it,” she says. “But I will also not work in really extreme conditions because honestly, my clients don’t expect me to either.” Escaping the heat isn’t just a matter of comfort. It’s a matter of health.



And, as the city looks to its future ahead of Melbourne Assembly, tree canopy experts are keeping a dogged watch over the state government’s plan to densify suburban transport hubs through designated “activity centres”. Tree canopy has a direct correlation with all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, and fatal or non-fatal heart attacks, an Australian study has found. The activity centres run vast lines through Melbourne, with one in four concentrated in the Stonnington council area, in the leafy east. But they also trace a path over sparse tree canopy hotspots, including West Footscray, Seddon, North Essendon, Brunswick, Thornbury and Preston. RMIT University urban planner Thami Croeser, who helped compile tree canopy data for The Age, says experts are waiting to see whether developers prioritise good tree cover across the suburbs. Historically, they’ve taken up almost entire parcels of land with apartment buildings, leaving little space for gardens or trees. Suburbs earmarked for Suburban Rail Loop stations could also bring in tens of thousands of new homes in towers of up to 20 stories across Melbourne.



“There is a bit of concern in the tree canopy space that it’s all housing-focused, and not on the vital tree canopy that needs to make that housing liveable,” Croeser says. “As we densify, we want to ensure we don’t crush every tree in the neighbourhood.” Editor's pick Melbourne Assembly Melbourne should learn from Sydney and stop turning its back on the bay As Melbourne’s skyline pushes outward and upward, urban designers say the environment below has never been more crucial. Among them is Kalms, whose app is putting that premise into practice. Walking comfortably and safely At the top of a tree-lined suburban street in Melbourne’s outer south-east stands an unassuming green metal fence. Taking a few steps beyond it reveals a ridge perched over a vast valley, where turtles crane their necks to break the surface of a lake cradled in its centre.



Rabbits burrow near the banks of the lake. And, up on the ridge at Wilson Botanic Park in Berwick, a kookaburra hops alongside the footpath, gobbling up a worm before it flies back to the oak tree from where it came. This is a daytime route on the YourWalk app, created specifically with women and vulnerable people in mind. Its walking routes prioritise tree cover, shade and accessible footpaths during the day, as well as adequate lighting at night – when many women don’t feel safe. Rubina Nawabi is one of them – a 55-year-old mother of four living in the City of Casey, where the local council has partnered with Monash University XYX Lab and spatial data studio CrowdLab to pilot the YourWalk app. The author at Wilson Botanic Park in Berwick – one of two routes tested on the YourWalk app. Ruby Alexander After dark, the Hallam-based social worker rarely goes out, unless she’s driving (not a given for women in Casey, where many families share a single car). She refuses to take her usual low-lit shortcut if she is out walking after sunset and fears for her teenage daughter, who recently walked home for three kilometres with friends from Westfield Fountain Gate at about 6pm.

World.title: Can’t hit your 10,000 steps per day? Try this instead
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessFitness Can’t hit your 10,000 steps per day? Try this instead Lauren Ironmonger September 22, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The ubiquity of wearable trackers and the oft-cited prescription of 10,000 steps a day mean we tend to focus on quantity above all else when it comes to our daily physical-activity goals. But findings from a large prospective cohort study, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine this month, suggest speed might matter just as much as steps when it comes to mortality risk. The Japanese practice of jogging at “niko-niko pace”, or “smiling pace”, is a more pleasurable way to exercise and improve cardiovascular fitness. iStock Researchers from Monash University and The University of Sydney found taking fewer daily steps at a faster pace, or more steps at a slower pace may substantially lower the risk of early death by up to 43 per cent. Data was drawn from the UK Biobank, comprising 64,743 participants aged 40 to 69 who wore a wrist tracker for seven consecutive days. Researchers then followed up eight years later.



They found similar benefits between walking under 5000 steps per day at a faster cadence, and walking 7500 to 10,000 steps per day at a slower cadence. Editor's pick Trends Forget 10,000 steps. The Japanese walking method is easier and faster The lowest mortality risk, unsurprisingly, was among those walking 7500 to 10,000 steps per day at a quicker pace. Previous population studies show an association between higher daily step count and lower mortality risk. Research has also consistently shown an association between higher intensity exercise – even in short bursts – with lower risk of chronic disease and mortality outcomes. But co-author Dr Nicholas Koemel, senior research fellow in the Turner Institute for Brain and Mental Health at Monash University, says few large-scale studies have looked at the association between intensity and step count.



“The real goal here was: can we find different avenues for people to achieve those same health benefits?” he says. “Everybody might not have the same level of motivation or time to accrue the traditional 10,000 steps per day goal that’s often touted around, especially those who have fragmented days or, like myself, are sitting in front of the computer screen all day.” For Koemel, it’s an important reminder to try to get the most out of the steps we might already be doing. The other side of this brisk walking coin is “slow jogging”, a growing trend that, as the name suggests, promotes running at glacial speed.



Developed by late Japanese researcher Hiroaki Tanaka, the idea is that jogging at “niko-niko pace”, or “smiling pace”, is a more pleasurable way to exercise and improve cardiovascular fitness. Editor's pick Fitness Six simple exercises physios wish everyone would do for lifelong strength The practice has since spread to other parts of Asia including South Korea and Indonesia, and has gained popularity in the west thanks to social media, even boasting its own dedicated subreddit, r/slowjogging. Emmanuel Stamatakis, professor of physical activity, lifestyle and population health at Monash University’s Turner Institute, says while there have been no large cohort studies on the practice, it’s an attractive idea. “Slow jogging appeals to me because it lowers the entry barrier to an intensity that many inactive adults would otherwise never reach, and the short, high cadence stride keeps the effort steadier than a conventional jog,” he says.



“What the trend does is maintain a running gait at walking speeds, often somewhere between 3km/h and 6km/h, which puts it closer to fast walking than running.” And the benefits go beyond the physical. As Koemel points out, most social media videos show slow jogging in group settings. “That’s really exciting because it creates a social structure, which is quite helpful for maintaining physical activity in the long run.” A recent, small study from the Massachussetts Institute of Technology also found even short bouts of very slow running improved mood and executive brain function. Dr Hunter Bennett, a senior lecturer in exercise and sport science at Adelaide University, says the benefits of low-intensity exercise like slow jogging depend on one’s fitness levels.





He suggests using breathing as an easy guide to gauge intensity. “You should notice it getting faster, and if intensity approaches upper moderate to vigorous, you would manage a sentence but not a comfortable conversation.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. World.title: ‘I’d love to see more of it’: Telstra backs data centre boom amid backlash
World.content:
Exclusive TechnologyTelecommunications ‘I’d love to see more of it’: Telstra backs data centre boom amid backlash David Swan September 22, 2026 — 5:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Telstra says Australia has a natural advantage in the global race to build artificial intelligence data centres, and wants to see more of them built here despite growing community backlash. Nathan Gumley, the telco’s executive for software engineering and IT, said the country’s combination of renewable energy and water set it apart from much of the United States, where developers are often forced to choose between the two. Data centres like NextDC’s building in Footscray, Victoria, are popping up around Australia. Eddie Jim “If you look here in the US, you can go where power is cheap because renewables exist, but there’s no water,” Gumley said in an interview at Salesforce’s Dreamforce conference in San Francisco. “Or you can go where water exists and there’s no renewables and power’s really expensive.” “We’re kind of blessed that we have both.”





Treasury has estimated $150 billion could be spent on Australian data centres by 2030. There are 162 already operating and about 130 more at the planning stage. Community resistance is building alongside the investment. Residents are campaigning against a $1.47 billion facility proposed for Spotswood in Melbourne’s inner west, which would draw 240 megawatts, roughly the consumption of 250,000 Victorian households. Telstra’s AI boss Dayle Stevens said the national resilience question for Australia lay in that infrastructure rather than in developing local AI models. Peter Rae In the United States, 18 states have passed moratoriums on new data centres. The company stands to benefit directly from any expansion of the build. It is constructing the Aura Network, a terrestrial fibre network connecting Australian capital cities, and has deployed more than 8500 kilometres of fibre with six routes ready for service. It owns or operates about 400,000 kilometres of subsea cable.



“We’re just incredibly well-placed to be able to connect to those things, particularly with intercity network,” Gumley said. “I’d love to see more of it.” Related Article Newsletter

Telecommunications Telstra had no shortage of warnings before its outage. How did it miss them? Telstra has signed long-term contracts across its fibre and subsea assets with Google, Amazon Web Services and Australian AI infrastructure company Firmus. Microsoft is the foundational partner on Aura. The company lifted its expected investment in Aura and a related satellite project to about $1.8 billion through to FY28 in results released last month, up from a previous estimate of $1.6 billion, citing inflation and site conditions. It expects a mid-teens internal rate of return and a payback period of around nine years. Chief executive Vicki Brady told investors the sales pipeline for Aura had increased significantly over the past six months.



Dayle Stevens, who leads Telstra’s data and AI function, said the national resilience question for Australia lay in that infrastructure rather than in developing local AI models. “Telstra’s role is connectivity,” she said. “It is not our job to be building sovereign models.” Stevens said the critical infrastructure underpinning AI, including subsea cables, would matter more as the broader economy adopted the technology. Inside the company, Telstra has deployed AI agents built on Salesforce’s Agentforce platform to process customer refunds and check security permissions, targeting internal processes staff had complained about for years. Gumley said the refunds agent removed 15 to 20 steps from what a call centre worker must complete while holding a conversation with a customer. Telstra keeps a person accountable end to end for each automated process, he said, with thresholds determining when a human must intervene.



Not every deployment has gone smoothly. Gumley said staff given an internal assistant to navigate about 5500 knowledge articles reported that it was producing poor results. Telstra has signed long-term contracts across its fibre and subsea assets with Google, Amazon Web Services and Australian AI infrastructure company Firmus, with Microsoft the foundational partner on Aura. Craig Sillitoe “Unsurprisingly, it wasn’t the agent that was broken, it was actually the knowledge articles,” he said. Late last year Telstra deployed what it calls an AI control plane, monitoring cost, performance, risk and compliance across its AI systems in real time. Stevens said it had not stopped any deployment yet, describing it as early days. Telstra executives have said reductions in software engineering came largely through attrition and slower hiring rather than redundancy, and that the company expects to be smaller again by 2030. Telstra’s direct workforce fell by 1219 roles over the past year, to 29,334.



Related Article Updated

Telecommunications ‘Accountability rests with me’: Telstra boss rakes in $6.8m but Triple Zero outage costs her “Most people at most companies have some amount of uncertainty about what the future of their roles are,” Salesforce’s chief product officer for Agentforce John Kucera told this masthead. “All of our roles are impacted by AI, and they evolve every day, which is uncomfortable.” Kucera argued that automating repetitive tasks is meant to free up staff rather than eliminate them: “You want to have the human when you need them most, while having the agent handle all the routine things.” Stevens declined to discuss July’s network outage, which cut off Triple Zero. She said Telstra was examining what AI could do for network resilience and for the staff who work on it. David Swan travelled to San Francisco as a guest of Salesforce. World.title: ASX set to rise as Wall Street surges; Oil prices fall; Road clears for $154b Paramount-Warner Bros merger
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise as Wall Street surges; Oil prices fall; Road clears for $154b Paramount-Warner Bros merger Stan Choe September 22, 2026 — 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks are climbing with markets worldwide after oil prices and yields in the bond market gave back some of their jumps from last week. The S&P 500 rose 1.5 per cent and pulled within 0.4 per cent of its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 348 points, or 0.7 per cent, in mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 2.2 per cent higher. Easing oil prices and bonds yields brought relief to markets. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 4.52am AEST pointing to a gain of 36 points or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX closed flat on Monday. The Australian dollar was steady at US71.22¢. They got help from the price for a barrel of Brent oil falling 3.4 per cent to $US100.29. While that’s still much higher than its roughly $US72 price from earlier this summer, it’s down from the nearly $US110 it touched last week.



Oil prices are swinging up and down as some crude from the Middle East is able to sail through the Strait of Hormuz, though nowhere nearly as much as the industry and customers would like because of the war with Iran. Morgan Stanley’s Michael Wilson said another leg higher in prices for oil, gasoline and other refined products is the main risk he sees in the near term that could keep the US stock market from rising to his forecasted target for the year’s end. The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline across the United States has already climbed to nearly $US4.48, according to AAA. That’s up from less than $US4.32 just a week earlier and from $US3.18 a year ago. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Trump’s war is strangling the world Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Monday’s pullback in oil prices helped lower the pressure coming from the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury eased to 4.97 per cent from 5.01 per cent late Friday after it crossed above the 5 per cent threshold last week for the first time in three years. Yields have been on the rise because of worries about inflation, big debt loads for governments worldwide and other factors. That hurts the economy because high yields make it more expensive not only for the US government to borrow money to pay its bills but also for households and businesses.



Worries remain about how much oil is available for customers worldwide, ING commodities strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson wrote in a commentary on Monday. However, they said profit-taking by investors after the recent jump in oil prices, together with hopes for constructive discussions at this week’s UN General Assembly and at a meeting between China’s and the United States’ leaders, helped improve optimism. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters following talks Sunday with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York that the US had “a very successful engagement” with the Chinese side. Bessent said talks with China touched on trade and AI. China and the United States have been discussing reciprocal tariff reductions on $US30 billion ($42.1 billion) worth of goods from each side. In Beijing, China’s Foreign Ministry on Monday confirmed that Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to the United States between September 23 and 25. Experts and policymakers believe trade, tariffs, and AI safety are likely among the topics to be on the agenda. The war in Iran and developments in the Middle East and ties between China and Iran could also be discussed. On Wall Street, stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry continued to stabilise following their worldwide slide at the start of last week. Leaders of the AI industry have recently warned a slowdown is needed in the industry’s development for the safety of humanity. Advanced Micro Devices rallied 8.8 per cent and could finish the day with a total market value above $US1 trillion, while Nvidia added 2.2 per cent.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Why higher interest rates are the new normal Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor Stocks enmeshed in the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, rallied after bitcoin’s price rose back above $US85,000 and returned to where it was in January. Coinbase Global jumped 4.8 per cent, and Robinhood Markets rose 4.2 per cent. Skydance-owned Paramount fell 1.6 per cent as it reached a settlement in lawsuits brought by 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild trade union challenging its $US110 billion ($154 billion) acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, which jumped 10.8 per cent. The parties worked through the weekend to reach the deal, which includes protections designed to limit the market power and ensure the editorial independence of the media giant, which will control two of Hollywood’s biggest studios, two major subscription streaming services and dozens of TV channels ranging from CBS to HBO. Paramount has promised to release 30 movies a year at the combined studios, a move designed to placate cinema owners and Hollywood talent who believed the merger would reduce film output. Under the terms of the deal , half of those films must be produced by the new company.



Stock indexes around the world also climbed thanks to the easing of oil prices and bond yields. Indexes gained 0.9 per cent in France, 1.2 per cent in Hong Kong and 1.6 per cent in South Korea. AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Super wars escalate as Coalition leans in to mortgage plan
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalSuperannuation Super wars escalate as Coalition leans in to mortgage plan Paul Sakkal September 22, 2026 — 5:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Coalition has locked in a three-way election battle with One Nation and Labor over superannuation, floating a plan to use retirement savings to make securing a home loan easier. The opposition was split this month when Pauline Hanson announced a policy to allow people to pocket a quarter of their super contributions as a wage top-up, which Labor said had set up an effective referendum on the multitrillion-dollar scheme. Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg. Alex Ellinghausen Some shadow ministers wanted to avoid a fight on superannuation after the Coalition lost two elections in a row advocating to use retirement savings for housing. Since then, however, senior MPs have largely united around the idea of making a splash with a fresh policy to give people more choice over how their funds can be used. Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg will use a speech on Tuesday to float a proposal, which is under consideration but not yet adopted, to use superannuation as collateral for a mortgage or to increase the size of a loan.



The Coalition’s policy at the last election allowed first home buyers to take up to $50,000 out of superannuation for a home purchase. The idea to use superannuation funds as collateral is seen as less radical because people would not draw the funds from of the super account. Related Article Exclusive

Superannuation Superannuation shouldn’t be untouchable, says expert: ‘People get hysterical’ The Coalition will also explore an expansion of the $50,000 proposal, though this is seen as less likely. “Policy must factor in the big changes since 1992, when superannuation started, such as the fact that it was assumed that most people would own a home in retirement. That is not assured today. It is even less assured in the future,” he will say, according to a copy of his speech. “The idea that we are stuck with the exact design features of the current system and there is no possible way to improve it is incredibly lazy thinking and exemplifies the frustration Australians have about their leaders.”



Labor will probably use Bragg’s speech to portray the opposition as willing to risk a world-leading pension scheme whose power to invest trillions has attracted the interest of the Trump administration. But there are growing calls to consider whether the $4.8 trillion retirement savings pool can help address contemporary economic problems. Emily Millane, author of an upcoming history of the private pension system, said a fortnight ago that the political debate on super had become “hysterical” and proposals to use the money for housing should be debated. Nicholas Gruen, a prominent economist who worked for Labor treasurer John Dawkins when Paul Keating established compulsory super, conjured World War I battlelines as he said Labor was defending “the Maginot Line they’ve spent the last generation building”. “It’s a neat trick for finance to pull off requiring people to pay them for mortgages which are necessary because they’re … forced to invest their savings in securities when they need to fund a home,” Gruen said on LinkedIn last week.



A Morrison-era review and the Grattan Institute have argued that the superannuation guarantee rate of 12 per cent is too high and probably depresses wages. Like Gruen, Bragg raised the issue of superannuation’s cost to the federal budget. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has argued that the Intergenerational Report, released on Monday, demonstrates that Australia is one of very few nations where spending on the pension is on track to decline. However, Bragg argued the concessional tax treatment of superannuation was projected to overtake age pension spending in the 2040s. Treasurer Jim Chalmers at the Australian National University on Monday prior to the release of the Intergenerational Report. AAPIMAGE Before entering politics, the Liberal senator worked for the Financial Services Council, which competes with industry super funds. He has been a frequent critic of the pension scheme. The MP was chastised by some colleagues for freewheeling on a range of policies in a press club speech in August. He is not in charge of superannuation policy for the Coalition, but leads ideas on housing. Bragg argues Labor was ideologically tied to super because many MPs, unionists and staffers moved onto the boards of industry super funds.



“Housing was always part of this discussion. Back in 1993, Paul Keating himself proposed a policy where $10,000 could be taken from superannuation for a first home deposit. His policy said ‘for most people, a debt-free home is as important a part of retirement security as superannuation income’,” Bragg will say. “The architect of compulsory superannuation was right that home ownership should be part of the system. In later years, Mr Keating has lost his imagination. He now subscribes to the groupthink position that super preservation until 60 years of age is a sacred cow which can never be discussed, reviewed or reformed.” Keating’s policy was eventually dumped because of fears about stoking house prices. Bragg said his looming policy on super-for-housing must be coupled with a radical unleashing of home building, which he argued was the main game in housing. But he said the super policy was also key because there was a growing group of renter retirees and nearly a third of lump sum payouts of super were used to pay mortgages. “If it is good enough for Singapore, New Zealand and Canada with these similar super schemes to allow for housing, surely it’s a debate we can have without scare campaigns,” Bragg will say. “The psychological benefits of a home that belongs to an individual are equally immense. We must be clear that housing sits at the heart of retirement policy alongside private savings, superannuation and the pension. Each element should work together.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Albanese signs declaration with world leaders calling for international AI safeguards
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAI Albanese signs declaration with world leaders calling for international AI safeguards Rob Harris Updated September 22, 2026 — 5:01am ,first published 2:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia has joined a call for international safeguards on artificial intelligence amid warnings from scientists and industry executives that the rapid development of powerful systems could outpace governments’ ability to control emerging risks. At the United Nations in New York, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese signed a declaration with leaders including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz calling for mandatory safety testing, independent evaluations and greater international oversight of so-called frontier AI models. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, pictured on the weekend as he visits the US. Dominic Lorrimer The declaration warns that capable AI systems have already been seen circumventing testing safeguards, exploiting vulnerabilities and gaining unauthorised access to real-world systems. “Leading scientists and executives are warning that the pace of development could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks,” the leaders said.



The release comes ahead of Thursday’s meeting between Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, with AI expected to be a major topic of discussion. Albanese has cited Australia’s role in shaping international rules for AI as a key plank of its bid for a seat on the UN Security Council. He said he hoped for a positive meeting between Trump and Xi. Related Article AI ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates The US and China are locked in a race to develop increasingly powerful AI systems, while Washington and Beijing have resisted calls from industry figures including Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, backed by OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceX founder Elon Musk, to slow the development of frontier models amid warnings that humans could lose control. The leaders on Monday (US time) stopped short of calling for a halt to development, instead arguing that AI’s potential to improve lives, advance science and strengthen economies should be preserved while stronger controls are imposed.



“AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control,” they said, insisting that it must be developed and used in accordance with international law. Albanese said AI had the potential to improve lives, strengthen the economy and productivity, and advance science and medical breakthroughs, but “humans need to be in control of it”. The prime minister said Australians wanted to know that “artificial intelligence won’t be in control of us” and that governments needed to shape how the technology rolled out. “Artificial intelligence will have a massive impact on the way that our lives and our work is conducted,” he said, arguing that humans needed to remain “at the centre of it” and in control. The declaration calls on AI companies to develop transparent safety protocols, including mandatory testing before systems are deployed and independent assessments by qualified evaluators given sufficient access to identify risks.



Governments and regional organisations are also urged to develop common standards, strengthen transparency and share reports of serious AI safety incidents. Related Article Data centres This is the data centre capital of the world. They’re starting to regret it The leaders want countries across all regions to have access to the scientific expertise, technical capacity and trusted evaluation needed to assess advanced AI systems. The declaration also calls on UN member states to explore creating an international institution that could set standards, enable verification and convene governments when AI systems cross agreed capability thresholds. The group warned that efforts to control frontier AI should not widen the gap between countries with access to the technology and those unable to benefit from its advances. World.title: John’s cancer patients were prescribed opioids. This key warning was missing
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCancer John’s cancer patients were prescribed opioids. This key warning was missing Courtney Kruk September 22, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cancer survivor Suellen Kirkegaard had been given six months to live when she was prescribed opioids, a group of strong, highly addictive painkillers. Doctors had discovered a metastatic melanoma three years after her breast cancer surgery and treatment. Immunotherapy – then limited and expensive – offered the only hope of improving her prognosis. “The oncologist I’d had for my breast cancer … [was able to get immunotherapy] for me on compassionate grounds,” she said. “Otherwise, six months wasn’t a lot to look forward to.” Cancer survivor Suellen Kirkgaard was not informed about the dangers of driving when she was prescribed opioids. Courtney Kruk Kirkegaard responded well to the treatment, but needed opioids to curb painful side effects; arthritis, joint pain, fatigue and regular bouts of pancreatitis.



“Without the pain medication, I just would not have been able to function at all,” she explained. While Kirkegaard understood opioids could be addictive, it wasn’t until she met Dr John Gillett, a Toowoomba-based palliative care doctor and Queensland University of Technology PhD researcher, that she learned about the risks associated with driving. “The medications say ‘do not operate heavy vehicles’ and I’m thinking, yeah, I’m not going to be driving a truck,” Kirkegaard said. “It was only when he [Gillett] mentioned opioids and the capacity to drive [that it] crossed my mind.” Nearly 3 million Australians are prescribed opioids each year. While strong painkillers such as morphine, oxycodone and fentanyl are not classed as sedatives, they can cause heavy drowsiness and fatigue.



Related Article Drug reform ‘Pick between driving or treating yourself’: Calls for change to zero-tolerance laws Patients rely on health professionals to explain possible cognitive impairment, but through his research, Gillett found both doctors and pharmacists were failing to perform this duty of care. “I [spoke] to a couple of younger women who said, ‘can we drive? Can we drop the kids off to school? I’m taking these drugs, but nobody can tell me what to do’,” Gillett said. “They wanted to ask the question, but nobody wanted to answer.” Reasons for the oversight were varied, Gillett explained.



In one study focused on pharmacists, many discussed the risk of impairment, but did not explicitly tell patients this related to driving, assuming they would make the connection themselves. “No, I probably never ask if they are driving or not,” one pharmacist told Gillett, continuing that they encourage patients to “decide how impaired you are and then you decide if you think you’re right to drive”. Another pharmacist implied that GPs bore greater responsibility to manage driving and opioid use: “I’ve even seen them drive their car and they haven’t even been able to walk in the door, so to me they shouldn’t be driving,” they said. “But the doctors will still sign off that they’re capable of driving, and I don’t know how they can do that.” Separate research exploring doctors’ role in assessing drivers found GPs gave mixed advice depending on their experience and relationship with patients.



Many doctors had not received consistent education on driving-impairing medications. “The book is very clear on epilepsy and it’s pretty clear on diabetes, but on medication, it’s quite vague,” one senior doctor said. “I think that pushes a lot of … responsibility and guesswork back onto the GP.” Overall, Gillett found health professionals leave it up to patients to self regulate driving and initiate concerns. “[Doctors are] not going to say ‘oh, I’m worried about these drugs you’re taking, but I know nothing about them’, and then pass that over to the patient,” Gillett said.



“That’s probably going to be worse than saying nothing.” Gillett was recently asked to be involved in GP training on the topic of auditing driving privileges, and has written submissions on assessing fitness to drive guidelines. He said recent cases highlight the importance of improving education across the health sector and ensuring GPs and pharmacists give patients consistent advice. In 2024, bus driver Brett Button was sentenced to more than two decades in prison for the fatal crash that killed 10 people and injured 25 following a wedding in the NSW Hunter Valley the previous year.



Related Article Science Jess gave birth on an opioid treatment program. It inspired her to start a PhD Throughout the case, the court heard that Button had an opioid dependency and had taken a large amount of the painkiller Tramadol through the day of the accident. He admitted he was impaired as a result of the drugs, but did not believe when he got behind the wheel on the day of the crash. “No one’s mentioned about the responsibility of doctors and pharmacists to inform [the driver],” Gillett said. Kirkegaard no longer takes opioids but agreed with Gillett’s calls for consistency and education. “You lose so much with a cancer diagnosis, from your hair to your dignity, your self-image … you want your independence [and] some form of normality,” she said.



“But you don’t want to put other people at risk either. A car on the road with someone behind it that’s not fully switched on, so to speak, isn’t good either.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.content:
RecipesCookbook extracts Four satisfying new Sarah Pound salads you’ll actually want to eat Packed with texture, zippy dressings and generous layers, these midweek-friendly dishes put crunch back on the table. Sarah Pound September 22, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A great salad shouldn’t be an afterthought or a bowl of leaves you force yourself to finish. It needs weight, contrast and purpose. For me, assembling a salad is about building layers: pairing hearty bases such as grains, roasted root vegetables or noodles with sharp herbs, big-hitting proteins, and a dressing strong enough to hold all the elements together. Once you stop treating salads like a diet requirement and start treating them like an actual meal, the options open up fast. The recipes below from Wholesome Made Easy reflect that exact approach – generous, textured and punchy enough to take centre stage at the table. Sarah’s salad tips Remember the crunch. Nuts, seeds, croutons, crispy noodles, fried shallots or even crushed tortilla chips can completely change a salad.

Nuts, seeds, croutons, crispy noodles, fried shallots or even crushed tortilla chips can completely change a salad. A great dressing matters. It’s what brings everything together, but add it gradually. You want to coat the ingredients, not drown them.

It’s what brings everything together, but add it gradually. You want to coat the ingredients, not drown them. Think beyond leaves. Grains, noodles, potatoes, roasted vegetables and legumes can turn a simple salad into a really satisfying meal.

Grains, noodles, potatoes, roasted vegetables and legumes can turn a simple salad into a really satisfying meal. Use what you have. You don’t need to follow a salad recipe religiously. Swap the herbs, vegetables, grains or protein depending on what’s in the fridge.

You don’t need to follow a salad recipe religiously. Swap the herbs, vegetables, grains or protein depending on what’s in the fridge. Balance is everything. I love having something fresh, something creamy, something crunchy and a little acidity or sweetness. That combination makes you want to keep going back for another bite.



Raw asparagus, hazelnut, celery and parmesan salad is simple but impressive. Mark Roper The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Raw asparagus, hazelnut, celery and parmesan salad Raw asparagus is unbelievably good. If you’ve never tried it, you simply must give this salad a go to understand how fresh, zesty and crunchy it really is. I’m completely obsessed with how simple this is, too. It uses just a handful of ingredients, comes together quickly and tastes so much better than you would ever expect. INGREDIENTS 4 bunches of asparagus (about 600g), trimmed and finely sliced on the diagonal

4 celery stalks, finely sliced

140g (1 cup) hazelnuts, toasted and roughly chopped

50g (½ cup) finely grated parmesan

25g (¼ cup) shaved parmesan, to serve

freshly ground black pepper



Shallot, lemon and chilli dressing 1 French shallot (eschalot), finely diced

3 tbsp extra virgin olive oil

juice of 1 large lemon

1 tsp salt flakes

pinch of chilli flakes

1-2 tsp honey or maple syrup METHOD Place the asparagus and celery in a large bowl. Whisk the dressing ingredients together well in a small bowl. Taste and adjust the seasoning if needed. Pour half the dressing over the vegetables and toss gently to coat evenly. Add the hazelnuts and grated parmesan and toss again. Transfer the salad to a large bowl and finish with the shaved parmesan and a good grind of pepper. Serve straight away. Serves 4



Storage tip: Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Chargrilled zucchini and broccoli salad with corn and rocket is a riot of interesting textures and flavours. Mark Roper Chargrilled zucchini and broccoli salad with corn and rocket The crunchy parmesan, seed and pine nut topping on this salad will change your life. Seriously, it’s so moreish you’ll find yourself sneaking some straight from the pan, and it works beautifully on other salads too. This vibrant and utterly delicious salad is the perfect combo of textures and flavours, and I love that it’s easy enough for a weeknight but impressive enough for weekend entertaining. INGREDIENTS



750g zucchini, cut diagonally into 1cm slices

300g broccoli florets

1-2 tbsp extra virgin olive oil

salt flakes and freshly ground black pepper

2 tbsp apple cider vinegar

2 corn cobs, husks removed

2 handfuls of rocket leaves

1 large handful basil and mint leaves Creamy basil dressing 2 tbsp salted capers, rinsed and drained

1 handful of basil leaves

1 garlic clove, roughly chopped

juice of 1 lemon

125g (½ cup) Greek yoghurt

pinch of salt flakes Crunchy topping 2 tbsp pine nuts

2 tbsp pumpkin seeds

2 tbsp finely grated parmesan



METHOD Heat a large chargrill pan or barbecue over medium-high heat. Toss the zucchini and broccoli with the olive oil in a large bowl, then season with salt and pepper. Cook for 3-4 minutes each side, until golden and slightly charred. Transfer to a large serving bowl, drizzle on the vinegar while still warm and toss to coat. Next, chargrill the corn cobs for 8-10 minutes, turning occasionally, until lightly charred and cooked through. Set aside to cool slightly, then cut the kernels from the cobs and add to the zucchini and broccoli. Next, add the rocket, basil and mint leaves. Combine all the creamy basil dressing ingredients in a food processor and blend until smooth. Add 1 teaspoon of water at a time, processing after each addition, until a nice thin consistency is reached. Taste and adjust the seasoning if needed. Combine the crunchy topping ingredients in a dry frying pan over medium heat and lightly toast for 3-4 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Drizzle the dressing over the salad and toss gently to coat everything evenly. Finish with the delicious crunchy, chewy and savoury topping. This salad is best served while the chargrilled vegetables are still slightly warm. Serves 4 Storage tip: Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Mediterranean pasta salad, with a choice of dressings, is ideal for summer entertaining. Mark Roper



Classic Mediterranean pasta salad Everyone loves a good pasta salad. I think the best ones are where all the ingredients come together – the juicy tomatoes, salty olives, crunchy capsicum, fresh herbs and creamy cheeses – to create the perfect mix of flavours and textures. It is full of the Mediterranean flavours I adore and is always a crowd-pleaser, wonderful for family meals, picnics or summer entertaining. INGREDIENTS 300g dried short pasta (such as spirals, fusilli or small shells)

200g cherry tomatoes, halved

60g (½ cup) pitted black or green olives, sliced (optional)

1 small Lebanese cucumber, diced

1 small red capsicum, diced

1 small green capsicum, diced

1 small red onion, finely sliced

1 handful of flat-leaf parsley leaves, chopped

100g salami, cut into small pieces (optional)

125g mozzarella, cubed, or cherry bocconcini

50g (½ cup) freshly grated parmesan, plus extra to serve (optional)

salt flakes and freshly ground black pepper

1 tsp dried Italian herbs DRESSING OPTIONS



1: Classic vinaigrette 80ml (⅓ cup) vegetable oil or half extra virgin olive oil, half vegetable oil

3 tbsp red wine vinegar

1 tsp Dijon mustard

1 tsp caster sugar

salt flakes and freshly ground black pepper 2: Creamy Italian dressing 125g (½ cup) Greek yoghurt

2 tbsp mayonnaise

1 tbsp red wine vinegar or freshly squeezed lemon juice

1 tsp Dijon mustard

½ tsp dried Italian herbs

1-2 tsp extra virgin olive oil (optional, for extra silkiness)

salt flakes and freshly ground black pepper METHOD



Cook the pasta according to the packet instructions until al dente. Drain and rinse under cold water to cool. Prepare your chosen dressing by whisking all the ingredients together in a small bowl until smooth. Taste and adjust the seasoning if needed. Combine the cooled pasta with the cherry tomatoes, olives, if using, cucumber, capsicums, onion, parsley, salami, if using, and cheeses in a large bowl. Pour the dressing over the top, season with salt and pepper and toss gently until everything is evenly coated. Chill the pasta salad in the fridge for at least 30 minutes before serving. Serve cold with a sprinkle of dried Italian herbs and some extra parmesan or black pepper, if desired. Serves 6-8 Storage tip: Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Expect to have roasted carrot salad with almond harissa crunch on high rotation. Mark Roper Roasted carrot salad with almond harissa crunch



Carrots are such an underrated and very affordable vegetable. I’ve made this salad so many times recently because it is easy, uses very few ingredients and comes together quickly to create a beautiful side dish. Plus, it is ideal for entertaining or taking somewhere – simply prep all the parts separately and pop them together just before serving. INGREDIENTS 1kg small carrots, washed and halved lengthways

2 tbsp extra virgin olive oil, plus extra for drizzling

1 tbsp honey

1 tbsp fennel seeds

1 tbsp dukkah or zaatar

salt flakes and freshly ground black pepper Almond harissa crunch 155g (1 cup) whole almonds (honey-roasted almonds are even better), roughly chopped

1 tbsp unsalted butter

1 tbsp harissa paste



Creamy dill base 250g (1 cup) Greek yoghurt

zest of 1 lemon

juice of ½ lemon

2 tbsp finely chopped dill, plus extra to serve

pinch of salt flakes To serve 2 spring onions, finely sliced

handful of mint leaves

100g soft goat’s cheese or feta, crumbled METHOD



Preheat the oven to 200C fan-forced (220C conventional). Place the carrots on a large baking tray and drizzle on 2 tablespoons olive oil and the honey, then scatter on the fennel seeds, dukkah or zaatar and salt and pepper, to taste. Toss to coat. Roast for 30-40 minutes, until the carrots are tender and caramelised. Meanwhile, make the almond harissa crunch. Heat a frying pan over medium heat, add the almonds and butter and toast for 5-8 minutes, until the nuts are golden. Stir in the harissa and cook for 1-2 minutes, until fragrant. Set aside to cool slightly. - Combine the creamy dill base ingredients in a bowl until smooth. Taste and adjust the seasoning if needed. Spread the creamy dill base over a serving plate. Arrange the roasted carrots on top. Sprinkle on the almond harissa crunch, spring onion, mint and extra dill, then finish with the goat’s cheese or feta and a drizzle of olive oil. Serves 4-6 Storage tip: Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days.
