World.title: Climate change could push many Melbourne women out of work. This app aims to keep them in it
World.content:
Petite Gardens owner Lisa Nicholson isn’t afraid of a tough day’s work. But, as Melbourne gets hotter, her workdays are getting earlier.

As temperatures rise, Melbourne will shift towards a nighttime economy. We trial a new app which makes walking more comfortable and safer.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

The morning has just turned light when Lisa Nicholson’s alarm sounds. She taps her phone screen to turn it off, before sitting up and stretching muscles still tired from the day before. After saying good morning to her teenage son, she walks out to her carport, where she hauls a lawn mower, whipper snipper, leaf blower and hand tools into the back of her little green Mazda 2. Peering above the pile of metal in her rearview mirror, she backs out of her driveway, and sets off to create lush sanctuaries in Melbourne’s neighbourhoods of concrete and brick. Monash University gender and urban design expert Nicole Kalms and CrowdLab founder and director Anthony Aisenberg, who co-created the YourWalk app. Eddie JIm Tomorrow, she’ll do it all again – but as the city heats up, her days are getting earlier. “I’ll try to get out and get all my work done in summer by midday,” says Nicholson, owner of gardening business Petite Gardens. “It’s a killer in the afternoon.



“Once the weather starts to really crank up – sometimes it’s earlier in the year, sometimes it’s later – it does affect the business.” Gender and urban design expert Nicole Kalms says that, as temperatures rise with climate change, cities including Melbourne will shift their work, commerce and recreation to the nighttime economy. Prioritising green space is a focus for Kalms, but she knows the shift to an after-dark economy also comes with an unintended cost for women. If women don’t feel safe out at night and in unlit areas, will they be excluded? The topic of healthy places and people is one of the key pillars of Melbourne Assembly, a civic forum The Age is hosting in October, bringing together the world’s brightest minds, industry leaders, key decision-makers and the community to shape the city’s future. Nicholson says that, if she didn’t have the agency to work around the heat, “I certainly wouldn’t do the work I’m doing”. “I’m not averse to being out there and working hard, and being sweaty and all the rest of it,” she says. “But I will also not work in really extreme conditions because honestly, my clients don’t expect me to either.” Escaping the heat isn’t just a matter of comfort. It’s a matter of health.



And, as the city looks to its future ahead of Melbourne Assembly, tree canopy experts are keeping a dogged watch over the state government’s plan to densify suburban transport hubs through designated “activity centres”. Tree canopy has a direct correlation with all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, and fatal or non-fatal heart attacks, an Australian study has found. The activity centres run vast lines through Melbourne, with one in four concentrated in the Stonnington council area, in the leafy east. But they also trace a path over sparse tree canopy hotspots, including West Footscray, Seddon, North Essendon, Brunswick, Thornbury and Preston. RMIT University urban planner Thami Croeser, who helped compile tree canopy data for The Age, says experts are waiting to see whether developers prioritise good tree cover across the suburbs. Historically, they’ve taken up almost entire parcels of land with apartment buildings, leaving little space for gardens or trees. Suburbs earmarked for Suburban Rail Loop stations could also bring in tens of thousands of new homes in towers of up to 20 stories across Melbourne.



“There is a bit of concern in the tree canopy space that it’s all housing-focused, and not on the vital tree canopy that needs to make that housing liveable,” Croeser says. “As we densify, we want to ensure we don’t crush every tree in the neighbourhood.” Editor's pick Melbourne Assembly Melbourne should learn from Sydney and stop turning its back on the bay As Melbourne’s skyline pushes outward and upward, urban designers say the environment below has never been more crucial. Among them is Kalms, whose app is putting that premise into practice. Walking comfortably and safely At the top of a tree-lined suburban street in Melbourne’s outer south-east stands an unassuming green metal fence. Taking a few steps beyond it reveals a ridge perched over a vast valley, where turtles crane their necks to break the surface of a lake cradled in its centre.



Rabbits burrow near the banks of the lake. And, up on the ridge at Wilson Botanic Park in Berwick, a kookaburra hops alongside the footpath, gobbling up a worm before it flies back to the oak tree from where it came. This is a daytime route on the YourWalk app, created specifically with women and vulnerable people in mind. Its walking routes prioritise tree cover, shade and accessible footpaths during the day, as well as adequate lighting at night – when many women don’t feel safe. Rubina Nawabi is one of them – a 55-year-old mother of four living in the City of Casey, where the local council has partnered with Monash University XYX Lab and spatial data studio CrowdLab to pilot the YourWalk app. The author at Wilson Botanic Park in Berwick – one of two routes tested on the YourWalk app. Ruby Alexander After dark, the Hallam-based social worker rarely goes out, unless she’s driving (not a given for women in Casey, where many families share a single car). She refuses to take her usual low-lit shortcut if she is out walking after sunset and fears for her teenage daughter, who recently walked home for three kilometres with friends from Westfield Fountain Gate at about 6pm.

World.title: Can’t hit your 10,000 steps per day? Try this instead
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessFitness Can’t hit your 10,000 steps per day? Try this instead Lauren Ironmonger September 22, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The ubiquity of wearable trackers and the oft-cited prescription of 10,000 steps a day mean we tend to focus on quantity above all else when it comes to our daily physical-activity goals. But findings from a large prospective cohort study, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine this month, suggest speed might matter just as much as steps when it comes to mortality risk. The Japanese practice of jogging at “niko-niko pace”, or “smiling pace”, is a more pleasurable way to exercise and improve cardiovascular fitness. iStock Researchers from Monash University and The University of Sydney found taking fewer daily steps at a faster pace, or more steps at a slower pace may substantially lower the risk of early death by up to 43 per cent. Data was drawn from the UK Biobank, comprising 64,743 participants aged 40 to 69 who wore a wrist tracker for seven consecutive days. Researchers then followed up eight years later.



They found similar benefits between walking under 5000 steps per day at a faster cadence, and walking 7500 to 10,000 steps per day at a slower cadence. Editor's pick Trends Forget 10,000 steps. The Japanese walking method is easier and faster The lowest mortality risk, unsurprisingly, was among those walking 7500 to 10,000 steps per day at a quicker pace. Previous population studies show an association between higher daily step count and lower mortality risk. Research has also consistently shown an association between higher intensity exercise – even in short bursts – with lower risk of chronic disease and mortality outcomes. But co-author Dr Nicholas Koemel, senior research fellow in the Turner Institute for Brain and Mental Health at Monash University, says few large-scale studies have looked at the association between intensity and step count.



“The real goal here was: can we find different avenues for people to achieve those same health benefits?” he says. “Everybody might not have the same level of motivation or time to accrue the traditional 10,000 steps per day goal that’s often touted around, especially those who have fragmented days or, like myself, are sitting in front of the computer screen all day.” For Koemel, it’s an important reminder to try to get the most out of the steps we might already be doing. The other side of this brisk walking coin is “slow jogging”, a growing trend that, as the name suggests, promotes running at glacial speed.



Developed by late Japanese researcher Hiroaki Tanaka, the idea is that jogging at “niko-niko pace”, or “smiling pace”, is a more pleasurable way to exercise and improve cardiovascular fitness. Editor's pick Fitness Six simple exercises physios wish everyone would do for lifelong strength The practice has since spread to other parts of Asia including South Korea and Indonesia, and has gained popularity in the west thanks to social media, even boasting its own dedicated subreddit, r/slowjogging. Emmanuel Stamatakis, professor of physical activity, lifestyle and population health at Monash University’s Turner Institute, says while there have been no large cohort studies on the practice, it’s an attractive idea. “Slow jogging appeals to me because it lowers the entry barrier to an intensity that many inactive adults would otherwise never reach, and the short, high cadence stride keeps the effort steadier than a conventional jog,” he says.



“What the trend does is maintain a running gait at walking speeds, often somewhere between 3km/h and 6km/h, which puts it closer to fast walking than running.” And the benefits go beyond the physical. As Koemel points out, most social media videos show slow jogging in group settings. “That’s really exciting because it creates a social structure, which is quite helpful for maintaining physical activity in the long run.” A recent, small study from the Massachussetts Institute of Technology also found even short bouts of very slow running improved mood and executive brain function. Dr Hunter Bennett, a senior lecturer in exercise and sport science at Adelaide University, says the benefits of low-intensity exercise like slow jogging depend on one’s fitness levels.





He suggests using breathing as an easy guide to gauge intensity. “You should notice it getting faster, and if intensity approaches upper moderate to vigorous, you would manage a sentence but not a comfortable conversation.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Property investors relieved at Labour's landlord tax deduction promise
World.content:
Audio player for " RNZ National " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1509858%2Fproperty-investors-relieved-at-labour-s-landlord-tax-deduction-promise

RNZ national

Chris Hipkins is speaking to RNZ's Morning Report shortly. Listen live on the player above, the RNZ app or your local RNZ frequency.

The Property Investors Federation is hailing Labour's decision to leave interest deductibility settings alone, if elected.

Labour has ruled out any changes to the settings, with leader Chris Hipkins saying the party was committed to a capital gains tax instead.

In 2024, the government reinstated landlords' ability to claim tax deductions for interest in residential investment properties - essentially allowing investors to claim their mortgage costs against their rental income.

The policy was forecast to cost $2.8 billion over four years, and reversed a decision made by the previous government, which had removed the ability for landlords to offset their interest expenses against taxes paid on rental income in the hope it would help first home buyers.

Despite still decrying the policy as "tax cuts for landlords" as recently as last week, Labour has opted to keep the current settings in place.

Audio player for " Jo Moir discusses Labour’s landlord tax deductibility decision " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1509858%2Fproperty-investors-relieved-at-labour-s-landlord-tax-deduction-promise

Jo Moir discusses Labour’s landlord tax deductibility decision Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Labour was expected to announce its decision following the release of the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update, but on Monday, Labour leader Chris Hipkins confirmed there would be no change.

Matt Ball, advocacy manager for the New Zealand Property Investors Federation, said landlords, and therefore tenants, could feel relief.

Ball said the group had been talking a lot to Labour about the impact it could have on the sector.

"It's the impact on tenants that's really important here. These are the people who are at the end of the chain, if you like, and the ones who would have been most severely impacted by this policy," he said.

Audio player for " Labour rules out changing landlord interest deductibility " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1509858%2Fproperty-investors-relieved-at-labour-s-landlord-tax-deduction-promise

Labour rules out changing landlord interest deductibility Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Ball had previously said reintroducing the ban on interest deductibility alongside the capital gains tax would make investing in residential property unprofitable, and people would exit the industry.

Following Labour's confirmation interest deductibility would stay, Ball said it would give landlords more confidence.

While he said the CGT "isn't great," interest deductibility was "way up on Mount Everest" in terms of impact.

"When you impose a tax like this, and don't forget it's a new tax, it just goes as a straight cost increase to landlords. And the only options they've got are to put up rents, cut their costs, cut maintenance, cut investment in their property or sell. And so it has a really detrimental impact on tenants, and especially also on on landlords," he said.

"So it's good news. It's stability for the sector. We're going to stop flip-flopping between policies, which is fantastic."

ACT leader David Seymour. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

Hipkins said when Labour had introduced its CGT policy, it recognised it would also have an influence around what it did around interest deductibility.

"I recognise that tenants are anxious about their rents, and I don't want to give any landlords the excuse of increasing rents at a time when Kiwis are already struggling with the cost of living," Hipkins said.

"Most of the evidence we received in government was that rents are more likely to be influenced by interest rates, and by people's capacity to pay, i.e. salary and wage growth. Those are still the two biggest things that drive rents. But I'm not giving landlords any extra excuse to increase people's rents. They're struggling to pay them now," he said.

ACT celebrates 'backdown'

The ACT Party, which along with National had campaigned to restore interest deductibility at the last election, said Labour's backdown on a policy it had invented was a "victory for common sense."

Leader David Seymour said removing interest deductibility in the first place was a "bizarre wrinkle," which added pressure on investors when all their other living costs were going up.

World.title: Guam demands consultation on CNMI deep-sea mining plan
World.content:
Guam's governor is demanding formal consultation over a proposed deep sea mineral lease sale in federal waters off the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI).

Governor Lou Leon Guerrero said Guam was left out of a process afforded to the CNMI.

Leon Guerrero said Guam qualifies as an "adjacent State" under US federal regulations and should have been formally consulted on the proposed Pacific Mineral Lease Sale, or PACM-2.

In a 15 September letter to US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Marine Minerals Administration officials, Leon Guerrero said the proposed lease area is about 47 miles from Guam, compared with 57 miles from Saipan.

The governor said the federal environmental assessment anticipates potential impacts on ports and infrastructure in both Guam and the CNMI, as well as possible effects on fisheries, air quality and shared marine ecosystems.

"Federal regulations carry the force of law," Leon Guerrero wrote.

"The leasing of seabed minerals is unprecedented, and that novelty makes careful, formal consultation all the more necessary to safeguard Guam's environment, economy, and people."

Leon Guerrero cited federal regulation, arguing it requires an adjacent state to receive the Proposed Leasing Notice and a 60-day period to review and comment before publication of a final leasing notice.

According to her letter, the proposed leasing notice was provided to the CNMI governor following its announcement on 17 August, but Guam was not given the same opportunity.

World.title: The unexpected call for law change prompted by weight loss drugs
World.content:
Aquaculture could rival the red meat sector by using open ocean fish farming, as global demand rises partly due to new weight-loss drugs.

That's the hope of officials, investors, chief executives, iwi representatives and other sector leaders who discussed the opportunities in a meeting with the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) on Monday.

They set an aspirational goal of increasing exports to 450,000 tonnes a year, targeting the premium market, with industry players confident those gains were achievable regardless of whether drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy would continue driving demand for healthy, lean protein.

They had been invited by Fisheries Minister Shane Jones on Monday ahead of the government's replacements for the Resource Management Act passing their final readings in Parliament this week.

Jones told reporters that with those reforms going through, industry players had agreed to share ideas with the government about growing the sector, starting by creating a regulatory system for open ocean farming.

They had reached the "hope and anxiety" stage, he said.

"What's needed is certainty around the entire chain of activity, if you're going to literally accelerate the emergence of a hitherto unknown industry, i.e. farming protein in the oceanic environment.

"No one is going to spend their money unless they're confident that they're going to secure the necessary statutory consents, which in itself is impacted by social licence."

Fisheries Minister Shane Jones. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Open ocean fishing in New Zealand's exclusive economic zone - the fourth-largest in the world - is currently limited to a handful of projects including NZ King Salmon's world's-first open-ocean king salmon farm the Blue Endeavour; Ngāi Tahu's Hananui salmon project approved under fast-track off Rakiura/Stewart Island; and Te Whakatōhea Mussel Farm off Ōpōtiki.

Jones invited a couple of reporters to attend the start of the meeting, and industry sources later confirmed to RNZ discussion had centred on the challenges facing the industry and how the government could help overcome them.

While proposals to develop a bespoke aquaculture law and regulatory regime were not official government policy, slides shown pointed to plans to expand well beyond the current goal of $3 billion in annual revenue by 2035.

MPI director-general Ray Smith said 93 percent of the food New Zealand was producing was consumed overseas, with the primary sector exporting about $64 billion worth a year, but at around $750m aquaculture accounted for less than 1.2 percent.

"We're big in dairy, we're big in sheep and beef, horticulture now is bigger than forestry and processing ... the aquaculture sector in New Zealand, if you think: we're surrounded by water - but we barely use it."

MPI director of strategy, insights and evidence Chris Kerr told the meeting the next 25 years would add "two billion extra mouths to feed".

"We are exceedingly confident in that medium to long term outlook or demand for protein, in fact I'd go so far as to say there will globally be a structural deficit in supply of protein."

He pointed to the rise of GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy.

RNZ composite/ screenshot

"Even in the developed world, the advent of GLP-1 drugs means there will be a surge in demand for that premium protein, nutrient-dense food."

Kerr highlighted the discussion should examine what would be needed for the regulatory system to support it, identifying a new aquaculture law, national standards, proactive spatial planning, development zoning, allocation and licensing, compliance monitoring, "saying yes to onshore infrastructure" and delivering on settlements.

From the private sector, investment would be needed not only into science, research and development and the offshore kit, but infrastructure for onshore processing and hatcheries.

"This is about building an industry, not administering or regulating the system."

Those gathered were agreed the focus should remain on premium products, with Akaroa King Salmon chief executive Stewart Hawthorn saying "we're not trying to be McDonald's, we're trying to be a high quality food that's good for people and good for the planet".

He said the government needed to be making consistent decisions in a centralised way with all departments operating together, acknowledging challenges the industry had faced with the Department of Conservation.

He suggested there may be opportunity to expand to Atlantic salmon, and there may be other species.

Whakatōhea Mussels chief executive Peter Vitasovich said species in warmer waters further north including kingfish, and ocean trout.

"I think that will complement our industry rather than being stuck in a single species with salmon."

World.title: 'She was a lost soul' - agencies under microscope at inquest into girls death
World.content:
A father has told an inquest into the suspected suicide of a 12-year-old New Plymouth girl in June 2017 she was a "little angel"' and a "fun loving kid" whose life got more and more difficult.

In a statement read by his counsel Quinn Katene-Rosa, the man - who cannot be identified for legal reasons - said he hoped the inquest before Coroner Heather McKenzie would provide answers about government agencies' response to his daughter's living conditions at the time of her death.

"Her life unfortunately sucked. She was a lost soul who did not receive the care and support she needed from the government and agencies and services that were supposed to be there for her. At times it felt to me like no one really cared or, to put it plainly, gave a shit."

Two years after the girl's death, a drug-addicted Taranaki woman was jailed for four years and three months for the physical and psychological abuse of three children.

The father said he hoped missed opportunities to help his daughter would be identified so other people didn't have to go through what he had.

"My daughter's life had value. She was loved beyond measure, and she deserved the opportunity to live the life she had ahead of her. I'm here today because I want to understand what happened to her, and because she can no longer speak for herself.

"I know that this inquest will not bring her back. What I do hope is that her lived experiences and the pain and distress that her and her two sisters went through can bring about meaningful change to a system so that, where possible, other kids in similar circumstances are supported and have a better outcome."

Coroner McKenzie earlier laid out the parameters of the inquest and apologised for delays to the hearing taking place.

She said it would not revisit the previous criminal case nor investigate the immediate cause of the girl's death, but would instead focus on the role of Oranga Tamariki, police and other agencies in her care.

Coroner McKenzie said it would then move to look what would happen today if a similar case arose and look at what recommendations could be made.

She acknowledged the courage of the girl's whānau in agreeing to be part of proceedings.

Counsel assisting the court Rebekah Jordan opened by saying the 12- year-old had been born in Christchurch, but lived most of her life in Waitara and New Plymouth.

While attending an intermediate school in the city, her appearance and behaviour resulted in staff visiting her home on several occasions and subsequently seeking help from Oranga Tamariki, police and other social agencies.

The key social worker involved in the case in the weeks before the girl's death was questioned at length.

The visibly upset social worker, who cannot be named, said a "report of concern" had been received from the school and she met with the principal and a community constable.

She said a home safety assessment was done and a whānau agreement drawn up which proposed counselling and substance-use support for the mother and individual counselling for the child.

"I advised police that Oranga Tamariki will remain involved under a family whānau agreement. On June 13th, I had communication with Tū Tama Wāhine o Taranaki, confirming via email that the mother presented once to their service but did not attend her next scheduled appointment."

A safety plan involving school staff, an aunt, neighbours, and emergency services was also agreed.

Under questioning from Jordan, the social worker said at the time she hadn't been aware of previous "reports of concern" from 2013 and 2015 involving the girl and admitted "it would've been useful".

She acknowledged a screening test done to assess the mood of the child found she felt "sad" and had "thoughts of ending it all" but didn't have a plan to suicide, although she was self harming.

The plan was to seek counselling for the child but there was little follow up on whether she or her mother were attending.

The social worker was quizzed by Jordan as to whether it was fair to to say that Oranga Tamariki had assessed the child's home as being safe and secure because she was left in the home.

The social worker answered: "I believe so".

She was pushed further to say whether it would be also fair to say that was Oranga Tamariki's conclusion until the girl died, but that changed after her death?

After some reflection she replied: "Yes, it changed, I believe, after that.".

Despite at times struggling to remember events from nine years ago, the social worker was adamant that Oranga Tamariki was unaware of any violence or neglect in the home before the child's death and did not have evidence supporting an application for custody.

A specialist teacher working in the area of student well-being and behaviour also gave evidence.

She had been seeing the child at least once a week before her death.

"My question now as it was back then is, if a 12-year-old child needs a safety plan to be in their home, what are they doing there? Almost 10 years later, I cannot say that I have really seen any changes."

She said the various agencies involved with the child worked in silos and did not collaborate closely enough.

The social worker and the police believed that the child was presenting with challenging behaviours and they were satisfied with supports being put in place for the whānau and that stronger boundaries for her were required.

"No one asked the why behind the actions and only viewed them as the actions of a naughty child.

The specialist teacher said all behaviours were a form of communication.

"When working with people in the way that our agencies do, it is important to understand that and not make judgements about what they see, but to ask what is underneath and to look for the why."

In this case the police looked at the legal side and if any laws had been broken and the social worker only saw the disruptive behaviours being displayed as acts of gaining attention.

"No one asked why or what she was trying to tell everyone. No one saw beyond the scope of their role."

Coroner McKenzie praised the specialist teacher for her efforts to help the girl and asked what her impressions of her were.

Addressing her father directly, she said his daughter was a wonderful young lady with a gift for music that was self-taught.

"When she was happy, when she was within herself, she would light up a room. Her laugh was infectious.

"You know, she had dreams. She wanted to go places and do something. And I was hell-bent on trying to get her there. I gave her a magic wand because I wanted her to have hopes and dreams because she didn't believe she had a right to them.

"She was an amazing young lady, and I enjoyed spending time with her."

Fighting back tears the girl's father stood and thank her for all she had done for his daughter.

"I just wish that the other agencies had listened to you, and maybe if they'd listened to you and the right support was put around her, this lovely girl would still be here today."

World.title: Has New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly created higher prices?
World.content:
The supermarket sector has become an election issue, and political parties are suggesting everything from government-run supermarkets to breaking up Foodstuffs in an attempt to create more competition.

New Zealand has high levels of concentration in the grocery sector. The two main supermarket chains hold 82 percent of the market, down only slightly from 84 percent in 2020 despite ongoing attention.

The Commerce Commission has highlighted that New Zealand supermarkets also appear to have high margins compared to those in other countries.

In its most recent grocery report, it noted Foodstuffs North and South Islands had EBIT margins of more than 6 percent, second-highest in its global comparison and ahead of Coles, Walmart, Tesco, Sainsbury and Carrefour.

Audio player for " Could I run out of money in retirement and other questions experts wish you'd ask " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/business/1509019%2Fhas-new-zealand-s-supermarket-duopoly-created-higher-prices

Could I run out of money in retirement and other questions experts wish you'd ask No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

Woolworths had a margin of 1 percent and features low on the table, although that includes recent substantial investment made by the supermarket chain in rebranding.

The current duopoly situation, in which New Zealand co-operatives Foodstuffs North Island and South Island compete with Woolworths, has been in place since the early 2000s, when the Commerce Commission gave clearance for Progressive Enterprises' acquisition of Woolworths.

OECD data shows no clear impact on the pace of increase in food prices before or after this amalgamation.

Supplied /Shamubeel Eaqub

Supplied / Shamubeel Eaqub

Supplied / Shamubeel Eaqub

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said New Zealand's food prices had been rising at a rate that put them somewhere in the middle of the range of countries we might normally compare ourselves to.

He said the problem was likely that incomes in New Zealand had not risen as quickly. "So that's where people are feeling the pinch."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said there were periods where New Zealand's rate of food inflation had increased sharply. "Sometimes that is related to weather conditions because a lot of the fresh food will be local.

"Because we're in the Southern Hemisphere we get slightly different weather patterns and impacts on foods…but overall food prices in New Zealand versus advanced economies seem to go on kind of the same [track]. It doesn't mean we're not all being gouged but we can't see it in the data."

University of Auckland senior lecturer in marketing Drew Franklin said while inflation might not have run ahead of the rest of the world, it did not mean the lack of competition had not affected prices.

"Any two countries can see their prices rise at exactly the same rate while one of them pays considerably more than the other the whole time. It's also worth noting that any comparison with Australia is a comparison with another highly concentrated market, dominated by Coles and Woolworths, so it's perhaps not a fair benchmark for what a competitive market would look like.

"When the Commerce Commission compared actual price levels and profits in its 2022 market study, it found New Zealand was the fifth most expensive grocery market in the OECD in 2017 and that between 2015 and 2019 the major supermarkets earned returns on capital more than double its central estimate of a normal return in a competitive market. Its latest annual grocery report found little change since then in market concentration or supermarket margins."

Eckhold said there was unlikely to be any reform that was a silver bullet to make food more affordable.

"It's important to understand that most of this debt is about a more marginal impact on prices. If you did make the market more competitive and if margins in supermarkets declined… you might be looking at reducing the profits by half in the sector but that's a small proportion of the total price that you'd pay at the supermarket."

Eckhold said it could be possible to create slightly cheaper prices or a wider product offering but it would take time. "Restructuring is quite disruptive for the industry, would have considerable costs for the industry and could actually result in higher prices for consumers for a while because competition might not appreciably change for a while.

"I think people are hunting for an answer to the cost-of-living problem but I don't think supermarket reform is the answer."

He said it was desirable to promote more competition in any part of the economy.

"But what problem are we really trying to address here? If it' the cost of living, I'm not confident that what's being discussed here is really going to substantially shift that very much."

World.title: House for adults living with intellectual disabilities picks up award
World.content:
A house providing round-the-clock care for adults living with intellectual disabilities in Auckland is being hailed as a turn-around success, giving residents the power to make decisions many would take for granted.

Te Anua Nua Trust's manager has picked up an industry leadership award for bringing mana to two houses in Manurewa, where 10 people live with the support of carers.

It comes amid calls for more accessible housing and support for those with disabilities.

Monique Collins has lived under the wings of Te Anua Nua Trust for 16 years, where she has a studio unit looking out onto the garden.

"I call it like a whanau home, you know the bosses the staff like a whanau home and I'm so proud I've got that," she said.

When Len Moodley came on board as the chief executive about a year ago, he introduced a new way of living that increased the choice and control residents have in their lives.

"Len is kindness, very kindness he brings joy in this house for all of us and my flatmates," Collins said.

Elderly gentleman Ben Taite has lived there for two years.

"What brought me here is a disability...the work that I do is the gardening, I'm sort of like a caretaker who takes care of the flowers."

He said those who live and work there had become his whanau.

Moodley received an Enabling Good Lives leadership award for turning around the management of the homes, giving residents more say in everyday choices such as what to eat and what activities to do.

He ensured the new staff team received training and that the systems staff use to record health and safety and finances were up to date.

"There's been a 180 degree turnaround from the time I took over. I think at the time of coming here, my priority was to make sure that we're giving the best possible service, respect and value to our clients that are being looked after at Te Anua Nua."

He said the residents now choose their activities and can also choose to stay home if they don't feel like an outing.

"We see the difference, we see what it's done to their moods. It makes them more happy, they want to go out and enjoy life like every other person would want to do. This is the exciting bit for me, when I get to see that excitement."

He travelled with the residents and staff on a recent holiday they took to Gisborne and often receives cards of appreciation from the residents.

"The expression of how they give it to you, it's just mind blowing and that's my greatest joy."

But there's a wait list - Moodley said he gets regular calls from people needing supported housing for their disabled relatives.

Te Anua Nua Trust plans to rebuild one of the homes, expanding the number of rooms.

"There's always a shortage of housing and there's a big waiting list and so we're trying to address it slowly but surely so we can do it well," he said.

Te Anua Nua Trust resident Ben Taite. RNZ / Amy Williams

Disability advocate Nick Ruane said recent official information shows very few social houses are accessible for disabled people.

Of the near 20,000 community housing dwellings, less than two-and-a-half percent are fully modified for accessibility, while about six percent are partially modified - for example with a ramp or a grab rail.

But more than half of those homes the accessibility is unknown.

Disability Connect provides information and advice including through its housing information service, linking advisors with disabled people and their families.

Its chief executive Mike Potter said he would like to see the government act faster to ensure more accessible housing is built.

"We absolutely need more of it, New Zealand is in a housing crisis particularly for disabled people. There's just not enough of the right type of housing," he said.

"For most people and their housing, you might think about affordablity, you might think of the number of bedrooms but for disability we're also thinking about accessibility."

A spokesperson for the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport said the government is undertaking a review of social housing to ensure support is focused on those with the greatest and most persistent housing needs.

"The review is considering how different barriers affect people's ability to access and maintain housing, including those with disabilities," they said.

Te Anua Nua Trust service manager Angel Liu Chan and chief executive Len Moodley, RNZ / Amy Williams

Accessible housing is delivered by a range of social housing providers, including Kāinga Ora.

The spokesperson said around 15 percent of social housing places funded through Budgets 2024 and 2025 were identified by community housing providers as accessible or accessible ready, in July.

They said the ministry is involved in the New Zealand Disability Strategy, working towards the strategy's goal for housing.

"This is that disabled people and their whānau access affordable, safe, healthy, secure and accessible homes that support their independence and wellbeing," they said.

Looking ahead, Potter said homes like Te Anua Nua Trust's are needed.

"The demand is there because people are actually living longer, and the parents of people with intellectual disability are also living longer, and they're getting to the point where they're not able to to care for their children," Potter said.

"On the way is a virtual tsunami of a number of disabled people, particularly people with intellectual disability, who will need somewhere to live."

He said if there is not enough accessible housing or supported living homes, that leaves institutional type care which is more expensive.

The day RNZ visited Te Anua Nua Trust's Manurewa home, staff were preparing a hangi for dinner and the residents were sitting down for a cup of tea and milo.

Angel Liu Chan is the service manager and said the favourite part of her days is the morning, when she is greeted with smiles and hugs.

"Arriving on the site it's fairly early and the residents are just big smiles they greet you with the warmest hugs, they lift me up in spirit," she said.

"Just watching them flourish is what delights my heart...I wouldn't even call it a job it's actually a second home for me and my staff as well they've actually become my whanau."

World.title: Four missing after overloaded boat carrying 14 people capsizes in PNG
World.content:
Audio player for " Second deadly boat incident in 2 months in PNG " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/pacific/1512412%2Ffour-missing-after-overloaded-boat-carrying-14-people-capsizes-in-png

Second deadly boat incident in 2 months in PNG Pacific Waves Download MP3 3m

Four people remain missing after a boat carrying 14 passengers capsized in rough seas in Papua New Guinea's East New Britain province on Saturday afternoon. It is the second maritime accident in the province in two months.

One person has died and nine people have been rescued following the incident.

East New Britain Provincial Police Commander Amanda Kates told Pacific Waves the boat left Kokopo Beach and was heading to the Duke of York Island on Saturday when huge swells overturned the vessel.

The boat was licensed to carry eight people but had 14 passengers on board. Not only was the boat overloaded, but it also went to sea despite weather warnings being issued before the group left Kokopo.

Search and rescue operations were launched on Sunday morning, with the Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary deploying its police patrol vessel, Manning.

Kates said one of those brought to safety was a man who spent the night keeping two children afloat.

"The man was absolutely physically exhausted because he held up the 11-year-old and the little baby all night, trying to keep their heads above water."

"He was just an absolute hero," Kates told Pacific Waves.

The search and rescue operation is continuing for the four people still missing.

The incident comes as the Pacific responds to the sinking of the MV Matui in Vanuatu, where dozens of people were reported missing.

But Kates said she does not believe the East New Britain incident points to a wider boat safety problem.

She said larger vessels in the province comply with maritime safety regulations, while the main issue is the reliance on small boats for travel between the outlying islands and Kokopo.

Kates said a better inter-island transport system was needed.

"Banana boats between Kokopo and the Duke of Yorks is not the safest way to travel on a regular basis," she said.

"We need a ferry, and we need a reliable transport system."

Kates said the province has experienced unusually strong winds and large swells in recent months, making travel by small boats particularly challenging.

World.title: New rural GP practice opening up in Central Hawke's Bay
World.content:
Audio player for " New rural GP practice opens in Hawke’s Bay " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1509020%2Fnew-rural-gp-practice-opening-up-in-central-hawke-s-bay

New rural GP practice opens in Hawke’s Bay Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A new rural GP practice is opening in Central Hawke's Bay, despite a nationwide shortage of doctors.

After fundraising more than $1.2 million, the Takapau Health Centre is transforming into a GP-led practice and moving into a brand new building.

The nurse-led practice has been caring for the community in Takapau's old post office building for 38 years, but from 5 October, patients will go to a new site just a few hundred metres down the road.

"We've got a really cool team of GPs and nurse practitioners joining us and everyone is really excited," clinical lead and community nurse prescriber Jo Ward said.

When asked how the health service managed to hire rural GPs during a nationwide shortage, Ward told RNZ it was because of the clinic's values.

"I think our reputation has helped us, I think the fact that what we are continuing here is a charitable not-for-profit trust.

"Our ideas and our ethos of what we are about - it's not about making as much money as possible, it's about looking after people," she said.

It's the same approach the Takapau Health Centre has always had, ever since it opened in 1989 after the local community, led by Anne Lloyd and Lyla Koppen, rallied together to buy the former post office building.

When the project to turn the centre into a GP practice began four years ago, it was estimated the cost would be over $4m. But thanks to a passing conversation between a patient and Kaweka Hospital in Hastings, the Takapau Community Health Centre Charitable Trust managed to buy a modern transportable building from the private surgical hospital for $1.2m.

"We were all here on a misty morning at 6am when it came down that road on the back of a truck and it was pretty awesome. It's quite special ... there's been a lot of hard work getting this here," Ward said.

Locals gather for the opening of the new Takapau Health Centre. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Project leader April Smith said it's been quite the journey, with plenty of ups and downs.

"It was only by chance that this building became available, then we had to negotiate and get money out of the funders.

"The building is amazing, there are so many rooms," she said.

More than 1800 people in Central Hawke's Bay are not enrolled with a GP, and Ward said many residents were facing numerous challenges in accessing healthcare.

"No transport, no public transport, a lack of finance ... So unfortunately they wait and wait until they've got really sick, because it's just too hard.

"There are too many barriers in the way for them," she said.

Those living in the community say the new service is a big win for the district.

"It's very special for us ... it's very handy for our old people, our parents, our kids. The way the price of things are going up with gas and stuff," one man said.

Local farmers Dave and Nicole Ellison are thrilled.

"It future-proofs the community and generations going forward, it's absolutely amazing," Dave said.

"For me it can be a month or six weeks before I get a doctor's appointment, so to have something on your doorstep is wonderful," Nicole said.

Judith Finlay, Jo Ward and Jason Ward outside the new Takapau Health Centre. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Local resident Judith Finlay has been part of the Takapau Community Health Centre Charitable Trust for over 30 years and said the idea to build a new GP practice began in 2022.

"It seemed like a pipe dream when it was first mooted because the old building was not fit for purpose. We'd outgrown it," she said.

The main funders are Royston Health Trust, Eastern and Central Community Trust and the NZ Lottery Grants Board, plus a huge number of local businesses and families who have donated time, money or labour to the cause.

Such as local plumber Willie Mathewson, who's donated his time and expertise to ensure all the plumbing and drainlaying is done for the new building.

"This is essential for the community, so that all the old people here including me don't have to shift to town to get health services,' Willie said.

It was his wife Kim who put him up to the job.

"This was an amazing project so we had to get on board and give what we could, because this benefits us, our children and our grandchildren," she said.

Takapau Health Centre's new treatment room. RNZ / Alexa Cook

The new digs will also provide opportunities for patients, with its large purpose-built treatment room.

"We're very excited about this room - it's a very cool treatment room and our GPs are very keen to do minor surgeries, skin excisions,IUD insertions, suturing, plastering ... this is a fantastic room for that," Jo Ward said.

All patients will be given 20-minute appointments, rather than the usual 15, which nurse prescriber Fiona Greene said is all part of their vision and vibe.

"It's like going back in time, it'll be a smaller clinic for the people of the community, like the good old days where you know who your patients are.

"We've been really lucky that we've got doctors and nurse practitioners who live locally and want to work here," Greene said.

Moana Barrett and Fiona Greene. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Health improvement practitioner Moana Barrett is looking forward to reaching more people with their services.

"We'll be able to see more patients, more whanau - and working together as a whole holistic team is going to be beneficial for all of Central Hawke's Bay.

"This is an amazing time for Takapau," she said.

Phase two of the project is already in the pipeline, with plans under way for a community meeting space in the old scout hall for gatherings, events and education.

World.title: NRL set to axe ref Klein after controversial semifinal ending
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL is reportedly set to axe top referee Ashley Klein for the preliminary finals after admitting the Warriors were wrongly denied a crucial late penalty in their 12-10 semifinal loss to Newcastle.

NRL officials today confirmed the Warriors should have been awarded a penalty for an escort infringement by the Knights' Tyson Frizell with a minute left in yesterday's Eden Park thriller.

Had the penalty been awarded, the Warriors would have had the chance to level at 12-12 via a penalty goal from just to the side of the posts and send the match to extra time.

NRL investigating Eden Park incident The NRL is threatening to ban spectators who threw projectiles at referee Ashley Klein, with the league's integrity unit investigating the aftermath of Sunday's semifinal in Auckland.

But the call was instead missed on the field, with the bunker unable to review the play, despite a stoppage for an injury soon afterwards.

A comprehensive NRL review of Newcastle's 12-10 semifinal did, however, back the bunker over two other contentious calls.

First, it was deemed that bunker official Chris Butler was right to rule that Warriors centre Ali Leiataua got a thumb to a ball before it went to ground late in the match.

The NRL also supported the bunker's decision to stick with the on-field call of a strip against Warrior Te Maire Martin.

But it is the non-call on Frizell that will annoy the Warriors most.

The Newcastle veteran appeared to get in the way of Leka Halasima as he chased through on a kick in the Warriors' last attacking raid.

Given the seconds that would have come off the clock while the Warriors lined up the shot, there would probably not have been time for a restart.

"I thought they were trying to find ways to take it off us," Warriors coach Andrew Webster said after the game.

Projectiles thrown at ref as Knights win Projectiles have been thrown at the NRL refereeing crew following Newcastle's upset semifinal win over the New Zealand Warriors.

"The last one, two points would have drawn the game, he is going across Leka, pretending to try and catch the ball which they've told us you can't do."

AAP understands Klein will pay for the error by losing his spot in the preliminary finals, with Grant Atkins or Gerard Sutton likely to be called up.

Klein has overseen every game of the past five State of Origin series and two of the last four grand finals.

He had been expected to referee last year's decider, before losing out to Atkins following 18 penalties in a Melbourne-Cronulla preliminary final.

Meanwhile, the NRL have threatened bans for fans who threw projectiles at Klein as he walked off Eden Park on Sunday night.

Vision showed a mass of bottles and rubbish being thrown at the long-time official, with Warriors great Shaun Johnson labelling the fans' behaviour "embarrassing".

AAP

World.title: Daicos wins first Brownlow Medal and sets new modern-day voting record
World.content:
Collingwood superstar Nick Daicos has finally claimed his first Brownlow Medal in a runaway victory with a record-breaking 47 votes.

The 23-year-old surged to a perfect nine votes from his first three games, led from round 11, then registered six consecutive best-on-ground performances between rounds 15 and 20 to seal victory by round 21.

Daicos won the AFL's greatest individual honour from Geelong star Bailey Smith (36) and Western Bulldogs champion Marcus Bontempelli (34).

The Magpie had 13 three-vote performances and beat the previous votes record of 45 set by Carlton champion Patrick Cripps in 2024.

Daicos, the son of Magpies great Peter Daicos, conceded he was relieved, having finally prevailed after runner-up finishes in the past two seasons, a third placing in 2023 and an eighth place in his debut year of 2022.

"I've just learned not to trust the the betting markets, to be honest," Daicos said at Monday night's vote count.

"But no, there is (relief).

"It's a massive award, and I'm so privileged to be up here. And yeah, I can't believe I'm a Brownlow medallist, to be honest."

The dynamic midfielder had already snared the AFL Players Association and AFL Coaches Association player-of-the-year awards this season.

It was the fourth consecutive year that Daicos was favourite, and with the umpires able to consult statistics for the first time, the star Magpie was irresistible.

Nick Daicos and partner Arlette Amor. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Daicos averaged 34.9 disposals, 5.7 clearances, 6.7 inside-50s and 1.1 goals.

The brilliant playmaker was edged out by Gold Coast's Matt Rowell last year and Cripps the year before, when Daicos polled 38 votes.

Daicos, the Collingwood vice-captain who's widely expected to be named skipper next season, is the club's first Brownlow medallist since Dane Swan in 2011.

Bontempelli and Smith were the next best performers ahead of Melbourne skipper Max Gawn (28), Brisbane star Will Ashcroft (27), Carlton's two-time winner Patrick Cripps (27) and North Melbourne's Harry Sheezel (27).

Port Adelaide superstar Zak Butters, set to join Bontempelli at the Bulldogs next season, was among the contenders before his late-season ankle injury and finished on 26.

Sydney's Charlie Curnow, Collingwood's Nick Daicos, Geelong's Bailey Smith and Collingwood's Josh Daicos. (Getty Images: Michael Wilson/AFL Photos)

Banned Sydney stars Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner weren't in the room as they polled 26 and 12 votes respectively.

Brisbane's Conor McKenna won goal of the year while Hawthorn dynamo Nick Watson was awarded mark of the year.

AAP

World.title: How Freo's former number one ticket holder has helped Brisbane's dynasty
World.content:
If the Brisbane Lions win a third straight AFL premiership on Saturday, they will be thanking a former number one ticketholder for the Fremantle Dockers.

Luc Longley, a three-time NBA champion with the Michael Jordan-led Chicago Bulls, knows what it takes to reach the top and stay there.

Longley, a Fremantle native, was also the Dockers' number one ticketholder in 2006 and 2007.

But a meeting the Olympian had with the Lions in July may be the catalyst for Fremantle's downfall this Saturday.

The Lions are in their fourth consecutive AFL decider, and are trying to complete three premiership triumphs in a row and join the list of all-time great dynasties.

Despite finishing third on the ladder and making it to the final day in September, the Lions' 2026 season has not been smooth sailing.

Brisbane lost their opening two matches of the season, conceded a record 86 points in the third quarter of their loss to GWS, were hammered by 76 points against Carlton, and lost the qualifying final by 53 points to an understrength Sydney.

But they have overcome all obstacles to be in another grand final, with several players telling ABC Sport of a meeting with Longley in July which has spurred them on.

Former NBA champion Luc Longley is from Fremantle, and was once the Dockers' number one ticketholder. (Getty Images: James Worsfold)

"The ability he had to share some of that wisdom and talk to us about what he went through, it was awesome," Lions star Cam Rayner said.

"Just being able to compare and bounce ideas off him and learn things from him about the ability to keep turning up and find that motivation again has held us in good stead."

The Lions had six wins and six losses through 12 games, but were on a five-match winning streak before meeting Longley ahead of their round 18 clash against West Coast in July.

Rayner said Longley's discussions with the team about keeping the desire to win, despite already experiencing success, resonated with the team as they strived for a third consecutive flag.

"The hunger to want to win and to continue to have that success. At the start of the year there were times that wasn't really there in our performances," he said.

"We were dropping in and out of games and struggling to really perform to the level that we could.

"You can't really question the hunger after the game last week. It's back to a level that it needs to be and it's exciting to bring it to this week.

"That's one of the messages Luc Longley brought to us, he said, 'If the game's not going to get you up, you're probably playing it for the wrong reasons'. I feel like that really resonated with a lot of the boys."

Longley was an important part of the Bulls' 1996-1998 championship run, without being the star player.

Michael Jordan was the star of the NBA, while Scottie Pippen, Dennis Rodman and Steve Kerr also enjoyed big-name status.

For experienced Lions' midfielder Jarrod Berry, speaking to a champion who was known for his team-first work ethic was exactly what he believed Brisbane's dynasty has been built on.

"He [Longley] was never the big dog, the star, the whatever. He got more satisfaction out of seeing his teammates succeed," Berry told ABC Sport.

"Our squad is so talented and we've got so many stars and whatever, but it's not necessarily those guys that are making the club so special.

"It's the other guys that are doing all the tough work and hard work and selfless stuff.

"It was really nice to highlight that. It's all about being generous to your teammates and doing it for them."

The Lions are attempting to become the sixth team to win three consecutive V/AFL premierships, and the first since Hawthorn, who did it from 2013-15.

The Lions won three premierships on the bounce in 2001, 2002 and 2003, then lost the 2004 grand final.

The only club to have won three consecutive flags twice is Melbourne, which did it from 1939–1941 and 1955–1957.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.

World.title: Wallabies eye Springboks scalp amid Dockers frenzy in Perth
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

This is how Wallabies flanker Carlo Tizzano wants this weekend to pan out: Fremantle saluting in the AFL grand final on Saturday and Australia beating world champions South Africa in front of a rocking Perth Stadium crowd on Sunday night.

Perth is abuzz with Flagmantle fever ahead of the Dockers' date with destiny against Brisbane at the MCG on Saturday.

It's little wonder the Wallabies' arrival in Perth has gone mostly unnoticed.

But rather than feeling a bit miffed, Wallabies players are keen to lap up the Dockers-inspired party atmosphere and hope they can add to the happy vibes.

Petaia in Wallabies squad Precocious outside back Jordan Petaia is back in the Wallabies squad for the first time since the 2023 Rugby World Cup as Australia brace for the Springboks.

Perth-born Tizzano is leading that charge.

"We're behind Freo all the way and hopefully they get a good win," he told AAP.

"The atmosphere here is crazy. You saw what Fremantle was like after their preliminary final win, and what a game that was.

"They're the minor premiers, so they've got a lot of momentum, and hopefully they win the grand final for the first time ever, and then we get the win on the weekend as well."

Like Fremantle, the Wallabies will start as underdogs when they face defending World Cup champions South Africa.

The Springboks beat Australia 30-12 in their last visit to Perth in 2024.

Tizzano was playing just his second Test on that wet and wild night, and although his team didn't come away with the win, the 26-year-old lapped up the experience of donning the Wallabies gold in front of family and friends.

Australia have won three and drawn one Test under new coach Les Kiss.

Taking into account the Wallabies' 57-10 win over Italy in Perth in Joe Schmidt's last match in charge in July, Australia are on a five-match unbeaten run.

Tizzano hopes the team can produce something special to take down South Africa, who arrive in Perth full of confidence following a 3-1 series win over New Zealand.

The Wallabies have included uncapped Western Force recruit Harry McLaughlin-Phillips in the 34-man squad.

But the biggest addition was the return of star back Jordan Petaia, who left the Queensland Reds in 2024 to pursue his NFL dream, and hasn't played for the Wallabies since the 2023 World Cup.

The Springboks arrive in Perth without Pieter-Steph du Toit and Damian de Allende after the veteran duo were released from the squad to spend more time with family.

AAP

World.title: The clause that may save Lions ace for AFL grand final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The AFL tribunal chairman was blunt: the "good bloke" clause does not exist.

Instead, tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC turned to a fresh provision in the AFL's laws, centred on compelling and exceptional circumstances.

It is the clause that could save Brisbane's Lachie Neale from being suspended for Saturday's grand final.

The Lions will challenge Neale's one-game suspension for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Neale's gut punch on Ginnivan was graded intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact.

On video evidence, Neale is guilty.

"There's no point putting energy into it until we know the result," Neale's teammate Jarrod Berry said today.

"We'll be sitting tight and praying that he gets off. But if he doesn't, we'll face it when it comes."

Precedents this season have resulted in one-game bans to numerous players. The most recent just last week, when Adelaide's Max Michalanney was suspended for delivering an off-the-ball gut punch.

Neale facing grand final ban The Lions will contest a one-match suspension handed to Lachie Neale, which would rule the two-time premiership captain out of the AFL grand final.

But what may allow Neale, a dual Brownlow medallist to play in the premiership decider is the clause that saved Collingwood legend Scott Pendlebury from suspension in March.

"Exceptional and compelling circumstances" is certain to be the anchor of Brisbane's argument at Tuesday night's tribunal hearing.

The Lions will cite Pendlebury's hearing on March 17 this year.

The acts in the cases of Pendlebury and Neale are starkly different.

The Magpie great was charged with rough conduct for a bump on Adelaide's Josh Worrell.

His proposed one-match suspension was downgraded to a $3,000 fine with Gleeson enacting the "compelling and exceptional circumstances" clause.

Pendlebury's advocate Myles Tehan successfully argued the ex-Pies captain "stands in a class of his own", having never previously been before the tribunal in a 21-year AFL career.

"It's frankly difficult to imagine how it could not constitute an exceptional and compelling circumstance (to avoid a ban)," Tehan told the hearing.

"I should say this is not by any means a good bloke clause or a get of jail free card or anything of that nature."

Tribunal chair Gleeson then interjected.

"I might add, it never has been. It's misreported as being something to that effect from time to time," Gleeson said.

"But people who read the guidelines and listen to what the tribunal says will understand it's nothing to do with being a good bloke.

"It's to do with whether the circumstances are exceptional and compelling."

The relevant clause states: "Players will not automatically receive a reduced sanction for a good record. However, if a classifiable offence is contested or referred to the tribunal, a player with an exemplary record may argue that their good record constitutes exceptional and compelling circumstances".

Neale, a 320-gamer, is a dual Brownlow medallist; a dual premiership captain; a four-time All Australian; a four-time club champion who, like Pendlebury, has never been suspended.

His exemplary history gives the Lions cause to argue, and hope for a reprieve.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Fremantle legend in tears as AFL grand final honour revealed
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Fremantle pioneer Shaun McManus will hand over the AFL premiership cup to captain Alex Pearce if the Dockers break through for their maiden flag.

Part of the inaugural 1995 Dockers squad, McManus has been named as Fremantle's cup presenter ahead of Saturday's grand final against back-to-back reigning premiers Brisbane.

The Lions are yet to name their presenter after three-time premiership player Jonathan Brown did so for last year's decider win over Geelong.

McManus was brought to tears when he was told he was the club's cup presenter during a segment on Perth radio this morning.

Peter Bell was named the club's presenter for the eventual 2013 grand final loss to Hawthorn.

Dockers chief Simon Garlick described McManus as a perfect embodiment of the club's values.

McManus began his AFL career as a 19-year-old, going on to play 228 games across 14 seasons.

He captained the team alongside Adrian Fletcher from 2000 to 2001, and played alongside current coach Justin Longmuir.

"Shaun perfectly sums up what a Fremantle person is," Garlick said in a club statement.

"He had a remarkable career as a Fremantle player, but beyond that he has been a champion of this club since our humble beginnings back in 1995.

"Those early foundation years weren't easy, and as a 19-year-old he came in, showed great qualities which resulted in him being named captain at just 24.

"The courage he showed on field speaks for itself, but ever since retiring he's been a passionate and positive influence, someone who purely lives and breathes Freo.

"If we are good enough to get the job done on Saturday, it will be a great moment to see Shaun present the cup to Alex, and his old teammate Justin."

McManus is the ninth-highest game record holder in the club's history and was the second behind Shane Parker to reach the 200-game milestone.

Retiring after the 2008 season, McManus remained at the club as a player development coach and transitioned through various off-field roles.

The 50-year-old became a Dockers life member in 2004.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.

AAP

World.title: NRL set to act over 'embarrassing' referee abuse
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL has threatened to ban spectators who threw projectiles at referee Ashley Klein, with the league's integrity unit investigating the aftermath of Sunday's semifinal in Auckland.

Footage from after full-time in Newcastle's 12-10 win over the Warriors at Eden Park showed a raft of bottles, cups and rubbish being thrown at Klein as he walked from the field.

Projectiles thrown at ref as Knights win Projectiles have been thrown at the NRL refereeing crew following Newcastle's upset semifinal win over the New Zealand Warriors.

Klein had to be protected by security as fans abused the veteran referee and threw projectiles.

The NRL immediately launched an investigation into potential breaches of its spectators' code of conduct.

An integrity unit investigator had been at the ground.

"If found guilty, they [the fans] will be banned for a period of time from attending NRL games," ARL Commission chair Peter V'landys said.

Auckland police have since confirmed no arrests were made.

They said there were "no issues to note", other than two pitch invaders.

The Warriors exited the finals following the loss to the Knights. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Sunday's crowd of 48,511 marked the largest ever for a rugby league match in New Zealand, after the NRL made the call to move the match from Mount Smart Stadium.

The spectator abuse came after two contentious calls went against the Warriors late in the match, including a decision not to penalise Tyson Frizell for an escort in the dying minutes.

Warriors great Shaun Johnson hit out at the response of spectators after the match, labelling it "embarrassing".

"It leaves a bit of a sour taste in your mouth [after] what has been an unbelievable night with the colours, the energy, the happiness and celebration," Johnson said on Sky NZ's coverage.

"But there is just no need for it. It's just embarrassing.

"Ashley Klein has probably refereed the best game of rugby league I have seen in a long time tonight.

Hawks fans facing bans Hawthorn supporters who threw bottles at umpires after a controversial finals exit face lengthy bans if identified by the AFL and Victoria Police.

"He didn't take any gamesmanship in terms of people laying down. He didn't let people approach him whingeing.

"He didn't make the game about him. He let the players come and play and they dictated the outcome."

Warriors coach Andrew Webster vented his frustration in the post-match media conference, highlighting a bunker strip call on Te Maire Martin and the decision not to penalise Frizell for a possible escort on Leka Halasima.

"The last one, [when] two points would have drawn the game, he [Frizell] is going across Leka, pretending to try and catch the ball, which they've told us you can't do," Webster said.

The incident came after AFL umpires also had bottles and cans thrown at them while leaving the MCG following Hawthorn's nine-point loss to the Brisbane Lions in Saturday night's preliminary final.

The AFL has condemned the behaviour and warned of minimum five-year bans for any fans found responsible.

Tech.title: GM can’t ‘bring back’ Apple CarPlay because it never left
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Last week, GM announced a new software experience for its upcoming Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks, including a new look for Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, the popular phone mirroring systems that the automaker made a big deal about removing from its electric vehicles in 2023.

Naturally, this led to some confusion about whether GM was “bringing back” CarPlay and Android Auto to its vehicles. Yahoo Finance reported it that way, calling it an “about-face” by the automaker, while Apple Insider’s headline boasted that GM “cave[d]” on its decision to remove the interface from its gas-powered vehicles. Even The Verge’s own commenters were a bit flummoxed about what was going on.

It’s certainly true that GM has not offered phone projection in any of its electric vehicles for the past three years. That means no CarPlay or Android Auto in the Chevy Equinox, Blazer, Bolt, and Silverado EVs; Cadillac Lyriq, Optiq, Vistiq, and Escalade IQ; or GMC Sierra and Hummer SUV and Truck EVs.

All of those vehicles have Google software products embedded in their systems, like Maps and Gemini. That’s because GM builds its operating system on top of Android Automotive, which is often called Google Automotive Services or GAS when bundled with the full suite of native apps. But if you’re hoping to plug in your phone, or connect wirelessly, and see the familiar app layout on the infotainment screen of a GM electric vehicle, you’ll be sorely disappointed.

The same can’t be said about GM’s many gas-powered trucks and SUVs. GM never disabled phone projection in its best-selling ICE models. Tens of thousands of owners of GM-branded vehicles regularly project their phones’ displays on their vehicles’ infotainment screens without any issue. And now CarPlay and Android Auto are both getting spiffy new picture-in-picture upgrades in the Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra, a sign that perhaps GM is learning to co-exist with phone mirroring.

GM is partly responsible for the confusion. In an October 2025 appearance on Decoder, GM CEO Mary Barra defended the company’s decision to prohibit CarPlay in its electric vehicles and indicated that the policy would eventually extend to GM’s gasoline-powered lineup as well.

Everyone freaked out for a second time. Removing phone projection in EVs was one thing, but many truck and SUV owners were understandably incensed about the prospect of losing the capability in their beloved GM-branded vehicles. But a few days later, GM seemed to walk back that statement, clarifying to a number of outlets that Apple CarPlay and Android Auto would remain available in its gas-powered vehicles “for the foreseeable future.” Last week’s announcement of a new software experience in the Silverado and Sierra trucks would seem to be included in that “foreseeable future.”

Allow me to add some further reporting here. For the Silverado/Sierra announcement, I spoke to Colin McCormick, group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles at GM. Here’s what he had to say about how GM’s position on phone projection has evolved over the years:

And so the way that I look at this is that we were one of the early adopters of CarPlay and Android Auto when it first came out. And we do have a small segment of EVs right now that don’t offer that, but there is a large majority of our vehicles that do offer that. And our big position on this is that it shouldn’t be two competing systems. So as we work together with Apple and Google to provide solutions that we think are best for the customer, this is what we’re representing in this new UI design. So I think we’re landing in a spot where … we don’t have a customer that has to decide, ‘Oh, I’m going to use projection,’ or, ‘Oh, I want to use the native system.’ That’s our sweet spot for us. And that’s where we want to live.

GM most likely realizes that its position on CarPlay and Android Auto isn’t popular. People really like mirroring their phones! It’s clean, it’s familiar, and it’s (mostly) dependable. The same can’t be said for most modern cars’ native software. Even the ones that are really well designed, like Rivian and Tesla, still struggle with some core functions like profile logins and messages. And you can find plenty of owners of both brands that would give their firstborn child for the ability to mirror their phone.

CarPlay and Android Auto aren’t perfect. They have dependability problems and connectivity problems aplenty. But they are worlds better than the majority of the native operating systems in cars today — most of which are just trash. Yes, they’re getting better. And GM is not wrong in thinking it can offer a better experience. But people get testy when you take away their choices.

So GM is finding ways to coexist with CarPlay and Android Auto. It doesn’t want to lose more customers over it, which is why we’re getting this most recent solution that includes picture-in-picture phone projection. GM thinks this solves the “two competing systems” problem, as mentioned by McCormick. But what it really does is get it out of the corner it backed itself into over phone mirroring.

Tech.title: Bungie says it’s ‘not done with Destiny’ and will bring back vaulted content
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Months after seemingly giving up on Destiny 2, Bungie now says it’s planning to restore vaulted content in the game like campaigns, destinations, and raids. The decision reverses the Destiny Content Vault that Bungie created six years ago, controversially removing older content from Destiny 2 that players had paid to access.

“We understand that removing these experiences had a lasting impact on player trust and enjoyment of Destiny,” admits Bungie. “We cannot change the decision we made, but we can acknowledge its impact and do the work to make it right by restoring these important parts of Destiny’s history.“

All Destiny 2 players will get access to the vaulted content, but it’s not a simple switch of a button for Bungie. The developer made big changes to Destiny 2 with the Beyond Light expansion, meaning it has to go back and update lighting, encounters, combatants, and other underlying systems for this older content. “That work will take time, but it is necessary to ensure returning content meets the stability and gameplay standards of Destiny 2 today,” says Bungie.

The decision to return this content to Destiny 2 comes just weeks after a “Sunrise” Destiny 2 offline preservation mod appeared. The mod lets players access older areas in Destiny 2 that had been vaulted, but not the exact campaigns and missions that players had experienced previously.

Bungie now says its own restoration project is the “first step to lay the foundation for how we reforge into new stories and games that you all deserve.” Could that be a Destiny 3 sequel? There’s no mention of such a project, despite fans desperately pleading for a successor to Destiny 2 in multiple high-profile Twitch streams in recent weeks. Bungie is only committing to building a “stronger long-term future for Destiny” right now.

Alongside the Destiny 2 efforts, Bungie is also admitting that Marathon, its extraction shooter, didn’t “reach as many players as we had hoped, and we also know and understand that the game needs to evolve.” That means Marathon will expand deeper into a survival experience. The changes are a little vague right now, but it sounds like Marathon really needs to change and attract more players if it’s to be a sustainable project for Bungie.
